question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer:
Well, let me just give you a sample of my daily routine. At this moment, I am a housewife, and I have three children. My daily routine starts with Fajr prayer, being a Muslim, and some dhikr afterward, and then getting the kids ready for school — waking them up, helping them get ready, packing their lunch. That's the morning routine, and I drop them off at school; they have different timings. Then I come home, and I'm currently studying — I'm working on a certification, so I work on that. And obviously it's a lot of housework — nothing really important going on, just what a woman is expected to do: the cleaning, the house chores, I would say. Then prayer comes, and after prayer I definitely have time for reading the Quran and tafsir, learning about my faith. It's in my daily routine. Alhamdulillah, I've been maintaining that for quite a while now, and I'm kind of proud of that, before the kids come home. I work on that, and after the kids arrive we actually do have after-school programs for them — Quran classes at the mosque, two to four times a week, sometimes four times, and activities, sports they do go to. I try to keep them busy, keep myself busy, and at the same time maintain — being a woman — taking care of my own health and hygiene, working out, sports, anything that I can do for my health. Yeah, it's not a bad idea.

It's a lot — well, it sounds like a lot, but I mean, it is a lot. And then at the end of the day, sometimes I get a comment like, "What did you do today?" I'm like, sure, let me just start counting. Sometimes I do feel like a woman's work is 24-7, especially being a mom with three kids, and it's not as valuable — society doesn't really accept it as you doing something, you know what I mean? I get that from my own family members — they say, "What did you do today? You've been home all day long." It's like, oh, okay, so I did nothing. It's amazing, but I'm still grateful. I have love for everything; I enjoy being able to provide for the kids, not just financially but spiritually — I can put them in classes; they have a morning Quran and an afternoon Quran. My goal is for them to start with the morning Quran and finish with Quran in the evening — the least I can give them. My goal is to teach them the Quran so the Quran can teach them everything in life, inshallah.

Ameen, for all of us, but for all the Muslims, especially living in the West — a lot of the influences out here, the environment is not as ideal, right?

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer:
You know, I was actually very lucky. My community is full of Muslims, alhamdulillah, and I like to surround myself with Muslims, even though my husband's side of the family are not Muslims — I like to keep myself close to our community more than any other, because I noticed in the past — before marriage and even after marriage, I'll be honest — I surrounded myself with non-Muslims, and without me wanting it, I saw their lifestyle and culture and was kind of trying to fit in, or maybe adapting to it somehow without knowing it. Like I said before, I wasn't a hijabi — I was very, I guess, modern, and everything you'd see in any other woman outside, non-Muslim or non-practicing, you could see I was one of them. I don't want to put anybody down, but what I mean is you wouldn't know that I was a practicing woman, even though I was praying and doing all the other pillars I'm supposed to be doing — fasting, giving zakat, everything — but I wasn't properly showing myself as a Muslim woman. It's not because I was embarrassed or anything, but that's just where I grew up, this is where we come from — being modest wasn't part of our culture, I guess. It was like the opposite.

I grew up in Uzbekistan, and I grew up in Russia — I grew up in parts of Europe, because my father was around the world, so we moved around with him a lot. I never actually got exposed to modest Muslim women; everybody around me was Muslim, but at the same time everybody was like me, so I didn't really have modest Muslim women around me growing up. I wish it would have been different, but at the same time I'm really grateful it wasn't that way, because I don't take it for granted — I feel like I respect it more now than if I had been forced into it while growing up. I came to start wearing hijab and wearing more modest clothes by my own will; nobody forced me into it. I learned about it, and Allah guided me to do it — he gave me that option of choosing it. It's not like my parents or the society I grew up in forced me into it.

I do appreciate that a lot, and I'm grateful for that as well. I just want to stress that enough. I've seen a lot of young women who unfortunately were forced into hijab, but then later on they took it off. I've met so many of them, but wallahu a'lam — it's not for me to talk about other people's reasons; people have their own decisions. But my experience of coming into being more modest, becoming a Muslim woman, came with my own decision through Allah's guidance.

How would I describe it? I would say that I think Muslim women are the freest women on earth. That's what I would say, because unfortunately non-Muslims don't have as much freedom as Muslim women do — at least in my case, in the case of my own family, the people that I know — because they think we're oppressed, they judge us by...

Well, let me take that back — I would probably explain to non-Muslims that Muslim women have much more freedom than they think. Muslim women have much more choice than non-Muslims in terms of going to work or not going to work, cooking food or not cooking food, working and giving the money to the husband or not — you can own it. Even with breastfeeding — a lot of that is the woman's choice. I didn't know that a woman can even charge her husband for it. I grew a lot in the past five years, I would say. Before that I was, mashallah, in my la-la land — I was not a really good example for anybody. I'm still not a great example for a lot of the non-Muslim women out there, but I try. If they were to ask me one thing about Muslim women and if I had to describe them, I would describe them as faithful. They are pious, and at the same time they're very caring and responsible women.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer:
No, I didn't have it. I started seeing myself doing what I saw in my mom. Mashallah, she's very well educated, she's a teacher, and once she started having kids she gave up her career for them — she raised five kids. I remember growing up sometimes we'd say, "Why do you do that? I don't want to do that," but I remember how she was handling us — it wasn't like, "You've got to do it, I'm your mom." It wasn't like that. She was more understanding, giving us choices, and guiding us through it in a calm way.

I see that in my mom — she was able to take care of everything without going to work. My father was the provider; she never had to work. All she did was take care of the family, the kids, the household — she even had to take care of the in-laws — giving her best to her kids. That's what I saw in my mom. And after having a kid myself, I started doing what she was doing — I don't know, maybe it's in the blood — and I saw, "This is what I'm supposed to be doing." Nobody told me; at that point my husband wasn't even Muslim, but he supported me in a way — he didn't push me to go to work. I didn't hear that from him. Or maybe I trained him naturally — "Hey, I'm a mom now, I have to stay home and take care of my kids, that's my priority." I remember those kinds of conversations too — my kids are my priority.

He supported it, so I just naturally did what I saw. I didn't realize it until very recently, looking back — "Oh my gosh, this is exactly what my mom did, and this is what I'm doing too." Then I started thinking about whether I wanted to go all the way through like she did, because she never went back to work. Allah knows best — I'm trying to be a little different from her, because the timing is different, the environment is different, the place I'm living is different.

I've been living here maybe close to thirty years — I've been back and forth between different countries, but yeah, it's been close to thirty years.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, AND HOW?
answer:
Yes, I do. If you asked me maybe three years ago, I didn't even know the Arabic letters — I didn't know how to read Quran. I'd never read Quran. I'm not proud of it, but I'm not ashamed of it either, because I was never exposed to it. It's not an excuse, but I never thought, "We should be reading Quran daily" — that came later, once I started listening to sheikhs online, on YouTube. You can increase your knowledge that way. I started learning about the religion because my husband started questioning me on a few things and I couldn't give him an answer — I said, "I don't know, we were just told we should do it," but he didn't accept that as an answer. He said, "That's not really an answer — that means you've been brainwashed." And I was like, "Yeah, you're right, maybe so — I'm going to start learning." I told him I'm obviously not the right person for his questions, that I could connect him with the mosque imams or find some information so we could both read.

He would say things like, "We don't do that, you should never let the kids—" well, I guess I can share this too — we were telling the kids they should start praying, they should go to Sunday school, and my husband said, "You cannot force your religion on the kids."

And I said, "Yes, I can, because they were born Muslim — this is what we intended, this is who they are, and they're going to have to start practicing and learning, just like we saw our parents doing it and started doing it naturally." But with them, they know they have a choice — they know they can celebrate Christmas and at the same time they can celebrate Eid. When they were asking, I said, well, because those aren't our holidays, we don't celebrate them — so we're going to have to learn our religion, our beliefs, what we can celebrate and why, why we don't celebrate other things. Those are things I started taking them to Sunday school for, and my husband would say, "Why don't you guys celebrate this, what's the problem, why can't the kids do that?" He'd ask the questions and I'd say, "Well, that's a really great question, and I'm not the right person to answer it."

But I started seeking knowledge, because I could see he was right — I don't have the knowledge, I can't defend myself. When you have little to no knowledge about something, you're speechless. So I started educating myself online, learning, reading when I could. I started listening a lot to — I think he was really the one who saved me — Omar Suleiman; that's why I have such deep respect for that man. I started listening to him a lot, and to people good for beginners, like Mufti Menk — he's really easy to start with.

I started seeking knowledge, I guess, and learning — "Oh, that's why we don't do this, that's why—" Once I started learning it, I started teaching it to my husband, sharing the knowledge with him, so he could learn for himself and so he'd never again have to tell me my kids should just choose their own religion. It started making sense for both of us. Before, I knew I shouldn't be doing certain things, but I didn't really know why — I would just obey because I knew we weren't supposed to do it, not because I understood it deeply. That's how I started — just doing it all. I still listen a lot online; that's where my resources for knowledge come from, I would say.

Basically, I led my entire family toward becoming more intentional about why we do what we do. But honestly, I give all the credit to Allah, because he's the one who guided me — if he hadn't put that situation in front of my family, if my husband hadn't pushed me the way he did, I probably wouldn't have stayed firm on that point.

If I hadn't, I wouldn't be sitting here talking to you right now — I would have lost it right there. Something inside me told me, "No, you can't do that, you need to start educating yourself." It's the situations that guide you to the light. It wasn't a happy moment at the time, but now I look back and think, I'm glad that happened, because I wouldn't know a lot of things — my kids wouldn't know a lot of things, my kids wouldn't even be memorizing Quran. Small things led to bigger and bigger things.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
A lot of things changed after hijab. Before, like I said, for most of my life I was without the scarf, but I felt more, being in a Western country, like you feel connected, you feel like one of them — it's such an awkward feeling, but that's how you feel. Even though I didn't wear hijab, I never dressed too openly — I was still fairly modest in my clothing, wearing loose clothes, but I just wouldn't wear a scarf.

How did I come to the scarf? I always knew the time was going to come, because I started seeing a lot of Muslim women at the mosque and thought, maybe I should start putting that on. I honestly thought — and this shows how little knowledge I had — that the scarf was a cultural thing. I'd see it on women from Pakistan, women from Afghanistan, and what I saw in the media was that their husbands made them wear it, that the family, the brothers, forced them — that's how I thought, which is very strange coming from a Muslim woman, but that's how I saw it: that these women wore hijab because their husbands made them, maybe out of jealousy or control. That's what I thought, until I started learning and reading the Quran, and I started seeing the ayat — "Oh, so I'm supposed to be wearing it too." It's not something somebody is telling me to do, it's my Creator telling me to wear it. That's how I came to it.

It was really a big decision for me, because I knew a lot of things were going to change around me — people were going to change around me. I couldn't do the same things I was doing before — you basically have to get rid of most of your closet, renew everything, adapt to a new look and to the people around you. It took me some time to work up to it, but once I decided, it didn't take long to actually put the hijab on — it was just one morning I woke up and said, "That's it, I'm starting today," and I've been wearing it ever since. It was just the decision I made once I found out it wasn't a cultural thing.

Oh my gosh, tell me about it — I've had a lot of ups and downs in my life. I still think I'm discovering myself; I don't know about other women, but I still try to find myself, who I am and why I'm here. Those are the things I always try to discover — why things around me happen, what the reason is. I always have that in the back of my head.

I don't regret putting the scarf on — I actually believe I earned more respect. Even before, in the Western countries, when you'd see a man, you'd shake his hand or give him a hug — it was very normal for me because I didn't know I wasn't supposed to do that. I didn't know I shouldn't be hugging a man I wasn't related to — I thought that's just how you greet people, and it was very common where I come from too. Then, once I started learning, it was like, "Okay, this isn't allowed, and here's why." I noticed that men in Western countries actually knew more than I did — when they see a woman in a scarf, they don't reach their hand out or try to hug her, they distance themselves respectfully, which I think is a great thing. They were more educated on that than I was. I think it's a matter of respect, because people I used to know stopped hugging me once I started wearing hijab — even family friends, people I know, they stopped doing that kind of thing.

It was great — I don't regret putting the scarf on, and I've seen it have a huge influence on my daughter. She's very young and goes to public school, and sometimes she comes to me and says she wants to wear a scarf to school. I say, "Are you sure?" and she says yes, so I say, "Okay, go try it, experience it, why not." She comes back and says everybody told her it looked so cute. I don't want to force her, but I want her to do something out of her own will — I want my kids to have a better education about this than I had myself, I guess.

question: HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO WRONG PORTRAYALS OF MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
I don't know — what do you mean by that, the portrayal of Muslim women?

The feeling is one thing, of course — I know it's wrong, what they're saying is wrong, at least I understand that now. But how would I explain it to them? I try to connect with them, relate it to their own religion or belief — like, why are Muslim women held to a much higher standard, much more piety, than they are — relating it back to their own religion. If you look at Maryam, the pictures and scriptures of her, or the pious women in the church, the nuns — just look at your own belief, your own religion, how you were commanded, before you even judge me. People have judged me a lot, and I say, "You go to church and put a scarf on too."

My own mother-in-law goes to church and has to have some kind of head covering on to pray, and I think, why is it okay for you to do that but not okay for me, a Muslim woman, to have my scarf on all the time? What's wrong with that? The Quran says that when you pray you should be covering — not just your head, but down to your arms, your form should be covered too. When you read that, and then — I don't want to sound like a hypocrite, because I was one of them, I wasn't wearing one either — I started relating it back to them, and then they lose the argument, because they know what they're saying is wrong.

Yes, everybody who goes to church wears something — it's not like us wearing a hijab, but they put a light veil on their head. It's a little tradition — I don't know if you've seen Jewish women, they just cover the back of the head. My mother-in-law wears a scarf like that, most of the time without it, but for church she wears it. So I say a more spiritual, more religious person would do it, because somebody who really knows their religion, who's well educated, would do it — you see that more in the older generation than the younger one. I don't know how the younger ones dress for church now, but they probably still have something like a uniform — they don't just go in whatever, they wear proper clothes because they know that's a place to pray, to glorify God, whatever they believe. They respect the prayer and the outfit, so — I respect my religion, I respect my faith, I respect my Creator, because he asked me to put it on. If that bothers you, that's your problem.

question: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN OR HIJAB?
answer:
I don't think it's that they misunderstand — it's judging, like, "Oh, she wears a scarf." A lot of people don't know my background — when they say things like, "Why are you wearing a scarf," assuming it's my husband — my husband isn't even Muslim originally, he's a revert, and he would never in his life tell me to put a scarf on. He was actually the opposite — he believes women are beautiful and should show that beauty, that's how he grew up. So that whole idea — that it's your husband or a cultural thing — doesn't apply to me, because culturally I'm not from there, and I'm definitely not forced by anyone.

It's probably her own decision — if somebody judges another woman for wearing hijab, assuming her husband is behind it. If somebody has the nerve to say something to me about my scarf, I don't bother engaging with them much, but I make sure I defend women — not just myself. If I'm being judged, I know other women are getting judged too, so I don't just defend myself, I defend all women in hijab.

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer:
It's a life challenge... Oh my gosh, I still struggle with that. I wish I was a better person to answer that question, but I still struggle with it — I still try to find the reason why things sometimes don't work out for me, even when I feel like I'm doing everything right. I'm not the right person, honestly — I still struggle a lot, I'm still working on that part of myself, trying to understand why things don't work out sometimes. But alhamdulillah, Allah has made it very clear to me, through a couple of situations in my life, why things didn't work out the way I wanted — by giving me a better solution.

I have full trust in Allah, but when you're frustrated, facing a difficulty, it's really hard to fight against shaytan — the thoughts that come to my head. I do struggle with it, but I've found that dhikr helps me a lot. Every time those dark thoughts come — why is this happening to me, I'm doing everything right, getting impatient — I do dhikr, and that's really helped me calm myself and stop the questioning, honestly.

question: WHAT INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS ARE PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer: It would feel bad — I'd feel bad for the person. I believe faith is something that should come to a woman by her own will. I've seen women who were forced into things — not hijab necessarily, but other things — and it goes in the wrong direction; they try to get out of the situation and it usually doesn't end well. So, like you said, it doesn't really relate to me — I've never been forced into anything in my life, alhamdulillah, though not everything I chose was correct. But mistakes are part of learning. As for a man who does that to women, I don't know if he's Muslim or not, whoever he is, I think they're mentally unwell — they should never impose something like that.

question: WHAT DIFFICULTIES HAVE YOU FACED WEARING HIJAB, AND HOW DID YOU RESOLVE THEM?
answer: No — like I said, alhamdulillah, after I started wearing hijab I actually started surrounding myself more with Muslims than non-Muslims, and I try not to pay attention to anybody. How you carry yourself matters too — people will usually bully you or say something to your face based on how you present yourself. I haven't had that, alhamdulillah, but may Allah always give me the strength to fight for it, for any woman. But I'm a fighter — if somebody says something, I say something back usually.

question: HOW DID YOUR FAMILY RESPOND TO YOU WEARING HIJAB?
answer: My father was shocked, because, like I said, none of my family members, including my sisters, wore hijab, and my mom only started wearing it after I did. She used to wear just a scarf covering the back of her head — we have this little tradition, I don't know if you've seen Jewish women do this, they just cover the back of the head. So she wore it that way, and mostly without a scarf otherwise. They didn't dislike it, exactly — they were shocked, in the sense of, "You're still young, why are you doing that to yourself?" — because we'd been, I guess, brainwashed by society, coming from a lack of knowledge. I like to share the knowledge with them; I tell them they should be wearing it too. It was good — after I started wearing it, my mother started wearing it, and then my sister-in-law, my brother's wife, started wearing it too. She thought, if you live in America, you're educated, you have everything you want, nobody's forcing you, and you started wearing it, then I should too — since she lives among Muslim countries, she felt she could start too.

question: HOW DO YOU MAKE SENSE OF WHAT IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL?
answer:
I push through it. I've had a lot of hardship, in different ways — relationships, finances, I've gone through all those roller coasters, alhamdulillah. I accept it as fate — I know it's temporary, I know it's going to pass, and I just keep working on it. I don't like to give up on anything. I know Allah doesn't give me any burden more than I can handle, so if he thinks I can handle it, I'm going to come out the other side.

Of course nobody likes hardship, but you accept it and work on it. I don't say when it's going to end, but I try to make sure how it's going to end, you know — it's good.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer:
I feel responsible to my kids, their future, their education, how they form early in life — and my family, I think.

I don't know — that's a very deep question. I've never thought about it.

Right, right... It's part of it, because they were the main reason I actually went on that journey deeper — there were questions I couldn't answer, and I didn't feel good about that. I'm the kind of person that if I don't know something, I don't feel good — I want to know why I don't know what I don't know, and I want to know it. I don't want to sound ignorant or hypocritical about what I believe is right. I want to get my facts right so I can teach someone. So I believe my kids are the main reason, my family — my husband, my kids — because it was all around raising the kids, that's the main reason we went that route.

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer:
In my household I'm a mom, and I know I should be responsible — I know my actions speak louder to my kids than what I'm saying. What I do in front of them is much more effective, so I take that responsibility very seriously, being a mom, a role model, and a good Muslim — I'm their first example. They see that in me and try to imitate it — my daughter, my kids, they know I pray at certain times, and they say, "Okay, Mom, I'm going to go pray," without me even telling them. It might not sound like a big responsibility, but it is — that's how we pass our religion on to them, so they can continue the faith we believe in. I believe that's my responsibility. On the community level, unfortunately I'm not too involved in community events, just smaller-scale things — I encourage my neighbors. There's a lady across from me, from Pakistan, who was always very open about everything, and lately I've been encouraging her to start putting her scarf on, maybe twice a week to start, slowly, and I feel it's been working — though it's not because of me, exactly. Her mother recently passed away, and I sent her a video of a woman talking about why she started wearing hijab, after she saw, for the first time, a woman's body being washed and shrouded — she saw the woman's body covered in extra layers, her hair covered just like a hijab. Hearing that story, I sent it to my neighbor, and she came back to me and said, "Oh my gosh, I saw that with my mom too — when they were shrouding her, only her face was open, but her head was covered just like hijab."

I haven't seen how it's done for men, but the woman's experience was that after her body was gone, they still put a scarf on her. Sending that to her was a reminder for me too, and for her — she was actually more modest than me before, and it was the opposite by the time she moved here. I was the one wearing shorts and things I'm not supposed to be wearing, and then I turned around 180 degrees, and I started seeing her change too.

I've been there — I know. It's not something somebody told me to do, I chose it, because I was on that side and it wasn't good — even though I was wearing certain things, I wasn't feeling good about it. I tell her she should be more modest. I see that as community-level work — sharing whatever knowledge I have with the people around me, on a smaller scale, but I want to slowly make a bigger impact in the community, inshallah. May Allah guide me.

question: HAVE YOU BEEN MADE TO FEEL YOUR FAITH CONFLICTS WITH YOUR COUNTRY?
answer:
Well, I haven't — no one has made me feel that way yet, I guess, but you can feel the pressure from how things are portrayed around the world, how the media, especially in Western countries, portrays Muslims. I don't think I'm a threat — they should think I'm a blessing to them. I think I'm a blessing to these communities, honestly, and I would defend that — if somebody dares to open their mouth, I will defend it.

No — in this small journey of wearing hijab and showing myself as a Muslim woman, alhamdulillah I haven't faced that. May Allah not let that happen to any Muslim woman who wears it. I believe where you live matters a lot — where I live is very diverse, people came from different cultural backgrounds, it's not a place where it's mostly one dominant group and I'm the only one who doesn't fit. It's much more diverse, so I haven't been in areas like that, though I've heard other women say they've faced situations where they were told to go back where they came from. Nobody's said that to me yet, but if they do, they'd better be ready for me to say something back — I'm not the accepting type. My face probably shows that too — I think people who say those things target women who look weak.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: Oh, I've started thinking about this a lot lately, because everything we do has a hisab. I think about it a lot in everyday things — what I can do to make my Akhirah better than this life. I've started practicing things I never did much before — small things, extra dhikr, extra prayers, extra du'as, sending du'as — small things that we think are small but really aren't. I've started doing that, and I hope to continue, and, well, when I have the means, inshallah, I hope to do a bigger sadaqah jariyah, to leave something behind.

question: HOW DO YOU MAKE SENSE OF WHAT IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL?
answer: All I know is, anything beyond my control is in somebody else's control, so I just leave it to him. I know God is in power — Allah is in control of everything.

question: WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR PRACTICING YOUR RELIGION IN THE LONG RUN?
answer:
If she wants to go on that path, of course, I wish she does, but I want her to have deep knowledge, so that when she faces any challenge in her life — just being a Muslim woman and standing up for her faith — she's ready. Really, the only challenging part of being a Muslim woman is your hijab; the rest of it, people wouldn't know who you are unless you show them, and showing them could potentially work against you in the Western countries. But I want her to understand that if she has deeper knowledge and understanding of why she has to wear it, of being Muslim and standing up for herself, she'll be okay if she has that strong foundation, and I hope she does. Egypt helped a lot with that too — I think she was really influenced by it, because she wanted, at one point, to wear niqab.

You can experience it — she wanted to put the niqab on and go to the market, and I said sure. People were looking at me — I was actually in a Muslim country, not a non-Muslim one, and she was wearing niqab and I wasn't, and people would say to my face, "You don't wear niqab, why are you letting your daughter wear it?" They assumed I was telling her to wear it — they didn't understand that a child has her own mind about things. They couldn't accept it. I told them, "You're missing the whole point, that's her choice and I respect it, and I let her do it."

I said I hope she keeps that will in her — when she wants to do something, even if I say no, she keeps pursuing it in a good way.

A lot of things — a lot of things — nothing really aligns with our beliefs here, so you have to really help them realign themselves with what we believe, make sense of everything they're doing. There are things they shouldn't be looking at or doing; they need to build enough tarbiyah of the nafs for themselves. I can only facilitate that through knowledge — I can't force them. I wish the West had the good morals that Muslim people have — unfortunately it doesn't, but I do appreciate that they have good manners here, they're at least kind to your face, and they have opportunity. So that's a good side, but there are other things that need to be taught — you have to guide them to make sure they know where they come from and who they are, and if we keep reinforcing that in them, I think they'll be okay.

question: WHAT IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR HEART, INTENTION, AND OUTWARD PRACTICE?
answer:
Of course — when I wear the hijab, I know I have to do things that align with it; I can't be wearing hijab and doing things that don't make sense with that. I really respect — I think hijab is a big responsibility in my life, one I didn't touch on earlier. I believe wearing hijab, showing people that I'm Muslim, is one of the biggest responsibilities I have, and you have to live up to it — everything you do, you have to really be conscious of it.

Inward, of course — like, if I'm wearing hijab and the prayer time comes and I don't pray, what's the point of me wearing the outward things if I'm not doing what's important? So I try to align the two. My heart, I believe, has always been with Allah — even when I did something small that was wrong, I was always scared, thinking, "Oh my gosh, forgive me, I know I did this wrong." I've always had that awareness that Allah is watching me, Allah is with me, that I need to seek forgiveness — that's always been with me in my heart. I didn't always show that outwardly, but inside, I believe it's something I was born with — I had a lot of opportunities to go in different directions, but something inside me was telling me not to do it, and I didn't do a lot of things that weren't good.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer: Submission, to me, is submitting to Allah with every decision you make, everything you do — praying, raising a family, working, the people around you — anything you do, you do for his ridha, so that he's pleased with you. That's submission to Allah. And believing in everything that happens in your life — even when something you wanted isn't given to you, or the person you wanted isn't with you — accepting that is submission to Allah too. It's hard, I'm not saying it's easy — for your research, whoever reads this should understand it's not easy. Submitting yourself to Allah fully is the hardest thing — I don't know for other people, but for me it's really hard. But I know if I push myself to it, it's going to be good for me in my heart. What keeps me submitting is hoping that one day he'll be pleased with me and grant me Jannah, grant my family Jannah, and the Muslims I know, and gather us all together — that's the one thing I know for sure if I submit myself. It keeps me going, though I know sometimes I'm off track, and I try to go back with istighfar, with tawbah, extra prayers — we're human at the end of the day.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer:
Liberated — I don't know, that's a really good question, but I don't know the answer, I don't... know, sorry.

You see, I'm actually the opposite — alhamdulillah, I've never been restricted on anything, I've never been oppressed on anything. Alhamdulillah. What's liberating is being capable — like, okay, I want to do this, I can go do this, without asking anybody's permission. Alhamdulillah, I've been blessed with that kind of liberation — Allah facilitated a lot of things for me without much hardship. There was hardship, but not in the way of somebody telling me, "No, you can't do it."

I was allowed to do things, even though I faced small challenges here and there, but I was never told I couldn't do something. I've been blessed on that, may Allah bless everyone. I think going more deeply into my religion, I've been liberated — my husband too, I guess Allah made that happen. That was something I chose to go through — I made a niyyah, an intention, and set a goal: that's it, I'm going to go to Egypt, I'm going to learn about Islam, I'm going to teach my kids Quran, they're going to memorize the Quran. That was a huge decision — leaving my husband, everything behind. I left my house, my car, everything.

It was a huge move; my husband was shocked, because I told him, if you're going to keep saying my kids can choose everything, I'm going to take the kids and put them in an environment where they have to understand what's right for them.

And somehow, that was Allah helping us — when you put your mind to something, Allah sends... look at this, it's amazing. He sent my husband to Kuwait after us — he was in the U.S. working at [GOVERNMENT SPACE AGENCY], and somehow he ended up going to Kuwait, to a military base. He made that happen for himself. We went to Egypt at the end of May, and he was there by September 1st. He'd had no intention of moving anywhere, no plan of going to the Middle East and working there, but he took the offer — he could have said no, but it was like Allah made that happen for him, and he understood, "Okay, so what she's doing is probably right." He started supporting the Quran, everything — he's always been a supportive guy, but something struck him too.

I think, not me — maybe he got liberated. He got exposed to something, or something opened up for him.

question: HOW DID YOU BECOME MORE INTENTIONAL PRACTICING ISLAM OUTSIDE A MUSLIM-MAJORITY COUNTRY?
answer:
Right, yeah. You see, something has to come with the foundation — our foundations, at least the seeds, were planted, so we knew who we were, we knew our identity, we knew we should pray, we knew we were Muslim. Even though we weren't practicing everything fully, we were doing the things we knew — we knew we should fast in Ramadan, we knew we should pay our zakat, we knew we shouldn't be bad to people, we knew we should respect our mom and dad. We'd been introduced properly, and that's super important for kids from a young age, I believe, because if kids are introduced to their faith early — they're already born Muslim, they're already born modest, in a way. I really noticed that raising my kids — when they think something is inappropriate, they start covering themselves, they start defending themselves automatically. If you're going through something and you cry, they cry too.

That's planted in the kids, but we need to nourish it more so they can grow with it. It's like when a child is very young, a toddler — I've noticed, sometimes when I'm helping her in the shower, with her hair, she starts covering the parts she should be covering, automatically. I never taught her that — I never thought to teach her that when she was younger — but she knows she should be covering that, like it's human, it's already planted in us from birth. It's just that society, without nurturing that education in kids, lets it start fading out. What I believe is that kids just need the right foundation fitted into them, small and small, when they're young — their religion, their faith — it shouldn't be a problem for them then.

To continue — and then letting that nourish itself and grow, like you help the kids until they can help themselves. Like our parents told us, "You should pray, you should do this," but on a smaller scale, not forcefully. What I'm trying to say is, we knew what we should be doing, what's right, what's not right, except for the outward things, the hijab and so on — but the main five pillars, we knew we should be doing those. So if kids are educated rightly, I think they'll be fine — whatever they go through, they'll be fine, they'll start practicing, and even if they go off track, they'll go back to it, by Allah's will, and I'll always pray for them, that Allah guides them all the time. The parents' influence is much more important than anybody else's, because whatever they see in the house is what they're going to start doing.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer: Well, I think how faith shows up every day would be through praying five times a day. Most importantly, starting my day with the Fajr prayer, before the sun rises — I get up, make an intention, do the wash that we do as Muslims, and pray to Allah, our Lord, our Creator. It's a time to talk to our Creator, to meditate, and it really starts the day in the Islamic faith. That's the start of the day, and then throughout the day, praying — I go to work and I pray at my job. There's a place where I can pray at my employment. At first I was doing it without anyone knowing, but then people would see me — I'm around people who aren't Muslim, so I had a little dialogue with everyone and explained how my day goes, that Muslims pray five times a day, and they would see me doing this. I got permission that it was okay for me to have a space to do so, and they were fine with it.

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer:
I'm sorry, repeat that again?

Okay, let's see — I'm thinking if I've had an incident with anyone who hasn't met a Muslim. Not to bombard a person, but if they ask me, or I'm just approaching them and letting them know — I think it's different if someone comes to you and asks; then it's more welcoming to freely talk in that type of situation.

Okay, yeah, so I've had questions — someone would come up to me and say, "Oh, I like your hijab," or maybe they don't know anything and say, "I like what you have on, I like your scarf," and I tell them, yes, it's part of my Muslim identity as a woman — we cover our hair, we dress very modestly, we cover parts of our body, so it's an everyday look. Then I've gotten the question, "So do you wear it at home too?" and I say no, at home I don't have to wear it — I'm dressed very comfortably in my house clothes, and I don't have to cover around my husband, my son, uncles. So I think it depends on the questions, and that's how I would explain it. And then, especially around the holidays, people will tell me "Merry Christmas," and I tell them I don't celebrate Christmas, and they say, "Oh, okay, so what do you celebrate?" So I can explain that we have two holidays throughout the year, and I give the details on the Eids we celebrate, and I tell people we don't celebrate Christmas because we don't believe Jesus is the son of God — we believe Jesus is a prophet. In Arabic his name is Isa. So it's a nice educational piece to share with people who aren't aware that some people don't celebrate Christmas.

They're very beneficial, because for people that don't know anything about Islam, or very little, it gives them some more in-depth insight that they wouldn't get otherwise. It breaks down assumptions and misconceptions when they stop and ask me instead of just seeing me and assuming. I really appreciate someone asking instead of assuming, so then I can clarify and break down whatever assumptions people may have, and then they can go into their community or their church and say, "I met a Muslim lady, this is what I asked her and what she explained to me." It spreads education about Muslims, because I feel like day to day we interact with a lot of non-Muslims just in passing, but we don't have much dialogue. There are a lot of Muslims here in [STATE 1], and from everyday interactions — passing in grocery stores and other common places we meet — it's important to have dialogue with people.

question: HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO WRONG PORTRAYALS OF MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
I haven't personally gotten any negative feedback — I can't think of a specific time. My immediate family is Muslim, but that's it; my cousins, uncles, aunts are not Muslim. I have family members down south — when you go deeper down south, into [STATE 2], [STATE 3], I have family that practice Christianity, in church every day, having Bible study. Some of them said, years ago, "What is this you're wearing on your head?" I said, "We call it a hijab, it's a covering, a form of modesty." And they said, "Well, how are you going to get married if you're not showing your hair?" I said, "Well, we usually marry someone of our same faith." They understand that this is a passage of righteousness, to cover and to be modest — it's one of the marks of being Muslim. I told them, as a Christian, you also have a look of modesty that you follow — if you look back at the Old Testament, at old photos, Christian women used to cover, used to wear a type of hijab, long sleeves, a long gown. Over time it's gotten shorter and shorter, and now you don't even cover your hair at all, but at one time you also, as a Christian woman, covered.

Then they said, well, if you don't take Jesus as your Lord, you're going to hellfire. I said, we believe we pray straight to the Creator — why don't you pray straight to the Creator? Why do you feel the need to go through a man to get to the Creator? It was a very long, complicated conversation, confusing coming from a Muslim, someone who has always practiced — I was never Christian, my parents didn't raise us Christian, so we never really studied it, but just knowing about the Trinity, three different people in one, is confusing to me. I didn't really get a good explanation from my family about what it was — it sounded as if they just practice it because it's stated to them, and certain things they couldn't clarify, why they do it, just that they do it because it's written. I know from the Quran and Hadith there are reasons why, as Muslims, we do things — the Quran states what is done, and the Hadith explains why it's done. It's very clear, in black and white, so for something not to be explained or clarified is confusing.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
That's a good question, because I didn't always wear hijab growing up. I grew up in the Midwest — there weren't too many Muslims at my school. In high school, I was the only Muslim, I think. We did have a few people from Palestine, Pakistan, India, maybe a few West Africans, but not too many, not like here on the East Coast. My parents didn't encourage us to wear hijab — we couldn't wear shorts or short-sleeve shirts or tight pants, but we didn't have to cover. So I didn't really have a Muslim identity — you couldn't tell I was Muslim. I didn't get any questions in school about my faith unless I wanted to tell someone about it.

When I started wearing hijab as an adult, I noticed I got approached differently — men didn't approach me anymore. I feel like I get a level of respect I didn't get before. Especially in the African American community — if I go into [CITY 1], people who aren't Muslim will say "Salaam Alaikum" to me, and even Muslims will say it, because in urban cities there's a predominantly large amount of African American Muslims. A lot of African Americans become Muslim — they weren't raised Muslim, but they convert — and they're already integrated in the community, so they have easy dialogue with each other. I get a lot of salaam alaikum, and people don't look at me a certain way because I'm not wearing tight clothes, not revealing my body — I get a more respectful look. It's a protection for me, wearing my hijab, for that reason — I'm in a safe space, traveling on my journey outside my home in a safe space.

I actually started wearing hijab when I got married. My husband was an influence on me, a gentle one — he didn't tell me, "You have to do this, you have to do that," it was more, "You should try," a level of modesty that's part of our religion. When I started covering, I didn't cover my neck — I just took a scarf and tied it behind my head, and my neck was showing. Over time, as I studied more and learned more about the religion, it deepened my understanding of the importance of why Muslim women cover, so I felt the importance to cover more, and I started covering my neck and draping it down over my chest, as it's stated in our Holy Book.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, AND HOW?
answer: Reading from the Quran and the Sunnah, and then my husband — he used to be an imam, he comes from a family of sheikhs — he teaches Arabic and translates to English, so he teaches people; he's a teacher himself. That was a big help, because I didn't have to go outside to a stranger.

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer:
Um, yeah... I think through praying, and praying over time, and having understanding — you can talk to Allah, and Allah will make your difficulties go away. I'm not a complainer; instead of complaining, I like to talk to Allah. So through prayer, it helps — asking Allah to guide me through difficult situations. There are certain du'as we say as Muslims. I don't know, I'm speaking in third person — is that okay?

Okay, because I know I'm speaking to another Muslim, but I'm speaking as if non-Muslims will hear this.

Yeah, so memorizing certain du'as is helpful, knowing the meaning behind it. I like to study du'as in Arabic, but I also like to memorize them in English, because it touches the heart when I know what I'm saying — speaking in Arabic is good, but not knowing what you're saying doesn't reach your heart, you can't have an attachment to it. So that helps — certain du'as, and the kids memorize them, we memorize them together, and I teach them, while teaching myself, that patience and perseverance will get you through any situation, and staying calm. How do we learn that? Through prayer — because through prayer you have to be patient, you have to focus, you don't rush. That teaches you a level of patience to deal with any type of situation. Alhamdulillah, I thank Allah for being Muslim when I say that.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer:
Who do I feel most responsible to? My kids, my husband. It was my mother, when she was here, but she's not here anymore. And I feel a responsibility to my siblings as well, because everyone is spread out, living in different places — my sister's in [STATE 4], I have a brother here, and another brother in [STATE 5]. As the oldest of my family, I feel responsible for keeping the connection going — calling them, checking on them, seeing how they're doing. This is important because they're the only family I have that's Muslim.

I think that's my first responsibility. My second responsibility is my passion for plants and teaching people the importance of growing food for themselves and their family, because I'm a health educator — it's very important to take care of your body.

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer: I understand it to be very important for well-being — it connects our spiritual, our mental, and our physical health, to stay connected. I feel like it's part of our DNA — we have to help one another out. We live here in America, and it's isolating here, so how do we break that isolation? We have to keep the community, we have to keep connected to one another, encourage each other, check on each other, see how we're doing. It's very important — it's part of our deen, but it's also part of our mental health, our physical well-being. That's why, as a Muslim, if someone's sick, you go to visit them. It's important to care for one another — it's part of our religion.

question: HAVE YOU BEEN MADE TO FEEL YOUR FAITH CONFLICTS WITH YOUR COUNTRY?
answer:
No, I don't feel my religion is a threat, to anybody or to my community. No.

It's hard to say, because I'm also African American. In a country that's so racist, and the world is so racist at times, depending where you go, sometimes I don't know if it's because of the color of my skin or because I'm wearing a hijab — some of the tension I'll feel, or the looks I'll get. But then, because I'm so optimistic, I try to give people — I think Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) said to give people fifty or seventy excuses — so it may not even be the color of my skin or my hijab; someone may just be having a bad day and take it out on me, not caring about my skin color or my hijab. Sometimes people have had a death in the family that morning, and they still have to go to work and function. Giving people those kinds of excuses, and not taking it personally, kind of breaks barriers between people, because then you're able to deal with someone who's maybe having a difficult day or acting in a difficult manner.

I never know what kind of response I'm going to get unless someone says something verbally abusive or aggressive — then I'd know how to deal with that. But I don't get backlash from people, alhamdulillah — I haven't had anyone come up to me and call me offensive names, I haven't had anyone pull on my hijab, like I've heard of certain incidents where some Muslim women are attacked or called certain names. I haven't personally had that, and I pray Allah continues to protect me in that way.

That hasn't been my experience, but I know of a situation with my sister — she used to wear niqab, and she lived in Canada for thirteen years, in [CITY 2]. She got a lot of harassment from white men because she was wearing the niqab, and she would go out with her kids without her husband, and men would approach her aggressively and say demeaning things to her — "take that off, go back to your country" — very offensive, negative words that they shouldn't be saying to a woman with children. So even though it's not my experience, I personally know my sister has experienced that.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: Okay, my awareness of the afterlife — it makes me very conscious about everything I do, what I say, how I walk, how I talk. I'm very conscious of that because of the world we live in — I think society is getting worse, generations are more — people act as if how they feel is more important, people want to do what they want to do. That makes me more conscious of my being and how I interact with people, what I do from day to day. I feel like it's more important to promote Islam, and I feel like, alone, women, as we cover, we're already promoting Islam by the way we cover — it's easier to start a conversation when you're covered. Alhamdulillah for that, and may it be a ticket to Jannah for all the women who wear hijab, because you have women who cover, who wear hijab, but you can't tell if their husband is Muslim or not — so a lot falls on the Muslim woman, I feel like, but in a good way.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer: I'm sorry, I'll say it again? Submitting to the will of Allah is putting my faith in Allah for everything that I do. Being God-conscious is the first act of my submission to Allah, and then following the five pillars of Islam is the submission to Allah.

question: WHAT IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR HEART, INTENTION, AND OUTWARD PRACTICE?
answer:
The way I speak to people, my kindness, being easygoing — I feel like that's why I'm easygoing, through my faith too. It's made me a relaxed person, I don't stress about things easily. Even though I'm human, I do stress, but I'm kind to other people — I try to be, because I want people to be kind to me.

Bottom line, it's about getting blessings from Allah — I can't go to Jannah, I don't want to go to hellfire, so I ask myself, what do I need to do to prevent myself from going to hellfire? The acts I do intentionally, my intentions and how they're put into action, are all based on making my connection to Allah strong, so I can, inshallah, get to Jannah — and I'd like a special place in Jannah, with my favorite plants. So you ask Allah for it, and it makes you look forward to going to a better place than here — through doing good acts of kindness, and also thinking good thoughts, and inshallah my work pays off.

question: WHO GETS TO REPRESENT MUSLIM WOMEN IN RESEARCH, MEDIA, OR AI?
answer:
Let me think... I did a little bit of research — it's called large language models. I wasn't familiar with it; I'm not a big computer person, not too much into tech, but there's so much going on, so many changes, and I'm not a big fan of AI. I thought that was interesting — I could see some of the language being historically slanted toward one group over another, and a lot of misconceptions coming up.

Is it like a male-dominated field?

Yeah, that's very important — representation matters, and everyone needs their own voice to speak their own story. I strongly believe that. And the way it's done doesn't have to be the way this society thinks it has to be — loud, aggressive, confrontational. You can speak your truth and advocate for yourself in a calm, reserved manner — it doesn't have to be boisterous or loud. I feel like that's how people think women should present themselves too, and it doesn't have to be like that — you can get your point across and speak your story in a respectful way and get respect back. I've noticed with the young generation, a lot of young girls are being taught that advocating for themselves means being aggressive, pushing people, it's all about "what I want" — and I don't think that's a good way to advocate for your needs. The way you present yourself is also important.

question: WHERE DOES YOUR APPROACH TO SPEAKING UP AND REPRESENTING YOURSELF COME FROM?
answer: Yeah, because I teach — I'm an art educator at a farm, with the homeschooling community, a co-op that runs for homeschoolers. I taught the middle schoolers this year. During the middle school years is a time when children are trying to find themselves, making friends, learning about themselves, wanting to socialize, but some of them aren't doing it in a positive direction, or aren't sure how. Common things — like when you come in, you should say hello to your teacher, ask how they're doing — these common things that help you socialize — when you don't have those skills, it's a struggle. I see that in the kids. One particular girl said she needs to advocate for herself and her rights, and the way she does it is by screaming and yelling, so I've been teaching her that you can speak calmly and address people with respect and get respect back — that entering a room expecting your presence alone to get what you need, in a dominating way, doesn't work, it doesn't create a peaceful environment. I try to teach the children that.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer:
Where in my life do I feel most liberated — where, meaning a particular place?

These are good questions, I never thought about this one. I feel like when I'm — actually, the work that I do — I feel most liberated when I'm teaching, because...

I feel like I have a presence, as the only Muslim, and the way I teach, I can incorporate a little bit of Islam into it, which makes me feel liberated, because I feel like I'm giving a community something they wouldn't get anywhere else — the people I work with are all non-Muslim, and I don't think they'd have the opportunity to approach any other Muslim and ask the kinds of questions they ask me, since they know me on a personal level. I feel most liberated when I can teach, and teach the youth too — I've taught them about some Islamic values that I wouldn't otherwise have the opportunity to share. Every morning, during our morning circle, I have seventeen kids, and I do a lot of social-emotional teaching, because I feel there's a need there — if they're lacking things based on how they act and what they say. I give a general concept, and then I'll say, "As a Muslim, we do this." So I'm able to educate the young generation, and my hope is that they'll embrace Islam, or at least they can say, "I had a Muslim teacher, and she taught us about Islam" — that I didn't just come and teach academics or art, but gave them something of myself. I feel like that's important and needed with the young generation coming up — I see that they're very open, they're not stuck holding tightly to any particular values, their minds are very free. This is a good time to educate them about Islam.

It's a good place to be, to reflect and see how I can best serve the children as a Muslim woman and as an African American woman.

Yes, and I feel liberated doing that, because I'm giving them a piece of information and teaching them a little about myself and how I practice Islam. Otherwise they wouldn't know — like when we had the Eid celebration, I brought goodies for everybody and let them know we celebrate — we don't celebrate Christmas, but we have our own celebration, and I welcome and share it with everyone. I don't think they'd otherwise see that — even my colleagues didn't know what Eid was. I came in one day — it wasn't the actual day of Eid, because I never work on Eid day, but it was a few days after — and I brought some cookies, and they asked, "What are the cookies for?" I said, "We're celebrating Eid," and they said, "Oh, what is that?" — people just don't know.

I feel good to be able to teach people about Islam. That's my job.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer: I'm a practicing Muslim, as long as I can remember, so faith is a big part of my day. I'm a mom — my kids are older now, so I decided to go back to school to finish my graduate studies. My day normally starts with prayer in the morning, before Fajr — that's been my time since I can remember, because I always had little kids; I got married early, so that used to be my time, waking up early before Fajr and spending some time praying. I do my Fajr, get my coffee, and then get my only daughter, who's younger, ready for school. I send her to school and then head to my own school — I have classes, I work in the lab, and then come back, pick her up, go back home. During the day, as a Muslim, I have to pray five times a day, so I do my prayers at school. I come back home with my daughter, get dinner ready, sometimes go to the gym, come back. I'm normally out of energy by around seven p.m., so I just wait until I do my last prayer, and the day ends for me.

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer:
Let's start with the self. Muslims in general, practicing Muslims, are very disciplined. First of all, knowing that God is overseeing everything gives a lot of discipline to your life — you know that not just every movement or action, but every thought, is monitored, so you work a lot on yourself to make sure you're doing everything pleasing to God, because we believe this life is temporary, that it's just a path to the next life, and it decides your life forever in the hereafter. So we're very disciplined people, in terms of our commitment to worship, to family, to community — we're responsible in every position we're in, not toward people but toward God, so you try your best to please God in every way.

In terms of community, this is something a lot of people don't know — since I've lived in the West for a long time, many people don't know that the Muslim community is very accepting, open-minded, and loving. Their discipline, their main goal, is to serve humanity and serve people locally. This is something I feel because of the media, because of the politics around us — a lot of people don't know that unless they actually engage with a Muslim or a Muslim community or community centers around them.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer:
I came here in 2000, so I've been here for twenty-six years. When I first came, it was actually a hard time, because September 11th happened a year after I arrived, so there was a huge campaign against Muslims. I came wearing my hijab, my full covering — I came young, I was twenty when I came, so I wanted to represent my faith in a good way to people here. It wasn't a good time when we came, because there was a lot of hate toward Muslims, a lot of misconceptions in the media, so it was a challenge, but I was pretty open about my faith, about my values. I remember a lot of times people would stop their car when I was outside and yell, "Go back to your country, go back to the camels," and even in the mall people would stop me and yell things. I always took every opportunity to help people understand — I would explain to them what my faith is, how the media misrepresents Muslims. It was a hard time, but it was also a good time — a good opportunity for me personally to open dialogue with other people.

I think age has a role. I had my kids here, after I came. I don't know if it's age, but I'm almost in my forties now, and I feel I'm not as strong as I used to be — I think it's because of age. I'm still open to answering questions, but I'm not fighting as hard as I used to, showing others the way I used to. I'm still trying to do my best, but I think I'm leaving that to the new generation now.

Fighting means fighting the mainstream idea that Muslims are violent, that Muslims are bad. I'm fighting those ideas, trying to show people what we're actually about, what Muslims are about, and how Muslims are misrepresented in the media. That's the fight I meant.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, AND HOW?
answer: Yeah, this is a blessing I always had. Wherever I moved — I've moved to many states here — I always had a good Muslim community, and I tried to always connect to other knowledge-seeking, Islamic-knowledge-seeking people. Nowadays I use YouTube a lot, always listening to new videos about Muslims, about Islam, more details on faith, explanations of the Quran. We also have a sisters' halaqa to study Quran — we've been doing it almost weekly for a long time now, something me and my friends established and worked on together.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
Hijab, back in our culture, in my country, is of course an Islamic thing, but a lot of it is mostly culture — when you get to a specific age, you're kind of expected to wear it. I started my connection with my faith early, around sixth or seventh grade — we had a really good Islamic teacher, a woman who explained Islam in a way you could relate to, and even though I was younger than the age you'd typically wear hijab, I decided to fully wear it — I wore hijab and what we call a jilbab, a long dress. My parents at that time weren't very practicing — they were more into the culture than the religion — so they were actually against it, but I stood my ground and wore it, and I still do now. It was a challenge at that time, because back home there was also a lot of misconception against Islam and practicing Muslims, so it wasn't very acceptable in the family either. But I decided to wear it, me and my older sister, and I've always been seeking to learn more about my faith, because with Islam you always have to revisit certain concepts to reinforce them in your daily life, and I've been doing that for a long time — alhamdulillah, that helped me a lot with wearing the hijab and practicing everything.

I remember when I first came here, a lot of friends would tell me, "Oh, you're going to the US, that means you're going to take it off," and it was confusing — why would I take it off, if I wear it for God, when I come here? So I came here, and it was a big part of my identity — I always looked different from other people around me. I joined school a couple of years after I came here, and I was almost the only person wearing hijab in my classes. It was good, though, because I always achieved in my classes, so it was a good representation for Muslim women with hijab. Since then, it's been a big part of my life.

When I grew up back in Palestine, Islam wasn't something you just grew up following — unfortunately, even in Muslim countries, there were a lot of campaigns to move people away from practicing the right Islam. Islam basically encourages you to think for yourself, to ask questions, and because of the dictatorships in many of these countries, they don't want people to think, they just want them to follow what the government wants. If you're a Muslim, a practicing Muslim, a Muslim who seeks knowledge, that's something they don't want, because to follow Islam properly you actually have to think about whether something is right or wrong, whether you're following what God wants or what people want, and they don't want that — they want you following what the government or the rulers want, because that's not always what's best for the people. There's no free will, no democracy, and the easy way to control people is by making them submit — especially when what the rulers want isn't what's best for the people, but what's best for themselves.

We weren't allowed — mosques now are open to young people, they're encouraged to ask questions, encouraged to think for themselves; that wasn't the case back then. You'd wear hijab just because it was the culture — you'd grow up, start going to college, and that's when you'd wear it. If you actually wanted to wear it because Islam wants you to, that wasn't encouraged — a lot of people viewed girls who wore hijab early as girls who were forced into it, not doing it for themselves. In my case, it was the opposite — I actually wanted to do it, but my parents didn't want people to think they were forcing me.

question: HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO WRONG PORTRAYALS OF MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
Are you talking about here, or in the West, or back home?

I still don't understand — what kind of woman?

Yeah.

I actually love when I'm in a situation like this. I've been in many situations where people would tell me, "Oh, we feel bad for you, you're forced to wear hijab, you're forced to listen to your husband, you're forced to—" and I love these moments, because that's a good opportunity to explain, especially for people who know me or interact with me — I'm very kind and open-minded, easy to talk to. There's this idea that Muslim women always get married through arranged marriage, and I've been told many times, "I feel bad for you, being forced to marry someone you don't know," and that's not the case at all. I love these questions, because it's a good opportunity to explain, since people don't know otherwise.

question: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN OR HIJAB?
answer: Yeah, this is — even at this time, with social media, people still don't know. I have a neighbor who, until recently, thought I was wearing hijab because I'm forced to, because my husband or my son are around — there was a situation where she told me, "Oh, go inside, your husband, your son is coming," as if I'm only wearing it out of fear of my son or husband, which isn't the case. I love when people do that, because it's a good opportunity to explain — you don't explain randomly, you need people to ask you these questions or say these things to you. I remember another neighbor who asked, doesn't it feel bad that you're allowed to drive a car here in the West — which is funny, because we drive cars everywhere, I don't know why they think that's something we're not allowed to do as Muslims. Yeah, until now, unfortunately, there are misconceptions about Muslim women.

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer:
You know, life is very hard — you go through things you don't imagine you can go through. I have a few things in mind... Maybe one of the hardest times we went through was when the war in Gaza was happening — this most recent one. My family is in the West Bank, so they were going through things too, but we felt shy even talking about any struggle my family was going through in the West Bank compared to Gaza. Just seeing the genocide happening in front of our eyes, and not being able to do anything to stop it, that was one of the hardest things.

What I've seen — it wasn't just me, I think it was a global feeling of helplessness, not being able to do anything. I always thought, how do people with no faith handle this? Because the only thing that made me, or anybody going through this, able to make sense of what was happening was faith — just knowing there is a judgment day, and everyone who committed any tyranny, any killing, any genocide, is going to stand in front of God and be asked. That gives a lot of peace of mind, knowing that God is just, that he's not going to let these people — the people who did the genocide, the people who supported it — go without being punished. Without faith, I don't know how people can handle these events.

question: WHAT INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS ARE PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
I feel like I have a responsibility — I always feel a responsibility to fix, or at least to play some small role in changing people's perspective, people's ideas. These things, when you have a culture, ways that have been there for a long time, it doesn't take one step to change, one action — it has to go through a period of time and a lot of change from other people. Just knowing that a word from you, standing for what you believe, can have a small change — I think that's always been my approach, to use these opportunities to make a change, to talk to people, to open dialogue, to help people understand why something is not right or needs to change.

As a young person, when you believe in something, you try to stand your ground. I remember hearing a lot of things from family members, like, "You're too young, why are you doing this to yourself, you're so beautiful, you shouldn't — you're eventually going to wear it anyway, why wear it this early?" But that didn't make sense to me. When I was that young, in seventh grade, I wasn't able to handle it the way I learned to later, especially with older people — you still have to have respect for older people, so sometimes negotiating or debating with them isn't very helpful. What I did was just stand my ground — I didn't listen, and I tried to surround myself with people who would support me, that I could go back to for support. When I got a little older, it became easier to actually discuss any opinion other people had and bring actual support for my position, from Islam, from religion, from history — the more you listen, the more you learn, the more knowledge you gain, and the better you become at defending what you believe in.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer:
Responsible for what?

I believe, for choices, the best bond is your bond with God, because you can rely on people, but with experience and a lot of disappointment, you learn not to rely on them too much, so you won't get disappointed. But I believe the most important bond, I would say, is the mother bond — I don't know if I'm answering the right question.

I believe this is the basic bond, that your bond with your mother shapes everything after that, and I was blessed to have one of the best moms. After that, also, as a woman, your relationship with your dad — as a woman, you need a male figure in your life, and if you don't have that with brothers, I had it with my dad. Just knowing there's a man who would always support you no matter what, love you no matter what, be proud of you — I think that mom and dad are the most important relationships, the ones that either fix or ruin everything after. Also, being a mother, your relationship with your kids — I think that's what makes life beautiful after that, gives you another perspective, another aim and goal, because once you become a mom, everything shifts, it becomes more about these lives, these souls, that you brought into the world.

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer:
There are many aspects — family is very important, I'm talking about extended family, parents, brothers and sisters. After God, they're your backbone, and if you have their love and support, you're good to go.

In my family, at this age — maybe when you're younger, they're your backbone, your support, but once your mom and dad get older, it becomes your responsibility to take care of them. That's a very important role, and no matter how busy you are, you always have to make time to serve them, because that's in our culture and our religion — this is what brings blessing to your life, taking care of the souls that took care of you when you were young. As a mom, in my own family, your role changes — when the kids are young, you're basically everything for them, the support, the source of love, security, advice, and that starts fading as they grow up, but the responsibility doesn't go away — you're always going to support them and love them and be there for them, no matter how far or how old they get.

I also believe I was more active in the community when I was younger than I am now — maybe I'm busier now. I use the community here to support myself, but maybe that's one of my shortcomings — I should have more of a role, support the community more. What I try to do is participate in many community events, but maybe I should do a little bit more.

question: HAVE YOU BEEN MADE TO FEEL YOUR FAITH CONFLICTS WITH YOUR COUNTRY?
answer: I think that happened after September 11th — a lot of people around us made us feel like we were a threat, that we didn't belong. It happened for a while. I lived at that time in an area where a lot of Muslims lived, and we had a lot of attacks on the masjids, on our apartment complex, on the street. We were told not to leave the house, because people tried, many times, to pull the hijab off some women's heads. It was a lot — that was one of the hardest times to be Muslim in the West.

question: WHAT DOES BELONGING FEEL LIKE HERE?
answer:
Can you repeat that question again?

I have many roles here — I'm a student, and I've been in the same school for a long time, so I feel like I belong there, I know a lot of professors and students, and having that support system makes you feel part of the belonging. A big part of feeling that I belong is the Muslim community here — we have a great Muslim community, and it's like home to me, especially because I don't have family around — they're my family, that's where I feel like I belong.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: It shapes everything — just knowing that this life doesn't end when you die, that it's just a gateway to the real, forever life. It shapes your perspective on everything. You know you're here as part of a test, here to be tested, to strengthen yourself, to get to know God, to build yourself in a way that helps you get to heaven, because we believe you have to work for it, you have to deserve it, and that takes a lot of energy, a lot of shaping in your life — every step you take, the way you think, interact with people, raise your kids, interact with your family, your community, people you don't know — everything is going to be judged, even your intentions, your thoughts. So it makes you work on every detail in your life — what you look at, what you listen to, how you talk to people, how you respond to others — everything is going to be judged, everything you're going to be asked about, so you have to try your best to deserve God's mercy.

question: HOW DO YOU MAKE SENSE OF WHAT IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL?
answer:
In the last two years I've been going through something that flipped my life — everything happened, and it was out of my control. I worked so hard for years to build something, and in the last two years it was destroyed. You don't question it exactly, but after something like that happens, you know that in this life, everything is in God's hands — it's not about how smart you are, how much money you have, how strong you are. The only thing that happens is what Allah wants, not what you want.

We know that this life is a test — we're not here just to have fun, live, eat, and enjoy. God will put you through things that bring out either the best or the worst in you, and that's how you get tested. It's like when you're in a class and you study — the professor, at the end of the semester, is going to test you, to see how deeply you know the material. It's the same way — God will put you through things that bring out what's actually inside you, and if you've worked hard on yourself, you'll be able to withstand any hardship, knowing that every pleasure here is temporary.
