Your kids are temporary, your health is temporary, it's all going to go eventually — you're going to lose your health, your kids won't stay with you forever, your wealth might go any minute. Even the simple blessings — your eyesight, your five senses, your ability to walk — these are all temporary. So this life is temporary, it's a test, and that's how you're able to withstand any difficulty, knowing that everything happens by God's will and for a reason.

question: WHAT IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR HEART, INTENTION, AND OUTWARD PRACTICE?
answer:
What I know is, everything is connected — whatever you listen to affects your understanding of things, your feelings. If you're surrounded by people who are very negative, always listening to negative comments, you're going to be affected, you're going to be down, you might end up like them. If you're surrounded by hardworking people, or if you go to the gym, it's going to boost you, because physical action does have an effect on the heart and mind. We believe that when your actions — remembrance of God, saying God's name repeatedly, reading Quran, praying — this always has a strong effect on the heart, it softens the heart somehow.

The number one intention, when you do any act of worship, should always be to please your Creator — just knowing that even if it has no other effect, you're pleasing the one who created you, the one who deserves to be worshipped. I think that's enough, but it also helps to know the reason behind an action you do. For example, wearing hijab — we wear it because God told us to, but it also has an effect on communities. I remember, back when I was doing my bachelor's, people would ask me, "Why are you doing this to yourself?" — but when people interact with a covered woman, they actually talk to her as a human being, not as a body. We know how visual men are, how affected they are by what they see. I always used to give this example: if you want to hire a secretary, and a beautiful girl, uncovered, showing all of her hair and skin, comes in, there's a big chance you're going to hire her because of how she looks, or talk to her because of how she looks, rather than what's actually going on inside her mind, whether she deserves the position. But as a Muslim, wherever we go, I feel like people judge us based on who we are as a human being, not as a body.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer: Submission to Allah has many aspects. One is obeying his commands, following the religion he sent, that he accepted for us, that he wanted us to follow. Submission also means accepting his decree — and I don't want that to sound negative. You try your best, and in a difficult situation you try to change anything you're not comfortable with, but sometimes things happen that are out of your hands, so at some point you have to know that everything God writes for you is for your own good, and you just have to look for the reason and accept it. I think that's a big part of being submitted to God.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer: A big part of my liberation is being Muslim — that's actually the source of my liberation, because I know the only ultimate submission has to be to God. Even when you submit to rules here and there, you submit to them under God's submission too — for example, when you live in a country, you have to obey its rules, because in Islam we're taught that when you're in an area, you have to submit to the rulings of that area, as long as they don't interfere with God's rulings. A big part of liberation comes from the fact that the ultimate entity you're submitting to is God, so any injustice, anything else — because as a human, you're going to submit to something, even if it's not to God, you might be submitting to social pressure or something else — but your ultimate goal should be what pleases Allah, and everything else comes after. Liberation comes from knowing you don't have to follow what other people follow. I think that's a big part of my liberation, because at the end, most people follow the trend, follow what everybody else does, but as a Muslim you don't do that — you follow what your religion is telling you, what God is telling you, what makes sense to you, not blindly, because Islam tells you to always think, read, and increase your knowledge. You don't just follow because everybody follows. I think that's a big part of liberation, I guess.

question: WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR PRACTICING YOUR RELIGION IN THE LONG RUN?
answer:
Number one, what matters most is doing it just for the sake of God — you're practicing not to show people or please people, your ultimate goal should always be to please God. But in addition, living as a Muslim in the West, you're not the majority, you're a minority, and unfortunately a minority that the media and a lot of people have misconceptions about, so you're a representation of the faith too — when you make a mistake, people won't say you did it as an individual, they'll blame the whole religion for it. So there's a lot of responsibility just living in the West, being on your best behavior, being a good practicing Muslim, showing what Islam is really about. I think this is a responsibility that people mostly in the West have as Muslims.

Representing Islam in the best way, in a way people actually understand — being a good Muslim tells a lot of people here what Islam is about, because you might be the only Muslim that person ever interacts with, so you can be a good representation or a bad one. That's a big responsibility.

There's a lot of misconception, I would say a war against Muslims here — Western media tries to stain us with all kinds of wrong ideas, that we're violent, terrorists, all about killing, all about forcing people to do things. And that's not true.

question: HOW DO WE CREATE CHANGE OR BETTER COEXISTENCE?
answer: First of all, be a good model to other people. Show the reality of Muslims, show how Muslims care about communities and other people and want the best for them. Talk to people, use any opportunity to open a dialogue and get your thoughts across to people who don't know, because that might be their only chance to learn about Islam from you.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer: So I am a mother of three, married for close to nineteen years now, and my day is a typical housewife's day. It starts with Salat al-Fajr, then we move on to making breakfast for the family. I'm a homeschooling mom, so we have schoolwork, then comes our second prayer of the day, Salat al-Dhuhr. My day basically revolves around our salah times — anything we plan, anything we do, is planned around salah times. If we have to go shopping, my day is planned accordingly. Right now it's summer, so the days are longer, and the time between the salahs is longer, so that's how my day is planned — between Salat al-Dhuhr and Salat al-Asr is my shopping time, my going-out time, and we have to be back by Maghrib, because the time between Asr and Maghrib is shorter. Then the day ends after Salat al-Isha.

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer:
I would say we are a very welcoming community. The people I'm living with currently are an amazing group of people. I'll give you an example — this past Thanksgiving, over the Christmas break, the churches were busy, and we have a mosque, a church, a synagogue, a couple of churches near our mosque, and the welcome among these communities is so profound that they share parking spaces with each other, they share food with each other. For the recent Eid after Ramadan, the masjid organized events to welcome outsiders to come in and see how we celebrate our holidays. I've personally experienced that in our community, and I've noticed it with my neighbors too, because they get invitations and have been experiencing it for some time. When we moved in — it's no exaggeration — almost the whole block, because as soon as we moved in I made some gift boxes and put in a small letter introducing ourselves, telling them about my family, how many of us there were, and sent it out to the entire block. Most of them brought back gifts — some brought flowers, some brought cookies. They were very open and appreciative that we introduced ourselves, and we told them openly that we're a Muslim family and wanted to introduce ourselves. We got so much love from our neighborhood, because they're used to other Muslims in the community. It was so amazing — I was honestly in awe of how welcoming they were.

No, not on our block, at least — I think we have one Muslim family about fifteen houses down. Everyone else is different ethnicities — South American, Caucasian, African American. Our next-door neighbor's family has been in the same house for over ninety years — the mom is in rehab now, but she was born in that house, so you can imagine how long they've been here.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer:
As in this house, or in the U.S.?

I've been here, well, roughly sixteen years. Honestly, I believe my iman has gone up in the U.S. compared to how it was, because I was born and raised in Pakistan, in [CITY 1], and I feel like I've been able to learn more about myself and my religion, and appreciate the blessing of being Muslim, more in this country than I ever did growing up.

I've seen how — when I see these reverts, I've learned a lot from them, from their struggles, and how much love they give toward their religion, especially the struggle they go through with their families and communities when they come to Islam. I was so humbled by that, because I was born and raised in a Muslim family, and we do not appreciate our blessings enough as Muslims, because being born and raised Muslim, we weren't taught enough. I've learned more from these reverts, from people actually trying to understand our religion. In my sixteen years, I've experienced some of my husband's close acquaintances accept Islam, and I saw the love they came with toward the religion, and I was extremely humbled — that made me want to learn more, appreciate more.

I've also become more confident. Coming from Pakistan, I wasn't born and raised here — I felt more conscious of myself growing up in Pakistan, because I was a hijabi and niqabi, wearing an abaya, and I was more conscious of the people around me, because I came from a relatively middle-class family attending expensive universities — that's the reason I'm able to speak English, because I went to an expensive school, an expensive university, and when you have elite people around you, you get self-conscious, at least that's how it was for me. Coming to the U.S., I've become more confident in myself, and I truly believe it's a blessing from my Lord, because I was able to truly accept who I am and be comfortable in my own skin.

I'm into working with my hands — woodworking, gardening — and I'll go to a Home Depot or a Lowe's in my abaya, in my hijab, and buy tools, buy wood. There was one incident I'd like to share — I was in a black abaya and a black hijab; I usually wear colored clothing, but that day I was in a complete black outfit because that was what I could quickly grab. There was an African American son with his mom at the store — he was a middle-aged man, and his mom was older — and he pointed me out, "Look, Mom, look at that person," and he showed so much appreciation for how I was dressed, in an aisle where you'd usually find construction workers. It made me so happy — it doesn't matter who you are, it's how confident you are in yourself. I've been able to become more confident in my own identity as a Muslim woman who can do whatever she wants within the limits my Lord has described.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, AND HOW?
answer: Frequently. We've been to [ISLAMIC EDUCATION INSTITUTE 1], [ISLAMIC EDUCATION INSTITUTE 2], our Deobandi scholars — in this country, I've been exposed to all the madhahib, all kinds of masjids we attend, anything we can. As I've grown older, I've come to understand that the bias we have within our community toward other madhahib is very deep, I think. So you have to be more open-minded toward other ideologies within your own community and your own religion, and take whatever positive you can from anywhere — you don't have to change your own ideology, but you can take whatever is positive. So we might not follow [ISLAMIC EDUCATION INSTITUTE 1] ideologically, but we attend their programs, and we've benefited tremendously, because I think all these institutions are doing tremendous work. Like, we attend [MUSLIM ORGANIZATION 1], where I might not agree with them on some points — the intermingling of the opposite gender, you'll see men, girls, boys all hanging out — but mashallah, I see the positive there too, that all the girls are in hijabs and abayas, very strict about not sitting together, they're on opposite ends, and you'll find all the boys in thobes, most with beards, so there's a lot of positive going on too, and I think our youth needs that. So I'll take all the positives that come from anywhere. We attend anything we possibly can within our time, because we have time issues, but we attend what we can.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer: I grew up in Pakistan, so in the beginning it was mostly because it's part of the society you grew up in — a middle-class society in Pakistan is more conservative compared to some other communities. I don't want to sound offensive, but there's a gap — the more educated, the more westernized you become, the more respect you get, but in middle-class communities it's more conservative, so you kind of have to cover yourself when you go out. So it was part of our culture, I'll say it that way — my hijab was more cultural than anything else at first. If I attended weddings I wouldn't cover myself. But my story became more specific — I was honestly searching, around seventeen or eighteen years old. I came across the Barelvi sect in Pakistan, which is more open to welcoming women into their circles. As Maulana Rumi says — I don't know how to explain it in English — every being wants to go back to its origin, and our origin is going back toward our Lord, so it's like a spiral moving toward its center; every human being looks for that. The Barelvi sect in Pakistan is more welcoming toward women; the Deobandi sect is mostly for men — women are supposed to stay home. Pakistan is a patriarchal society. So when I was looking to find myself, I was introduced to this sect and started attending their programs, and that's how I became closer to deen. I started covering my face, started doing hijab and niqab, more for deen than culture. I did go to an extreme at some point — I started covering myself from all men, even my own cousins. I went very extreme, but then slowly calmed down, and I am where I am now. That's the short end of it.

question: HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO WRONG PORTRAYALS OF MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
It makes me feel sad, because I think we're an amazing group of people if we follow everything properly — Sharia has been given such a negative connotation in this world today, and it's the complete opposite. Just yesterday, something came up in conversation with my sister-in-law — one of my nieces' friends asked why it is that, in inheritance, men get double the share of women, and it was a valid question — like, if a father passes away, the son gets more than the daughter. It's not just Western society; I think even among us Muslims, the lack of education is affecting people so much. Yes, it is so because Sharia made it so, but Sharia also made it so that, even though a daughter gets half of what the son gets, the society is supposed to take care of the females — it was made so she's not left alone. Unfortunately, culture has taken over — nobody really follows Sharia the way it's supposed to be followed. All we see is how strict everything looks. It's not really strict — it was made so the whole society takes care of the weaker sex. We're not as strong as men, and that's okay — I'd still like to do what I want to do, even being weaker than them, that's fine, if I accept that and follow my dreams, I'm better equipped to do what I want. So the concept of equality in our society really hurts me — feminism should be more about equity than equality, because everybody has equity in the world we live in, nothing is equal, it shouldn't be equal. I believe in the idea of equity compared to equality.

Okay.

I'll be honest, I haven't experienced that on a personal level at all, from outsiders. I've experienced more prejudice from my own people, to be honest. I was at a gym once, an all-female gym, and I still wore my hijab, because even though it was an all-female gym, there were male instructors, guards, security. One of the ladies there, who also happened to be Muslim, told me, "Why do you need that? Why do you do that to yourself? You don't need to do that, it's a female gym." I was taken aback — honestly, all I told her was that it's none of her business. That's kind of how I feel toward anybody who doesn't have a deeper understanding of how things are but still makes judgments — unfortunately we live in a world where judgments are abundant. So I haven't experienced any prejudice from any non-Muslim on a personal level, I'll be honest.

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer:
Do you mean a personal difficulty?

In terms of religious — in terms of my hijab and religion, is that how you'd mean it?

I came across — I don't remember the scholar's name — this sounds like a generic response, like you say Alhamdulillah and move on, but in that moment it's hard to just say Alhamdulillah and move on. As a human being, it's very hard — it's like if I get a paper cut, my finger hurts, it's painful, and if somebody tells me I should be grateful because there are people without arms or legs — yes, and may Allah bless them all — but my paper cut still hurts right now. If somebody tells me I should be grateful, I will be, but I'm still in pain. So I've come to understand that it's okay to be in pain, okay to be angry, as long as you don't let it affect your iman. It's been a struggle for me, because life throws a lot at you — nothing in life is a straight path. As I've grown older, I've become more calm, but I'll say this, and it will probably go on record — I did go through a lot being in the United States, and because there's more awareness here, I had more opportunities to get help. There was a point I had to reach out to the [MUSLIM MENTAL HEALTH ORGANIZATION] — I won't give details of what those issues were — and I had to get therapy. It did help. At this point I'm on anxiety medicine, because it did get extremely difficult. So when it comes to understanding my deen, I've come to see it this way: if you have help available to you, see it as a blessing and make use of it. It's not wrong to do that — it's a blessing from your Lord that you have the means to get help. I truly feel that this has given me some peace, in terms of getting close to my Lord and finding peace inside — I've seen the things available to me as a blessing.

question: WHAT DIFFICULTIES HAVE YOU FACED WEARING HIJAB, AND HOW DID YOU RESOLVE THEM?
answer:
Let me give a brief summary — it was very specific, to be honest. I was at a business school in Pakistan, one of the only three niqabis in the university. Looking back now, as an adult, I think I could have opted for being a hijabi instead of a niqabi — I was still a teenager, and I see it now as a teenage rebellious phase, but I was a niqabi. This was one of the top business schools in [CITY 1], with thousands of students, and I was one of only three niqabis in my year — that says something about how big the gap was. There were many hijabis, but even beyond that, most girls didn't wear hijab at all — just shirts and kurtas, no scarves. So that's how big the gap was, and I only had one friend who would stick by me. I was extremely conscious that most girls didn't want to hang out with me because I was a niqabi, because they felt I wasn't part of their circle. I came from a middle-class family, and a lot of these students were upper-middle-class, and in my heart I felt uncomfortable — it could have been my subconscious, I was biased against myself, I don't know the exact reasons, but I was kind of a pariah in my year. I didn't have many friends, just this one girl who was from Saudi Arabia, who'd moved to Pakistan for higher education — I guess she understood, maybe she'd had niqabi friends before. But within two semesters I got married, so I left, I didn't continue my higher education in Pakistan.

In my family, my mother's side has no segregation at all; my father's side has extreme segregation, so much that if the women are in one house, the men are in a different house altogether. My mother's side, everybody hangs out together. That was really confusing for me as a teenager, attending events in both families. That made me more conscious. Then I got married, and even my in-laws, though culturally religious, had these issues — they would cover their faces outside the house but not inside the house, from their own cousins and male family members. For them, covering was mostly about the people they didn't know, not the men in the family. So that was also confusing for me. Holding on to my hijab, my niqab, was hard, but all I did was keep moving on — that's all I could do. Eventually I stopped doing niqab and found a middle ground with just my hijab, but I didn't let go of my abaya, because that was something important to me. So even at family events, I'll have longer, looser clothing, and my hijab is just a part of me — like your arms and legs — so I just kept moving on despite all the confusion around me.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer:
I don't understand — what do you mean?

I think our whole lives are supposed to revolve around the boundaries Sharia defines. If I get into an argument with my dad, I have to be respectful — yes, there's some cultural aspect to it, but at the end of the day it's more about religion, because Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala has ordered us to take care of our parents and not raise our voices against them. Keeping that in mind when I deal with my family members, based on those boundaries, I think that helps, because there are times you get into arguments with your husband and you just want nothing to do with them, but you have your boundaries to follow. Everything in my life, if I'm nice to anybody, sometimes as a human being I don't even want to look at certain individuals, but my Lord has given me boundaries to keep in mind, and holding on to that makes things easier — it helps bring your anger down, your frustration down. I'm close to forty now, thirty-nine this year — in all my years, I was more emotional when I was younger, but as I've grown older I've come to understand that no matter what, some things just are, because that's what your Lord wants, that's what the Sunnah explains. I've been able to deal with so much based on that.

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer:
My role is as a caretaker. As a female, everything in my life — like I said, I'm on anxiety medicine, and I've been studying and learning and understanding how my being can help me deal with things as a human being — I see myself as a caretaker. Even with woodworking, which I love, I've been able to find enjoyment while taking care of my family — I'll build outdoor furniture, not sheds, because that's too much work, but furniture that helps my husband save on expenses. I garden, which also helps my family save money. So it gives me happiness, and it helps my family — anything I do at this point, as I get older, is finding ways to make myself happy while helping my family as a caretaker.

I don't know how to explain that — I'm an extreme introvert. If I can avoid people, I do, to the best of my ability. I'm not really friends, to be honest, more like acquaintances with my husband's friends' wives, because that's the connection I have. Overall I'm an extreme introvert — I don't participate in masjid events and things like that, because it gives me a physical reaction at this point, I get palpitations, so I avoid anything outside my comfort zone. I would have pushed myself at some age, but now, this is who I am, I'd rather do what I can. I interact with people through my homeschooling circles, because my daughter has classes, so I'll take her there and interact with those people for five or ten minutes, then go hide in the library — I don't even sit around. That's just who I am.

question: WHAT DOES BELONGING FEEL LIKE HERE?
answer: Respect. It's not just about the West — I think overall, belonging, whether to an individual or a community, is about how much respect you get for the choices you make, for who you are. If there's a group of people you've been close to for a long time and they don't respect who you are, you don't really belong to them at heart — you're around them because sometimes you don't have a choice. I feel like it's all about respect, and respect, in my opinion, usually comes from the heart — if you truly respect somebody, you accept them wholeheartedly.

question: HAVE YOU BEEN MADE TO FEEL YOUR FAITH CONFLICTS WITH YOUR COUNTRY?
answer:
I think I'm more open with my choices, I have more freedom, to be honest. In Pakistan, we were there for two years when my sons were doing hifz, and I couldn't even walk down the street without male supervision, which was bizarre — I'm just going to the store — but here, nobody cares, to be honest. So I feel more comfortable with the freedoms of this country in terms of my religion and my identity.

No. Maybe because I'm an introvert, I keep my head down, say hello, and move on. I haven't experienced that on a personal level at all.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: Everything revolves around it. Sometimes — my anxiety maybe stems from that too — at night I get these feelings, like I'm not doing enough, I'm not prepared, because death is a foregone conclusion, but I feel like I'm not doing enough. But again, that's just being human — you just keep moving forward and keep trying.

question: HOW DO YOU MAKE SENSE OF WHAT IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL?
answer: As I grow older, I've learned to just let go. There's a saying in Urdu — if there's a street you're not heading toward, don't even ask for directions to it; if that's not your goal, why would you worry about the address to that location? That's how I see everything — if something doesn't concern me at all, if it's not going to affect me, I just let it go. And if it does affect me, and it's not in my control, if there's nothing I can do about it, I've learned to let it go. I've truly learned to let things go, but I think that's something that comes with age and experience.

question: WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR PRACTICING YOUR RELIGION IN THE LONG RUN?
answer: I think we need a lot more for the youth. The problem, in my circles — my husband follows the Deobandi and Tablighi sects, though we're not extreme in that regard — is that there's a lot happening for the older generation, middle-aged people, more mature people, but not enough happening for young people. They're Western kids, they don't know Eastern society at all, it just doesn't work for them, so we need more for the younger girls and boys — they need to be able to connect, because right now I truly feel that deen and dunya are so separate. It shouldn't be that way — deen is the way of life, it should not be separate. But living in Western society — my son attends university, he has lots of non-Muslim friends, he attends a [RELIGIOUSLY AFFILIATED UNIVERSITY 1], because my husband works there and we get a tuition discount, which made sense given how expensive education is here. It's primarily white, non-Muslim students, and when he wants to go out with them — these are older boys, eighteen, nineteen — they do things that aren't appropriate for Muslim boys, and for him it's confusing, because it's not haram, but it's not appropriate, and it's hard for him to understand that doing something inappropriate, even if it's not haram, might lead to something haram. So we need to find a way to love who they are, living in the society they're living in, and help them hold on to their deen while living where they live.

question: WHAT IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR HEART, INTENTION, AND OUTWARD PRACTICE?
answer:
In the beginning it was harder, because I saw myself as different. At this point in life, it's become a part of me — I don't even go into the backyard without my hijab, I'm very conscious of that, because even though it's an enclosed space, there might be neighbors, someone looking out a window. I don't even give it a second thought anymore — anytime I leave the house, I have to be covered appropriately.

I'd say it's for my identity as a Muslim woman, because those are the boundaries that were set, and I have to stay within them. It's how I see driving on the highway — there's a minimum and a maximum, but sometimes you're allowed to go a bit above the maximum, and on some highways people go even faster because no one's watching the road. Further out in [METRO REGION 1] I've driven ninety miles an hour because I knew there was no police nearby, but there's still a limit to how far I can go, and a limit to how low I can go. I just stay within those limits, and my intention is simply not to break the rules, not to step outside the boundaries set for me by Sharia — that's just what I do.

For me, Sharia is the rules and laws set by our Lord and explained by our Prophet, peace be upon him — it's not just a set of rules, it's the way you live. Everything the Prophet did teaches how to live as a human being until time ends on this planet. I don't know all the rules, obviously, but as I grow older I keep learning more, and I consciously try to learn more — if I don't know something, I'll ask. The way you get up from bed, the way you sleep, everything has been explained, and Sharia goes deeper into some rules and regulations, but for me it's just a way of life.

I don't know how to explain this one, what I see...

I'd say having clean intentions makes a big difference — I was taught at some point that your intentions have an effect on how other people vibe with you. Your intentions in your heart affect your atmosphere, so I've made a conscious decision to keep my intentions as clean as possible, and I always make du'a that Allah ta'ala helps me keep my intentions clean at all times. What I mean by clean intentions is not intending harm on anybody, not having avarice — if something happens that's out of my control, I ask for forgiveness, but I mean not intentionally intending evil or wrong. If I keep my intentions clean, I think people around me will see it — I truly believe Allah helps put good in other people's hearts if your intentions are pure.

That's a very deep question. It does make you feel good — I don't know how to explain this one. So, basically, you're asking how I would feel if somebody saw me feeding somebody.

There might have been a time when I was concerned, but as I've grown older I've seen how people will judge you if they have biases against you anyway, no matter what you do, so I've stopped worrying about what people think. I'll do what my gut tells me is the right thing to do without going out of my way to show the world that I'm a good person. I've stopped worrying about the fact that if somebody doesn't like me, they don't like me. At this point in my life I've genuinely stopped caring — yes, sometimes it hits you, sometimes it worries you, sometimes you get sad, like, I haven't done anybody any harm — but if they don't see my intentions, Allah knows my intentions, and I try my best to worry about what my Lord thinks, because as I get older, I don't have the energy to worry about human beings — we really don't have the time, they're just not nice sometimes.

I just don't like people anymore, man. There are one or two people I click with. I've stopped caring about the rest — I'll see them once a year and get through it, that's it.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer: That's a deep question. What does submission to Allah mean for me? It's showing my love and being grateful, I guess — following the path of our Nabi, alayhi salatu wasalam, and having the hope that one day we'll get to see him.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer: Moving to the US gave me so many opportunities — I've been able to do what I like without worrying about people. When I started woodworking, I got a lot of pushback from some adults in the family — they called me names, essentially calling me manly for doing manly things, and for me it was very offensive, because I was inside my house, not going out, not hanging out — it was offensive that there are individuals in your own family who see it that way, just because it wasn't something women from their culture did, wasn't seen as the right thing to do. So I've been liberated in the sense that I've been able to do more with the financial freedom I have — being in the U.S. gave me more financial freedom than I had before, and I've been able to use that to pursue whatever hobbies I wanted, within the boundaries set by my Lord.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer:
My husband, my kids, and my brothers, to be honest — my brothers have been amazing supporters. There was a point when I kind of gave up on everything, even my gardening. My husband, too, to some degree, though he has responsibilities toward his family and can't stand up to them, because that might backfire on him. But on the side, he kept supporting me — he's the one who supported me financially, and my sons have given me so much encouragement, my brothers too. I do appreciate these individuals immensely in my life.

I'm very close to my brothers — there was a point my brother was having marriage issues, and I pushed him not to leave his wife, because I felt for her, in her place as a female, and I felt my brother was doing wrong. I'm close enough to him that he listened to me. With my sons too — my older one comes to me and opens up to me, my younger one is more of a shy kid, but my husband, too, I know I can talk to him openly. My relationships are close, alhamdulillah.

Yes, 100%. All my choices are made based on how my relationships are — the people I'm closest to, yes.

question: IS IT YOUR COUNTRY OR YOUR CULTURE THAT CONFLICTS WITH YOUR RELIGION?
answer:
I'm middle-aged now, and my life experiences are vastly different from what younger kids are going through. My sister-in-law, who was born and raised in the U.S., traveled to Pakistan with her daughter, who was also born in the U.S. — she's a hijabi, mashallah, sixteen, turning seventeen soon, and a very strong hijabi, wore her hijab through public high school, was on the volleyball team, very strong in her identity as a Muslim hijabi teenager. But in Pakistan, when she visited, she actually faced backlash, because people there saw her as an extremist. I think if you want to look at hijabi women, you should include these teenagers — I can introduce you to my niece and some of her hijabi friends. I think that would give you a perspective on what western society, especially people from the subcontinent, are facing, because our culture, in my opinion, and our deen clash all the time. Culturally hijabi people are very different from people who actually hold on to their hijab as their Muslim identity.

Yeah, the question should be, is it in conflict with your culture? I guess — or, is your religion in conflict with your culture, because even though we live in the West, our culture influences us a lot. I think our culture affects our religion more, from my experience, than Western society does, because for individuals who have to go out into the world, surrounded by other ethnicities, non-Muslims, it's different — but for me, a homebody, I face culture more; my religion clashes with my culture more than with the society I live in. It varies personally, I think.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer: As-salamu alaykum. Faith shows up multiple times, because our faith has different aspects. In terms of spirituality, of course, the morning starts with Fajr prayer — waking up and remembering Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala first thing in the morning, regardless of how bad the night was due to a baby waking up or kids being sick. It's a requirement, and it also roots me to my faith. Throughout the day I find myself making silent du'as anytime something is disturbing me or difficult, just asking Allah for help, whether I'm stuck in traffic or in the pickup line at my kids' school. Faith shows up spiritually in my prayers throughout the day — Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib, Isha — and it shows up anytime I'm struggling with something; I have this constant remembrance of Allah. It also shows up in supermarkets, sometimes at the mall. I won't say every time I go out I meet somebody, but at least once a week I'll have someone complimenting my hijab or asking why I wear it, whether I'm taking my kids to swim classes or at the mall. Something I find interesting is especially when I'm shopping for makeup — there are different concepts people have about Muslim women, like whether we're able to go shopping by ourselves or spend money on certain things. Sometimes people have a very different perception about our religion, and that would be the third form where faith shows up: when people ask questions related to my faith.

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer: We are very welcoming and hospitable. I want to be transparent: the majority of my community, where I live, are open-minded people who will be warm and welcoming, who will share about their faith and answer your questions. That's what I would say about my community. Of course, my community is also very diverse, with different backgrounds and ethnicities — even the Muslims in my community differ in their religious background. Some are very religious, some are just learning their religion, some are Muslims by name, and some are practicing. As an individual, I would describe myself as confident and vocal, someone who is proud of her Muslim faith and understands that her Muslim faith can help her fit in anywhere and succeed in her life.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer:
I was born and raised in the United States. Over time, things definitely changed. In my elementary school years I never wore hijab, so people often thought I was Hispanic. Even then I was very vocal about my faith — when Ramadan came I would tell my classmates why I was taking off school for Eid, which wasn't very common back in the '90s. On Eid I would actually go to school and bring goodie bags and gifts for my classmates just to share my faith, and when they offered food to share for someone's birthday, I would openly say if it had gelatin in it I couldn't have it.

I also didn't go to a diverse elementary school — I was the only Muslim girl in my entire school. Then in middle school and high school, 9/11 happened, and everybody had a perception of Muslims depending on what they'd watched or which news channel they followed. That's when I started wearing hijab. I remember being in a [GROCERY CHAIN 1] with my father just buying vegetables, and a very upset woman came up and asked me if I was Bin Laden's niece — it was a very straight question, no beating around the bush. Instead of getting scared, I explained to her that no, I wasn't, and that not every Muslim is related to or (is) a certain person. During that time I didn't meet many accepting people, and I was living in an area that wasn't diverse at all — we were the only Muslim family in our entire neighborhood, and the only brown family too. That's the kind of community I grew up in. Later I went to an Islamic boarding school, so at that point I was mostly around other Muslims. But when we would go out, during middle school and high school I saw the way people reacted to how I was dressed, or the things they would say, happening more and more. Then I started driving, and there were quite a few times I was at a red light — I wore hijab from a pretty young age, and my father is your typical elderly Muslim man with a long beard — where the car next to us, someone would say something to us with their hands, with their fingers. That happened quite a few times.

Later, as I got older, I got married and had my children, and that's when it hit me that raising a child in the West who is proud of their Muslim identity is very difficult. You have to put in a lot of energy, you have to be strong, you have to have a lot of conversations with them — it's not just about giving them a Muslim name and expecting them to grow up (proud). That's when I realized how much effort our parents probably had to put in to make us proud of our religion and not fear what people would say to us. That gave me a completely different perspective. When I became a mother, it was more about how do I make my kids love my religion, love their faith, not just mine — especially in this world of social media, where people have more and more exposure and more and more perspectives depending on who they're following and what they're watching, and that's how people's mentality about Islam gets shaped. It's a really hard time to raise children. That's when I found myself doing a lot of research to make sure my kids love their faith and are proud to represent it, not scared of it — especially because that's also when Islamophobia started increasing, especially for women. A Muslim man can be walking on the street and you won't even know he's Muslim until you ask him and find out his name is Muhammad or something, but a practicing Muslim woman wearing hijab is automatically recognized as Muslim. So she's more prone to Islamophobic crimes than a Muslim man is. Raising girls in that environment made me look at my faith in a very different way and teach it in a very different way as well.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, AND HOW?
answer: I went to [ISLAMIC BOARDING SCHOOL 1], an institution in [CITY 1], [STATE 1] — that's where I sought my religious knowledge. Currently, yes, I continue to receive religious knowledge. I'm a student, or in the mentorship, of Shaykh Akram Nadwi. I haven't taken consistent courses, but he's someone I speak to, and I follow some of the courses and classes he offers, even though I haven't taken any certification — that's someone I'm mentoring with at this point, and I'll continue to do so. Religious knowledge is never something you can say you've completed, like now I have a certificate and I'm done. Because the world is rapidly changing, having knowledge about contemporary Islamic rulings and fatwas, and how we can apply Islam at this point in time, is really important. That's why I think it's going to be a continuous journey throughout my life.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
I'm from a cultural family, and nobody explained to me in the beginning why I should wear hijab — I was told I had to wear it. It was an honor thing for my mother, never really pushed by my father. My mother's family was very pro-hijab without the religious background behind it, so it was like, you wear hijab but only in front of servants, not in front of cousins — it was really confusing. I just knew you had to wear hijab when you left the house. I was the person who wore hijab and took it off at school, and who only wore hijab when my mom was around, because my father never pushed it — ironically he's more religious than my mother.

Then I ended up at the Islamic institution in [CITY 1], where the uniform was niqab, not just hijab — if you left the madrasa for a field trip, the mall, or the airport, you wore an abaya, a hijab, and a niqab. I started wearing niqab there because I had to. Over time I accepted it, and then, as we studied Qur'an tafsir, I understood the point of hijab — that it's in the Qur'an, that there's a purpose behind it. I was one of those girls, even in the 2000s, who thought, why do girls wear it and boys don't — I actually had that mindset. But slowly, alhamdulillah, I came to realize the wisdom, the hikmah, behind it, and that you get to a point where you love Allah and realize there are certain commands from Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala that you don't sugarcoat — you just wear it.

My niqab journey is a bit different. We also have to understand that many of these madaris are culturally influenced — in the Indo-Pak subcontinent, most madrasas that stem from there hold that niqab is mandatory, because according to Imam Abu Hanifa niqab is wajib, especially in times of fitna. When I was in madrasa I started wearing niqab too, and since I'm not the type of person embarrassed to do or say anything in public, it wasn't hard for me to wear it outside. Over the years I got used to it, and it became my second skin — I couldn't live without it, and I did everything with my niqab on. All the milestones people find difficult to achieve with niqab — I got my license, I finished college, I got married — all of that happened while I wore niqab.

Then, three years ago, I was teaching, and a student asked in my class, "Is niqab an obligation?" The room went silent, because that student and everybody in the class wore niqab because of how they'd been taught, and I wore niqab too. I don't know if she wanted my personal ruling or preference, but she asked, and I ended up saying no, niqab is not an obligation. When I said that, it became a big deal in my workplace and community — people started talking. That's when I started thinking: if this isn't fard, why am I wearing it myself? When you're twelve or thirteen and start at an Islamic school with a uniform, that makes sense, but over the years you get a mind of your own and need to do your own research and understand why you're wearing something. I have daughters, and I'm not the type of mother who forces her kids to wear niqab, so when I came home and shared that with my younger girls, they asked me why I wear it. That's when I went through this whole research process: why do we wear niqab, where does this ruling come from, why is it most prominent in certain schools of thought or cultures. Parenting really changed my perspective on how I was going to teach and learn my faith, and this was one of those moments — if I want my daughters to grow up knowing what is actually in their faith versus what is culturally influenced to the point where we call something mandatory in every situation and don't let girls ask questions, (that) was a real turning point in my journey.

So I actually removed my niqab. It was one of the toughest things I've done — I got bashed for it a lot. I removed it this year, though it took three years (after starting to question it) to actually take it off, and I did it cold turkey, just took it off one day. Honestly, after taking my niqab off, I've become closer to my deen. It sounds funny, but it's because at this point I feel like whatever I'm doing now is for Allah. When I was wearing niqab, I always felt like people assumed the stereotype of niqabis — that we're rigid and quiet — which is wrong; niqabis are some of the friendliest people in the world. But people would assume that because I wore niqab I must be so righteous and pious, and I'm not — it's just that with niqab, people assume it. So I felt like I was somebody I wasn't. Honestly, after taking it off, I really feel like someone who is actually following their deen.

For me, hijab makes me follow a command of Allah to get close to Him — that's the first thing. The second is that hijab, especially in the West, represents me as a Muslim woman, and maintaining my religious identity while living in a country that's a melting pot of religions is really important to me. The third is that it's a constant reminder, when I'm outside, that I'm doing everything for the sake of Allah, that I'm going to do everything He wants me to do. It just makes me get closer to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. The funny thing is I understood this only after all these years, as a mother — this isn't something I understood in my teenage years, how hijab makes you close to Allah. But now hijab is a constant reminder to me that Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala is with me.

question: HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO WRONG PORTRAYALS OF MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
Honestly, it doesn't even make me feel bad anymore, because the portrayal is already wrong within the Islamic community before it ever gets to non-Muslims. I come from a South Asian background, and I feel South Asians have stripped Muslim women of their rights more than anybody. I come from a culture where if a woman marries by her own choice, she's considered to have committed the worst sin in the world. I come from a culture where women who memorize the Quran aren't allowed to recite it in public, because we've taken the ruling that "a woman's voice is awrah" to a whole other level. If you're outspoken, in politics, or whatever, people think you're not even religious anymore, and if you are religious, you're expected to be confined to your home. As someone who graduated as an alimah, when I started teaching at the local masjid and speaking at events, my own classmates and family considered me to be doing something wrong — and it's funny, because Arab Muslims don't think it's wrong, Muslims from the African continent don't think it's wrong, but for some reason in my culture it is.

I don't even blame non-Muslims, because Muslims have ruined it for themselves. We've created a culture in our community where every single thing Muslim women were allowed to do in Islam, we twisted. For example, in the cultural Muslim community, the story of Aisha is taught to encourage girls to get married young — they'll mention that she got married young, but not how she never thanked the Prophet ﷺ after her father told her to, when the verse was revealed clearing her name of slander. That's so empowering — when her father told her to thank the Prophet ﷺ because the verse had been revealed and her name was cleared, she said no, I'm going to thank the One who sent the verse. In South Asian culture — and I'm sorry if I keep mentioning South Asian culture, but it's the culture I'm speaking from — we tell women that even if her husband is extremely abusive, well, he provides for you, so thank him. Even the way we teach Islam to our girls in South Asian culture, we make them start hating Islam most of the time, because we use Islam to tell them "you can't do this, you can't do this, you have to be like this." We use sabr as a kind of trophy — if you're living in an abusive relationship, well, Islam says to have sabr.

So, like I said, when a non-Muslim says something bad, some perspective about a Muslim woman, it doesn't upset me because I already know that person is ignorant. What upsets me more is when Muslims say things about Muslim women that are completely out of line — someone born and raised Muslim, not even a convert, from an "Islamic Republic" of this or that, and they don't even know what their own religion says about women. So yes, it upsets me, but not as much, because I already expect that from a non-Muslim, not from a Muslim. Muslim men and women have set the bar so low for Islam and for women that I don't even get surprised anymore.

Honestly, I think it's all about how someone was taught Islam. I know a few converts who became Muslim in a community that was prominently South Asian, and they actually think certain things are part of Islam that aren't, because culture and religion have mixed up over the years. South Asia, for example, was colonized for many years, and after that Hindus and Muslims lived together, and Muslims there ended up adopting a lot of Hindu customs without realizing none of it has a base in our religion. So people from those areas actually think they're doing something Islamic when they're not. It does depend on where somebody is from, and on who taught them and how they were taught.

To give the [ISLAMIC BOARDING SCHOOL 1] example — I remember being told that going to college is haram for girls. Why did that person say that? Because that's what they were told, and what they actually believed. We still have people in our community who say girls going to college is haram because of fitna, there being boys and men around. I'll say, well, isn't it haram for men too, then, since there are women there? And I'm told, no, men need an education to be providers. I say, well, they could run a burger stand — they don't need an education for that. So when I say "who," I mean: were you taught by somebody who was brainwashed into thinking culture is their religion, who was never taught the difference and will teach you the exact same thing — and in certain Islamic schools you can't even ask why, because that's treated like the end of the world? Or did you learn from somebody who actually did their own research and was taught by somebody who wasn't culturally influenced, versus somebody who is culturally influenced and needs to make things a certain way because it fits their culture and appeases the men in their community? That's the "who."

The "how" is also important, because of the way Islam is taught. Take the story of Aisha again — one person can teach it focusing only on the fact that she got married young, and another person can teach the same story and talk about how the Prophet ﷺ treated her, how she never lost herself, how she actually established an even stronger identity because she remained who she was — the fact that she'd knead dough and a goat would come and take it, because that's how relaxed she was; she wasn't walking on eggshells worrying about what she'd cooked before her husband got home. Now you have women in their fifties who panic because their husband is home and the food isn't cooked and he's going to yell at them. But that same story of Aisha, when I hear the elderly women in my family use it, is used to say things like, if a girl is twenty-two and says she's not getting married yet, "oh my God, she should already be married at this age" — that's the only lesson they take from it. So the "how" is: how do you teach Islam to your students so they understand that, as Muslim women, they have an identity.

question: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN OR HIJAB?
answer:
Within my culture, definitely, people don't expect me to speak up. It's funny — when I used to wear niqab and started speaking about women's rights, somebody said to me that the way I dress and the way I talk are very different. In my culture, I'm expected — and this happened a year ago, I was doing a Hadith intensive and speaking about how the joint family system has no basis in Islam — an elderly, very educated lady came up to me afterward and said, "stop saying stuff like this, you're going to ruin the lives of a lot of girls, they're going to demand separate houses." I looked at her and said, well, that's the hope. My culture expects that if I have Islamic knowledge and wear hijab, I'm probably going to be saying something like "cook for your husband, that's going to get you to Jannah" or "don't go to college because it's haram." That's the perception within my culture.

Outside my community, it's sometimes a shocker when I start speaking English without an accent — it's funny that even now, people's faces change when they hear me speaking, whether at a store, hospital, or bank; you can tell, "oh, she's actually speaking English." A lot of people who aren't well versed about Muslim women just assume she's going to need an interpreter or won't be able to explain herself.

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer:
I've had six miscarriages, and I think really understanding what Qadr was at that time really helped, especially with the first three, which happened after my first child. I didn't want to only have one child, for personal reasons, and when I went to the doctor they said I had unexplained infertility — they did everything and couldn't find anything, which is even worse, because there's no medicine, nothing they can do; everything is fine, so why is this happening? As a human being you just want a solution for everything. Alhamdulillah, Allah gave me three healthy children after that, but during those times it was about telling myself that Allah does whatever is best for you.

I should throw this in too — I'm from South Asian culture, so I had three girls, and I loved them to pieces; my husband and I never thought our family wasn't complete, and we were done having children. But it was funny, because everywhere I went, if I seemed really happy or at an event or a da'wat, some auntie had to say, "everything about your life is good, but they can't give you a boy" — and people don't understand that that actually hurts. You've gone through an infertility journey, you have three beautiful, healthy daughters, you're so happy with your life because you thought you'd only have one child and then got more, and then suddenly you're made to feel incomplete.

Then it was from Allah — I never in a million years thought I would have more children, and then I was expecting, and I didn't even care about the gender. I made du'a to Allah that He only give me a boy if I could raise him to be a good man — that was my only du'a; if I was going to raise a terrible man, give me a girl instead, just give me a healthy child, but a boy only if I could raise him to be a good man. During that pregnancy, things were showing up on the ultrasound — that he had fluid in his head and other issues — so it was like I was getting what I prayed for, because maybe Allah knew I could raise a good man, but now I was going through all these medical issues. Faith came in again: Allah does whatever He does for a reason, Allah will do whatever is good for you, Allah will give you whatever is in your Qadar.

From my miscarriages, I think it all has to do with infertility — those were some of my darkest times, especially the consecutive miscarriages, and then the journey to having all my healthy children. For people who've had a miscarriage and then get pregnant again, that pregnancy is the longest year, the longest time of your life. I think that's when faith really helps: Allah will do whatever is good for me.

question: WHAT INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS ARE PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
That makes me angry — if you want it in one word, it makes me angry, it makes me upset, because sometimes I think, how do you even say things like that? And the fact that it's often religious scholars backing it up just makes things worse, and it scares me for my own kids. It's funny — anytime I see stuff like that online it puts me in a spiral, so I sit my kids down and give a whole lecture, because I think that will help them. It makes me upset, but it also terrifies me, because especially with social media, it's so easy to influence and brainwash young children into thinking Muslim women should be a certain way.

This morning, for example, we had a conversation at the breakfast table about the word "daraba" in the Quran and how it has multiple meanings — I'll pick up any topic, but this one came up because one of my daughters asked why she can't just read the Quran translation by herself. That's something I don't allow my kids to do; they can't read the Quran translation on their own, only when I teach them or when they're with another teacher. My oldest doesn't ask that anymore because I've already taught her, but my youngest, who's nine, asked why she couldn't just pick it up and read it. I explained that translations, especially Urdu translations, often carry a lot of the translator's personal preferences, and you can't do justice to the Arabic language by just reading a translation of one ayah — you have to understand the complexity of the meanings, the nouns, and how certain words are used. So a lot of our conversations are pretty intellectual, and they usually come from something I see online that's out of line, or from the girls' own questions. One of my daughters has a classmate who's Syrian, and they're really good friends, so a lot of our conversations are about treating people with kindness and respect, while also understanding what our faith does and doesn't accept.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer: At this point in life, and I'll sound selfish saying it, it's my children — though I don't think it's selfish, because whatever I want for my children, I want for other people's children too. Since I'm a face in the community, I never want to give advice to anyone's daughter or son that I wouldn't give to my own kids. For the past year or two especially, now that my oldest is sixteen, it's really important for me to do things right in terms of my faith, so my kids have that confidence, that structure and framework, and know who to look up to.

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer:
For my community — this is going to sound terrible, but I've reached a point where I've realized certain people in my community are a lost cause. There's no point in me sitting down with someone much older than me and telling them they can't expect their daughter-in-law to cook for all their sons every single day; there's no point having that conversation, because they're well-rooted in their culture and to them I'm just being disrespectful. I did that with my own family for a while, and then I realized I was wasting my energy when I could use it to change the upcoming generation instead. So I stopped trying to fix what was already damaged and tried to salvage what was left — the upcoming generation, who might otherwise assume whatever our elders are doing is right. I put my focus on women my age, women younger than me, women getting into adulthood right now — for a while I worked with teenagers. That generation is something I can fix, or at least attempt to, so the upcoming generation has a good version of what deen, what Islam, really looks like. That's where I stand in my community. I respect the elders. I'll share a funny story — I was leading a halaqah with people of all ages, and someone asked about tarawih, saying she'd had a long day. I said, look, it's Ramadan, if you can't pray tarawih at the end of a long day, that's fine. Afterward, a very elderly, respected community member came up and told me I was the first person she'd heard say inside the masjid that you don't have to pray tarawih. I said it because the woman who asked has five children, all under six, and is living a tough life — what am I supposed to tell her, that she'll get sin for not praying tarawih at the end of a long day when her husband is at work all day and she's with the kids and fasting? I don't want to disrespect the elders, I don't want to change their ways, I can't change their ways, so I respect them, I always ask for their du'as, I respect their decisions because that's what they know and what they thought was best. But my focus in my community is on my age and younger, the youth.

As for my family — as a South Asian (woman), I don't really have a role. I'm a wife, a mother, a daughter, a daughter-in-law, a niece. That's it. The one thing I have control over is my kids, and, surprisingly, whoever reads this one day will be shocked at how hard it is for a South Asian woman to actually have control over her own kids — even getting to the point of making decisions different from what my parents made for me is a battle. My mother thinks my kids should go to (the school in) [CITY 1]. According to my mother, I'm raising my kids all wrong — why does my daughter go to public school, why doesn't the younger one wear hijab yet like my oldest does. For a while I thought I was failing at parenting because of everything being said in my family, and then I reached a point where I didn't want my kids growing up thinking that being (a woman) means complete control over you, especially as a girl. So my role in my family is that I'm a mother — that's where my influence comes in, whatever religious changes I can make. Besides that, no.

question: WHAT DOES BELONGING FEEL LIKE HERE?
answer: I was born and raised here — I belong here. This is home; you're born here, raised here. When somebody asks me where I'm from and I say I'm from America, and they push back with "no, where are you really from," I ask them where they're from, because unless they're Native American, why are they asking me that? I'm born here, I'm raised here, I'm American — I'm a [STATE 2] native, born and raised. I never even left my state. Belonging means I should have the safety of practicing my religious identity, because that's what my country represents. As long as I can wear hijab here, which I should always be able to, and live my life according to my religion, I belong here, and I don't think anyone has the right to take that away from me.

question: HAVE YOU BEEN MADE TO FEEL YOUR FAITH CONFLICTS WITH YOUR COUNTRY?
answer: No — I mean, I have been made to feel that, definitely, from that woman who asked if I was Bin Laden's niece, to things I hear about my community all the time from people who are supposedly highly educated, who hold certain roles in the community or government. When they say things about Muslims that are messed up, yes, it makes you feel upset. But then I always remind myself of what Allah says in the Quran — that when the ignorant address you, you say "peace." There are ignorant people (everywhere).

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: That's why I'm nice to people, take my word for it. My relationship with Allah is like a friendship, it seems — maybe this is too private to share, but there's the ayah in the Quran that says Allah is closer to you than your jugular vein. I've never really said this openly, but I feel like Allah is always there — I mean, of course He's always there, but anytime I'm having a hard time I'll say, "what's going on," and I feel peace in it. That's my relationship with Allah. As for the Akhirah, it makes me fear certain things — I fear having a full meal when the servants of Allah have nothing. That's the kind of thing the Akhirah shakes me over: what have I done to help those people? Sometimes I want to be really mean to somebody because I just don't like them, but then I won't be, because there's accountability, there's judgment, and maybe I'm just treating this person wrong for no reason. So the Akhirah shapes my hukm, the way I treat people.

question: HOW DO YOU MAKE SENSE OF WHAT IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL?
answer: It's from Allah. It took me a while to get to that point, but my miscarriages are what got me there. I just tell myself it's from Allah, there's nothing I can do. There's a certain level of faith, a lot of struggle, you have to go through to get to that point, but once you get there, life becomes so peaceful.

question: WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR PRACTICING YOUR RELIGION IN THE LONG RUN?
answer:
That my kids stay Muslim — I know that's controversial, because people will say, don't you care who they marry, how they dress? I care about all of that, but I've sat face to face with students who wear hijab and never take it off, yet say they're not Muslim. My most important thing is that my kids, my grandkids, my great-grandkids, are rooted in Islam: Allah is One, Muhammad is the last Prophet, we don't commit zina, we don't drink alcohol — all the major things that come with Islam. That they just stay Muslim — I make du'a for that. Of course I want them to be practicing too, but people don't realize that practicing doesn't equal belief, and belief comes first. That's so important — for them to stay Muslim, to love Islam.

I make sure. Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala has always put me in situations where I learned — I was a middle school and high school Islamic studies teacher for eleven years, and it taught me so much. I always remember one student who came to my class and wouldn't talk to me for three days; she hated my class. One day I had a one-on-one with her and said, every other teacher says you're really good with them, why don't you like me? She said, I don't like Islam, and your class is Islamic studies. I asked why she didn't like Islam, and she said Islam doesn't let us do anything — her brother has a girlfriend, she can't have a boyfriend; her brother goes to prom, she wanted to go last year and couldn't, and now she's stuck in this Islamic school. I told her, look, your parents aren't raising your brother right — they can't control your brother, and that has nothing to do with Islam. They're typical Pakistani parents who believe boys are boys and can do whatever they want. She didn't believe me at first, but three weeks later her mom called, came in, and said I'd turned her daughter against her. I said I hadn't — if that's how you're raising your son, you can't tell your daughter that Islam doesn't allow her something while it allows him. That girl still reaches out to me — she's a nurse now, and she still thanks me. She told me that if I hadn't (talked to her), her plan was to leave that Islamic school, go to college, and leave Islam — she had no intention of ever staying Muslim once she left her parents' house. That's just one story, and I hear that kind of thing every single day.

So my role has been to let my daughters ask questions, to let them know how much Allah loves them, to let them know the "why" behind why they can't have boyfriends, why we don't do drugs, the wisdom behind all of it, why we have to cover. Alhamdulillah, I thank Allah every day that I was able to get to the point of telling them that Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala put things in the Quran for their own benefit, and I'm blessed that my kids have actually come to understand that — but it took a lot of work. A lot of Muslim parents use Islam for parenting — "my kids can't have sleepovers" — not because Islam says so, but because I tell them, your dad and I don't allow sleepovers. We don't use Islam as a tool to stop our kids from doing something, because I've heard the whole "you can't sleep at so-and-so's house, it's haram" — no, it's not haram, be a proper parent when you have to be a parent, don't use Islam to control your children when it's not necessary. That's the role I've played, and it's been a struggle, and it's still a struggle with my younger kids — talking to them every single day, helping them understand what is actually haram and what is just something I don't want them to do, so they don't think everything is haram.

question: WHAT IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR HEART, INTENTION, AND OUTWARD PRACTICE?
answer:
Nothing is really going on consciously, but I can never leave the house without hijab — it's like a part of me. It's that Allah told me to do it, so I'm doing it, and I love Allah and Allah loves me.

I come from a culture — again, am I the only one who talks about culture so much? — where log kya kahenge, "what will people say," is a very big deal; you can ruin your entire life over it. Alhamdulillah, I actually thank my culture for being that intense about it, because I don't even care what people say at this point. I think it was pushed so much, for all the wrong reasons, that for me it ended up going into my heart instead. Taking the niqab off is one of the biggest examples — people said so much, they're still saying so much; somebody literally took a picture of me and sent it in a WhatsApp chat to ask if it was really me and why I'd taken it off. You get to a point where you think, I'm doing it for Allah, I don't care what people think.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer: Allah is my friend, and Allah is always there. He's closer to me than anything in the world, and He will resolve everything that I need.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer:
It's in my personality and my daily life. I wish people could actually peek into my heart and realize I really don't care, except for Allah. I'm at a point where — and this is going to sound disrespectful — I don't care what my parents say, and that's one of the most taboo things a South Asian woman can say. For me, if Allah is happy with me, that's what matters; it's in my daily life, my personality, the way I hold myself, the way I take care of all my daily affairs.

My mom is almost eighty, and she believes that if she takes her niqab off, she's going to Jahannam. She doesn't really know that I've taken mine off — when I visit her my niqab is off because I'm coming from the car, and outside she's not on social media so she doesn't see any flyers or posts. I've told her two or three times that I've taken it off; I don't think she realizes the depth of it, though one time she said, "do whatever." My dad knows — I told him — and he said he'd always wondered why I wasn't (taking it off already).

It's not just about my parents, though, it's about anything. I feel liberated when I'm able to follow my deen without (worrying), knowing that, alhamdulillah, I'm a good Muslim — maybe I don't know how my salat or my fasting is being measured by Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, but I'm liberated because I don't need the definition of Islam from anybody — not my aunts, uncles, in-laws, spouse, children, parents, or the Muslim community. It's all because my connection with Allah is so strong that, alhamdulillah, I feel like I'm at a point in my journey with deen where I know that Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala — I don't want to say He's happy with me, because I don't know if He's happy with me or not.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer:
As a student, an ordinary day consists of waking up, studying, praying, studying, then getting ready for school or going to my next set of classes and completing assignments. Coming home, I either do more studying for school or occasionally attend a halaqa if my local university has one going on before I head home. Then I come home, eat dinner, and sleep.

Faith shows up during the five daily prayers — whenever Dhuhr or Asr comes, I have to go pray; that's one place it comes into play. It also comes up generally when I'm interacting with non-Muslim colleagues — for example, if a guy extends his hand to shake mine, I have to say, actually, I don't do that, and if they're curious I explain why. It also shows up through the Muslim Student Association, or generally when I'm interacting with other Muslims. I also do some Islamic studies on the side — sometimes I go to my local masjid to study Quranic Arabic, and sometimes I go for hadith — so that's where it shows up as well.

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer: I would say the Muslim community is very open and very welcoming. At least from what I've seen, nobody has ever shunned anyone based on their faith, their identity, how they practice Islam, or how they don't practice it. Everybody has been pretty nice to everyone, generally. It's very open, especially on my campus — we've had so many converts, subhanAllah, that it's a very unique place to be, I think, compared to other universities. Generally it's a nice space to be, and I feel like when you're in a community where people share the same moral values and faith as you, it's easy to get along with them, communicate with them, and be a part of (it).

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer: I've lived in the area I live in for the last, I want to say, fifteen years, and I definitely think it's shaped who I am as a Muslim. I was born in an area where there were a lot of Muslims, but I was raised here from the age of five, so I grew up around a lot of Muslims, whether Indian, Pakistani, Arab, or African — a bunch of different kinds of Muslims. I got to experience that, and I think it gave me a generalized sense of multiple perspectives and made me open to dialogue and conversation. For example, some people follow a certain madhhab and others follow different ones, and having open conversations about that without anyone being offended — I think being in a very diverse Muslim community has made me very open about these topics and very accepting of many different views.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, AND HOW?
answer: Yes. I attend some classes — I've done hifz school, so I still do Qur'anic classes and review. I occasionally listen to lectures online; I think that's the main thing I do now that I'm in undergrad, because I have less time for a structured course. I sometimes try free online courses where you sit and listen to lecturers and take notes. Mostly I'll attend halaqas, or at my local masjid we sometimes have lectures or a scholar's seminar that comes through, so I'll go and attend those. That's generally how I seek my knowledge.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
That's a good question. My hijab story is pretty straightforward — I think it's the story that happens to many youth who have parents who wear hijab. When I was younger I saw my mom wearing hijab, so I decided I would do it too because I thought it was cool, and I started wearing it when I went places. I also wore it because I went to Islamic school when I was young, so it was part of our uniform anyway, but then there was a point where I wanted to wear it all the time, so I just ended up wearing it. So when it came time for it to become mandatory for me, it wasn't a huge shift — I was already doing it because I liked to, I thought it looked cool, so I ended up keeping it on. Of course I wasn't doing it for the right reasons at that time, but it kind of just became a natural thing for me.

I mean, I think originally, when I was a kid, I just did it because I saw my mom do it — you're influenced by the people around you and you kind of just follow what you see. But as you grow older you get a better understanding — this is an actual commandment in the Quran, women are supposed to wear hijab, they're supposed to be modest in a certain way. Of course there were struggles with it — hijab isn't just the headscarf, it's also the way you carry yourself and the kinds of clothes you wear generally, so that was a struggle growing up, especially when I transitioned to college. I was a homeschooled kid, so my community at that time was just the Muslim people I saw at my masjid, so wearing an abaya and hijab was easy then. But when I went to college, everyone was wearing shirts and pants and those kinds of things, and I kind of wanted to mimic that — but then you have to realize you're breaking the codes of hijab if you wear tight pants or a tight shirt. So that was a struggle, but alhamdulillah I was able to maintain it — my mom used to dress-code me quite a bit, so it helped.

It definitely singles me out. In a lot of spaces I've been in, at least growing up — in high school and college — I was typically the only hijabi. In university I studied engineering, so a lot of times it was either a male-dominated room or a room full of people who weren't necessarily Muslim; in my graduating class in college, I was the only practicing Muslim.
