It's interesting when people come up and start asking, "I've never seen you do this, why is that the case," or "why aren't you coming to the bar with us." They also look at you kind of strangely — I think a lot of hijabis have experienced this, where people see a hijabi walking into a room and think, "oh, that's a little different."

question: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN OR HIJAB?
answer: I don't think they misunderstand anything per se — it's more their ignorance about it. I haven't had anyone make assumptions when they've walked up to me; it's more curiosity. A lot of them are just confused — I've been asked things like, "are you Hindu or something, is that why you wear that?" They just don't know what I'm wearing or what it means, so I have to explain it to them. They'll ask, "do you ever take that off," and I'll say, yeah, I take it off at home — explaining these simple things to them, because they generally just don't know. I don't think they have any bad assumptions about it, at least from what I've seen.

question: HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO WRONG PORTRAYALS OF MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer: Honestly, I think it's a mix — first it's like, oh, I didn't realize people don't know this, because growing up in a very heavily Muslim-dominated community, especially as a homeschooler, I kind of forget sometimes that people don't know what Muslims are. So first it's surprise that this is even a question people would have. But then it's also kind of nice, because I'm glad they're asking me instead of just going to Google and wondering, "what's that thing she's wearing on her head?" I find it kind of endearing, honestly — like, you're nice enough to be curious and take the step to ask me these questions. It makes me feel nice, I guess.

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer: I guess I can talk about difficulties with regard to academics. A lot of times you can put in as much effort as you want into your studies, or taking an exam, or applying to a certain program, but things don't necessarily end up the way you expect relative to the effort you put in — you can write the best essays and that won't necessarily translate into the outcome you're expecting. In those moments, the biggest thing I've embodied through undergrad is Qadara Allahu ma sha'a fa'al — whatever is best is going to occur, and Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala knows best; I've tied my camel and left it up to Him. That's how I manage difficulty generally — realizing I'm not in control. I have to try my best in everything, that's something we have to do, but if things don't turn out the way I want, that's okay — Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala sees my efforts and knows what's best for me. You don't know if that job was the best for you or not.

question: WHAT INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS ARE PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
Definitely. I think everyone has a different way of practicing Islam, and when somebody sees someone wearing hijab and an abaya instead of loose pants and a t-shirt, they automatically assume, "oh, this girl is hyper-religious, she might be a hafidha, she might be like this or that" — so they have these expectations of you when they interact with you. Even elders will have these expectations, but then when they actually talk to you for the first time they might be like, "oh, she's just a normal person, just like us, another undergrad." Sometimes these expectations make me a little uncomfortable and make me feel like I don't belong in certain communities. I used to go to a school called [ISLAMIC SCHOOL 1] in the [METRO REGION 1] area, and at one point I left that school. Whenever I go back to that community — I still keep in contact with my teachers and have a lot of friends there — sometimes I'll go pray salah there on my way home, and when I see certain teachers or students, I feel like they look at me like I no longer belong, just because they're wearing their full black abayas and hijabs and I'm not necessarily wearing a black abaya, I'm wearing a different long dress or something, and that might single me out to some degree. Or the way I carry myself nowadays — I've changed since I was young, I behave a little differently, I talk a little differently, I'm more outspoken about my opinions, and I've noticed that changes how people treat me. My friends and teachers who know me treat me the same way, but other people in the community treat me slightly differently, and that makes me a little uncomfortable sometimes. So I do think expectations are placed on people based on their perceptions of you, though that's not the case everywhere — I think it's a matter of exposure. You might have a perception of the Muslim ummah based on one community, but if you've been exposed to many different communities, you're more open-minded and don't have these preconceived notions about people.

Yes, I'd say I've had a lot of difficulties, internally and externally, with the way I dress. Externally, as I grew up through my four years of undergrad, my mom especially would talk me through it — I might come out of my bedroom about to leave the house wearing something I thought was modest, and she'd say, "[INTERVIEWEE], I think this isn't a good idea, this part is see-through, I don't think that's good," and I'd be like, okay, but I really liked this outfit, why do I have to change right now — but then I'd go change. That was a little tough, but eventually I realized my mom was saying what's best for me, and it's better to be corrected by someone close to me than by some random auntie telling me, "beta, that's not the right thing to do," so I appreciate that.

Internally, I think the struggle — this might sound shallow — is that growing up, you're surrounded by so many pretty girls wearing really nice outfits, and if they believe that's the correct thing for them, they should do what they want. But if I believe that's not the correct way for me to dress, I should stay with my moral compass, stay with what I think is right — though it's tough, because sometimes you think, I also want to dress like that, but I can't. Eventually I got through it by shifting my style — I'm not necessarily wearing a black abaya, but it's still modest; I like wearing colors, so I worked out what colors to wear, going shopping with my mom and asking, "do you think this is okay to wear to school?" That's definitely helped.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer: I think — not a person, but Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. As a hafidha, I have this thing lingering over my head all the time, that I'm a walking Quran, so I should be behaving and carrying myself in a way that's conducive to that. Whenever I read Quran translations, or go to halaqas, it's like it's speaking to me directly and correcting me on certain things, so I definitely feel responsible, as a person who has accumulated at least this amount of knowledge, to act upon it. On top of that, I feel responsible to my family — these are the people who raised me, I'm the youngest in my family, they shaped my moral standards, and if I can't even follow the basic things they've taught me, that's not good. I agree with everything my parents tell me — they're very learned people and know what they're saying, so I should follow them. The last group I feel responsible to is the next generation — I'm pretty active in my local masjid and in the MSA community, and a lot of times you'll meet freshmen, sophomores, or high schoolers and middle schoolers at the masjid who look up to you because you're a bit further along in life; they ask you for advice. Making sure the way I behave, talk, and give advice is aligned with the Quran and Sunnah, something I'd want to be told as a youth, not misguiding them in any way, and being a good role model for them — those are the three groups.

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer: I think, family-wise, it's just a natural thing — I'm the youngest, I'm also the only daughter, and I live in a Desi household, so the role I play in my family is kind of natural. Growing up, my mom would show me, "if this happens, make sure you do this, your job is to do this," those kinds of things, and also just watching my mom generally, I think I followed her footsteps — if I see something that needs to get done, I'll do it. I don't know too much about my role within my household beyond that; it's kind of just a natural thing I learned by watching. In terms of my community, my role is mostly as a member — I try not to take leadership roles because I don't like being the face of things, but if people need help with something, I'm always in the group chats, whether it's volunteer planning or anything else — "we need an idea for this," "could you help me out with this," "we need someone to sub for this class because the teacher suddenly needs it" — and I'll say, yeah, I can definitely help out if I'm free. So I kind of fill in the gaps where I can, and I'm also just a general student in my community — my local masjid holds a lot of Arabic classes and tafsir classes, so I go and attend, because it's my weekly slice of Islamic knowledge that I try to incorporate into my life.

question: WHAT DOES BELONGING FEEL LIKE HERE?
answer:
To me, real belonging is when you enter a space and you don't feel on edge — you know that when you get there, people won't treat you as different, as someone they don't know. When you walk into the room you can easily greet people, and even if they don't know you super well, they'll treat you like a friend. That's belonging to me — you're not shunned, you're immediately accepted, even if you don't hold the same values or you differ on a certain topic; you're all respectful of one another and treat each other well.

I think so, yes, and in many of the spaces I'm a part of, I definitely feel that way.

question: HOW DOES LIVING HERE SHAPE HOW YOU PRACTICE OR SHOW YOUR FAITH?
answer: Honestly, I think I'm very lucky. The non-Muslim spaces I've been in — whether people are Black American, Hispanic, these kinds of things — they've all been very respectful of my differences in faith, and they've also taught me about their faiths. At my university, people who are Jewish would tell me they fast on certain days too, and I'd be like, wow, I didn't know that, tell me more, and they'd tell me everything about it. At least in my experience living in this country, I haven't faced discrimination from the communities I've been part of, whether undergrad or the workforce — people have been generally very accepting, very curious. I genuinely feel confident as a Muslim living here in the US. I know there are other countries where it's much harder, like India or Uzbekistan, but at least here, in the area I live in, everyone's been pretty open, and I feel confident being a Muslim. If I have to pray and I'm at, I don't know, a gym or something, I'm okay with just taking out my prayer mat in the parking lot and praying there — I don't expect anyone to jump me or anything, I'm confident enough to do that.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: I think that comes into play whenever I'm making decisions I'm a little wary of. When I think of the Akhirah, I think of judgment — how my actions are going to be weighed on the Day of Judgment. For example, a guy acquaintance at school might ask if I want to grab coffee, and even if it's platonic because he has a girlfriend and other joint acquaintances are coming, I personally try to avoid going out with a group if there isn't a higher girl-to-guy ratio — I just try to avoid it. Things like that I keep in mind, because you don't want to get close to even doing anything that might be sinful. Or it might be salah time and the window is closing while I'm in the middle of class, and I have to debate whether to leave the classroom — will the professor treat me differently if I leave? Technically I could just leave and he won't say anything, but he might have a skewed perception of me — but do I care about his perception of me, or the Lord's perception? So in those moments I have to think about whether to do it or not. Or saying no to certain invites — during graduation season, a lot of my acquaintances are guys, so they'll text me invites like, "you should come to my grad party," and I have to say, sorry, I can't come, and make up an excuse, because I don't feel comfortable going to a guy's grad party, especially because he's a guy. So, things like that.

question: HOW DO YOU MAKE SENSE OF WHAT IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL?
answer: When something's beyond my control, it's the Qadr of Allah — everything happens for a reason, everything has been pre-written, and there are certain things you genuinely can't control. So you just have to acknowledge that and keep it in the back of your head: I do what I can, and if things happen a certain way, then that's okay. That's the main thing I hold onto.

question: WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR PRACTICING YOUR RELIGION IN THE LONG RUN?
answer:
I think making sure you still get down the basic things of being a Muslim without compromising, even if you live in the West — salah is a big thing, making sure you don't compromise on your salah, or fasting, even when, for instance, there's a lunch meeting and everybody's ordering food and you just have to sit in the back. Making sure you don't compromise on the fundamentals, and also remembering that being a Muslim isn't just praying, fasting, or reading Quran — it's also being a good person. I feel like a lot of people forget that Islam is peace; you should treat everyone well despite their moral standards, their perceptions of things, their religion. Being a Muslim in the West is a combination of keeping down your basics and also being a good person, following the Sunnah of the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, treating everyone well — Islam is a way of life, and living that out as a Muslim the best that you can.

My friends say I'm a very level-headed person — I don't get upset, I don't show very strong emotions, and if I show any strong emotion it's mostly joy. They think I'm very calm and understanding, though I don't necessarily see that in myself, maybe because I have a different perception of myself at home. But usually when I'm outside, I'm calm, nice, and people think I'm extroverted even though I don't think I am. I do try, if I see someone who might not be included in a group, sitting on the side, to go introduce myself and try to make them feel more welcome, whether it's a Muslim or non-Muslim space. I think that's generally how I try to embody being a Muslim in outside spaces — and also not compromising. In undergrad it's come up a lot of times where I have to tell my teammates, in an in-person meeting or working on a prototype, "hey, it's my prayer time, do you mind if I step out for five minutes," and I'll go to a corner of the building, pray, and come back — everybody's been super nice about it, nobody's ever said anything against it. So it's about being confident in your values, explaining it to people if they're curious, and just being a nice person.

Before, if you'd talked to me in my freshman year of undergrad, I might have been very hesitant to say these kinds of things and explain them to people. Maghrib time, for example, is a very small window — you have to pray within thirty to forty-five minutes — and sometimes I wouldn't even say anything to my friends, I'd just leave and come back and say, "that was a long bathroom break." At that time I was a little shy about it, but over time I became more confident. The biggest thing that shifted my mindset was realizing — I'd been seeing this growing up but never actually acknowledged it — why are Christians so confident saying "we love Jesus," coming to your doorstep, these missionaries, and why are Jewish people so confident about their holidays, throwing a party, being proud and confident about their religion — and why weren't we as proud and confident about ours? People understand the different holidays and practices these other groups have more than they understand Muslims, even though, at least at my university, we're almost the same size, a very large Muslim community. Realizing that made me ask, why am I not confident in my own religion, why am I not educating people? Nobody treats conservative Christians or practicing Jewish people badly for it, so they shouldn't treat a Muslim person badly either. So I started doing that — of course it was a little hesitant at first. My friends actually think I'm insane — in the engineering department we have these giant workspaces, basically a bunch of lab benches, and if Maghrib is coming in while I'm working on something I can't walk away from, I'll just pray right there, and my Muslim friends look at me like, "[INTERVIEWEE], why do you do this?" And I'm like, nobody's going to do anything, why should I be afraid? So I think in the beginning it was hard, but over time, acknowledging that people just generally don't care — they really don't care, and if they do care, it's mostly out of curiosity. I haven't met a "Karen," so to speak, who has called me out for my Muslim practices, alhamdulillah.

Not really — if anything has happened to me, it was more of a passing situation. I did an internship in a certain area of the US that was known for its drug and poverty issues, and sometimes walking from the train station to my workplace and back, there'd be people who'd say strange racial slurs and Islamophobic slurs, but it was just a thing of passing — I'd walk past them and not give them too much mind. In professional spaces, academic spaces, or fun spaces like the gym, nobody's ever said anything.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer:
Before I went to undergrad, I was always surrounded by Muslims, always surrounded by girls — I wasn't really doing anything besides being at home, going to a masjid, going to Islamic school or hifz school, so my community was very — I'd say sheltered, if that's the right word — everyone was the same, nobody was challenging any of my moral standards, nobody was thinking anything differently from what I already knew. Coming into undergrad was the first time I was in a space where — this might sound strange, but it was my first time being in a class where everybody was my age, because I attended community college and did homeschooling, so I either didn't have classmates or the people were much older and didn't really talk to me. So coming into undergrad was the first time I had people my age, the first time seeing Muslims who practiced Islam differently from me, the first time meeting people of different religions. I learned a lot about different people's ideas of religion, identity, and moral standards, but I also learned what I value, because growing up I had this perception of what my moral standards were, but after experiencing more you get a more open mind, you learn to shift your ideas on certain topics based on what you've learned. My ideas on certain topics have definitely shifted quite a bit — religion is a big one, and also how I treat people; my perception of the LGBTQ community has shifted quite a bit, my perception of people generally, growing up with "stranger danger" (thinking).

My biggest growth was going from an introvert to more of an ambivert or extrovert — being nice to people, being proactive in spaces, being open-minded. I grew a lot; I just don't know how to explain it fully.

I think it's a mix of both. Growing up, faith was always described to me as Islam, Quran, salah, tafsir, studying Arabic — these kinds of things — and not necessarily as, how do you embody Islam in your character, how do you embody Islam through your reactions in certain situations. That's something I learned in undergrad. So I think faith has driven a bit of that, but also just my personal curiosity — I'm a generally curious person, I like getting to know people and learning about different topics — but I do think faith has definitely shaped my attitudes toward things as well.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer: Submission to Allah, to me, is remembering that nothing is in my control — everything is a ni'mah, even taking this breath, speaking this word, nothing comes without His permission. Just understanding that — I don't want to say it like this, but — you're kind of just a pawn in this larger game of life, and your movements are partially determined by your decisions, but the end result of the whole game is already predetermined, and you're just living through it without much control over it. Your goal as a pawn in this game is for everything you do to be to please Him, because before we came onto this earth, Allah said, you're going to be human, you're going to have your own decisions to make, your own society, your own nation, you're going to be judged on the Day of Judgment — are you ready to do this? And we said yes, back then. So you have to be the best person you can be and hope that whatever you do, as long as you do it with the best intention and believe it's the correct thing to do, then inshallah you'll do your best to enter Jannah — but in the end it's only up to His mercy that that happens. So submission, for me, is realizing that I'm a pawn in this larger game of life, and my job is to do my best, and whatever the result is going to be is up to Him.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: I think I mentioned this before, but awareness of the Akhirah, knowing I'm going to be judged at the end of the day — even Islamically, learning through the stories and hadiths we know, like what the Prophet sallallahu alayhi wa sallam saw happen to people who lied, or the punishment tied to committing zina — knowing these things guides you toward what you should and shouldn't do, and that's awareness of the Akhirah. Knowing these hints, these really scary things that could happen to you for doing things that our modern society might think is normal but that are Islamically forbidden, major sins — it definitely shapes the way you act in certain situations, at least for me.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer: For me, I feel most liberated when I'm with my closest friends doing something we enjoy — but also something my parents approve of, and that we know Islamically is something that benefits us. One of my favorite things to do, and the thing I feel most free about, because my parents are also very approving of it, is going with my friend to a weekly halaqa we really enjoy. My mom is kind of strict and doesn't let me go hang out with friends very often, so when I ask, "Mom, can I go with so-and-so to this halaqa," and she says yes, that's fine — I'm like, wow, you really don't let me go do anything else, but you let me go drive solo with her to this one thing. That's a moment when I feel liberated, because I have my parents' trust, and I'm able to hang out with someone I genuinely feel I can be myself with, have real conversations with, and we're doing something we both enjoy, whether it's the halaqa, or going to a cafe, or going for a hike. I feel most liberated when I'm doing things I enjoy, that my parents approve of, and that I hope Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala doesn't think is incorrect, and when I'm spending time with people who genuinely get me, who are open-minded, people I grew up with and am comfortable around.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer:
An ordinary day — I am a teacher, a middle school teacher. Right now I'm on summer break, but typically during the school year I would wake up around 4, 4:30, get ready as far as praying Fajr and all of that, prep my work for the upcoming day and go over everything, then leave the house around 5:30, six o'clock. I work in [STATE 2], so I have a bit of a drive. I start my job around 7:10, usually come home around 4, 4:30, spend time with family, then prepare work for the next day, and start the cycle all over again.

I'm really lucky because, obviously, I'm Muslim, and one of the benefits of salah is that we pray five times a day, which gives us the opportunity to constantly recenter ourselves — I'm so grateful for that. Salah is an important time in the day because it helps you recenter what's important and remember that, honestly, all the stresses you feel day to day are not important. I think that influences how I view my job and my work, especially working at the school I do — it's not a very diverse school, and for that reason I think I have a different outlook than a lot of my coworkers, who are very stressed on a day-to-day basis. One of the things I really like about myself — and I do attribute a lot of this to salah, to constantly recentering myself — is not getting too stressed out during the workday, because as a teacher you're kind of working throughout the day. I also mentioned I work in [STATE 2], so I have a bit of a drive — I really force myself to use that time to listen to Quran, make dhikr, or listen to a YouTube lecture. I've come to enjoy my drive; it's actually my favorite time of the day. I think because I'm so busy during the day I can find myself not fitting in dhikr or Quran, so I use the time on my commute — an hour there, an hour back. On the hour there, I don't allow myself to listen to any news or a podcast; I always put on an Islamic-related video. On the way back, I allow myself to listen to a podcast or the news.

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer:
To be honest, I don't really think of myself as different, so I think I would struggle to answer that question directly. If I had to describe myself, or my community, in a couple of words, I would say that I live in a very close-knit community. I have a very small circle, and I like it that way — I feel like my circle and my community are very supportive and very inspiring. I feel like we're all striving to be better, to better ourselves.

If they expressed interest in coming to my community, I would be a hundred percent for that. I think I would describe it as a place where they may encounter things that are different from their normal life, but I think there's still beauty in that. I also think my community is unique in that there are so many different cultures you can notice when you're visiting the masjid — it's a melting pot, everyone's from different places, but everyone sees past that because the number one unifier is that we're all Muslim, which I think is very similar to other places of worship. So I think they would see things they resonate with, and I think they would also see things that shock them, that are different to them.

In terms of rituals — and in terms of places of worship. I've visited churches and synagogues before, and I'd say mosques are kind of the closest in terms of... I think it comes down to cultural practices, but there's a lot of hugs, a lot of kissing on the cheeks, that kind of thing. I think that would be one small thing that would shock them.

question: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN OR HIJAB?
answer:
I think there's definitely a range. With social media, I feel like people are able to see — and it's tough, because with social media there are accounts that reaffirm what you already think a Muslim woman is like, and then there are accounts that may surprise you. I would say that in the area I live, [CITY 1, STATE 1], it's so diverse that I don't tend to think much about how other people view me — I feel like people have an accurate view of what a Muslim woman is because they interact with Muslims so much day to day. But in the area where I work — I work in [CITY 2, STATE 2], which is a very rural area, and I am one hundred percent the only Muslim on the staff. They have a diversity issue across the board — basically the entire staff is Caucasian. I know for a fact that a lot of the kids I teach, I am the first Muslim woman they've met. This is my sixth year teaching here, and I feel like it's gotten better, but my first year was a very interesting experience, because when the kids would walk in on the first day, a lot of them would do double takes. A lot of the kids have told me, you're the first woman in a scarf I've seen in person. I think with that comes a lot of responsibility.

During, I'd say, around October, whenever they're doing their unit on Islam in social studies, they ask things like, have you ever been to Mecca, why do you wear your scarf, why do you wear long sleeves and long pants. To be honest, I'm glad they're asking, because sometimes I can tell some of the kids have a question but don't ask it. The kids who do ask will ask things like, what does your hair look like, how long is your hair. Whenever someone does ask, it gets really quiet around me because everyone's waiting to hear what I'll say.

Not as much as you would think, with the adults. I don't know if it's because nowadays you can Google any question you have, or if it's culturally, in American culture, considered rude to ask certain questions. I've gotten a couple of questions, but I could count on one hand the number my colleagues have asked me. I think it's honestly just because you can Google whatever you're curious about.

To be honest, I don't know how they see me. They were a very welcoming group. I think at points I view myself as different, but at points I don't — my mom is American, I grew up here, so there are points where I feel different, and points where I feel like I'm American — I don't know, my mom's from [STATE 3]. I feel like I can fit in, but then there are points where I stand out. When I was younger I did mind that I stood out, that I was different — I don't know if I've gaslit myself into thinking it's okay that I'm different, but now, at twenty-seven, I almost like the fact that there's something special about me, that I am different. I kind of like the different parts about myself, as cheesy as that sounds.

The fact that I wear a scarf, for example — it's such an evident thing, it's almost the first thing you see about me. And there's a little bit of pressure I've always felt with that — I always feel like I have to, and this could go back to what others think of me; maybe I'm cognizant of the fact that people may have perceptions about what a Muslim woman is, so I'm always smiling, always upbeat, positive — I constantly feel like I have to manage people's impression of me. But, in a strange way, I do like the bar I feel like I have to set for myself. I like that I feel like I'm representing something bigger — I like the fact that when my students leave me, even if they're not going to stay in touch, they had the opportunity to interact with me and see what a Muslim person is, if that makes sense at all.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer: I think it definitely has changed. I'm very lucky that I went to an Islamic school until eighth grade — I always talk about the small circle I mentioned earlier; all of my closest friends, we all went through nursery, elementary, and middle school together, and some of us went to different high schools, but we're still very close. We always talk about how grateful we are for the foundation we got at an Islamic middle school and how we have a strong understanding of our faith — not all of us are hijabis, or some of us started out as hijabis and now are not, so even within my close group of friends, due to our experiences, we're all at different places. I think my childhood, growing up, I was very much surrounded by other Muslims, and for that reason I had a very strong sense of self, just because it was very affirmed when I was younger. I don't think I lost that going through high school and college, but there was a time when I got almost insecure about my sense of self — you go through that time of questioning what you were taught, which I think is very healthy, like, do I really believe this. Nothing to the extreme, but then in my young adulthood that strong sense of self returned, and now, at twenty-seven, I have a very unshakable sense of self — I truly feel like I know who I am, and I'm okay with that.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, AND HOW?
answer: I would say yes, I do, and I'm really grateful because I have a lot of sources for that. I'm really into podcasts. My dad is an imam, so I can always go to him, and he's always sharing different things. I really enjoy going to Jummah when I can — unfortunately during the school year I'm not always able to. The mosque I prefer for Jummah is [MASJID 1] in [COUNTY 1], in the [CITY 3] area, and the imam there is [IMAM 1] — I really enjoy his khutbahs, so that's been my go-to masjid for the past four or five years. Even when I'm not able to make Jummah, if I remember to on a Friday, they livestream their khutbahs, so I'll listen to those. Other than that, I think you just stumble upon videos with short snippets of Islamic knowledge on a daily basis. So I get knowledge from a variety of places.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
My hijab story — there wasn't really a point in time I remember saying, I'm going to wear the hijab today. By the end of middle school I still wasn't wearing my hijab a hundred percent — I would in public, but if I got in the car after school I would immediately take it off, then put it back on before going into Walmart or somewhere like that. Going into high school, my mentality was that it would be so much harder to put it on and go into school one day wearing it, then start wearing it, and if I ever wanted to take it off, take it off (later) — so I decided to start off wearing it (from the beginning).

I think, like I mentioned earlier, I'm very grateful for it because it's a constant reminder that I am Muslim, and with that comes a certain standard for myself. I do appreciate how people treat me with it on — this is something I've come to realize the older I've gotten — I think there's a certain level of respect that people give you automatically if you wear a scarf, and I've noticed that very frequently in daily interactions. But yeah, I'm very grateful for it.

question: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN OR HIJAB?
answer:
I do know that people have different views of what Islam is and what Muslim women are like. When I was younger, in my teens and as a young adult, I did harp on that and constantly think about what other people thought of me, and I think that was due to comments people would make. My mom is a convert, and her family isn't Muslim — recently my little sister got married, and she was telling me a funny story about something our grandmother asked her.

Basically, to cut the story short, our grandmother was asking her a bunch of questions about her husband, who, due to various circumstances, she hadn't met yet — she wasn't able to come down for the wedding. Our grandmother said, don't tell your mom I asked you this, but does your husband treat you right? My little sister started laughing and said, yeah, he treats me right. Then our grandmother said, you know, he has that stereotypical Arab look, doesn't smile in pictures — he's very sweet, but he doesn't put his hands on you, right? And my sister said, no! That's my own family holding those views. Even when my mom married my dad, my grandmother had a lot of strong opinions about it, because that was a long time ago. I think there are things people think about Muslims, and things people think about Arabs, so that's like a double whammy. I know people hold those views, and to be completely honest, there are probably people in the world those stereotypes apply to, but the problem is that those are overgeneralizations — people take one cultural practice and apply it to a whole group of people. But honestly, I can see that changing in the next couple of years — there are so many Muslim voices on social media, and as the world, especially America, gets more diverse, I can see people interacting more with Muslim people and Muslim women on a day-to-day basis. I think that's what truly helps change those mentalities and preconceptions, when people actually ask those questions and hear from Muslim women straight from their own mouths. I feel like that will start to change, and I can see it changing.

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer: What I was mentioning at the beginning of the interview was just my mentality in life — I'm not sure if it's a defense mechanism or a healthy practice, but truly I don't allow myself to harp on small things. If it's something that won't matter in a year or in five years, I'm not going to get angry about it — I'd rather just let things go, let it roll off my back. It's the same with difficult times in life — I know they're going to get easier. I'm not sure where I get that from, or if it's naturally my personality; it's not how people around me, my family and my circle of friends, deal with problems, so I don't think it was modeled for me. I don't know why I'm like that, but I don't harp on things too much. For example, my mom recently went through a health scare that involved getting sent to the emergency room — yes, I was worried about her, but I had a very positive outlook, telling myself we're going to get through this. She's doing great now, alhamdulillah. I try not to say to myself, "you're dealing with this right now," because, to be honest, I don't feel like my problems in life are that significant compared to other people's, so I don't like to complain or say "I'm so stressed" or "I have so many problems." I don't really operate like that. Again, I'm not sure if that's a defense mechanism or a healthy or unhealthy thing, but it would probably take a lot for me to shut down.

question: WHAT INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS ARE PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
I do. I think the expectations for Muslim women are a little higher than they are for men. Even growing up, I have three sisters and three brothers, and there's just... To be honest, I think that religiously the pressures and expectations are pretty even, but culturally, I do think that, the way things have progressed, there's more pressure on Muslim women in how we conduct ourselves and carry ourselves than there is on Muslim men.

Both — within the community and outside of it. Within the community, I just feel like your image is very important. The way I've always viewed it — and again, no one has ever explicitly said this to me — is that you're always a representation of your family, and I think that's a cultural thing. I was always a bit of a goody-two-shoes in school, and I think the reason was that I always thought whatever I do is going to get back to my parents, is going to be a representation of them. My parents raised my siblings and me in a way where they would trust us until we did something to lose that trust, and I think how they raised us made me never want to lose that trust and always want to present myself in a positive way, because I always felt that pressure — whatever I do is a representation of them.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
So, when I was younger — and again, I said this a little bit earlier — I did struggle a lot with being different, with getting stared at. Oh my gosh, I am very sensitive to being in an area and getting a lot of stares. My mom is from [TOWN 1, STATE 3], a very small town, and whenever we go there... I have a vivid memory of being in high school, going to a buffet with her family, who are not Muslim, and just being in such a crowded restaurant with everyone constantly staring at our table, it felt like. I don't know what they were thinking, but I think I did used to make a lot of assumptions about why they were staring at me. When I was younger I really, really struggled with stares, and even until now, I don't really like going to the beach in a bikini — I guess some of that is still there, I don't like standing out. There are certain times I wish I wasn't different, so I'd say that's the biggest difficulty. I've never found the concept of hijab itself to be difficult — I've always seen the women around me wearing hijab, and actually the hijab itself I really love. I have a great respect for the concept of modesty. I'm not opposed to the hijab — I think I'm just opposed to what other people think of me, or just the staring, and knowing that they may be thinking this or that.

No, and I think a lot of people would find that surprising, considering my dad is an imam, but I can't remember a time when my parents said, okay, you have to wear hijab, or why aren't you wearing hijab — I really can't remember a time when they said that. All of my sisters and I started wearing hijab full-time at different times — my older sister loved the hijab, she's in baby pictures wearing it at five or six years old, she's just always worn it. My younger sister was wearing it by second grade. Me, like I said, I wasn't fully wearing it until high school. But I don't remember a time when anyone in my family, or my parents, said take it off, or don't wear it, or you have to wear it.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer: Probably my family. I think it has a very strong impact on my choices — what's coming to mind is kind of what I just talked about, how I act in public; I think a lot of that I get from my family. But at the end of the day, I don't feel like I have to do things because of my family... what I'm thinking of is like me deciding to become a teacher. It's not that my parents were opposed to that, but I did feel like I had to go a certain route career-wise that I didn't end up going on. Was that from my parents? No, that was more so culturally — my parents have never explicitly said, we want you to become this or that.

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer:
I'm number five (in my family). Not really — I don't feel like I have to lead by example in that particular sense.

I think I stand by what I said earlier, that I do feel like I have certain expectations — not that anyone has ever explicitly said that to me, but I feel the need to overcompensate in that respect. Where I'm struggling with the question is the word "role," because if anything, I feel like I truly have almost a background role — I'm not really someone who has a leadership role in my community, and I don't really feel the need to get involved in my community to that extent. Even when I go to Jama'ah, for example, I'm in and I'm out — I don't really stay and converse too much with people, not because I don't like the people there, but I just like having a very background role; I kind of just go and do my thing and leave. In my family, I guess I have different roles at different times. I do have the role of being an older sister — I have a younger brother and younger sister, so with that comes checking in on them from time to time, being there whenever they need me. As far as my parents, as they're getting older, all of my older siblings have either moved out or are no longer in the state, so I've kind of taken on that caring role for my parents — I'm the oldest child they have here in [STATE 1], and I've started to feel that in the last couple of years.

I think I would run away from anything that requires me to be too out there, if I think of "role" that way — I would really rather be in the background.

question: WHAT DOES BELONGING FEEL LIKE HERE?
answer:
I think belonging here in the West means getting to a point where you're comfortable with the culture, to the point where you're familiar with the area around you, you can speak the language, you understand the nuances of how that society functions. Once you've attained that, I'd say you have a certain sense of belonging — on a day-to-day basis, when you can maneuver through life without much difficulty, I'd say you've attained a certain sense of belonging.

Absolutely, I think I've attained that. Like I said, I grew up here, and my mom is American, so I feel like that gives me a sense of — not ownership, but like, no matter what anyone says, I always know that I am American. If someone were to say something like "go back to your country," I do feel like this is the country I belong in. Conversely, my dad is Syrian, and I wouldn't say that if I went to Syria right now and lived there for three months, I think it would take a while for me to feel like I belong — which is interesting, because I do covet the Arab and Syrian sides of me a lot. But I think if I went to Syria right now, I wouldn't feel like I didn't belong exactly, but I would feel like I had to get to that point of being able to maneuver in that society, because I think I belong here more than I do there — which is kind of sad to say, because I do covet those Syrian parts of me and hold them very near and dear to my heart.

I think it's a combination of all of it — me knowing that ethnically I am American, that my mom is from [STATE 3], that her dad was Native American — I feel like, to an extra degree, I do belong here, and I feel like I check all the boxes of being American, as far as my comfortability being here. I feel like I don't have that with my Syrian side, and I think I covet it so much because I'd love to be equally as comfortable with both languages and really understand the culture. But to be honest, I think this is because I grew up here — some aspects of American culture I prefer over the toxic side of Arab culture.

question: HOW DOES LIVING HERE SHAPE HOW YOU PRACTICE OR SHOW YOUR FAITH?
answer:
I think a lot of times I don't feel like there is a conflict, because of the idea of America as a place where people of different religions and cultures should come — this country was built on immigrants, that kind of thing. Conceptually, my story and my family's story is what America is all about. But if I'm not thinking conceptually, if I'm thinking about what America actually does, about its actions — those are very distasteful, and that's where the conflict comes in. There are certain things America stands for, not what America says it stands for, but what it does, that conflicts with things I hold dear. So those two things are kind of on opposing sides.

Take Syria, for example — I really don't appreciate how America conducts itself on the foreign stage. Regardless of the president, it's not really about the president, it's about America's actions — how involved we are in stirring up things overseas, or with Gaza. Am I proud of my home? Yes. But sometimes I'm not proud of the fact that I live in a country that supports certain things and does certain things overseas. It's not a singular event — if you really look into certain things, it's not pretty.

question: HAVE YOU BEEN MADE TO FEEL YOUR FAITH CONFLICTS WITH YOUR COUNTRY?
answer: Do I think there's a conflict between my faith and the country I live in — again, conceptually, no. Even though America is kind of considered a Christian country, I don't really view it like that. I think that on a day-to-day basis, if you take the news out of it, people, from what I've observed, enjoy the fact that America is that diverse. I was at the airport the other day and there was a guy praying in the parking lot, and no one was disturbing him, and he felt comfortable enough to do that — that's the really beautiful part of living in a country this diverse. So I don't really feel like the country, or my faith, conflicts with the country, because I do feel like we still have religious freedom — the fact that you can live your life and wear a hijab loud and proud, walking around with it, is a testament to the fact that you have religious freedom. In that respect, I don't think they're at odds.

question: HOW AND WHERE ARE YOU ABLE TO PRAY DURING YOUR DAY?
answer:
I do pray in my classroom. Now, that being said, do I lock the doors whenever I pray? Yes. Would I feel uncomfortable if someone were to walk in on me praying? Yes. I'm not sure why — I don't think anyone would say anything if they walked in and I was praying, but I think it's just a personal thing, because, like I said earlier, when I was younger I did really care about what people thought of me, and I don't like being stared at. I kind of gaslit myself into seeing those parts of being different as being really good, and to an extent that is true, but there are certain parts of me that also just want to be like, no, I'm normal, I'm the same. But will I secretly be in my classroom praying? Yes.

I think it's not that I think anyone would mind — if I'm being completely rational, if someone were to walk in, they'd think, okay, she needs a second, and come back later. Rationally, I don't think anyone would mind. But I think the irrational part of me is like, no, I have to close the door. I don't know.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: I think it kind of makes that part of me that doesn't really sweat the small stuff even more pronounced — there are more important things to be worrying about. It's not that the people around me are like that, but truly a lot of things just don't matter to me, because there are certain things that are more important, and I think ultimately it does boil down to the Akhirah — this world is really insignificant, and I know that. Again, I'm not sure if it's a defense mechanism, but that's really the only thing that should be stressing me out, if that makes sense.

question: HOW DO YOU MAKE SENSE OF WHAT IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL?
answer: I'm comfortable with the fact that things are out of my control. I'm very comfortable with it — the idea of Qadr, of fate, that everything happens for a reason. I'm very comfortable with that. And yes, a thousand percent, that's what makes me more relaxed compared to my colleagues.

question: WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR PRACTICING YOUR RELIGION IN THE LONG RUN?
answer: What matters most to me is being a good representation of Islam, and also not being too flashy about it — not constantly saying things, just knowing that I did them, that's important to me. And on the other side of that coin, not being hypocritical — saying one thing and doing another — really matters to me.

question: WHAT IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR HEART, INTENTION, AND OUTWARD PRACTICE?
answer:
Yeah, ultimately I'm doing it for the benefit of the Akhirah, not at all for the benefit of this world. Aside from being a good person — I feel like being a good person is very important because, although it's like a drop in the bucket, it's almost like paying it forward — if you're a good person, since you can't control what other people are doing, at least you're trying to be a good person, at least you're acting how you wish people acted.

I don't know, but I just know that it is really important. I feel like it's a conjunction of different things — part how I was raised, part religious reasons, part because I'm a representation of my family. I think it's a whole bunch of different things that have just been reinforced throughout my lifetime.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer: I think it means, kind of like you were saying earlier, relinquishing control, knowing that there's a bigger plan, and that at the end of the day everything is written and there's a reason for everything, whether you like it or you don't.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer: I think I feel most liberated at home, because I'm the most myself at home. I feel like around your family you can say whatever you want and do whatever you want — you don't really have to watch your words, because your family knows who you are the most, so even if you say one offhanded thing you didn't mean, no one's going to take it the wrong way. I feel like around my family is where I feel safest, and that safety kind of leads to feeling liberated.

question: DO YOU FEEL A RESPONSIBILITY TO REPRESENT THE COMMUNITY WELL?
answer:
Every woman — because if you were caught, like how some people are caught acting up on an airplane or being super rude to somebody at a store, and you're wearing a hijab, I would be disappointed that you're negatively representing Islam, that you're reaffirming, maybe, if someone does view Muslim women negatively, that view, by acting that way. So I think it's the second one.

Remember when I said, when my students leave, if I was the only Muslim woman they interacted with, I would want them, when they think of a Muslim person, to think of me. I don't think it's necessarily a bad thing, but ultimately I do feel like, because we're obviously a minority, it's very important to always be your best. I do see what you're saying about the danger in that mindset, how it can lead to overgeneralizations, but I feel like that's where you have to use your critical thinking. If there's a video of someone acting up on a plane, I'm not saying that person is negatively representing the whole Muslim community or Muslim women — I'm saying that to some people who do have misconceptions, it could reaffirm those negative misconceptions. I'm not saying it does, I'm saying it could. So if you're going to wear a hijab, there is, in my opinion, a big responsibility, because you represent something bigger than yourself — but that's just my personal opinion.

I think so, because it's right there in your face, that you're Muslim, and it's not something to not be proud of — I think it is something to be proud of. But, at least in my mind, in my opinion, that's how I view it, and I'm not sure if I put that standard on myself, if that's all in my head — it's possible. But would I ever want to change that or try to convince myself otherwise? I don't know, because I like that I constantly feel like I have to be at my best. I like that I feel like I need that — not that I'm a hypocrite, I do things when I'm not wearing a scarf too — but I feel like it's almost a challenge to myself, to always remember; it kind of checks me.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer:
Keeping my house in order — that's pretty much it, along with family and work.

Faith is basically what our day revolves around. We have to wake up for prayer, so we're constantly reminded of our purpose — whatever it is that we do, we have our faith in mind. For me, as a Muslim woman wearing hijab, when I go outside I'm a representative of my faith, so I carry that with me everywhere I go.

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer: That depends on how they approach me and what questions they have. I've worked with Islamic nonprofit organizations, and we do a lot of da'wah work — of course, any interaction, everyday interactions, can be da'wah, a means of educating others about Islam. So basically I tell them that we live lives that are constantly conscious and aware of the existence of a Creator, and we obey the commandments He sent. For us, the most important thing is monotheism, the belief in one God, following the prophets He sent, and just being the best human beings we can be.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer:
I've been in the US for probably thirty-two years, and in the [CITY 1] area for about twenty years total.

I'm a convert — I converted to Islam when I was twenty years old, but I started learning about it fairly young, in my teens. My experience has been a little different than maybe someone raised in a Muslim family. I came from a Catholic background, was raised in that faith, and always believed in God, always prayed to the Creator, but I didn't know at that time exactly who that Creator was, and I was confused about that for a long time until I found Islam and started comparing Christianity to Islam. When I first converted, I wanted to go all in — since I'd already been exposed for a few years before converting, I wanted to start wearing hijab and start practicing right away, but I met some resistance from family members, so I had to hold back a little. With the hijab specifically, I'd say it took about a year before I was able to start wearing it properly. I actually converted a year before September 11th, so once that happened, it also caused a lot of friction with family members, but eventually they understood that I was committed to my faith and wanted to live it wholeheartedly, including wearing hijab. I think the biggest change after that came after I got married and had children — that's when hijab doesn't just become part of you, it becomes part of your family, because you're constantly with your children as a woman, so you're visibly Muslim, and you become either a target or an ambassador, depending on who you're dealing with when you're outside. That has shaped me to become more aware of my surroundings, stronger in my faith, and more prepared to answer questions and to protect myself and my family with regard to any hostility that may arise from my identity as a Muslim woman.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO ISLAM?
answer: I started learning about Islam when I came across the autobiography of Malcolm X. I started reading it when I was about fifteen, sixteen years old, and I also watched the movie, directed by Spike Lee, about his life. I was fascinated by Islam, and specifically by what happened to him after he made the pilgrimage to Mecca — before that he was part of the Nation of Islam, more into the Black power or Black Muslim movement, but once he went to the Middle East and saw Muslims of every race, culture, and ethnicity, he realized Islam was actually a unifying force for good rather than something that divides. He realized that racism wasn't a problem throughout the world in the way he'd thought, but rather a problem specific to the United States — of course it exists elsewhere too, but he was able to separate the two and see that Islam was the answer to those kinds of isms, like racism and colorism. When I learned about that, I was very curious what exactly Islam was. About a year after I was exposed to Malcolm X, I met a Muslim family from Egypt, and they helped me get hold of literature about Islam and answer questions I had. I actually approached them with my questions, and they graciously answered and offered me whatever reading material I needed. That's how I started reading about Islam on my own, and that eventually led me to convert.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
As I was reading about Islam, I already knew that if I was going to start practicing this religion, I wanted to wear hijab, because covering was something that was already constant in my life, even as a Catholic — I was raised around nuns, I was in Catholic school, and the women there, in the school and the church, wore a habit very similar to what a Muslim woman wears. As a Catholic, the figure of the Virgin Mary is very important, and at home, church, and school I would see images of her wearing a veil. So I always knew that covering was something that would make a woman closer to God — as Catholics we learned that the Virgin Mary, peace be upon her, was the epitome of a righteous woman. So it didn't seem strange to me, when I learned about Islam, that women should cover — it seemed like the natural thing to do, something that had been lost in other cultures and religions. So I embraced hijab wholeheartedly, and I wanted to start wearing it right after I converted. But I was living with my parents, and they didn't really approve of that, because it was new for them, even though they were Catholic too and saw the correlation — they were also more aware that society doesn't accept this as a normal thing, especially from someone of my background. So at first I had some resistance, and I would only wear it to the masjid when I went to pray, or if I was going out with other Muslim girls to a Muslim gathering. Eventually, a few months after I converted, I was able to get a job with a couple of Muslim doctors who had a practice, and because they were Muslim doctors I convinced my parents that, since I'd be working in their office, I should wear hijab to work. My parents agreed, and I started wearing hijab to work. Then, a few months later, September 11th happened, and at that point my parents asked me to take the hijab off, because they thought it was too dangerous for me to wear it outside, given the hostility toward Muslims right after 9/11. So what I would do is put the hijab in my purse when I left the house, then put it on once my parents didn't know, and remove it before coming home so they wouldn't realize I'd been wearing it outside. That happened for a while, until I eventually moved away for college, and at that point I told them I was going to wear hijab full-time. They saw that I was able to get a job — I actually had a job interview wearing hijab, and I got the job. When they saw I was able to do those things with hijab, they accepted it, and I've been wearing it ever since — I think it's been since 2002 that I started wearing it regularly.

I think it's just as the Qur'an says — it's an identifier, a form of obedience; you're following the commandment of Allah. It also separates a person from everyone else, in the sense that Allah says you'll be known as a believing woman. Another thing it does is deter you from doing things that aren't becoming of hijab — when you're covered and outside, people understand you're a Muslim woman, or at least a woman of faith, so they won't expect bad behavior from you, indecency, rowdy behavior. It really makes you aware of God, raises that God-consciousness, and puts a standard on you of modesty and decency that maybe you wouldn't have without that constant reminder that you're representing your faith the moment you step outside.

question: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN OR HIJAB?
answer: There's this prevailing misunderstanding, or stereotype, about Muslim women being oppressed, or obligated to wear it, forced to wear it by the men in our lives — our husbands, our fathers. That's just not the case; it's a very personal decision. I'm sure that in some cultures women may feel more pressure to wear it, but for me it wasn't pressure at all — it was something I wanted to do for myself. There's also this notion that Muslim women are uneducated, that the more covered you are, the more uneducated you are, but I've found it's completely the opposite. Honestly, out of all the women I've met in my life, I think Muslim women are among the most educated, the most successful academically and professionally. I'm really proud to be among Muslim women, especially those who've chosen to wear hijab, because it's a courageous thing to do, especially now, in this age.

question: HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO WRONG PORTRAYALS OF MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer: I try to help inform people, but it does get frustrating at times, because there are people who choose to remain ignorant. I think the more years pass, the more fed up you get with these different attacks on Muslim women and on Muslims in general. But you have to choose your battles and know who to ignore and who is genuinely searching for truth versus who just wants to attack Islam by any means possible — usually they'll attack women because they feel it's the easiest target, and that's just sad, not really worth our time. At the end of the day, I've also learned that this is just part of our test in this life — dealing with the ignorant haters. All the prophets had to deal with the same thing, and I'm sure the women of their time did too. So we just have to keep moving on and being strong for our faith.

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer: I've moved around quite a lot in my life, because of the nature of my father's work — we used to move every two or three years. I've had to be uprooted so many times, and even after I got married we still moved around quite a bit. What that has made difficult for me has been establishing friendships and having a sense of belonging in my community, and I think that's made even more difficult by the fact that I'm a convert, and that I'm not of the same ethnicity as the majority of people in our congregations at the mosque. That lack of support, of genuine friendships, is difficult, because it can get very lonely — I don't live in the same city as my parents, so I don't have family around; I only have one older brother, and he lives pretty far away. That's been, I think, probably the most difficult part of my life. But the way I see it, if it hadn't been for these moves and these interactions, people coming in and out of my life, even without producing lasting relationships, it helped — had I stayed back home and not moved around so much, I would have never had the opportunity to learn as much as I have. So I'm grateful for that.

question: WHAT INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS ARE PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer: There are expectations placed on women from all angles. We're expected, not just as Muslim women but as women in general, to be able to have a perfect life, a perfect household, to carry ourselves with perfect adab, perfect manners, at all times, to keep it together, stay beautiful, stay fit — so many things, but it's not realistic. Then, of course, from within the Muslim community, there are expectations about how to behave, what's acceptable and what's not, and who is "more Muslim" than other people. I've had encounters where people question your faith, question your knowledge, basically because of who you are or your background. As for how to overcome that — we're all on our own journeys, we all know the difficulties in our own lives, so we just have to ignore people's expectations and know that the only One we serve is Allah, at the end of the day, and that's who we're returning to. As long as we're doing what we have to do to please Allah, anything else is really just noise.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer: Alhamdulillah, I haven't had many difficulties. There was a period when I wore niqab, just to test it out — the community I was in at the time, the majority of women wore niqab, so I would wear it to the masjid. Then I moved to Egypt for a while and wore it there, and came back to the US expecting to continue wearing it. But I found it was very difficult — I felt disconnected from people, and the level of discrimination was even more intense with niqab. So it eventually became a decision I had to make, to stop wearing it altogether. I wore it maybe a year and a half to two years — a year and a half consistently, maybe two years on and off. It was a huge burden to decide to take it off, because I felt like I was doing something wrong, but then I had to reconcile with that. I read about the rulings on it and concluded this is not an obligation for a woman, and that it would be better for me, for my family, not to wear it. I was also attacked — not physically, but verbally, in front of my children, on more than one occasion, when I was out in stores wearing niqab. That was another deterrent — I said, I can't bring this attention to myself, because I'm not just bringing it to myself, I'm bringing it to my kids, and I want to keep them safe. So that was the reason I stopped wearing it.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer:
My family, absolutely — my family, my children, my husband, and then my parents. I think they shape my choices a lot — definitely for anything professionally, academically, economically, all decisions really go back to keeping my family in mind. Of course, my family is second to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, so any decisions that concern my religion, I have to know I'm serving Allah first, but after that, it's my family.

No — I think faith is something personal. I guess if you go back to the niqab issue... but ultimately I decided I didn't want to wear it, and even that decision was shaped by my relationship with Allah. I was asking myself, at the point where I wanted to take it off, was I taking it off for people, was I putting it on for people at this point, or was I doing it for Allah? And I realized I wasn't doing it for Allah anymore at the end — the reason it was so difficult for me to take it off was because I kept thinking about what people would think, now that they were used to seeing me like this, if I took it off. So at that point I said, I'm not doing it for Allah anymore, so that's why (I stopped). But any other decision that has to do with my faith always goes back to Allah, not people.

Not that I'm aware of — it was difficult for me, but I didn't feel anything outwardly; at least no one let me feel anything. I discussed my decision with other sisters I knew, and I was surprised when one of them told me she had done the same thing — I had no idea she'd worn niqab before, but she told me she took it off because of her children, because of the safety issue. Once I saw it wasn't something rare, I felt more comfortable, and it was just a matter of me overcoming my own fears about what people would think or how they would react.

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer:
That's a deep question. I understand my role in my family as raising my children and being the best example for them, making sure I'm doing the things that please Allah the most, and that I'm taking care of my household and being a good wife. Outside, in my community, I feel like family takes priority, but community comes second — how can I serve my community? I think being able to do whatever you can, being present, is important, helping whenever help is needed. But I have to admit it can be difficult to juggle both — I have a bigger family, a lot of children, and they take a lot of my time, so knowing I can't do as much volunteer work can sometimes make me feel guilty that I'm not doing enough. But I try my best.

Alhamdulillah, I've been given the opportunity to do a lot of nonprofit work, work in da'wah outreach, and also in education and writing. I think my writing is my biggest contribution to the community — I write on issues that affect our community, and that feels like the biggest way I give back. I used to be more active going out into the community, doing more things physically, but that was when I had fewer children and was younger. Now I have a role that's more in the background, but at least I feel like I do something, and that's a blessing in itself.

question: WHAT DOES BELONGING FEEL LIKE HERE?
answer: Belonging — I feel like it's difficult to feel a sense of belonging, especially with rising Islamophobia and anti-Muslim bigotry. We often feel othered, and that's on a macro scale; on a micro scale, even within our own community, we can sometimes feel like we don't belong, depending on whether we're people of color, whether we're of a different ethnic background than the majority of the congregation, or whether our level of practice is different from other people's — we may feel like we don't belong in certain spaces. At the same time, there are moments when the Muslim community feels like your safe space, because of how much hate comes from other groups. I also feel like people of faith in other communities offer that sense of belonging, because they're going through some of the same things the Muslim community is going through. I've had the opportunity to study interreligious relations alongside people from different faith backgrounds — Catholic, Christian, Jewish — and you see that people who are committed to social justice, committed to their faith, are fighting some of the same battles we're fighting, and they recognize the difficulties, so they offer that sense of belonging too. But ultimately you have to be in a place where you feel like you fit in, where you feel close to Allah — I think that's the ultimate tranquility, having that reminder that Allah is with you no matter what.

question: HOW DOES LIVING HERE SHAPE HOW YOU PRACTICE OR SHOW YOUR FAITH?
answer: I think what Muslims are facing is definitely different, because we're not the majority — we're just a little over one percent of the population here. The anti-Muslim hate, the xenophobia, the Islamophobia, is a real problem. But there's also an underlying problem: this society has become less and less attached to religion. Some people call it a Christian nation — it wasn't founded on Christianity, but it is a Christian-majority nation — yet even Christian churches have lost a lot of their congregations; a lot of people have abandoned their churches. People of faith, especially in leadership positions, see these dwindling numbers of people going to church, being involved in their places of worship. There are seminaries throughout the US that house not just Christians and Jews but also Muslims, studying in these institutions, and there are dwindling numbers of students there too — some institutions have had to close down or shift to online learning to offset costs. Because of that, leadership sees a threat coming from people who want to do away with faith altogether, or with public displays of religion, and they see that the Muslim community, since we're the biggest target of that, means there can be a threat to themselves as well — if you do away with one faith, eventually it comes down to the next one, and the next one. I think that's what has sounded the alarm on that issue.

question: HAVE YOU BEEN MADE TO FEEL YOUR FAITH CONFLICTS WITH YOUR COUNTRY?
answer: Honestly, outside, I have not. You sometimes feel an air of tension depending on where you are, because of your faith, because of the way you look, or at least you assume that. But I think the place you see a lot of the hatred, a lot of things boiling, is online. We've had this shift to social media over the past ten or fifteen years, more and more on our phones, our devices, interacting with people online, and you see the polarization, people spewing all kinds of hatred online, and that makes it more apparent that there's a problem. When we're living our day-to-day lives, going outside, going from place to place, our jobs, school, or even just to the supermarket, we don't feel the anti-Muslim hate — if we're blessed enough, we're not going to experience any physical attacks or anything like that. But when we go into that online space, where people interact without any filters, you see the things people are saying, and you wonder, is this what people are actually thinking, because they've been emboldened by having a screen to hide behind, so they're able to say whatever's actually on their mind. That creates a kind of tension when you go out and wonder if the people you see online are the same people you're interacting with outside.

question: WHO GETS TO REPRESENT MUSLIM WOMEN IN RESEARCH, MEDIA, OR AI?
answer:
The reception has been mixed. Some people are open and welcoming, and there are others who still have some suspicions, or who have expressed how difficult it is for Muslims to get a platform to even speak on their own religion — which I find really fascinating, because I've heard from Christian scholars and speakers who are out giving lectures, offering classes, and speaking on Islam. I asked, why is it that Muslims aren't able to speak for themselves? And I was told that people don't trust Muslims. It's eye-opening that people would choose to listen to someone outside our faith to explain our faith, rather than speak to one of us directly, so we can explain ourselves and our motivations behind our decisions to practice.

In academia, especially, to be white and Christian and male gets you a pass — that's the first tier. To be white, Christian, and female gets you the second tier. Academic spaces are dominated by white Christians, so they get the credibility and the opportunities to speak about others more frequently than people of color, and definitely more frequently than people of minority religions, regardless of race or ethnicity. So, as Muslims, we don't have the same clout to speak, and that's because there's a system in place that really suppresses the voices of people of color, of people of minority religions, in this country and elsewhere in the West.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: The Akhirah is a reminder — we're only here temporarily, so we have to prepare for leaving this world, and anything we do, we have to maximize our effort to do something good. I think about the concept of sadaqah jariyah, ongoing charity — what can I do that's going to help me even after I leave this world? That's why I really enjoy writing; I feel it's a powerful way to leave a lasting message, because writing is something that stays with us. Books, articles, even online articles, can stand the test of time and continue to offer me a chance to do good, even when I'm gone.

question: HOW DO YOU MAKE SENSE OF WHAT IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL?
answer: Allah is in control. Allah is always in control, and we fool ourselves into thinking that we control things, but at the end of the day we have to remind ourselves that Allah is in control of everything, and we have to put our trust completely in His infinite knowledge and wisdom.

question: WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR PRACTICING YOUR RELIGION IN THE LONG RUN?
answer: What matters most, of course, is doing these things with sincerity, for the sake of Allah first and foremost. But one of the worldly benefits is that we're here as a minority religion in the United States, and we have the opportunity to show people what Islam really is — so we have that responsibility because we're here. As for me, I was born in the Western hemisphere, so this is my home, and I don't have much choice in that matter — of course I could pick up and try to move to another country, but it's much more difficult for somebody born in the United States, with a US passport, to move their family to a different country and stay there permanently. So we're here, and we have the opportunity to show people what Islam really is, to contribute to this society in a positive way, and through our daily interactions to show people who Muslims really are. Those of us living here have that great opportunity to acquire good deeds and show people the best of us, so they can see that Islam is more than what they see on the news or depicted on television and online.

question: WHAT IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR HEART, INTENTION, AND OUTWARD PRACTICE?
answer: Self-awareness — I think I mentioned before that hijab provides a reminder, and I think it's the same with acts of worship: praying five times a day, fasting, they all serve as a reminder that God is watching, and that we're responsible to Him for our actions. Those acts of worship deter us from doing things that are evil or don't align with our faith, so they provide a certain awareness and mindfulness of who we are. For me, as a Muslim woman, I feel like hijab and the things I do as a Muslim are part of my identity — they become part of you, and I think this is especially the case for Muslim women. Hijab becomes part of you, you can't separate yourself from it, because hijab is the first thing people see when they look at you, so it just becomes part of who you are.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer: Liberation is freeing your mind — freeing your mind of what people, of what society, is choosing for you, or what the majority is doing, or what people deem acceptable or unacceptable, man-made trends and things like that.
