Freeing your mind from those things is liberation. Liberation is being able to practice your faith and know that no one can take that away from you, and being able to choose what you want to do in your life — to me, that is liberation. There's this notion in this society that women need to be liberated, especially Muslim women, because people see us in hijab, and hijab is supposed to be something that oppresses. But meanwhile, women in this society aren't free either — they're not free to choose to be a person of faith; a person of faith who dresses modestly is looked down upon. Only about a hundred and fifty years ago, all women in this country dressed modestly, no matter their religious background. So there's this hypocrisy about what women should and shouldn't do, and that's not liberation — that's more oppressive, for women not to be able (to choose modesty) and to work and be like men and things like that. I feel like that's more oppressive than a Muslim woman who's able to protect her modesty, isn't harassed outside because of the way she looks, and is able to practice her faith freely and live her life according to what she believes is best for her. To be able to choose that for yourself — that is more liberating than anything else.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
Submission to Allah — it's just a beautiful way that we say it in my language, instead of submission we say surrender, like surrendering yourself. That is surrendering every part of you, everything that you do, to your Creator.

Submission can feel like it has a negative connotation, like you're submissive, right? But when it comes to the Creator, you're surrendering yourself, you're giving yourself to your Creator, your deeds and your actions, to the Creator. When you think of it that way, you realize that, because we belong to God, we're admitting to ourselves that we're not in control, and that we owe everything to our Creator. So we give ourselves, we surrender ourselves, to Him.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer: There's a hadith that says the world is a prison for the believer and a paradise for the disbeliever. So when you think of yourself as submitted into this world, you're a prisoner to this world, but when you think about the Creator, that's beyond this reality — submitting, surrendering yourself to your Creator, goes beyond that and is liberating you from this world. Our paradise is with our Creator, but our prison is in this life.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer:
Right now I'm a recent graduate from [UNIVERSITY 1], so I'm taking life a little slow, just relaxing, and working my side job, which is nannying. I drive to my shift, usually in different parts of the [METRO REGION 1], but a lot of times they have shifts in the [SUBURB 1]/[CITY 1] area, so I drive down there, clock in, watch the kid I'm assigned to, then clock out and go home — that's been my daily routine the past couple of weeks. In regards to interacting with people, that happens a lot when I'm shopping and stuff like that, and I'd say most of my experiences interacting with people have been positive, now and in the past. I've been wearing hijab since I was about five or six years old, from a very young age, and at one point I even wore niqab, but that was only for about a year, and I never took it off since then, or the hijab. So alhamdulillah, I don't think I've ever had a negative experience, and I would attest that to me mainly being around Muslims.

I grew up going to [ISLAMIC SCHOOL 1], which is a private Islamic school. I was there from pre-K all the way to eighth grade, so most of my childhood experience was being at that school, where everyone was Muslim. My extracurriculars were also at that school — I did karate there too, predominantly with Muslims as well — and with my family we would go around to the rec center and the pools, and that's the way I would interact with other people from different faiths and people of all kinds.

But I would say I never felt isolated or targeted because of my hijab. I will say that when Islamophobia was extra targeted in the media, there was a rise in attacks — it's still happening now, but I'd say maybe around 2018, 2019, around those years — I felt a little scared, seeing the things that were happening to people who looked like me, people who were Muslim, people who wore hijab, how they were targeted, and hearing their experiences. I definitely felt scared sometimes to go outside with my hijab, and especially during the time I was wearing niqab, I was even more scared. But alhamdulillah, I think Allah blessed me with being around good people, and I never had to interact with anybody who had negative thoughts of me or who would hate me for wearing hijab. I will say people definitely have questions — I've encountered that a lot, people coming up and asking why I wear it, if I'm hot in it, and stuff like that. Since I grew up around Muslims, I was happy people asked, to show that they were curious and actually wanted to learn, so I answered them happily.

Faith is a very big part of my life. I try to use it as a guide every step of the way, so I think it shows in every choice I make — it's backed up by my religion, always at the forefront of my mind. For example, let's say I'm clocking into my nannying shifts — a lot of times I'm working with different families who don't know me, so I'm meeting them for the first time when I knock on their door. One time I knocked on the door and the father answered and held his hand out, like, "oh, nice to meet you, my name is this and that." As a Muslim woman, I'm not supposed to shake hands with another man who isn't a close relative. That doesn't happen too often, since I'm not really interacting with men much, but when it does, I get a little shy or embarrassed to say no to that person and shy away their hand, or say, "oh, I can't do this, I'm a Muslim woman," and state my values right then and there. I've been more intentional about that, so when that incident happened, I put my hand to my chest and said, "oh, I'm sorry, I don't shake hands with men," and the person was very responsive to that. I guess that's one way my faith showed up in that moment, when I made that decision to stand by my faith and my values.

In other cases in the past, when a man held out his hand and I had to say no but was too shy or embarrassed, I didn't say no, and ended up shaking his hand, and felt really guilty, like I hadn't stood by my values — which is what led me to be more intentional, to stand by my values even if nobody else around me is, even if there are Muslims who sometimes shake hands with other men. That's sometimes why other people, non-Muslims, don't understand when I say no. I had an incident once at school where I made that decision to stop shaking hands with men, and said, "oh, I'm sorry, I don't shake hands with men," and they said, "oh, but this other person did" — and that other person was a Muslim woman — and I said, "yeah, but everybody goes about their life their own way and makes their own decisions." So that's one way where, even if other Muslims aren't doing something and I have to be the odd one out, my faith stands up for me.

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer: I don't think I've been asked that question, but if they were to ask, I would say that my community is very close, and we're very much bound by our faith — our faith very much connects us, and we're always there for each other. I'll say specifically my local community, instead of the entire Muslim community: I'm talking about the [MASJID 1] community, because that's what I've been around the most. Even though I did grow up around [ISLAMIC SCHOOL 1], I haven't been there in many years, so [MASJID 1] is now my community. We're very connected, and we all have different strengths and play into each other's strengths. We meet often, we have different youth events, and I love that we can all come together and talk about our issues and relate to each other, especially living in the West, where sometimes you don't meet someone going through the same thing as you and can feel alone in that. To come to a masjid and be around my community, we can all talk about what we're dealing with and feel less alone, because we know the other person is most likely feeling that way too. Yes, I've been part of the [STATE 1] community all my life.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer:
From when I was a child, I grew up around predominantly Muslims, so that was just what I am — I'm a Muslim — and it was something I didn't even have to think about, it was very ingrained in me. But that was part of an issue for me too, because eventually I needed to go find who I am outside of that community. Since I'd been around this community my whole life and been told certain things my entire life, when I wasn't around these people, I didn't know where I stood, what my values and opinions were outside of it.

After I went to college, I was actually in an environment with very few Muslims — going from being around Muslims literally all the time to a space with barely any. I tried to look out for Muslims there and made friends, though those friends happened to be from the mosque and went to that same school, so I stuck with them. In the first semester I didn't really know anybody — the friends I'd made from the mosque weren't there yet either — so I was basically alone. I didn't feel like I really connected with anybody, and didn't even feel the need to, I guess, because I felt faith was such a big part of me that I wouldn't be able to connect with someone of a different faith, since we didn't hold the same values. So I isolated myself a little, and also started dressing differently because I wanted to fit in and not stand out. I had always worn abayas — that was my dress code, I never wore anything else — but at that school I didn't want to wear one anymore, because I didn't see a single person there wearing one. So I started wearing pants and shirts, sometimes skirts, which I'd worn before too, but not the abaya specifically — that I stopped wearing.

At first it was a little exciting, something new and different, but I'd say I also felt a little empty, like I was losing part of myself. Even though it seemed small, it was still a value I held closely, connected to my faith, a big part of me, so shying away from it made me lose myself a little. After that semester, when I reconnected with friends from the mosque who came to that same school, I stuck around them, and we hung out for the rest of my time there. I felt more comfortable wearing abayas again, and then I also started seeing other Muslim students at the school wearing abayas, so I felt even more comfortable.

The biggest difference was when I transferred to a bigger university, [UNIVERSITY 1], which had a lot of Muslims. I was so happy to go there, because at [COLLEGE 1], the previous school, there were barely any Muslims — there was Jumu'ah and an MSA, but it wasn't really active or pushed, so I never went, and my schedule didn't align either, so I never made it to the events they had. But at [UNIVERSITY 1], everything was very different — I saw Muslims all the time, always around, saying salaams, dressing the way I'm most comfortable dressing. There was Jumu'ah, and I started going back to it — I hadn't been able to at [COLLEGE 1] — and I felt a lot more connected to my community and my faith that way. They had a lot of events, and even though I think it's a PWI, I found a lot of diverse communities there. There were also other cultural communities — I'm Somali, Egyptian, and Yemeni, so there was a Somali club and an Egyptian club, a lot more opportunities to connect with different parts of myself at that school.

So that's how my faith and identity changed as I grew. First I was in a stage where I was constantly around people like me, around my community a lot, and that was all I knew. Then in my adolescent stage, figuring out who I was, I felt a little lost and wanted to get away from the community to figure that out on my own. Then I went into college and was put in an environment where I was literally alone — that was a struggle, and I did lose a bit of myself wanting to fit in and not stand out. Then after reconnecting with my community, I reconnected with my values and what was really important to me. Yeah, that's where I am now.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, AND HOW?
answer: Besides the videos I get on my IG and TikTok feed, I don't seek it out actively, but that's something I want to do. In the past, since I was at Islamic school and after that went to Quran school, a big part of my life I was actively seeking Islamic knowledge, more than my secular studies. That played into me losing that later in life, when I went to college and got really into my secular studies — I didn't have time, or didn't make enough time, for Islamic studies. Now that I've graduated, that's something I really want to put all my focus into going forward.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
When I was younger, for as long as I can remember, I absolutely loved the hijab. I started wearing it around age five or six because I loved it so much — I loved playing around with different styles and dressing it up different ways. I don't think I wore it every single day from age five, but for sure by the time I reached puberty, around nine years old, I wore it every day, and I haven't taken it off since. I love my hijab. I struggled a little with wearing it the correct way — in my adolescence, around thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, I had thoughts of not wanting to wear it correctly, wanting to show my hair, wanting to experiment with different styles. I went through that phase, and I'd say I still go through some of those struggles — I want to experiment with different styles, even though I know what hijab is; I see other people getting to experiment with styles in their lives, with hijab too, people wear it so many different ways, and I want to experiment sometimes too, even though I know it may not be the most correct way.

Even though I do struggle with it, I can never see myself taking it off — it's part of me, that's who I am, I can't imagine not wearing hijab, that wouldn't be who I am. I'd say it's also been a protection for me, from things that are bad. When I see people in the streets and they compliment my hijab, say how much they like it, and know I'm Muslim, they come up and start asking me questions about Islam. I'd say wearing hijab is a representation of my religion, and since my religion is a big part of me, I really value that.

At the beginning of my life, I wore it just because that's what everyone around me did — my mom wore it, everyone around me wore it, that's just what everyone did. Later in life is when I had to understand and learn the real meaning of hijab — not that I wasn't taught it, but I had to seek that out for myself. I learned that later, and I'm still learning. Despite struggling sometimes with hijab, and not always wanting to wear it the right way, I have to understand there is a certain way ordained for Muslim women by God, for reasons He has told us, but also some reasons are just (part of) His wisdom, and I have to trust that. That's something I took in, I'd say, later in my life.

question: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN OR HIJAB?
answer: I'd say sometimes non-Muslims may be a little intimidated by people in hijab and think we're all the same — that all hijabis are a certain way, act a certain way, are very rigid, and don't have personality. Sometimes I do have that in the back of my head — whenever I'm meeting someone who doesn't know much about Muslims, or it's their first time seeing a hijabi, I have that thought that they probably think I'm a certain way, that they have a preconceived notion of who I am. Then they get to know me and it's like, I'm not what they thought a Muslim woman would be. I think people sometimes don't think of Muslim women as actual people who have different personalities — we're not a completely different kind of creature, we're all human, we think similarly, we work the same, it's just that we have different values, and this head covering is part of something that I value.

question: HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO WRONG PORTRAYALS OF MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer: I've never encountered any discriminatory acts toward me because of my hijab. I will say I've seen some false representation, not specifically in my life, but in the media. In certain shows I watch, I see people wearing hijab and they're not really representing it the way it should be — for example, there was a Spanish show where a girl was a hijabi and later took the hijab off because of a boy; the meaning of hijab wasn't really represented accurately in that show, I believe. I see that often in small clips here and there in the media — shows and movies where the actual meaning of hijab isn't really talked about, you just see the covering, and it's not really addressed why this person is covering. So I don't think it's been represented accurately in the media, but I'd say recently we're getting more accurate representation. Growing up, I never saw an accurate representation of Muslim women unless it was from YouTube and Instagram, from personal accounts of Muslim hijabi women — I would follow those because I thought that was very relatable content, since they were Muslim women doing editorials and daily vlogs and stuff like that, so I thought that was accurate because they were representing themselves. But from the broader media, growing up, I didn't see any accurate representations.

question: WHO GETS TO REPRESENT MUSLIM WOMEN IN RESEARCH, MEDIA, OR AI?
answer: Yes, I for sure think self-representation is very crucial, because we know ourselves best and can represent ourselves the best. Like I mentioned, I felt the most represented by watching people represent themselves — Muslim women, Muslim hijabi women, whether on YouTube, Instagram, or in interviews — because they represented themselves and talked about their own experiences. Even though it's important for the broader media to represent different kinds of people, Muslim women included, I think it should come from Muslim hijabi women, because they know best how to represent themselves. Even though we go through different experiences, we all understand our collective experiences — because of our religion, I'd say.

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer:
Let me think — a difficulty I faced recently, I'd say financial difficulties. Before going to [UNIVERSITY 1], I knew I had to be the one to completely pay for my tuition myself. At that point I was just working my nannying job, my babysitting job, and that's not consistent — I had to find another job, find a way to pay my way through the next two years at university, and it was a lot more money than community college, so I was very much stressing. But I really had conviction that I wanted to go to [UNIVERSITY 1], so the previous month I took a semester off and saved up as much as I could, but I only saved enough for one semester, so I decided to go with that and look for jobs during that semester to pay my way for the next three. That was a really stressful time, because looking for jobs itself is stressful, and looking for jobs that fit my school schedule was even more stressful, since it was also my first semester at university and the workload was a lot different than at community college. It was really hard adjusting, and I was constantly in the mindset of needing to make this money, needing to find ways — it was a constant stress on me.

During that time, I relied a lot on my faith, relied a lot on God, and put my conviction in Him that He would help me, even though I didn't see a solution in front of me. I didn't have one, I just worked as much as I could, but it wasn't amounting to the amount I needed. I really held on to my faith, and thankfully I graduated, and I do have some money left to pay, but not a lot — I don't have much debt. I give a lot of credit to my faith, because I tried my hardest — I really did tie my camel — I tried as hard as I could to find ways to make money, even while in school, and with my reliance and conviction in God, I made it through and overcame that difficulty and stressful time.

question: WHAT INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS ARE PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
Yes, I do think there are some internal expectations within the Muslim community, especially for Muslim women. We're kind of the representation of Islam — when Muslim men go out in public, you can't really tell if they're Muslim. So I'll say yes, Muslim women, hijabi women specifically, are meant to act a certain way, because we're basically representing Islam.

I was basically saying that because Muslim women outwardly represent Islam through hijab, you can quickly identify that a woman is Muslim if she's wearing one, in contrast to men, where you can't really tell if they're Muslim or not. Because of that, Muslim women are expected to act in a way that represents Islam — she can't really do wrong, or do things that contradict Islam, because then she'll give people the wrong idea. So I think there's extra pressure on women who wear hijab to be, in quotes, on their best behavior, because people are watching and they know you're Muslim. I think that pressure of always having to act right, in a certain way, kind of intimidates some Muslim women who want to wear hijab from doing so, because of that pressure. I see a lot of Muslim women actually taking off their hijab because of that, because there's so much pressure from their community to be perfect.

As for external expectations, from outside people, I'm not quite sure — I don't assume so, because they don't really know what hijab is or what it represents. When someone sees a Muslim woman, they kind of judge the entirety of Islam based off that; it's almost an inherent reaction, like: this hijab-wearing woman I know is a Muslim, she's acting this way, so this is how all of Islam is, how all Muslims act. So when someone sees a Muslim woman wearing hijab, they may judge other Muslims based on her actions, whether good or bad, because they associate her with other Muslims.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer:
I'd say I feel most responsible toward my family first, and my community — they're the people I'm most connected to, so naturally I feel most responsible to them, or for them.

They very much do shape my choices. A lot of my choices are shaped by my family and their opinions, and also by my community and how they do things. Even though my community's outlook is similar to my family's — that's what I grew up around — if I ever have differing opinions, I'd say my community is more responsive to a difference of opinion and nuance than my family, where it's more their way or the highway. I'd say my family shaped me in the way that I have to act in a mature and responsible way — I'm also the oldest, so that's inherent — and that, in turn, shows up in the way I act around my community.

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer: Basically what I was taught growing up — I'm the oldest, so I have to be mature and responsible and look out for everybody. That was kind of how it was growing up, and it shows up in my community too, where I know I have to respect my elders and everybody, and help everybody out when I can. It's not just about me and my needs — there are other people I have to take into account, and I have to show up for them too.

question: WHAT DOES BELONGING FEEL LIKE HERE?
answer: Belonging in the West — I guess just feeling appreciated and accepted for who I am, no matter what I believe in. I think I'm feeling that more lately than in the past, and I give a lot of credit to representation in the media — TikTok is a very big outlet now, and a lot of Muslim women are posting videos, talking about themselves and their lives, and I feel more accepted. These are women who live in the West, some in my community, some in others, but still in America, and them posting those videos and educating the broader community about who we are is making other people more comfortable and inclined to accept us, not just based on negative preconceived notions pushed by the media in the past. So I've been feeling a lot more accepted recently, and a lot more comfortable and safe around people who aren't Muslim. I think people who act negatively toward Muslims are just very uneducated, and probably live in parts of the U.S. that are, I won't say far from civilization, but if you own a phone and are on social media, more often than not you're more accepting of a variety of different people. I definitely give a lot of credit to that.

question: HOW DOES LIVING HERE SHAPE HOW YOU PRACTICE OR SHOW YOUR FAITH?
answer:
That's a good question. To answer it, thinking about people's experiences in Muslim countries in contrast to mine — I see myself longing for that, to be in a Muslim country where you go out and a lot of people, maybe not every single person, are Muslim. You don't have to find Muslims in the crowd, they're just there, and people automatically understand things about you, particularly faith-wise — they just understand and accept it, and I don't have to explain certain choices I have to make. In Muslim countries, they celebrate Ramadan and Eid, and those celebrations are a big thing, whereas in this country it's not.

Here, as a faith, we're a minority, and some parts of our faith aren't really accepted the way they are for other faiths — for example, Christian holidays like Christmas and Easter are a big celebration, people get work and school off for them, but for Muslims we don't get that for our celebrations. So there's kind of a divide, where certain parts of my faith aren't really made for this country, whereas in Muslim countries it's the opposite.

Eid isn't celebrated the way we celebrate it ourselves. It often falls on different days during the year, and sometimes it lands on school or work days, so you don't get time off, and it doesn't even feel like a holiday, whereas for Christmas and Easter there's a lot of advertisement in stores and you get time off — it's a big, accepted thing here, where Eid and Ramadan aren't. Another thing is halal meat — recently there are more stores selling zabihah halal meat, but in the past there weren't. I remember going to [GROCERY CHAIN 1] a couple of months ago and seeing they actually have a halal section, and I was really surprised, I was shocked. I know Costco has it too now, maybe for a couple of years, I just hadn't noticed. But those things weren't normal growing up — you couldn't go to a regular store and ask for halal meat, it would have to be a halal store. So there are certain things where you have to put in extra effort to accommodate your values, whereas other people don't have to, because it's embedded in this country — I'll say specifically the Christian faith. There are also stores, like [GROCERY CHAIN 2], that have a kosher section, so they're accommodating Jewish culture too, but I don't see any halal sections in those stores. That's where I see the difference and the divide.

question: HAVE YOU BEEN MADE TO FEEL YOUR FAITH CONFLICTS WITH YOUR COUNTRY?
answer: I've never seen that, thankfully — in my personal experience I haven't experienced that, but I do know people, and I've seen it a lot in the media, where they've experienced those kinds of interactions, where people are scared of them or very discriminatory toward them. But thankfully I haven't gone through that experience.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: That's a good question. I think a lot of the choices I make day to day are about how this will benefit me not only in this life, but the next life too. For example, when I was struggling to find a way to pay for school, the easy way out would have been taking a loan, but that would have meant incurring a lot of interest, and interest is a really big no-no in our religion. Even though it wouldn't have had immediate consequences, I knew it would have been a very big consequence for my Akhirah, for the next world. So I told myself I was going to try my hardest not to take that, because I know it would hurt me in the next life. That's one example of how thinking about the next life shapes the decisions I make in this world.

question: HOW DO YOU MAKE SENSE OF WHAT IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL?
answer: I ultimately understand it through the way that God's wisdom is infinite — He plans, and I can plan the best I can, but His plan is always better. I trust and have full conviction in God that He wants the best for me, and even if a decision may seem bad to me in the moment — let's say something happened that wasn't what I wanted at all, not how I planned it to go — I have to understand that this is just the way God wanted it to happen, and it will lead me to something even better than what I imagined.

question: WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR PRACTICING YOUR RELIGION IN THE LONG RUN?
answer: I think it's just really holding on to it, not compromising certain values just because other people are doing so. By holding on to my values, my future family and I would stand out, and we'd probably have to actively seek further opportunities to better accommodate what we want in our values. That matters a lot to me — just making sure I really hold onto my faith, no matter what climate or what's going on around me.

question: WHAT IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR HEART, INTENTION, AND OUTWARD PRACTICE?
answer: Yeah, I have the intention behind doing these things — not taking certain opportunities, or showing my faith outwardly — because I want to please God, and because I know doing these things will lead to my success, not only in this life, but also in the next.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer: For me, it means completely submitting to what He has decreed and ordained for me, whether I understand it or not. Full, complete submission, even if you don't understand it — there are certain matters where I don't understand the wisdom behind them, but ultimately I have to realize that my view of wisdom, my perspective, is very, very limited, in contrast to God's — He has a much broader perspective than me. There's a hadith, or a saying, that in comparison to God's throne, we're like a ring in a very vast desert — if you dropped a ring in a very vast desert, that's how small we are in comparison to the throne of God. I understand and realize that my perspective is very limited, I don't understand everything. I also think back to other times in my life when something happened that I really didn't want to happen, and I thought it was the worst outcome, but later realized it was actually the best outcome and worked out in my favor. So I reflect on times when things didn't work out in my favor, and that strengthens my conviction in God.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer:
I think liberation means the freedom to express yourself in any way you want. I experience that, I guess, through my faith, and through feeling accepted, being able to explore and do what I want while also still being accepted by my community and the people around me. That's how I feel liberated.

I felt really liberated seeing all the Muslims around me doing what they do — they were all in different clubs, and a really big one was the MSA. They held many different events — a barbecue, an event where you could play bowling and pool and different games — a bunch of different activities, whether directly related to faith or just recreational, and that was very liberating for me, because I could be around like-minded people and still do all the activities that people in other communities do. If those other communities did those activities, I might not feel as comfortable going, because I don't really know anybody, and I don't feel like I'll connect with anybody, since we don't have one big thing in common, which is religion. So those were certain times I felt liberated, and joining [UNIVERSITY 1] was a very liberating experience, especially seeing Muslim hijabi women wearing long clothing — I also saw a lot of niqabis there, which was very surprising, because I had never seen a niqabi at my previous college, even though it was smaller. Just seeing young adult Muslim women sticking to and holding onto their values and faith, even in a big college like [UNIVERSITY 1], which is a PWI, so there are so many different people who may not understand why you do what you do, and sometimes you're in classes where you're the only POC, or the only hijabi, or the only Muslim — seeing those people still hold onto their values made me feel liberated. It made me feel more comfortable to do the same.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer:
I'm an only child. I have two parents who work full-time, so I think a lot of my day is me left to my own devices, kind of getting through my day, in general.

Well, I sleep late, so I wake up late — the first time I wake up is for Fajr, and then usually I go back to sleep and wake up again for the day. Most of the time my days include college classes; in the past three years they have, before that it was classes in general, so I'd say I'm a student above everything else. I'll have something to eat — most of the time I do skip breakfast — then I'll try to do some work after whatever class I have, and I'll end the day with an episode of something.

Faith shows up in Salah most consistently, and it shows up in conversations with people. When I speak to someone, it always starts with salaam — that's when I'm speaking to Muslims, which is the majority of the people I surround myself with. The only time I was surrounded by non-Muslims was my two years at [UNIVERSITY 1], and even then Islam showed up in my conversations, because even when I made friends, I'd tell them, for five minutes I'm just going to go pray, and sometimes I'd explain, sometimes I wouldn't. In the past two years is the first time I even had a non-Muslim friend, so all of these experiences were pretty brand new for me. Just talking about Islam is probably where it shows up, and it shows up on Fridays, because I try to be more involved — I try to do more Quran on Fridays, I try to go to Jumu'ah, kind of reconnect. Another part of my routine is a Quran class once a week that's not on a Friday. I think those are the most consistent ways Islam shows up in my life.

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer:
I struggled with that a lot in the past two years. I went to [ISLAMIC SCHOOL 1] — I would have a hard time explaining it, so what I ended up sticking with was that [ISLAMIC SCHOOL 1] is a K-through-12 private Muslim school, and that's kind of how I'd introduce myself to people when they asked about my schooling experience.

I would explain that I spent my time there on the girls' side — my teachers were women, my classmates were girls — and that influenced the way I saw things, like group projects, where I had a hard time communicating with my male classmates. Eventually, in my last semester, I got really good at treating everyone properly — not professionally, just without being intimidated, I guess. I'd say my community is really close, and I had to remove some of that closeness when I was interacting with people at [UNIVERSITY 1]. For example, my teachers at [ISLAMIC SCHOOL 1] versus my professors at [UNIVERSITY 1] — there was more distance, and that was hard to transition into, because in my environment you know someone's grandparents, their siblings, their parents, how they live their lives, for the most part. As Muslims, we know everyone's at Jumu'ah on Fridays, or this day is special — Ashura recently came in, and that's something that brings me closer to my community members, because I kind of know them. It was different to explain that to people, because they'd be like, how is it possible that you're close to this many people, or that you know such things about this many people? And I'm like, the base is that we're all Muslim first. I'm not going to lie, eventually I just ended up not explaining — even with Salah, toward the end of my time at [UNIVERSITY 1], I would just say I have a meeting, and then I'd leave and come back to whatever we were doing.

It would be like the list of questions — hi, what's your major, what high school did you go to — because there were a lot of networking-type events, so I was constantly introducing myself. Hi, my name is [INTERVIEWEE], I'm an econ major, and then the follow-up questions, but it would be a couple minutes long and then you'd do it with the next person.

I had this one friend — she's Indian, and India has a lot of Muslims, but her family wasn't Muslim — and she knew enough about me that when I had to go pray or anything, it wasn't even a conversation, she'd be like, oh, okay. But she had Muslim friends too — two guys specifically — and whatever I told her about being Muslim was contrary to how they were acting. For example, she had a graduation party, and the boys were drinking at the party, and I'd say, I don't drink, I'm Muslim, and she'd look over and see the guy drinking, and I was like, okay.

They were Muslim, and I would constantly be — this was the first time I'd been around Muslims who weren't from my community. The Muslims I grew up with had a certain standard of practicing Islam, and the Muslims I ended up meeting came from everywhere in the U.S., from backgrounds that weren't maybe as strict as the way I was raised, so I'd end up contradicting myself in front of non-Muslims who had met these other Muslims. Sometimes I was kind of dumbfounded, like, now what do I say? It was a tricky thing to navigate. I remember, I told her I was Muslim and she still invited me to the party — it was really just at her apartment, a couple people — and I went, said hi, and then left, because they were acting a little, you know, as these things go.

A more specific example would be interactions between opposite genders — I'd have a certain boundary and other Muslims wouldn't, so I'd look like the more extreme side of the spectrum of Muslims at [UNIVERSITY 1], if that makes sense. Girls would be giving guys hugs, and I'd be like, no — I'll stand over here, or I'll wave, whatever the case may be, and it would confuse a lot of people. Over time I ended up just saying, I have a meeting, when I had to pray, instead of saying, I'm going to pray. But for the people who did understand there was a different spectrum of Muslims — there was another girl, she was white actually, from [STATE 1], and her background gave her more interaction with Muslims. I wasn't her only Muslim friend, and her previous Muslim friend also prayed, so when I said, while we were studying one day, hey, I'm going to go pray, she'd say, yeah, it's probably around the time, and I was like, how do you know that? So it was a degree of interactions, and they were all different.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer:
I've been in this community, I think, since kindergarten — I haven't really left this nook of [MASJID 1], [CITY 1], I've lived here a really long time. But my sense of self —

I'll draw a parallel to my time in [CITY 2], since I've been there twice now, each time about two weeks. When I was in that community, my sense of being a Muslim woman changed, and when I'm in my community here, it's also different. The way I grew up, everything was pretty harshly stated in terms of how I, as a Muslim woman, was meant to dress, act, and speak.

When I went into an environment where Muslim girls were encouraged to do things, I hadn't even thought that a whole community would be okay with their daughters — the girls of the community — doing something like that; it would just be natural there. I felt myself more inclined to make Islam a part of my — Islam is a huge part of my identity anyway, but more often than not it feels like a responsibility here. In [CITY 2], I remember thinking it was easier to be a Muslim woman in an environment where people aren't constantly telling me how to be one.

At first I thought it was because a lot of the Muslims I was meeting there followed the Hanafi madhhab, whereas [MASJID 1] is Hanbali — over in [CITY 2] there are a lot of Hanafi masajid. I had an easier time thinking about my future and what was possible, whereas here I feel very confined to a certain path — it's like you either do this or you don't, and that's what makes you a good Muslim woman, when you look back on your life at the end of it.

Here, something that comes to mind is post-grad life. I'm being told that I'm getting older, that times are changing, that people need stability and family before they reach for other goals. In interactions with friends, we're subconsciously mirroring to each other what we've been told, and when we have accomplishments, like getting a job or traveling, it becomes a bigger, more complicated conversation. With parents, family, and friends — even yesterday I went to someone's graduation party, and the group of girls there had been together since elementary school at [ISLAMIC SCHOOL 1], and we were discussing how we weren't allowed to travel, not even out of state for college, or when someone has a better opportunity, like an internship a couple months long in another state — it's an amazing opportunity, good for your resume, good for your career trajectory, good for figuring out if you even like this career path you picked at twenty years old. But we're not being allowed — it's more confinement, everyone's being pushed toward staying home in a very frustrating way. I'm seeing people have different reactions in personal interactions that they wouldn't have if they were able to leave their homes and experience things and become more evolved as people. Instead I'm seeing girls I grew up with backtracking to looking like they were raised in the 90s — not that the 90s were super confined, but I feel like we're moving backwards.

I think it might be my circle of people — even when I branch out a little, I'm hit with the same set of values. When I was in [CITY 2], I met girls from different states, specifically at the [ISLAMIC INSTITUTE 1] community, and all those girls had come in from out of state for education, for learning. Hearing their life experiences, I remember thinking I wished some of the girls I knew here had parents who would release them a little to have some of those experiences. It didn't make me sad, but it made me understand our differences more starkly.

I don't know why, because it's not by ethnicity — every friend I have is from a different ethnicity, and all the girls I met over there were too, so I don't think it's culture. It might be that our parents are trying to preserve Islam the best way they think they can, by monitoring us, trying to make sure we don't lose what they think the U.S. is making us lose — what they've taught us, what we've learned. And we've learned a lot, I think. At this point I'm 23, my friends are around 22 to 24, and I see such a difference in our development versus that of our peers, whether at school, at work, or in different states. Everyone's talking as if our lives are over, and I think that's so detrimental, because I feel like I have a lot left to do.

Now everyone's kind of just waiting for marriage, then talking about getting married, having a kid, raising it, and I'm like, I want to do different things — maybe I want to go study overseas in two years and learn something, or move to another state and take a job opportunity and figure out how to do that.

My parents let me travel for my friend's [ISLAMIC INSTITUTE 1] graduation — I didn't study there. When I was there for two weeks, I went to a lot of their final parties, a lot of the halaqas, and met a lot of new people. Another thing I'm noticing is that when you have experiences, you think differently, and then you act differently, and when you don't have a lot of experiences, you're more confined to daily suffocation — mundane things become very suffocating, and then you take it out on the people closest to you, if that makes sense.

I'm seeing that in a lot of my friends now — post-grad, a lot of us are looking for jobs, and it's not easy, so there's like one to two years at home, and their parents are like, well, you can't go out, you can't do this, you can't do that, so everyone's kind of banging their head against a wall trying to figure out how to have the pressure released from them.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, AND HOW?
answer: I do. Attending [ISLAMIC SCHOOL 1] was my mom's way of me seeking religious knowledge, and it was very helpful — I got a good base of Quran, Arabic, Islamic studies. On my own, I would volunteer at [ISLAMIC SCHOOL 1], for the youth — I was there for like four years. At [ISLAMIC INSTITUTE 2] I was a consistent volunteer, and I'd attend those classes, and the local masajid as well. I'm also enrolled in — I don't know if you know — [ONLINE ISLAMIC ACADEMY 1]. It's kind of like a catch-all two-year program for all the bases of Islamic knowledge, though I hesitate to say exactly where they're based, since it's [ONLINE ISLAMIC ACADEMY 1], it might just be through the Saudi government, I'm not sure. I'm going to start in August. Along with my classes, my dhikr, tafsir classes — I do try to seek Islamic knowledge, but inshallah I want to do it in a more structured way in the future.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
I've been wearing it since I was a kid, so it wasn't really an active choice, but I'd say when I was in middle school I wore it looser, and that was probably the closest I got to not wearing it the way I do now — I think now I wear it pretty coveringly. I think hijab is also your clothing, so the journey to skirts and abayas was also something that took time. Even now I'll still wear pants from time to time, but looser-fitting. I don't think I really had a problem with that — sometimes it would just be that something didn't fit and I'd need a size bigger so it would sit closer. Overall it was pretty simple, I guess. I think hijab in an environment with Muslims is one thing; in an environment without Muslims, you tend to gravitate more toward pants and less loose clothing, just to fit in. But I don't think I ever went to the side of just not wearing it.

Maybe a couple years ago, when I started looking into hijab materials and abaya styles and things like that, that's probably when I started thinking more about how to make myself feel good in hijab instead of just wearing it out of habit. It makes me feel more comfortable going outside, and I think I first noticed that specifically when I went to Saudi for the first time — I chose on my own to wear niqab there, because I was more comfortable in that country, since if you're the only face people can see, you're the only face being looked at. Hijab just makes me feel comfortable.

question: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN OR HIJAB?
answer: That even amongst girls who don't wear hijab — I have family friends where my mom told me, when I was growing up, that people had questioned her about why I was wearing hijab so young. She would literally put hijab on me and I'd be running around in a short-sleeve shirt. I think that was important, because for me it wasn't something I had to think too long about — it was just something I always did, like when you get ready to go outside, you wear hijab. Those same people, their kids are now very grown, mid-20s, late-20s, early-20s, and they're not covering at all — and it's gotten worse, they're more on the side of non-Muslim attire than just regular attire and not wearing hijab. That's something I noticed. Another thing is that the same people I grew up with, we probably had similar lives, but they would isolate me for being too religious, or it would be an assumption. I'm actually not the best Muslim ever, I promise, but it would be more difficult to connect with some people because I'd be isolated for being too religious. No, it would be an assumption — not based on conversations, just the hijab.

question: HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO WRONG PORTRAYALS OF MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer: Yes. If I was in a position of closeness to the person who misunderstood, I would clarify. If I wasn't, I'd kind of just let it slide, unfortunately, because it would become a thing they'd talk to their friend about, and it would turn into an altercation. I really don't think that if someone misunderstands something, it's my place — I'm not an alimah, I'm not a sheikh, it's not my place to give nasiha like that. But if it's someone I'm close to, I'll say, hey, this is actually wrong, Islam doesn't say that, this is how I've always practiced it — whether it's the hugging thing, the shaking hands thing, or praying salah on time. Those are things that if I know the person who misunderstood it, I would clarify, because I know that to be true and I know what this person is doing is not. That's as far as I would take it. If I'm close to the person, I'd correct their misunderstanding; if I'm not close to them, I wouldn't want to put myself in a position where they go talk to the Muslim person and put me in a situation of drama — it's not what I went to school for.

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer:
To stick on the theme we've been talking about, I'd say my identity as a Muslim woman in the [UNIVERSITY 1] environment is something I had to think about a lot. There were points where low iman found me more often than not, because I was constantly surrounded by people who seemed like they didn't put in as much effort into doing certain things, but they still got the same results as me, sometimes better — not in terms of academics, but maybe it was easier for them to make friends and maintain them, or easier to get internships or jobs, or have these achievements, and I'd find that frustrating in the moment.

But when it would be summer or winter break, the frustration would dissipate, because I'd be in my own environment again, and I'd understand the way life kind of goes, and my iman would go back up. So I faced this up and down — there was a lot of turmoil in that for about two years straight, and I think, hopefully, now that I'm out of there, it'll go back to normal.

question: WHAT INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS ARE PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
I think if there was something I could say to a lot of people, it would be that I wish we saw our lives in a different way. There's so much opportunity out there, so many experiences waiting to be had, so many different ways of achieving the same thing, that I really wish, instead of monitoring each other, instead of being jealous, instead of being scared that someone's going to put your experience down so you don't share it, and everyone isolating themselves to protect themselves from evil eye or whatever it may be — it would be better if we could see that we all have time, we all have the opportunity to live full lives without just waiting for marriage, or even graduation, to happen to us. If we could take it easier and stop waiting for the next thing, we'd have fuller lives, and it would make us happier people, because we have, mashallah, a lot of time and energy, and support from our parents, financial or emotional, and if we could take all of that in and let go of what might or might not happen, we'd have better experiences of living — because I look around and see girls who are anxious and exhausted and depressed, and I think we can really make a choice not to live this way.

Culturally, communities that have — for example, in Morocco, there are Christians, there are Jews, there are Muslims, but there's also a culture of not giving too much information, for everybody, whether Muslim or not. But when you come to the West, to our environment here in the U.S., people are much more open with their lives, so there's a lot more connection, and I feel like Muslim girls are constantly scared of each other, maybe subconsciously — how close can you be to someone when all you ever say to them is, hi, how are you doing, alhamdulillah, and that's it? There's nothing below the surface in terms of connection. How are you going to connect with someone if you don't know anything about them?

question: HAS WEARING HIJAB CREATED BARRIERS IN EDUCATION OR EMPLOYMENT?
answer:
I think I didn't feel like myself in a lot of my interactions there, because I was putting on this persona of disinterest and nonchalance, because that's how everyone around me was acting. There were people I went to class with two semesters in a row, saw multiple times a week, and I couldn't tell you their names — it was so distant, and that was really hard for me to go through, but I learned, I guess.

I think my degree of practice played into it — I'd wear abayas to school, and hijab of course, and there were times my entire row would be empty, everyone sitting in front of me or behind me. It was the strangest thing, but over time you get used to it, and when I'm outside school I have community, so it wasn't something that put me down, but it was something I noticed.

I'd look around at other Muslims and their experiences, and the ones who did have friends of the opposite gender, or connections with non-Muslim classmates, were living lives I didn't want for myself. So I decided if the alternative was to get involved in things that might distract me or reduce my iman, even though I'm already struggling with it, it wasn't really worth getting hung up on — though that wasn't my initial reaction, that's a conclusion I came to after thinking about it. My initial reaction was loneliness, feeling like, how is this fair — but then you get over it.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer:
My parents. It shapes a lot of my choices — my major, the school I went to, the job opportunities I even apply to, much less accept or reject. It shapes everything.

I think in my house we're not as cultural as the homes of people I know — a lot of people have a lot of culture in their house, but I couldn't tell you a couple things from either of my parents' cultures. Even so, if they're more cultural than our household, we still have some of the same experiences. Being the only child plays a role too, yeah.

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer:
In my family, I'm kind of living what they were unable to do. Even my major — one of my parents began college but wasn't able to complete it, and that was their major, their program. Even finishing high school — one parent wasn't able to do that, so school is connected to that.

In my community, I guess I'm a volunteer, because I end up in situations helping out — event childcare or just being part of helping — that's probably my most consistent role.

As an only child, I feel like I have a lot of free time, for some reason, or maybe I want to make my time free, but I think a lot of people I know seem to have less, so I just go out and help. It helps with connection — I'm the kind of person who feels better interacting with people, whether I've met them before or not, and then I come home feeling better than when I left. Maybe that's why.

question: WHAT DOES BELONGING FEEL LIKE HERE?
answer:
Belonging — I'd say in employment, belonging would be a workplace that lets you be employed without releasing you from your responsibilities as a Muslim. What I look for in a workplace is a place that will allow me to take off during the last ten nights of Ramadan, somewhere to pray salah. At [UNIVERSITY 1] we had the MSA space, which allowed for salah during the day, and a space for weekly Jumu'ah. Belonging in the West would be the same as belonging anywhere else. When I was in [CITY 2], the masajid gave me a lot of belonging, because they had spaces for wudu, where you could wash your feet the way I do at home, and handheld bidets in the bathrooms. Belonging as a Muslim there made me feel like my wudu was accepted, my salah was accepted — on this side, that's more what I get from my house than my workplace or school.

Yes, a little — not that people need to be thinking about me twenty-four seven, but basically, yes. It's literally just wudu and salah, being comfortable knowing I'm able to pray in whatever space I'm in. In general, I'm one of those people who walks around with a prayer mat and will just take it out and start praying — everyone will look at me, but I don't really care. Me and my friend go to [CITY 3] a lot, and we both have those little things in our prayer mats, and we'll just pick a corner of the grass and pray. Nothing has happened to us so far, and inshallah nothing does. If you want to belong in an environment, you'll figure it out.

question: HOW DOES LIVING HERE SHAPE HOW YOU PRACTICE OR SHOW YOUR FAITH?
answer:
This country — I think the older I get, the more I realize that perhaps we didn't belong in the first place. I was just really young, so it wasn't as stark for me, but the older I get, the more I realize that very systemic things in this country are anti — not only anti-Islam, but anti any structured religion.

Even before getting into the different sects — when I meet Orthodox Christians or Orthodox Jews, the non-extreme ones, I find their experiences relate to mine in unexpected ways. I'd met Christians before [UNIVERSITY 1], but at [UNIVERSITY 1] is the first time I met Orthodox Jews, and a lot of them had the same struggles I did. I met a girl who also went to a Jewish private school, and it was the funniest conversation — every single point was matching. She was shocked about how wild some of the students could get, how distant the professors were from students, how there wasn't really respect in professor-student relationships — for example, at the end of every lecture, some students, while the professor is still talking, will just get up, pack, zip up their bags, and leave, because it's the end of the time slot. I'm like, he can finish his sentence, thirty seconds isn't the end of the world — and she was relating to all of it. I remember thinking, I wish you didn't love Israel the way you do, because we could have been friends.

She was part of the student union, and I saw her walking around with those shirts on October 7th, but she was a nice person right up until I found that out, so it was conflicting information for me — why am I relating to you so much? But I did meet very normal, very nice Orthodox Jews too, same situation. I remember that one girl specifically because she hit every nail on the head of my experiences as well.

question: HAVE YOU BEEN MADE TO FEEL YOUR FAITH CONFLICTS WITH YOUR COUNTRY?
answer: A threat to what? Not personally, but I do know of Muslim girls in the MSA who were being stalked around campus after October 7th, and the police were called on them. There was a Jewish Students for Peace group, and another one, and they'd host events on the main mall at [UNIVERSITY 1] with police surrounding the perimeter, as if the Muslim students were going to attack them. I found that very funny, because the aggressors and stalkers of Muslim girls on campus were the ones being protected with police from Muslims — that dichotomy was very, very annoying. I told my mom about it, and that day she called me early and told me to come home, because it was getting dangerous on campus. That was my fault, because I told her something that had happened — things don't really escalate on that campus more often than not, there's no escalation, but she was freaking out, she literally told me to skip class and come home. That was the first time that ever happened. It was a bunch of conflicting situations, but it did not happen to me personally, feeling like I was a threat.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: When I was younger, in high school, it wasn't as prevalent — I was in Islamic studies at [ISLAMIC SCHOOL 1], hearing about the Akhirah, the Day of Judgment, hearing that everything happens for a reason, that if a du'a isn't answered you might get something better in the Akhirah, or even in this life. But it didn't really sink in for me until around 2022, when I started thinking that we have entire lives left to live. I started zooming out from my day-to-day experience and seeing it as part one of a journey: life in the grave is one part, the Day of Judgment is one part, and then the last part is when you're actually in wherever you end up — inshallah, for all of us, Jannah — but that's another life to live. When you zoom out from your experiences, everything becomes easier to deal with — disappointment, isolation, loneliness, all of it doesn't affect you the way it once would have. Even if you feel it temporarily, even very strongly for a while, it's still not as much as you'd feel it if you didn't think about how this is just part one of several.

question: HOW DO YOU MAKE SENSE OF WHAT IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL?
answer:
Before, I used to want a lot of control over what's happening around me, what's happening to me, what kind of experiences I'm in — I wanted to know all the details, all the questions answered, the plan. I still am like that, but now I'm more certain that things are going to work out however the chips fall, and I have a more hands-off approach.

If I'm sure I've done everything I could to do things the correct way, even if I make a mistake, I still tried to do it correctly — that gives me peace and comfort, makes me less stressed, less anxious about the situation. When I look around at some of my classmates, I see they don't have that same peace, and they're having different experiences, acting very wild, and I don't want to live what I've seen someone live through. Even if my experience doesn't make me feel pretty when I look in the mirror — because as a Muslim woman, you dress well for the sake of Allah — and even if I'm having the worst day, no makeup, all of that, the alternative doesn't attract me. Yeah, the broader, non-Muslim community — that's what I mean.

question: WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR PRACTICING YOUR RELIGION IN THE LONG RUN?
answer:
When I think about practicing in the long run, what I'm working on right now is making sure my secular experiences are of benefit, and to increase my Islamic knowledge and have that shape how I do things secularly — what company I work for, what job I do, what repercussions come from the work I do, and who I give my energy to.

I mean, in the wider world — if I work for a company that does bad in the world, and my job strengthens that badness, I don't think the repercussions just go into the air. If you work for a place that does bad things, you get a portion of that. I want to be able to do work where I'm certain the repercussions are positive.

question: WHAT IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR HEART, INTENTION, AND OUTWARD PRACTICE?
answer: If it's at a park, I have a lot less stress. If it's on a sidewalk, or even at school in a hallway, I'm more aware of my surroundings — not being afraid to be openly Muslim, and consoling myself that I'm genuinely not doing anything wrong, so there's no reason my heart should be pounding like this.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer: It means just trying my best to fulfill my obligations, trying my best to have supplementary acts of worship outside the obligatory ones. I think it just means trying my best, even if the scope of what I'm doing is small. It sounds easy, but it's actually really hard — something as small as praying on time could be a battle for some people and not for others, or just having tawakkul in Allah. Especially now, I feel like the culture of the U.S. is very anti-tawakkul — propaganda, people's think pieces, even pop culture, all these things pull you away from having tawakkul in Allah. A lot of it is fear-mongering, or just makes it difficult to say, I know everything is going to be okay. It's about finding a balance and bringing that into my personal life.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer:
Liberation? I think when you travel, you feel liberated, because — there's a hadith, or an ayah of the Qur'an, where we're told to travel Allah's earth — and just thinking about that makes me feel like traveling is liberation, because you go somewhere and see different things, but the one thing that remains no matter where you go is making sure you're fulfilling your obligations to Allah — praying on time, making proper wudu, making ghusl on time if you get off your period, not letting it drag a day or two. It's making sure that no matter where you are, you have your set of things to do — your adhkar, your du'as — you're not alone.

The more I travel, the more I realize that. Traveling is liberating because when you come back to your environment, you see things differently — where you might have thought, this is such a frustrating thing I have to do every day, now you come home and think, thank God I have this, alhamdulillah for this. Or you come back with different experiences, and when you talk with your community or family, you're able to help someone out of their struggle, give them a different way to see things.

Earlier I was talking about feeling confinement, and I guess I said that because it's the most relevant thing to me currently, something I was struggling with.

It's liberating because it helps me see what's actually important, where my priorities are, and that liberates me from the stress of the job search, since I recently graduated and it's a huge theme in my life right now. It liberates me from being anxious about the future, because even if things are delayed, even if there's no stream of income currently, I still know my top priorities are in order.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer: An ordinary day in my life usually starts with school. Between my childhood and three years with family, I went for a GED, and then continued with career and academics thereafter. That's how I began my career.

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer: We are people dedicated to our families, kind-hearted, wanting the best for others as we wish for ourselves, and making a positive impact in the lives of ourselves, our families, and the community we care about.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer:
I've been in the United States since 1998, so that would be about 28 years this year. Comparing from the time I started in this country till now, there's been a lot of positive changes, and also a lot of negativity, and that actually spurs from 9/11, when the World Trade Center was attacked. From there, being a Muslim became more difficult, especially as a hijabi — walking around the streets became more difficult. Having the fear that I could be attacked always came to my mind, and especially going to school, completing my undergrad was really challenging, because working as a student, not having a car, having to move around — even on public transportation, at least about 75% of the time, I always faced negativity from people on the bus and around me. That really impacted how I felt in terms of my confidence level. As much as I was confident, the attack and Islamophobia really affected how I did things, how I tried to embark on things and make decisions. I preferred to be within a community, or within the house, where I felt more comfortable, rather than going outside — even working was difficult, because it was more dangerous, since people would call me names just because of my identity. But I did not want to back down, and I continued wearing my hijab — my dressing was part of me, so I was not going to back down on it. But I realized it affected the way I went about my daily life outside the house. I'd say that was after 9/11, thereabouts, maybe around the mid-2000s.

That gave me a little bit of confidence, because of the environment I found myself in and the people I worked with — they loved me for who I was, and also protected me. If there was any backlash from anybody outside when we went out, they were there for me, even though they were non-Muslims, because of the way I already carried myself around them — it felt comfortable, that as a Muslim, we're just like other people who want the best for ourselves and our families. That helped me regain a lot of confidence, starting with my children and all of that. I guess now the backlash is back, because of the political atmosphere, but I think overall the confidence I gained back then has helped me navigate the challenges of now.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, AND HOW?
answer: Yes, I do seek religious knowledge actively. I turn to scholars, I turn to my husband — he's more knowledgeable in the faith than me — and I turn to the Book of Allah, the Quran, for guidance, and also the sayings of the Prophet, peace be upon him, for guidance on how to face whatever challenge I may be dealing with.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
My hijab story is so funny. I started wearing hijab back in my native country, Nigeria. I went to a Christian school — being in that Christian environment, we were forced, not even given an option, to practice Christianity. My dad was not enforcing hijab, my parents did not enforce us to wear it — we didn't even grow up with the knowledge of girls wearing hijab. We were only taught to be modest in dressing and to have the best of characters representing ourselves outside our homes.

I remember I got sick at a period of time, and that sickness really impacted the way I viewed life. That was around the time I was going to get admission into college — that year, me and my sister were supposed to start college, but I couldn't, because of my sickness. That sickness made me turn back to Allah, and I started reading the Quran. As I read, I started realizing all the falsehoods we'd been taught in high school. That strained the relationship I had with my siblings and my parents, because me and my sister, who went to the same school, had that mindset that Christianity was the answer, that it wasn't a sin. But now, going outside my own shell, outside the knowledge my parents had given me, I had to navigate the challenge of finding the truth. It was either I continued with Christianity, what we'd been forced to do, or I found a way to understand — if Christianity was the answer, I'd understand what I was doing, and if Islam was the answer, I'd understand that too. So I started reading the Quran, and the more I read, the more conviction I gained that this was the truth.

The next year I gained admission — I went through the application process again and got into a polytechnic in Nigeria, and that really changed my perspective, because when I stepped into that university, regardless of the way I dressed, the people who came to my aid — this was a place I didn't know anybody, didn't know where I was going to sleep, had no idea how I was going to live my life there — the people who came to my aid were Muslims, and they weren't even fully practicing hijab or anything. I met a friend I still have a relationship with now, as a sister — she took me by the hand when she saw me crying, and we went through the admission process together, how to register and all of that. I realized Islam was just the truth — Islam, the way of life, was what gave me that peace of mind, that regardless of what I did, I could go back to Allah and ask for forgiveness and not be criticized, not be put down. After my first semester, I saw a lot of sisters wearing hijab, and they started attending Muslim Students' Association meetings, and I just fell in love with the way Islam was presented — it wasn't hard, it wasn't harsh, it was subtle, in a way that made me feel, okay, even without wearing hijab, I could be a Muslim who could become better and understand the reason why Allah asked women to wear hijab. Once I understood the ayah Allah revealed about covering, in Surat al-Ahzab, I realized this was a conviction I would obey my Lord with — I would be better, rather than trying to please the people around me who wanted me to be part of them. So the struggle of trying to balance it out — I decided no, I was going to stand firm on my deen, my religion, and get better at it, because I understood it more. That's also what led me to make sure that when I have kids in the future, I'd be able to help them understand the reason behind hijab, rather than just putting it on them.

The hijab protects me, it gives me confidence, it gives me the reassurance that obeying Allah is the ultimate, and when I obey my Creator, everything else becomes easy, because Allah said with hardship comes ease as well. So regardless of what I may be facing, I know that hijab is just an outer covering — it comes from my inner self, from having the conviction that Allah is the one who told me to cover, and in obeying Him, He has told me in the Quran that whoever obeys His commands will surely get a reward, which is happiness. So anything that happens to me, I know it's only by the design of Allah, not any human being. My hijab has given me the confidence to navigate challenges in life and know that this is just a passing trial, and the ultimate goal is working toward the life we're promised in the Akhirah.

question: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN OR HIJAB?
answer:
I think people categorize us as — maybe privileged, subdued, that we cannot make it in life, that we should not make it in life because we are women. The misunderstanding the media has portrayed to people of the Western world has been really negative, and that's the reason a lot of people in America, or the Western world, who have no real knowledge of hijabis, of the role of women in Islam, misunderstand us as women wearing hijab as being subdued — that we cannot have a career, cannot make it in life, that we're subject to harshness and can't make it past a certain level, even in education. For example, that education isn't something we should have.

I remember a time I was teaching, and a parent came to me — her child was in my classroom — and I believe she looked at me because of the hijab and thought, how can this person even be a teacher, she's not worthy of being a teacher. She tried to challenge me one day, and as she did, she wanted to know my educational background. Once I told her, she just apologized to me, because she'd had it at the back of her mind, from the way the media has portrayed Muslim women, that we're not able to have a good education, not given that opportunity, and she'd had that negativity pushed onto her. That really changed her perspective toward me from that day onward — the respect she gave me afterward was much more than the way she treated me at the beginning of our relationship as her child's teacher. That person was non-Muslim.

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer:
I remember, in 2015, after having three of my children, I faced the reality of either sending my children to public school or being in an Islamic environment. My house was far from the school, and I enjoyed my career as a teacher, I loved teaching, but I had to face the reality that it was becoming too stressful because of the distance, and we didn't want to live outside our means — whatever we had as income, me and my husband, we were going to live within it, we weren't going to get a house or a place of living that was more than our income could sustain. So we had to face the reality of either homeschooling our children to still give them the best education, or sending them to public school, because the alternative was just too stressful. That was the challenge we faced, and I remember trying to think, why do we have to go through this? But one thing was certain to us: our children were not going to go to public school, no matter what. We were not going to face the same challenges we'd faced with hijab, and the stories we'd heard from Muslim colleagues about children facing a lot of bullying in public schools, especially children who wear hijab — that could affect their confidence, and we didn't want our children to face that. We had girls, so it was a tough decision, but looking back, we're thankful to Allah that He guided us to make it — it's not a decision we've regretted one bit. Navigating it was the first challenge: how were we going to give our kids what we wanted them to have, and also let them have a social environment for their own well-being. We were able to balance that with activities for the kids, and alhamdulillah, they're young ladies now, thriving, in college, and I believe they've navigated the challenges they've faced as well.

First, we had to do some research — me and my husband had to sit down and decide, okay, it's only going to be one income, sustaining a family of five. So we sat down and wrote out all our expenses — what could we cut off, like cable TV, things that were more luxury than necessity. Cutting those off didn't impact our life in any way. My husband had to double down on his work, and I had to be the one staying home with the kids. We had to draw up a plan for how we were going to teach the kids the curriculum, to make sure they'd be able to keep up with other kids outside the home, and when it came to any state testing, they'd be able to pass, to be at the same level as kids outside our house. We consulted with people who were homeschooling, and got support from a few friends and our family too — when you don't stand alone, when you learn from others, you realize how much easier things can be. Having the right support, our family was there for us for the times I needed breaks, and that's how we navigated the situation.

When we made that decision, I realized, okay, I trained to do that work as a teacher, teaching other kids, and I also wanted to be in an Islamic environment — I didn't want to teach in a public school. I had gone through public school for my teacher training, and I'd made that decision within my heart that teaching in a public school wasn't something I'd want to do, except as a last resort. When we'd weighed all our options, I realized I could continue teaching, just teaching my own daughters instead. Especially for my five-year-old, who wasn't in school yet, I decided to take that on myself — I could take the same grade level I was teaching in school and put that energy into my daughter, and see if I could have a positive impact on her, if she could accomplish what the kids in my classroom could accomplish. I looked at that as a success for me. I realized the flexibility of homeschooling let me do a lot of things I was able to do more of outside the classroom, but also use my teacher mindset to teach her. When we decided to put her in an online Islamic school, and she went through testing, she was two grades above level, and that's how I looked at it as my success — that was what made me happy. I gave up something, but I saw something else in my own daughter that I probably wouldn't have seen had I not made that decision to stay home with my kids.
