question: WHAT INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS ARE PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
Definitely. The first thing, as a Muslim woman, you must be educated — you must be well-rounded to be able to have an impact. When we hear the stories of Aisha, radiAllahu anha, and Khadija, radiAllahu anha, and all the other wives, all the Muslim women back then, that's our own pathway too — we should also have a positive impact, and one of the ways we can do that is to be educated. You need to know what society is learning and be able to differentiate it, so you're not just in your own bubble, thinking this is the only way to approach things. Understanding what others who are non-Muslim think, understanding their thinking, and how you can make a positive impact, is what we build our community upon. A Muslim woman, even if she's going to be a stay-at-home mom, must be well-rounded, educated in the Western world and also in Islamic studies.

I think it goes back to our own parents. For me, at least within our Nigerian community, I'd say almost everybody had the same orientation from our parents, giving us that educational background — it wasn't a choice, you had to go to school, you had to learn — so that when people confront you with challenges, when people come to challenge your deen, you're able to understand where they're coming from and answer whatever questions they present. If you're living in ignorance, the way people will treat you, the way you'll be impacted by their thinking, you'll realize you'll be leaving your own being and your own beliefs to believe in what other people believe, because you don't have that deep understanding of what you've been leaving.

Yes, we had Islamic education at home, but it was on a basic level — not the way I'm teaching my own kids now, it's different. Yes, my school in Nigeria was a Christian school, but at home, and I lived in a boarding house, so it wasn't as if I was seeing my parents every day — we'd spend the whole semester at school, going to church and all of that, and then come home and practice our deen again.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer: I feel most responsible, first of all, to my family, my nuclear family, and to myself. And to my Creator — I'm responsible to follow and obey the commands of my Creator, Allah, and responsible for myself, since the actions I take will either impact me positively or negatively. Once the decisions I make for myself impact my own family, if I've made positive decisions, I know that positive attitude carries through to my children, my spouse. But if I make wrong choices, there's a tendency I'll bring down my own family too. As the adage goes, show me your face and I'll tell you who you are — the people around you say something about the type of person you are. So if I try to be a good person, if I try to follow the commands of Allah, the decisions I make, for the most part, mean I want people of that same mindset around me, my circle, to help me when I'm going through difficulties. So definitely, my responsibility is to love my family, my extended family, and my community as well.

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer:
I think going back to the Quran, it lays down the basics of the role of a woman, the impact she has. Even for those who don't have a spouse — they always say, behind every successful man is a woman. I even look at, for the non-Muslim example, someone like Bill Clinton, the former president — when we say he was a successful man, even through his struggles, his wife was beside him, and that's how non-Muslims think of it too. For a Muslim woman, it's even more — you have that impact, you're the one training the next generation. When you train a child well, you train the nation well, because that child goes out to train others, and the cycle continues. But if the mother is ignorant of her role, of the importance of having a positive impact on her children, you'll realize you'll lose them, because society will take your children away with their own stories, their own falsehood, and you'll see the children drift from believing in the oneness of Allah.

I believe it's something wider society shares too, not just an individual belief. A lot of people, even non-Muslims, don't send their children to public school, because they believe the way they want to raise their children is different from the way the public system trains them, and a lot of that comes from the larger curriculum being taught — as an individual, you don't have the role to make changes in that system, so you either go along with it or find a way to create your own system, one aligned with your belief system. So I believe it's more of a general thing than just an individual thing.

question: HOW DOES LIVING HERE SHAPE HOW YOU PRACTICE OR SHOW YOUR FAITH?
answer: My faith and the country I live in — it's challenging, and it also gives me the assurance that the more people understand me as a Muslim woman, the more they go back and learn about Islam, and accept it, because they can reason, they can understand — it's not about logic, it's the truth, but you have to understand it, and understanding it means you can't be in ignorance, can't just follow someone saying something on social media. You have to sit down and educate yourself, and when you educate yourself, you empower yourself, and when you empower yourself, you can stand on top of the mountain knowing your empowerment and your knowledge are based on understanding your faith, and you're able to navigate anything based on that understanding. So what I've found is that standing my ground, not backing down on hijab, has helped me a lot in this country — it's given me the confidence to navigate things, in a respectful and firm way, so that people understand me, and I can have an impact through how I present myself to others. When I represent myself well, people can say, this person is a Muslim, and this is different from what they've heard about Muslim women, and that can lead them to educate themselves and understand Islam.

question: HAVE YOU BEEN MADE TO FEEL YOUR FAITH CONFLICTS WITH YOUR COUNTRY?
answer: Oh yes — going back to 9/11, it was a huge challenge, because I was working as a student. When we came to this country, it was just me and my brother — my parents brought us and went back, so we were left to navigate ourselves here. We had family friends, but the main navigation was left to us — either based on what our parents had taught us, and we continue that legacy, or we let society drift us away from that path of being Muslim. When 9/11 happened, even the first few days after, I remember getting on the bus, sitting down just like any other time, and I never realized how that would affect me. I remember a white woman screaming right in my face, calling me all the words they called us back then — you're Osama bin Laden, you want to kill us in this country, you need to go back to your country. It wasn't easy — I'd go home and cry, not want to go to work again. We didn't have a personal car, my brother didn't either, so we had to take public transportation to school and work and back home — it wasn't just getting on the bus once, it was an everyday thing, so that threat grew more and more. My boss offered, at that time, that one of my colleagues could pick me up and drop me off close to my house, but I realized, how long was that going to last? People were ignorant, people were angry about what happened, and they put that anger on Muslim women, because for men it was easier not to be identified as Muslim, but for a Muslim woman wearing hijab, they'd consider you a terrorist, Osama bin Laden, here to hurt them. I never made comments to anybody — I understood why they were angry, but I didn't understand why they had to direct that anger at me, an individual just trying to go about my daily life like them. That was the threat I faced then, and alhamdulillah, it strengthened me, it strengthened my iman — I knew this was a test from Allah, and the only way to pass it was to stand my ground on being a Muslim woman, and nothing less.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: About Jannah — that's one thing we do, sharing reminders as a family after morning prayers. Allah's promise to those who do good, who pray their salah, pay their zakat, do good to others, be kind — simple things — is that if you do these things, inshallah, by His mercy, you'll gain the pleasure of Allah and get into Jannah. That's written clearly in the Quran, that He has promised this. He created the heavens and the earth, He makes the night turn to day and the day turn to night — the signs around us give us that understanding that the One who created all of this is the only one who can give us the hereafter, His paradise. Following those simple things He's said in the Quran isn't complicated — just go about your daily life the way that pleases Allah, and continue to seek His mercy. Those are the simple, uncomplicated things we talk about in my family — smile at others, be kind, when you see someone holding something and want to go through a door, hold it for them, that's an act of charity. Those little things count, and you don't know which one thing you do that pleases Him. We also remind ourselves of the story of the people of the cave, trapped in that cave, each pleading to Allah that this one thing I've done, use it to open this gate for us — and Allah did. We use all these examples as our own reminders, that when we do good, we can use that to hope for the best outcome.

question: HOW DO YOU MAKE SENSE OF WHAT IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL?
answer:
Not everything is something we would understand. I remember, I lost one of my sisters in 2014 to cancer — she was a medical doctor, and I kept thinking, she was a medical doctor and yet she couldn't cure herself. No matter all the things she'd read, all the things she did, none of it was going to cure her from that cancer. That journey lasted about six years, and she passed at 24. Throughout that journey, it gave me the insight that regardless of the trial, you just put your trust in Allah. It's tough, it's difficult — I couldn't make sense of it, that a doctor couldn't cure herself — but looking back, Allah has said He will test us with life and death, and that really opened my eyes, my horizon, that regardless of who you are, you'll be tested, and regardless of whether you can make sense of it or not, you just put your trust in Allah. With that sadness came the fact that my mom had passed away just four years before my sister — that grief was still there, but carrying on with the hope that Allah has my back. Even if I have to sit down and cry for a moment, it's okay, because I know He has my back through this ordeal. I don't need to, like in my country, where people will say, oh, maybe someone did this to this person, maybe someone cursed them — no, there's no reason to navigate that when you have Allah. That's what allows for the sakeenah to get you through the test.

Alhamdulillah, the grief is there all the time, but we always look back and say, alhamdulillah, she died as a believer, peace be with her.

question: WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR PRACTICING YOUR RELIGION IN THE LONG RUN?
answer: About the long run, I think it's just having that confidence and understanding that you're only answerable to Allah, not to humans. I always think, when it's time for Salah, and I'm scared that maybe if I try to pray something would happen to me, someone would attack me — which does happen — but I know that if I'm doing what pleases Allah, and He takes my soul at that point, I'll be happy, I'll have that sakeenah. When we're at the mall with my kids and it's time for salah, we try so hard to work our schedule around salah, but sometimes it does happen that we're still out shopping, and that's how it goes. I've taught my children, and led them by example — even at a funeral, we always have a prayer mat in our bag, and we go and pray, then continue whatever we're doing. Salah is our priority — if anything happens to us because we delayed too much, we'd find ourselves asking, why didn't I pray? Why didn't I pray on time? So to the best of my ability, me and my husband, we've tried to instill that in our children. Even when we're traveling and it's time for salah, we can combine our prayers — we find a place to stop, combine our salah, and continue the journey. Once salah time comes, you start to feel uneasy, you won't be at peace with yourself until you pray, because it's already part of you, and something that's part of you is hard to tear away, except if you put yourself in a community where Islam isn't practiced. So we navigate it so that our salah comes first — if we want to go out, we ask what time salah is coming, maybe we delay going out until after salah, or if it's a place where we know we won't be able to pray at all — like the airport — things have become much easier there too, you can find a place to pray now. Society has changed over time, and we're seeing that a lot of people see Muslims as just as good as them, or even better, and that's what we believe.

question: WHAT IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR HEART, INTENTION, AND OUTWARD PRACTICE?
answer: This is in obedience to Allah — that's what Allah wants me to do. My wudu is my key to my salah, and my salah is my key to my hereafter. When you're praying, you're in total submission to your Creator, you're obeying Allah at that time, because that's what He ordained us to do — as it's said in scripture, He created us for nothing but to worship Him. So when that time of salah comes, what I'm thinking about is that this is related to Allah, and nothing else comes before Him. After that, Allah makes everything else easy — even the difficult things become easy, by His grace. Sometimes when I'm finding something very difficult — like I said, my day begins with tahajjud — I put it in front of Allah: make things easy for me, make this decision easy for me, the decision that's best for me. That's total submission to Allah, alhamdulillah.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer: It means everything to me, actually. It means my conformity to my religion — my dressing, my eating, my mingling, my whole life, because Islam is a way of life. Everything I'm doing — the Prophet, peace be upon him, said that your daily activities, if you have the right intention, can be an act of worship. If I'm going to find a means for my family to eat, a source of income, or cooking for my children, for my family to be healthy, to not go hungry — that's an act of worship, because it's what Allah wants us to do. Everything connects — when I give my children food, Allah has given us the sustenance and the ability to cook it, and it's all an act of worship. When you have that mindset, subhanAllah, even when you're feeling tired, that energy comes to you, because you know every day won't be a perfect day. Even the best of man, the Prophet ﷺ, said, I'm nothing but a man like you, I am not perfect, there's no perfection. So I don't work toward perfection, I work toward doing my best, and when I do my best, I know Allah takes care of the rest.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer: Liberation is knowing you're not answerable to anyone, you're not begging anyone for your sustenance. Maybe someone comes to you and says, if you don't practice your deen, I'll give you this much money, I'll give you this, I'll give you that — but you feel a great surge knowing you're not begging anyone for sustenance, that whatever little you have, putting your trust back in Allah, gives you that liberation. Especially with money — people feel that's the number one thing they're answerable to, that if I don't have it, I can't do this, I can't go. But if Allah's given me this, I can be happier than someone who has much more and has a lot of worries. Because the barakah is there — Allah puts the barakah in it — I can have one dollar and feel on top of the world, because I know my life is in His care, that He has my back in everything I'm doing. That's when I feel most liberated, every day, because when it comes to my daily activities, my husband trying to work according to company policy — but anything that's against our deen, we find a way to let his boss know, no, we don't practice this, I don't go for happy hour. I don't have to bend to your culture to have my Islam taken from me — I would not bend to that. I do the work, I can do what I need to do to take care of my family, but anything that crosses the line with my Islam, I go with my Islam, and I know Allah will take care of me, because I'm doing what He wants me to do.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer:
An ordinary day in my life: I'm a homemaker and a homeschooler mainly, and a mother of three. In my spare time I teach Halaqa, the Islamic study circle, and I teach Quran one-on-one. A regular day would be, after I wake up in the morning I do my morning worship and have breakfast. On school days I would drop off my oldest child, who is a college student, at the train station, then come back and either exercise or have breakfast, then wake up my third child, who is in middle school, so she can start her day — that would be homeschooling, or maybe we would go to a homeschooling co-op. If we come back before lunch, I give lunch too. I also have my father-in-law at home, so I give him lunch, or if we are gone the whole day I set his lunch out. By afternoon I do dinner prep, and dinner would be around before or after Maghrib. Most of my Quran one-on-one teaching is in the afternoon on some days. I guess that would be a typical day.

How else does faith show up in a given day? Well, first of all, there is all the compulsory ritual worship — the five prayers. In the morning I do extra; I'm trying to memorize Quran, so a lot of time is for that, and some other worship habits I'm trying to build — sometimes successfully, sometimes not. I'm still training myself to have those habits. A lot of it is because I teach Quran and have to prep for my halaqas, and then there's teaching my kids, especially my youngest. Faith is basically the center — I can't really answer that separately, because your life is faith, and everything else is because of your faith. My service for my family and my in-laws is all based on faith. I don't really see a dichotomy where faith shows up sometimes and doesn't show up other times.

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer:
I would say that I'm somebody who believes in God and tries to center her (life on that). I guess somebody who's never met a Muslim woman would assume I'm not Muslim, so I would center tawhid first — that we believe in absolute monotheism, that our faith centers around God, and a Muslim woman would be somebody who — and that's why I wear the hijab, because it is an act of obeying God.

The Muslim community would be a community of people with diverse backgrounds. It would be a community that believes in one God and believes in the existence of the prophets and the holy books. I guess I would center it around the pillars of faith and what we believe, but then I would add that we're a diverse community with many backgrounds and cultures, and also different levels of understanding and different levels of practice.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer:
The community I'm part of right now — I would see myself as part of several communities. I'm in [CITY 1, STATE 1]; there's a mosque five minutes from me, so you could say I'm part of that community. I'm also originally [COUNTRY], so I'm part of the [COUNTRY] community in [CITY 2], which is further away, and I teach in a different masjid, so I see myself as part of that community too, although maybe a little loosely since I just teach there and I'm not there day to day or at their events. And I feel very much part of the [RELIGIOUS INSTITUTION] community because I attend the events regularly and I'm actively volunteering, so I consider myself part of all these communities.

How has it changed over time? My immediate community in [CITY 1] — when my kids were small and I first moved into this place, I was much more involved and much more regular; for example, I would attend every Jumu'ah, and I even started volunteering in the school based in that masjid and became a teacher there for about two years. When I stopped teaching, I still went there regularly, but as time went on I felt less connected to that community because there's a predominant culture there, and as a person who's not part of that culture, you feel it — you feel that you're not really seen. When the masjid leadership changed to a younger, more American-educated person who was more open to input from all communities and held events inviting community input, I got excited and active again. Then that new leadership was overturned by the older leadership, back to something that isn't exactly exclusive — nobody would say we're not open to other cultures, everything is technically open — but the atmosphere and feel of it is a kind of hidden, subtle exclusivity, I guess I can say that.

I've been in this community as long as I've been married, since 2005, so twenty-one years. I'm an idealist, so I always say the masjid is Allah's house, and the ones running it are people, and people aren't going to be perfect. So I was very doggedly just attending, attending, attending. Some of my friends, especially those more born and bred here, even though they're part of that culture, moved away because they felt it was too cultural, but I'm the one who's not from that culture and I kept saying no, this is Allah's house, you focus on Allah's house, and Allah's house is maintained by believers. For almost two decades I tried not to let the atmosphere affect me, but I think I kind of gave up a little, especially when someone made a harsh comment about my daughter, who was in her early teens, about her wearing pants. That was a small thing, but she became masjid-averse, and that affected me. Then COVID came, and we were inside and didn't go for Jumu'ah at all, and when we could go back to the masjid, I had by then found [RELIGIOUS INSTITUTION], and that spiritual need was fulfilled by [RELIGIOUS INSTITUTION] — Alhamdulillah, it really fulfilled that spiritual need. My eagerness, my idealist drive to always go to the masjid, kind of waned. After COVID, I stopped going to my closest, local community masjid as much for Jumu'ah — I come now and then, depending on the events, but not as regularly as before. For taraweeh, I still come regularly out of love for it, but outside Ramadan I'm not as consistent as before. So that has changed.

As for my sense of myself as a Muslim woman — Alhamdulillah, Alhamdulillah. Yes, it's definitely changed since I started wearing the hijab in my mid-20s, and I can say that was my gate to Islam. Before that I practiced Islam more ritualistically and very inconsistently — if I felt like praying, I'd pray; if it was convenient, I'd pray; if not, I didn't. I led a lifestyle that didn't refer to Islam at all; I just followed what felt good, what I thought was good, and how [ETHNICITY] culture and society were, so that's what I followed. Hijab became my gateway into Islam, because hijab was the hardest thing for me to apply. I went back and forth for nine years after I found out it was compulsory, and once Allah allowed me and made it easy for me, everything else after that became easy. I would always check whether something was halal or not; Islam became my guidance. I started learning, taking classes, and all my remorse over my previous lifestyle and my gratitude that Allah allowed me to change propelled me forward. The learning is a lifelong thing. So the evolution has been more learning and being more careful about the deen. Knowledge-wise, Alhamdulillah, I've improved a lot — I'm almost fifty now and I wore hijab at twenty-six. But I have to point out that sincerity-wise it's a struggle, always a struggle. In the early days I would read Yasin and tears would just come; I remember long tahajjud with tears, and that's kind of my benchmark, because I remember how passionate and remorseful you are when you first come to it, like a new convert. So I try to remind myself that knowledge-wise I'm exponentially further along, but sincerity-wise it's always up and down, and I have to fight within myself, especially now that I'm in spaces where I'm teaching — I have to remind myself about sincerity, about not taking it for granted, and about not letting it affect me when people are very respectful toward me. I can't say how the evolution is sincerity-wise; I just ask Allah to accept it and help me, but I get scared because I remember how sincere I was in those early days. I try to stay aware of that.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, AND HOW?
answer:
Yes, actually. When I first wore hijab I was in [STATE 2]; there was a masjid but no imam, so it was mostly from the internet. I remember reading the Quran, reading the ayah and right away reading the translation, and over the course of two years or so I became very familiar with Arabic and started noticing the root patterns — this means the same thing but the word is different, and then you see the letters are the same. It was very much self-taught. The masjid had a small library; people left cassettes there and I would listen to all of them. I printed out Q&As from the internet and that's how I learned. There was also a halaqa taught by an auntie, going through a tafsir book, though it wasn't as structured — that was also part of it.

When I moved to [CITY 2], things opened up for me — I found out there's a word-for-word translation, which was what I'd been doing all along by hand. I went to more classes, [ISLAMIC EDUCATION INSTITUTE 1], and online institutes like [ONLINE ISLAMIC INSTITUTE 1]. I should also mention there's an organization for [ETHNICITY] Muslims in America with regular halaqas, and a phone halaqa program I started around 2004 that I'm still part of — they were very instrumental in my early days. I would go to [ISLAMIC EDUCATION INSTITUTE 1] seminars when they came to [CITY 2], and I stumbled on a Quran institute while trying to memorize Quran after my parents passed away, because I wanted to do something for them. That memorization program didn't stick at first because my kids were smaller and I couldn't keep up, but I later found a Quran institute that taught tajweed and qira'at, and Alhamdulillah I got an ijazah from them. Then I found [RELIGIOUS INSTITUTION]. From the qira'at program I realized that if you really want credibility, you have to go through a structured system — halaqas are good for spiritual maintenance, but a structured program gives you a foundation, a chain of teaching you can point to, even though there are different opinions, say, on pronunciation. I looked for an Alimah program, but I'm Shafi'i and most online programs were Hanafi. I tried one program that wasn't very organized, then I Googled a Shafi'i Alimah program online and found [RELIGIOUS INSTITUTION], which is very organized, Mashallah, so I stuck with it. In my [ETHNICITY] community I'd somehow gotten invitations to teach, even though my knowledge was just from halaqas — the [ETHNICITY] community in [CITY 2] is small, and there aren't alimahs the way there are in the Desi community, so I felt a responsibility to be in a more serious, structured program, which is why I sought out the Alimah program. I didn't leave other institutes, but [RELIGIOUS INSTITUTION] became my main place of learning.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
Hijab is tied to my conversion story. I have to go back to my family — my parents. My father was gentle and soft, and we would organically pray together, but he never presented it as Islamic rules; we just prayed together. He was a diplomat, so we moved to different countries, and in every small [ETHNICITY] community we found ourselves in, he basically became the imam, even though he wasn't traditionally educated, just well-read and devout. It was never presented as rules. I remember being maybe seven or eight, him taking me to an outdoor restaurant at night, his face against the night sky full of stars, talking about Allah — I don't remember what he said, but I remember the feeling of awe. That was Islam for me.

Then I went to college in [COUNTRY], and the campus had a very strong Islamic movement and Da'wah movement, where the tangible benchmark of a successful da'wah was getting someone who didn't wear hijab to wear it. I was a rebel, and that approach didn't work on me — I reacted the opposite way, thinking, you think I'm a bad Muslim because I don't wear hijab? Fine, I'll color my hair purple. I still wanted to be spiritual, though, so I looked for a halaqa outside my campus, and I found one that turned out to be a misguided sect, almost a cult, actually banned by the government — they wanted a bay'ah (pledge) before moving to a new topic, and I refused, being the rebel that I am. A classmate I trusted helped me realize what it was, and I asked her to teach me instead, treating me as someone starting completely from zero. When we got to the topic of hijab I got stuck, because I realized that practicing Islam truly meant changing my lifestyle — and at the time my lifestyle was very un-Islamic; even my boyfriend used to drive me to these lessons. I wasn't ready, and I put religion in the back of my mind after I graduated and moved to Austria.

Then I moved to the US, and September 11 happened, and people started talking very badly about Islam — I was shocked, because I thought Americans were open-minded and advanced, and yet they couldn't see that religion is sacred. Around that time, a white convert who had taken off her hijab was staying with my roommate and me while she tried to get back on her feet and find work in that post-9/11 atmosphere. In my heart I protested — she was already there, already a Muslim, already someone who could show people Islam wasn't backward, and she was giving it up. That made me turn inward and ask, what about me? I'm educated too, and I do believe Islam is true. I started rethinking hijab and Islam. One day I decided to wear it, and then I had a kind of breakdown, because it had been nine years since I first learned hijab was compulsory back on my campus at seventeen or eighteen, and now I was twenty-six in [STATE 2]. I always thought that once I wanted to do it, I'd be able to. So when I wore it and then physically couldn't leave my apartment, I thought there must be something fundamentally wrong with me. I called my dad, who said it seemed like this had been on my mind a long time, and asked how my salah was; I said it was fine, I prayed. He told me to improve my salah, not to get angry, and if I found my mind going blank with nothing to think about, to do dhikr instead. I later realized that was like tazkiyah — my mind had accepted hijab, but my heart needed to be purified.

A few months later I went to the masjid, where I would always wear a loose hijab just for the visit. Driving back one day I thought, maybe I'll start wearing it properly in Ramadan — then I thought, how do I know I'll live through Ramadan? So as I was driving I thought, I'm wearing a hijab now, I just won't take it off again. And it was so easy, Alhamdulillah — that's Allah. From then on everything was easy; I stopped playing music in the car, and there was a thirst to learn everything I could. That's why I collected all the cassettes from the masjid. I became remorseful about my past lifestyle and became active in the community, volunteering in the Sunday school of that masjid in [STATE 2], and I realized I loved teaching. I changed my focus toward studying Islam and becoming a teacher. So hijab was the gate. It's very important to me because it took nine years, and I could have died in that time — I put myself in so many reckless situations, like wanting to try drag racing, going out with guys I didn't really know. Now that I have kids, I think, I was such a fool.

That nine years, from realizing hijab was mandatory to actually wearing it, Allah just got me to that point — Alhamdulillah. Hijab is very special to me because it's my gate to Islam, and I try to be mindful with women who don't wear it, because I remember what it felt like to be pushed and judged before I was ready. It can come at any point in someone's journey toward Allah, but for me it was really my gate, the hardest thing to submit to, so being able to do it is very special. Thank you for this interview, honestly, for reminding me how special it is.

question: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN OR HIJAB?
answer: Yes, definitely. I've had people ask me, did your dad tell you to wear it? And I just laugh, because my dad never told me to. It's a common misunderstanding — the internet gives people the perception that you're oppressed. But I feel like now it's much better.

question: HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO WRONG PORTRAYALS OF MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer: I haven't had that kind of direct question in a while — that was mostly early on, in my twenties. Especially here in [CITY 2], because it's so diverse, people are used to Muslims, but the encounters are more subtle now — like being in a grocery store and noticing a woman looking at me, clearly scared. I just smile and try to be friendly, though I do feel a pressure, when I'm out, to be more agreeable no matter how I'm actually feeling — though you don't want to fake it either. As a hijabi you're conscious of things — I'll always put my cart back where it belongs, even if I've parked far away, because I'm aware someone might see me and think, look at that Muslim woman not following the rules. I remember once talking to a white, non-Muslim friend about an issue I'd had, and she said, if it were me I'd just complain. I went quiet, and later I realized I hadn't complained because I'm a hijabi and I don't want to seem disagreeable in public. That used to weigh on me — you feel like you have to act nicely, be agreeable, because you assume people don't understand you or might be prejudiced, which I don't like, because then you're defeating yourself by assuming the worst. But I think somewhere in my forties you just stop caring so much what people think in general, so I feel freer now. I still act the way I should, but it doesn't weigh on me the way it used to.

question: WHAT INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS ARE PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
I didn't relate what I described to "the community" so much as to myself. At the local masjid I've weaned myself away from, their approach to women is really based on their culture. When I'm in that community, I do feel there's an expectation for women to be a certain way — for example, at iftar, you can feel the men get preference in how food is distributed; if there's a limited amount and a lot of people, the men tend to get the better portion. My mother-in-law, who's also from outside that culture, and other women who aren't from it, would look at each other, because we feel it, whereas the women from that culture just accept it since that's what they're used to. In [ETHNICITY] culture it's not like that — it's equal, or sometimes women even go first.

At another masjid with that same predominant culture, I was there with my homeschooling kids and it got a little noisy, and someone behind the curtain shushed us rudely — you don't find that at the [ETHNICITY] masjid, which doesn't even really have a partition, just a low, loose one. At an iftar there, the women were cleaning up and laughing about something, and women from another culture started taking pictures of them, asking why. My son, who hadn't been to the [ETHNICITY] masjid in a while, noticed on the drive home how different it was — that the women were noisy, but nobody shushed them. It made me realize the women are really the engine of a community, and that the women taking pictures were probably struck by how joyful and free the [ETHNICITY] women seemed. I don't want to say one culture is better, but I do notice the difference in expectation as I move between communities — in that other community, women are expected to conform and just take it, and maybe they're used to it, so it doesn't register to them as repressive, but from my outside vantage point it can feel a little repressive. At one meeting about Ramadan that included some girls and women, the man leading it spoke in a way I found condescending toward the girls, and the girls themselves just stayed quiet and seemed okay with it. That worried me, especially for a girl who is also American — I wondered, what happens when they meet men outside the community who talk to them respectfully and sweetly; will they be too easily swayed because they're used to being talked down to at home?

I don't want to throw my brothers and sisters under the bus by saying "it's the culture, not Islam" to outsiders, because that's still my community, even when I've been to a masjid where the women's section is small and dingy, or the carpet isn't nice. I remember once, when I was working at that masjid school, we planned a bake sale where the teachers would run the table, and the masjid board said they didn't want the sisters standing out there selling — not wanting to put them on display, which felt disrespectful from where I stood, though I tried to understand it might be a different notion of respect from their point of view. Islam does teach respect for women, but the practicality of it passes through the prism of culture and comes out in different colors. I try to look at it that way, to empathize rather than think badly of others, but after two decades here I do sometimes feel a resentment toward this predominant culture, because it's become so dominant in the Muslim American sphere, and there are a lot of masjids like that — I think it's partly because back home, women don't go to the masjid, so there was never a need for a bigger space. As an [ETHNICITY], a minority within the American Muslim experience, I sometimes feel resentment, especially when I read that "Islam is oppressive to women" — no, it isn't; it's just different cultural ways of doing things. Sorry, this became a bit of a rant.

As for external expectations — meaning from non-Muslims — I try not to think about it too much, but let me give an example. In my late twenties, in [STATE 2], I entered a graduate research competition and won second place, already wearing hijab. When I received the award, a woman told me, you should be really proud of yourself. I smiled, but later I wondered why she said that — it seemed harmless, but there was something in it. I realized it was probably because I'm hijabi, and she assumed my faith was oppressive, so my succeeding defied her expectations, like I was somehow out of the norm. So maybe that's the external expectation — that when you succeed, it surprises people because of how they view us.

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer:
My parents passed away about seventeen years ago, on the same day, and that was one of the biggest difficulties I can recall. How I made sense of it goes back to our belief that there's a decreed time written for each of us — there's no way around it. That's how I accepted it, though it was still painful and sad. Looking back, I feel it was humbling, because I realized I had subconsciously been treating my parents as a kind of backup plan — I married someone outside my own culture, and when they died I felt a sense of loss like a safety net had been pulled out from under me. I wondered why I felt that so acutely, and realized I'd been relying on them in a way that meant my reliance on Allah wasn't as complete as I thought. I might have gone through life thinking I was a good Muslim without ever recognizing that gap. Their passing made me realize that and, in a way, made me stronger — it pushed me toward wanting to do hifz for them and toward deeper Quran study. So the answer, again, is that I went back to my faith, trusting that it was Allah's will, and over time came to see it as something that was ultimately better for my iman — and certainly better for them, since neither of them suffered a long, difficult old age; my dad was sixty-two and my mom was fifty-seven or fifty-eight.

There's a hadith that your parents are crowned on the Day of Judgment (through good deeds like memorizing Quran on their behalf), and that became a big motivation for me. In the worldly sense, I felt like I hadn't done much for them — I finished my master's, worked a little, got married, had kids, and didn't really work after that — so I thought maybe I could present this for them, inshallah.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer: I feel responsible for my kids. There's also a duty to myself. If I said only my husband, I wouldn't be being truthful — I feel more like an equal there, not really "responsible for" him. I owe it to myself to try to do well in this world and to be safe in the Akhirah. So I try, as much as I can, to make choices that wouldn't jeopardize my Akhirah.

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer:
I'm responsible for my family. There's a kind of balance, though — when I was taking a halaqa from my [ETHNICITY] teacher, she said we have a little responsibility to everyone: you're responsible for your family, yes, but you also have some responsibility to your community, and you should contribute what you can in your capacity. My husband is from a different culture than mine, and in the beginning there was a bit of a clash, because in his culture the expectation is more that family comes first and everything else is extra. He's since become more flexible about it. I'm someone who feels that if you wait for the house to be perfectly clean before doing anything else, you'll never get anywhere, because the house never ends. So I follow my [ETHNICITY] teacher's approach — she's understanding, Mashallah; when a halaqa runs a little longer, the women will say, okay, let's end now, because they know the husbands might not be as patient. Back in [STATE 2], the [ETHNICITY] women in a room upstairs would take their time at events, but you'd see the husbands tap the steel stair railing with their keys to call their wives down, and whichever wife's husband it was would go running. We were more relaxed about it, I suppose. Sorry, I don't mean to make this about one culture versus another; it just comes up.

For instance, when I was younger and talking to a brother — someone other than my husband — from a certain culture, I asked a friend from that same culture to help me, maybe teach me a dish so I'd have something to talk to him about. She asked, why would you consider him? Your women are more free. I didn't understand what she meant at the time, being young, but with more experience I came to understand it. I've heard similar comments since, from friends about Southeast Asian men in general — that they're less rigid about domestic roles — though I also know plenty of men from that other culture who are loving, gentle, and exactly how I'd expect a good man to be. I know it's a stereotype, and it's probably unfair to the men who aren't like that, but that's the impression that's out there.

As for my role in the wider community: I feel I have some responsibility to it, so when I'm invited to speak or teach, I try to make it work, fitting it in around my family without waiting for everything else to be finished first, because if everyone only looked out for their own family first, the community itself would suffer. It's a together thing.

question: HOW DOES LIVING HERE SHAPE HOW YOU PRACTICE OR SHOW YOUR FAITH?
answer: Between Islam and America — if America needs Islam, it definitely needs Islam. All the ills you see in society — the unhappiness, the pressure on women to look a certain way, where appearance determines how people treat you and how successful you are — hijab takes that pressure away. It's not about your looks, it's about your character and conduct. I feel Islam is an answer to a lot of the ills of our society, but the society doesn't want it — it's a Judeo-Christian society, after all — though I think the more open-minded non-Muslim Americans become, the more they learn and, inshallah, the more they might see the good Islam can bring. So the relationship is kind of love-hate: America needs Islam, but America doesn't want Islam, or parts of it think they already know what Islam is and don't want it. I guess it's up to us as Muslims to conduct ourselves in a way that people can see the beauty of Islam.

question: HAVE YOU BEEN MADE TO FEEL YOUR FAITH CONFLICTS WITH YOUR COUNTRY?
answer: That time in the grocery store, when an elderly woman was looking at me and I saw so much fear on her face — that wasn't right after 9/11 at all; it happened much more recently, here.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: Subhanallah, that's everything. It's everything. That's all I could say.

question: HOW DO YOU MAKE SENSE OF WHAT IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL?
answer: When something is beyond my control, I understand it as something Allah has allowed at that time. Even though it's painful or very hard, I surrender to it, accept that I don't understand it, and surrender.

question: WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR PRACTICING YOUR RELIGION IN THE LONG RUN?
answer:
What matters most is that we're free to practice, and respected for the way we practice — that matters to me. Alhamdulillah, I feel better about that now than I once did.

If I could change something for the future, for my kids and grandkids, it would be the prevalence of Western culture's push toward just going after what you feel like, what you desire in the moment — I don't want to call it godlessness exactly, but there's a strong sense of chasing desire without restraint. That doesn't really align with Islam, where you can express yourself, but within a framework of what pleases Allah. I wish there were less of that pressure on kids and youth, though I don't know how you change something so built into the society.

question: WHAT IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR HEART, INTENTION, AND OUTWARD PRACTICE?
answer: Yes, of course. My intention — I try to keep Allah at the center of it. Who am I really doing it for, or policing myself for? That's the question I try to keep in mind.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer: Submission to Allah means letting go, understanding that Allah is Al-Hakim, the most wise, in everything, including his timing and the things he allows to happen — that even when you don't understand something, or even feel an aversion to it, you surrender to Allah, trusting there's something good in it, or that this is simply the way of the world. It means accepting things that happen, including things that cause you pain or sadness, and letting go of the idea that you know what's best. That's what submission to Allah means to me.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer: I feel most liberated when I practice, because then you're focused on one thing, instead of being affected by what people think or say. When you practice, it's not about what people think, it's about Allah, and that's very liberating — who cares? Homeschooling is a good example — it goes against the grain, but my first motivation was raising my kids with Islam in mind, and centering on Allah, trusting this is a gift and a trust from Him, makes it not matter what people think about homeschooling. Or with hijab, or even just getting ready to go somewhere — I used to spend so long choosing clothes and putting on makeup, wondering who I was trying to impress, and realizing modesty means not needing that. That became liberating too — not caring what people think, because you care what Allah thinks, becomes freeing. I'm not saying you stop caring about people entirely, but when the focus on Allah takes over, that's liberating.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer:
Right now I work from home, so an ordinary day would be getting up around Fajr, doing my morning adhkar, a simple morning routine, and then logging into work from home. Usually after work I have either masjid events I attend or social gatherings I like to attend, just to keep myself out of the house for some time.

I do try to maintain consistent reading of the Quran. It's not a set number of pages every day, but I try to incorporate it in some way, whether that's Surah Al-Waqi'ah after Salat al-Maghrib or Surah Al-Mulk after Salat al-Isha. There are also portions of the Quran already incorporated in the morning and evening adhkar.

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer:
I would describe myself as someone who is considerate, open-minded in the sense of not discriminating based on how someone looks, and just willing to help. My community would say that I show up — I'm pretty loyal to my commitments; when I say I'll organize an event or volunteer or show up somewhere, I keep my word.

My community itself is open. We are very warm hosts and we love to feed people — food is our love language, so anyone new to our community will get to see that firsthand for sure.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer: I've been born and raised in America, in [STATE 1], for about fifteen years. I'd say I was raised in a bit of a bubble — surrounded by Muslims in my social circle, and in school too, since I was fortunate enough to attend Islamic private school. As time went on and I switched to public high school and then university, where there are people from all walks of life, it made me realize I am different from my community, but there are a lot more similarities than differences between me and my peers. So although I have to follow my religion based on what I think is right, that doesn't really affect my social interactions with people who aren't similar to me.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, AND HOW?
answer: I do seek religious knowledge actively. I just finished a two-year program at my local masjid, and I'm currently learning tafsir through my local masjid's imam's wife. She's kind of the teacher for the entire sister side, so I turn to her for any questions or fatwas.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
Hijab has always been present in my life. I was in Islamic private school, so it was part of our uniform, so transitioning from wearing it exclusively for uniform to wearing it full time was, Alhamdulillah, not at all difficult, because I was already used to it — it was just natural to wear it to the grocery store, for example. What does it do for me? I feel there's a level of inherent respect most of the time when I'm out in public around a majority of non-Muslims. I think there's a sense of modesty and boundaries that my hijab easily portrays to other people, so they understand I'm not one to mess with, for lack of a better phrase. Alhamdulillah, it has given me a layer of protection that I didn't fully realize until I had the hindsight to see it. There have also been unfortunate moments — hostile glares, or a clear difference in customer service, for example — but alhamdulillah, nothing major, so overall it has acted as a protector for me.

I officially started wearing it full time everywhere in middle school. In late high school, when I joined public high school, I came to understand that I chose to stick to the version I believe is right not just because I was constantly surrounded by it, or because my mom wears it, but because of the knowledge I sought out and the reasoning behind the commandment, and because I'd seen firsthand the protection it provides me in everyday life. So based on my experiences, knowledge, and introspection, I came to an internal decision that this is right for me, even though I had already been wearing it before reaching that decision. My schooling was a combination — elementary, middle school, and the beginning of high school was Islamic school, and then I transferred to public high school partway through.

question: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN OR HIJAB?
answer: I think to the common person there's an obvious misunderstanding — that this is forced on me, that I'm oppressed, that if I didn't wear it my dad would hit me or something. That's pretty common, I think, because the word "freedom" when it comes to wearing anything tends to lean toward one definition rather than the other. In America, as the years have gone by, the freedom to let a woman wear whatever she wants usually tends to mean she can show however much of her body she wants, but when it comes to the other end — covering up however much she wants — that's not seen as part of the definition of freedom; anything more than usual is deemed as something that must have been forced on her, that it can't be her choice. So I think that's a lack of understanding from the general public.

question: HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO WRONG PORTRAYALS OF MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer: There were a couple of times, especially during COVID when I was in college and we were all wearing masks, when I was ordering coffee and there was this inherent bias that I wasn't able to speak English, so the barista would start showing me cup sizes with their hands — "this is small, are you okay with small, or do you want medium" — like a side-by-side demonstration. I'd just say, I can speak, and they'd be taken aback. That happened a couple of times. Honestly, I just took it as a humorous incident. I don't try to look too deeply into it, especially when there was no negative reaction afterward — I'd say maybe it was an honest mistake, but I try to give people the benefit of the doubt.

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer:
When I was graduating college, I had a difficult time finding a job. The job market was pretty bad at that time, and honestly still is. I was seeing people around me get a lot of offers, but at companies I didn't feel comfortable being part of. I ended up getting a position on campus at the school where I studied, which worked out in my favor, but during graduation, when everyone was talking about where they were heading next, I didn't really have an answer, and I felt kind of singled out in those conversations. I had to sit back and realize this was my test — was I willing to overlook certain company policies just for the sake of money or a title right after graduation, or was I willing to wait and see what God had planned for me? That time was pretty difficult.

This was around the time of the Palestinian conflict, when everyone was starting to realize where these countries even are and what history has to say about these events, and it was becoming clear who held which stance. Some companies were so blatant that it would have felt like a betrayal to myself as a Muslim to become part of them — whether defense companies or companies actively providing financial support to causes I don't think should be receiving that support. I tried my best to avoid those blatant betrayals of myself — of whether I'd be able to earn income from that, eat food bought with that money, live somewhere bought with that money, and tell myself that was correct.

question: WHAT INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS ARE PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
Of course, yes, a lot. The first thing that comes to mind is obviously wearing hijab a certain way, talking in a certain way, choosing certain fields of work and study — just this common trajectory of going to school and then immediately getting married and immediately starting a family. At least in my community I see that as a prominent factor; if someone over a certain age is still in college, still pursuing her education, or working in a career that doesn't leave room for a family yet, it's seen as her missing out, or not following the script.

When it comes to internal difficulties tied to hijab: when visiting places where I know diversity isn't present, I would internally tell myself not to be loud, verbally or physically — to be very pleasant with whoever I was talking to, take care of my own things, and not rely on people. For example, I visited a state that doesn't have many Muslims or immigrants, and it was pretty clear in convenience stores and restaurants that service workers were already uncomfortable seeing a woman in hijab. So I put an expectation on myself — if they got my order wrong, for example, I wouldn't call them back to fix it the way I would at home in [STATE 1], where diversity is present. There I would just take it as it is, try not to be the cause of anyone's inconvenience, and stay on the quieter side — meaning not calling back or sending food back, not constantly asking where something is when I could just look for it myself. I wouldn't say this resolved anything, really — it just prevented friction, in the sense that I could at least tell myself I wasn't causing anyone inconvenience or making them go out of their way for me.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer: My parents. A lot of the time, when it comes to structuring and scheduling my day, or looking at the events I'm going to or the people I'm spending time with, there's this internal dialogue of, will they be okay with that? They know all my friends, and I feel this inherent responsibility to make sure they're never displeased with me, so they always know where I'm going and who I'm with. It's simply because there's a strong emphasis in our religion on this — displeasing your parents, in some sense, is displeasing God — and I want to make sure that's never the case for me. If that means constantly telling them where I'm going or who I'm with, that's totally fine by me.

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer:
I'm the eldest, so I have this inherent responsibility to make sure everyone's needs are taken care of — if my mom needs to go somewhere, I'm going with her; if my dad needs an appointment made or something done, I try to make sure that's taken care of. Beyond that, just making sure errands run smoothly and no one has any major issues that need attention.

Within my community — we've had a smaller batch graduate from the Islamic course I mentioned earlier, and we've been kind of involuntarily, but happily, recruited by our masjid to serve as the face of the next generation — leading youth events, teaching semester-long fiqh classes, and so on, since we've been given certification to do so. We're kind of the go-to people in our generation for that. So I feel a sense of responsibility to make sure the kids in elementary and middle school at least know someone closer to their age they can reach out to with religious questions.

question: WHAT DOES BELONGING FEEL LIKE HERE?
answer:
Belonging is a pretty loaded question, but I'd say it means I personally don't feel like I need to keep moving. When I was visiting that other state I mentioned, I noticed I was internally always on the go, but in [STATE 1] I feel like I don't have to go anywhere — I can stay, mingle with people, and I don't have too many people questioning me. I'm just part of the background, essentially. That comes from my everyday experiences and interactions with all sorts of people, Muslim and non-Muslim, here.

In that other state, the first obvious thing was the staring — that struck me immediately — followed by curtness in replies, or just an unwillingness to help out. In a restaurant in [STATE 1], a server usually keeps an eye on their section and is willing to check on you, but in that state it wasn't the case; I'd even say we were being ignored and pushed to the side, with no one really willing to reach out and make sure we were okay or needed anything.

question: HOW DOES LIVING HERE SHAPE HOW YOU PRACTICE OR SHOW YOUR FAITH?
answer:
It has its pros and cons. The religious freedom here in the West lets us follow the religion in a way that makes us comfortable, whether or not that's "right" is a different conversation — in other places, people trying to enforce religion do it in a way that doesn't conform to everyone's lifestyle. The trade-off is that it's sometimes a topic of conversation in certain gatherings — like at the library, someone asking why I actually wear the hijab, or whether I can really not eat pork, some of the more common questions.

Honestly, it makes me feel happy most of the time, because I give people the benefit of the doubt that it's coming from genuine curiosity rather than a way to dissect or validate their views on Islam. I like seeing the recognition on people's faces when they hear about the commonalities in our religions — that Mary also covered her hair, for instance, or that pork isn't allowed in some other religions either, and they see that common ground. I really enjoy it; it doesn't make me uncomfortable, though I think it takes reading your gut feeling and the intention of the person asking. If someone had malice in their heart, I imagine it would be best not to engage.

question: HAVE YOU BEEN MADE TO FEEL YOUR FAITH CONFLICTS WITH YOUR COUNTRY?
answer: I'd lean toward no.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: This reminds me of a quote — the summer heat is hot, but Jahannam is hotter — so we really have to stick to what we know is right, straighten our intentions, and hope that Allah accepts us. I've seen people struggle with the idea of living comfortably in the West, but especially after seeing the Palestinians suffer, I've come to this realization that Islam is Islam — we know what's right and wrong, and we can't try to conform it to fit other people's insecurities, because we'll have to answer for every single action in the next life. Just imagining having to answer for what I'm doing right now scares me, so I try to follow whatever I can.

question: HOW DO YOU MAKE SENSE OF WHAT IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL?
answer: A few years ago, I would have thought it was a punishment for my sins. But I'm starting to realize that a lot of the time our experiences or difficulties are either a means of protection or Allah's way of making sure we stick to the right path and don't falter over something small. A lot of the time, once it passes, we realize in hindsight that we got through it, and that we're stronger than we think we are.

question: WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR PRACTICING YOUR RELIGION IN THE LONG RUN?
answer:
Safety. Although prayer is important, especially as a Muslim woman, we're told that if, say, Maghrib starts while I'm driving on the highway, it's not a smart idea to pull over and pray on the road, because you never know who else is driving, and when we pray we're not in full awareness of our surroundings, so the concern is safety, both mine and that of the people around me. When it comes to practicing, I make sure it's not somewhere I'm truly visible — in college, I'd usually find an empty conference room, or some corner that didn't make me stand out, mostly for my own safety rather than to avoid making someone else uncomfortable.

Besides Salah, dress matters, obviously, and making sure what I eat is halal, which can be difficult sometimes.

question: WHAT IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR HEART, INTENTION, AND OUTWARD PRACTICE?
answer: A lot of the time it's become muscle memory, but there are moments — especially in Ramadan, or during the ten days for Hajj — when I'm physically putting the hijab on in front of the mirror and I have to stop and remind myself that my intention in wearing it isn't just habit, it's that I'm trying to please Allah and that this is an act of worship, and I make the du'a that Allah accepts whatever I'm doing. It's unfortunately not an everyday practice for me — that's a personal weakness — but it does show up at certain points.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer: Submission to Allah simply means following whatever He said, without misconstruing it to make it fit your daily life — the key word is misconstruing, rather than making it fit. For example, we're always told to pray at the earliest time, but sometimes that's literally not possible, like when you're traveling on a plane or a train, and if you have to wait a little to pray, that's okay. But misconstruing would be something like saying interest is actually fine because it's everywhere in this country. So to me, submission to Allah means knowing what's absolutely wrong, making sure you stay away from that, and trying to live the rest of your life according to what He said is good.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer: Liberation, to me, is the personal freedom to practice Islam. Alhamdulillah, for most of my life I've been in a state where I can wear hijab, or even wear the abaya to university, and the next day wear jeans, and no one is going to scold me or attack me for that personal choice.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer: I wake up in the morning for the Fajr prayer — right now that's around 4 a.m. Then I go back to sleep after praying, and I wake up again to go to work. Right now I work at a private practice; I'm a physician, so I see patients for consultations. I have a short break between 1 and 2 p.m., though I'm usually running late, so it's closer to 2 p.m. when I end my morning consultations, around the same time as the Dhuhr prayer, so I eat and pray, then start the afternoon consultations again, and usually finish after 6 p.m. and go home.

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer:
There is no single Muslim woman — there are as many different Muslim women as there are women in general — but Muslim women are supposed to be helpful, kind, respectful, and shy; these are values they're supposed to hold, among others.

As for my community: they are awesome. I don't think there's just one community — here in France alone there are many — but we are supposed to take care of each other like a family, like members of one family caring for one another. That idea comes from the recommendation we get from our Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him; it's one of his teachings.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer: I've always lived here. As for how my sense of myself as a Muslim woman has changed — I feel a responsibility to show good values, to show, not exactly "excellence," but the best version of a human being, so that when people look at me, they see only good things. That's important to give a good vision of Islam; I feel we should all be examples for others who don't know Islam — women and men both, but because women who wear hijab are more recognizable, we carry more of that responsibility. It's a feeling I've had — for example, during (medical) school there was a voice in my head telling me that because I wear hijab, I have to be better than the others. I couldn't be a bad doctor; I had to be a good one, so I had to study more, learn more than others, so I would have the right answer and set a good example — not particularly about Islam, but in general, during (medical) school, around scholarship and academics.

question: HOW DOES LIVING HERE SHAPE HOW YOU PRACTICE OR SHOW YOUR FAITH?
answer:
Yes, certainly. First of all, I had to take off my hijab when I was a student, whenever I went to school or the hospital. When I was a student, and also during my five years of work after my diploma, hijab was forbidden in the hospital, so I had to take it off every time I entered and put it back on when I left. That job was mandatory for me to get experience, so I had no other choice but to go to the hospital, and I felt I had no other choice but to take it off. I would take it off in my car, in the parking lot, before going in. That's hard — at first you completely disapprove, and you feel obliged to do something you don't want to do; you feel treated like some kind of criminal, like you're doing something wrong when you're not. You also feel that they don't want the full you, just a part of you.

It's enforced with pictures — like signs showing it's forbidden, clearly written. If you don't comply, there have been many problems for sisters who wanted to keep it anyway — some couldn't work, couldn't go to school, lost their job. There's a recent story of one who had received scholarship money for her studies, and since she didn't want to take off her hijab, they dismissed her from the hospital, and she had to return all the money, for something like four years of study.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, AND HOW?
answer: Yes. I seek it through an online institute — I take classes on weekdays.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
I started when I was twenty. I was born into a Muslim family — my mother always wore the hijab, so it was natural for me to wear it eventually; it was just a question of when the right time was. After medical college, I decided to put it on — I had moved cities at that point, to the south of France for three years, so it was like starting a new life, and I started wearing it there. I already knew the French law about hijab when I put it on: it was strictly forbidden in high school, not forbidden in university, but forbidden in the hospital, so I knew I would have to accommodate that. I knew it was temporary — just for a time, to get my diplomas, and then afterward I would do what I wanted, and that's what I did.

Something is still missing, though, because I left the hospital, a place I really liked working — now I'm in private practice, but I loved working at the hospital and I left because of the hijab restriction, so they lost a doctor who wanted to stay, and I lost a team I liked. I did decide to leave because I couldn't wear my hijab there. In my private practice now, I am able to wear a form of hijab inside — not exactly a scarf like this, more like a small cap; I don't know quite how to describe it.

question: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN OR HIJAB?
answer: I don't know if people understand anything — they just assume what they hear from politics and the media, that Muslim women are obliged to wear it, that it's not their choice, and that it's the opposite of freedom for women. I think that's what they think when they see a hijabi — not most people, but people who don't live around Muslims. There are places in France with very few Muslims, and I think that's the feeling there.

question: HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO WRONG PORTRAYALS OF MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer: It's not so much about Muslim women in general as about the hijab specifically — I've heard that I'm foolish, that it's not my choice, that I'm siding with women being dominated by men, that kind of thing.

question: HOW DID WEARING HIJAB CHANGE PEOPLE'S INTERACTIONS WITH YOU?
answer: In high school, before I wore hijab, my life felt normal, like anyone else's — even now I feel I have a normal life like anyone. But the interactions did change: I felt more isolated after I started wearing the hijab than before. People don't come to you as easily as they did before.

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer:
Racism is part of this too. In high school, before I wore hijab, I still felt racism from my teachers and the school administration. They didn't want me to pursue medical school; they pushed me toward literature instead, insisting a lot, because my grades were better in literature than in science — though not catastrophically different. I'm sure that if I hadn't been Arab, things would have gone differently. One teacher told me plainly, are you serious, you will never be able to do medical school, just forget about it, and called my house many times. They had a plan for me to go study literature in Belgium and then possibly transfer to medical school there. My mother, who wears hijab, didn't want the principal to see her and put even more pressure on me because of it, so she sent my father instead.

There were so many stories like mine, of children from North African or Arab immigrant families being steered away from higher study and toward something more like a trade, rather than being guided toward what was actually best for them. When I asked directly, they didn't hide it — they told parents plainly that it was better for their son or daughter to go a certain route instead.

question: HAS WEARING HIJAB CREATED BARRIERS IN EDUCATION OR EMPLOYMENT?
answer: The admission process is through a website where you list your choices; back when I applied, there was no in-person meeting — it was based on high school grades and recommendations, not a physical interview. I believe that's changed now, and there is an interview process today. I honestly don't know of any case of a hijab-wearing Muslim woman applying to medical school and being able to attend that interview wearing hijab — it's a recent change, and I just don't know.

question: WHAT INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS ARE PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
I don't know that it's about the community so much as internal expectations — from myself and my family, more than from the whole community. We come from immigration, an economic exile, so there's an expectation that we should build a better life than our parents and the first generation had after leaving their countries. When it comes to religion, my family transmitted it to me and expects me to grow in it.

As for expectations from the broader French society: there are certainly some. They expect Muslim women to be visible and engaged in society, in teaching, medicine, law, so we're not left on the margins, so we can help each other and build ourselves up. But there's also a different expectation from the non-Muslim French community — they tend to favor Muslims who aren't very practicing, who might drink at parties with colleagues, or otherwise seem "integrated," or really, assimilated. I don't know if that's an expectation aimed specifically at Muslim women, but that's the general pattern. It's really associated with immigrants more broadly — since a lot of immigration here is from North Africa, and most of those immigrants are Muslim, and Africans generally are Muslim too, so when people say "immigrant," they often mean "Muslim."

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer: It depends on whether a decision affects my family or is personal — if it's about the community, I'm responsible to the community; if it's personal, it's for myself and my family. I don't know if this is a good answer, but I'd say you have to have a good intention, and the outcome should be good — not to hurt anyone. That's the important thing, I think.

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer: The role is the same in the family and in the community — to be present, to help others, not to hurt them, and to set a good example.

question: WHAT DOES BELONGING FEEL LIKE HERE?
answer:
Belonging means being part of something. When you're part of a community or a family, you have to be present, to interact with others in a good way, to set a good example, to help others in need, and, when you're in need yourself, to be able to expect that same support from someone in your group.

Yes, I belong in France — because the story of my family is bound up with the story of France. We didn't choose that, but that's how it is, so yes, I belong. But I don't feel treated like every other French citizen; I don't feel my place is quite equal to (that of) other citizens, even though I do think my place is in France. It's not exactly the same story as my family's, but a mixed one — because of the colonization of my country, my family ended up in exile here, which is why there are so many North African immigrants in France, and that's why we belong here too.

question: DO YOU FEEL YOU BELONG HERE — ARE YOU SEEN AS FRENCH/QUEBECOIS?
answer: I'm not sure the French, ethnically French people, see me as French. On paper we have the same rights, but in daily life we don't feel that we have the same rights — we can't rise as high as we'd like; mosques are closing, Muslim schools are closing, we can't go swimming because they won't accept burkinis or separate swimming times for women. It's not a huge thing on its own, but it still signals that you're not treated like any other French citizen.

question: HOW DOES LIVING HERE SHAPE HOW YOU PRACTICE OR SHOW YOUR FAITH?
answer:
Alhamdulillah, there are still many ways to learn about the religion here — you can go to mosques, gather with other Muslims, sit and learn Quran at the mosque. There are many things you're free to do in France, one hundred percent, and probably worse elsewhere, so there are good things too — many French imams you can learn from, ways to travel and learn about your religion. But the more time passes, the more restrictions there are — like I said, Muslim schools are being closed because they're accused of "separatism," meaning that going to a Muslim school is treated as separating your life from society, wanting to stay only among Muslims, and that's forbidden, so they close the schools. There was also the controversy around the abaya — they stopped girls in school from wearing long dresses, even dresses that weren't technically an abaya; if you looked Arab, or like an immigrant, or Muslim, and wore a long dress, you couldn't enter the school. That law was around 2003 or so. There was also a recent law about the surgical cap some Muslim staff wear in hospitals — a nurse was dismissed from her job for wearing one, and there was another case of a non-Muslim woman who had a hair-related medical issue and was asked to produce a certificate proving she wasn't Muslim. It's terrible. It feels like they're watching for this constantly, especially before elections, when they start targeting Muslims more.

On the faith side, there are also closures around prayer — if you can't get to the mosque during prayer time, you simply can't pray; when you're outside, you can't pray anywhere, because it's forbidden.

question: HOW AND WHERE ARE YOU ABLE TO PRAY DURING YOUR DAY?
answer: At work, I'm at my desk, in my own room, so I pray there. When I was in school and university, you simply don't pray there — usually you pray when you get back home.

question: HAVE YOU BEEN MADE TO FEEL YOUR FAITH CONFLICTS WITH YOUR COUNTRY?
answer: I don't know — they never made me feel that I was a threat. I don't know if they feel it, but I've never felt that myself.

question: ARE MUSLIMS TREATED DIFFERENTLY FROM OTHER RELIGIOUS GROUPS IN FRANCE?
answer: Jews and Christians have their own schools, and those schools aren't being closed — it's specifically Muslim schools that are closing. Jewish schools have police protection; you can't touch anything related to Jews, because that would be treated as antisemitism, so no one says anything against a Jewish school. Islamophobia is a problem in France, but officially they try to deny it.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: When you're convinced about the Akhira, you have to judge yourself every day — was this a good action, is this something forbidden, is this something that pleases Allah, is this a sin or bad behavior?
