Before I was Muslim, I wouldn't really tap into that — I'd call out to God or go back to church or pray only when I was in real need, but I'd forget to do it in times of good. Now it's constant: it doesn't matter what happens in a day, a week, or an hour — if it's good, it's thanks to God, and if it's not good, it's still thanks to God. It's constantly thinking that way; that connection continues no matter what's going on in my life.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer: I feel more liberated in that I'm free to practice my religion and really immerse myself in the community — going to halaqas, going to meet friends at the mosque; that's kind of the place where we go. Part of it is also my age — I'm going to be 55 this year, and I don't have the responsibility of small children, so that plays a role too. Younger women have more constrictions from responsibilities, but for me now I'm free to spend my time doing the things I like to do — I like to spend my time at the mosque and seeking knowledge. I'm free of those mundane responsibilities toward others, so now I can spend my time doing what I want to do.

question: WHAT INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS ARE PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer: There's definitely (an expectation). I think there's an unspoken idea of things you need to accomplish by a certain age — by 23 you've got to be married with three kids. I see younger women struggling with not having good candidates for marriage, or this cultural idea that if you're 29 you're too old and nobody's going to want to marry you. There's a lot of baggage placed on women that isn't really religious, it's more cultural. That's true externally too — there are misconceptions, because people will also think... Well, there's a couple of things people get confused about. When they see, oh, my friend is Muslim and she doesn't wear the hijab, why do you wear the hijab? — you have to explain that. But again, I can't speak for your friend, I can only speak for my own choices, or how I want to identify, so I better not speak for her. And I'm also not going to say wearing the hijab makes me a better Muslim — she may be more knowledgeable than me, she may be more respectful, she may be more submissive to God. Wearing the hijab does not make me better.

question: WHAT IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR HEART, INTENTION, AND OUTWARD PRACTICE?
answer: The internal (matters), because everything external — people can pretend. But if you don't have that sincere desire to purify your heart, to seek the pleasure of God, to stay in that state of communion with Him daily throughout the prayers, then what kind of Islam would you have if you're just faking the prayers, or covering because you think it makes you look more religious? It's not (real).

question: WHAT LED YOU TO TRAVEL TO MOROCCO?
answer:
I only got hints — I'd never even, I didn't even know where Morocco was.

But I got a bit afraid. I was at work, and I'd been preparing, saying, okay, I'm going to have two whole months off — that was my sabbatical. And one thing I did is, I didn't want my children with me — I really felt like I needed a break from my life — and I said, what's the most remote place I can go to? It just so happened that I had hired an employee who was from Morocco. He knew I was going to be gone for two months and was curious — how can I do that? I told him, you're going to have to work ten years here before they give you a sabbatical. But then I said, I'm struggling — I know I don't want to go back home, I want to go somewhere completely new and different than anything I know. And he's the one who said, you should go to my country, you should go to Morocco.

People are nice, and he put me in contact with his family — he said they could pick me up from the airport and help guide me to where I wanted to go, and since I'm a woman traveling alone, they could watch out for me too. Then another employee, who'd started just two months before, was also from Morocco, and he also said, go visit my family there. So I ended up spending one week with one family, one week with the other family, and one week by myself.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer:
Depending on when we wake up, we'll start the day with breakfast — I'll make breakfast. Before that, early in the morning, I pray Fajr and do some of my adhkar. My little one is a toddler, so after breakfast we'll do a little playtime or story time, and then he'll take his first nap. When he wakes up we'll eat lunch and either go on a walk or do some activity — each day is a little different. After our afternoon activity, whether it's a walk, playtime, or an excursion, we'll come back home, eat, and then start settling down for nighttime.

I prioritize my salah — whenever it's time to pray, that's the main priority. My day is organized around the obligatory acts of ibadah.

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer:
I would say, for me personally, there's a strong sisterhood — I've built a strong sisterhood for myself. I have a lot of friends who are also like-minded, and they help in terms of reminding me and being a source of emotional support whenever there's a need. We can rely on one another. It's a very strong community, not just spiritually but emotionally — they help financially if needed. Overall there's just a really strong community and sisterhood.

I'd say it's a community of young women who are all striving towards the same thing, whether in our worldly lives or our afterlife, because that's mainly where we're striving. But we're also pretty ambitious when it comes to our worldly life — we're either in school or working.

I would say we're practicing — I can speak for my group of friends. We're all visibly Muslim, whether we're wearing niqab or hijab. We're visibly Muslim, but on the other hand we're also not too different from the rest, since we have the same goals and aspirations as everyone else.

I'm from [CITY 1]. I've lived in Canada my whole life.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO ISLAM?
answer:
I came to Islam in 2016 — I was quite young at the time.

I've always grown up around a lot of Muslims. I'm predominantly Lebanese, Moroccan, and Somali — I'd say Somali was the more predominant community I was around. I always had them as neighbors, and they were really welcoming; there was a strong neighborly presence, if that makes sense, because now, depending on where you live, you don't really see that — neighbors don't tend to really know each other. But growing up, neighbors were always around; if they were cooking, they'd be feeding us, and we'd be feeding them. There was a strong bond there. I always had Muslim friends growing up, and then in high school I started doubting my own personal beliefs. I grew up as a Christian.

Some of my Muslim friends would tell me things, whether it was a hadith or something from the text of Islam, and it would resonate with me — I believed it. There was no doubt in my heart about what they were telling me. Eventually I started doing my own research. My friends would bring me to the masjid or to gatherings of Muslims where sheikhs would be speaking, and I believed everything I was hearing. I did delay my shahada for some years, but at the end of my high school career I decided to finally do it, due to the advice of a friend, and I just did it.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer:
There was definitely a lot of growth. At first I didn't really know much. At the time my friends weren't necessarily practicing — they were more cultural Muslims — and I stayed with them for maybe two years as friends. Then I realized I wanted to grow, to evolve as a Muslim; I knew I didn't want the same lifestyle I had before.

I attribute this to Allah — I think it was Him removing people from my life and introducing new people into my life. I started frequenting the masjid more often, even though I was anxious to go alone. At that time I didn't have much knowledge, and I would still consider myself new even after two years, because I wasn't wearing hijab yet, and I don't think I really knew how to pray correctly until I actually started frequenting the masjid, getting myself out there, and asking questions. Around 2018, two years after my conversion, I decided to put myself out there — I started learning more about my religion, dressing more modestly, and becoming friends with more of a practicing group of sisters. Up until now that was kind of my trajectory, going up, up, up, up, and then now I feel like I've plateaued. But I'd like to definitely increase in my iman and keep growing and learning.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, AND HOW?
answer: Now it's mainly online, just because I'm a mother. But when I can, I try to go to the masjid or the local markaz here in my city whenever they have classes. Before, there were a lot of different resources here in the city — there was one masjid that had an Arabic program, and I went there. Even before that I was always learning Arabic, since 2018, once I decided I wanted to seek knowledge about the religion. From 2018 to about 2022 I was really immersed in seeking knowledge — I was studying Arabic, learning about Quran and tajweed, and I started memorizing the Quran. These were all programs in the city, but now it's mainly online.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
In 2016 I didn't jump into wearing hijab right away — I was doing more of a turban and dressing more modestly, long pants, long shirts, long cardigans. After two years, when I started frequenting the masjid, I noticed a lot of sisters were wearing really long hijab, really long khimar, and I liked that — I thought it was beautiful, so I started emulating them and dressing like them. For about two years I dressed like that, with long hijabs and long abayas, and then in 2020 I decided to wear niqab. I decided to wear it mainly because of the mask mandate — I wanted to take that decision into my own hands. I didn't want to be forced to wear a mask, and I thought the mask at the time was uncomfortable. I said, you know, I've always wanted to wear niqab, so why don't I use this as a gateway to wear it. Since then I've been wearing niqab, jilbab, and abaya.

I personally think it's empowering. I really feel the most feminine and the most empowered being able to take modesty into my own hands and not be objectified. The older you get, you realize certain things and you're more aware of how the world is, and I definitely feel safest being covered. When I'm engaging in conversations with people, they're not just looking at me because of how I look — they're engaging with me because of me and what I have to say, genuinely. So I definitely feel a lot safer, in the sense that I'm not being objectified.

question: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN OR HIJAB?
answer:
I do feel like it's really misunderstood. Prior to the past couple of years, people were more open-minded, I find, especially in Canada — there's this stereotype of Canadians being super nice and polite. But I feel like now, maybe with the political climate, people are becoming a little less open-minded, because I've personally noticed a lot more hostility towards niqab specifically. Which is strange, because I've always lived in Canada and I've worn niqab for the past six years, and it's only become an issue in the last year. I used to be able to work with it on, to live my life wearing it, and I never really encountered any issues until recently.

I definitely think a lot of people misunderstand it and view it as something oppressive — mind you, this is a personal choice that I made as a young woman, and most young women are not deciding to fully cover. So they might view me as oppressed or extreme, but I obviously don't think so, because it was definitely my own decision, before I even got married. I think there's definitely a misunderstanding — most people don't really want to hear the reality of why a woman decides to cover or fully cover. It's more that they want to believe what the media is telling them instead of actually being open-minded and understanding why a young woman would want to fully cover.

question: ENCOUNTERS WITH HOSTILITY AND HARASSMENT
answer:
I've encountered — I can remember about three instances that were memorable, and here and there people who stare and give you dirty looks. One time I was driving from Costco, and you know how Costco is usually really busy with lines of cars trying to leave the parking lot — a pickup truck quickly swerved around me, and when he saw what I looked like, he cussed at me and said the F-word. I pulled up beside him eventually, when the traffic was light, and I rolled down my window and asked him if there was something he needed to say to me, and all of a sudden he went quiet. You notice that when you talk back and ask them, they kind of shut down, because they don't expect you to be a person under there, to defend yourself or ask them what's going on — if you have something to say, say it. You could tell he dialed back his aggressiveness, but that was just superficial, because he had this big pickup truck and I was driving a small sedan with my baby in the car. I just thought it was overly aggressive for no reason — we're just going grocery shopping on the weekend, there's no need for this.

More recently, we were at the grocery store closest to my house — my baby and I had gone on a walk and then stopped by the grocery store. Women I've noticed will more just give dirty looks or glares, or say something and walk away, but men I find are more aggressive. This guy came up to me — I had my AirPods in, and I knew he'd said something vile because of the look on his face. I took my AirPod out and asked if he needed something, and then he started with a whole verbal attack, getting really aggressive and screaming — people on the other side of the store could hear. He was getting red in the face, you could tell he was extremely angry for absolutely no reason; I guess the way I dressed aggravated him. He was talking about how I should go back to my country, that I should go blow something up, stuff along those lines, cursing and using all types of foul language. That was the most unsafe I've felt, because this person seemed like he could actually be of physical harm to me.

He eventually walked away. Obviously I was shook, just because this is a man and I'm a woman with my child — I wasn't expecting that, and this is my local store, so they know me. Eventually they got security involved and banned him from the store, and then police were involved, because I actually saw him the next day or two days later, so I realized he's someone who lives in my neighborhood. I definitely needed to safeguard myself, so I called the police and made a report — that's being taken care of.

In another instance, a woman was driving and slowing down her car — mind you, these are all within the past year, so I'm surprised it's been back to back to back. She was an older woman; she stopped her car and stared at me, and I just waved and gave her the peace sign. I guess she didn't like that, and she got really upset with me, so I just walked off — I don't have time to be interacting that way, I have my own stuff to do. There have also been little instances like people slowing their car or honking. Another instance, a white guy drove past and used an Arabic slur, a really derogatory word regarding women — I was shocked, because I'm a fully covered woman, so why would you use that word to describe me? He yelled it out of his car, which was embarrassing, humiliating. There have been a lot of weird instances like that in the past year — this is in [CITY 1].

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer:
When I first started practicing, around 2018, I was in university. At that time I had learned that interest-based loans are haram, so they're not permitted, and that caused me some difficulty because I was in the middle of my university and needed that financial help to pay for schooling. I ended up not taking the loan — in [PROVINCE 1] we call it [PROVINCIAL STUDENT LOAN PROGRAM], which is what a lot of people use to pay for school. I didn't want to take the loan; I was taking grants, but it became difficult to pay off the rest of the tuition because I had to work and take semesters off to work, and that became exhausting. I ended up actually leaving school because of that. It was a hardship — I wanted to finish school, but it was really difficult to manage and pay it all off. At the time I decided to work full-time, and I found a lot of fulfillment in that, because it was in a field where I was happy, working with children, and I decided to go down that path instead. I was able to go to college, and I found college a lot easier — I was able to manage working full-time and full-time studies online. I think it was a good decision for me, to be patient and eventually find something I wanted to do.

For me it was because ultimately I'm doing it for Allah's sake. I knew there was going to be no real repercussions — I'm winning at the end of the day regardless of what I'm doing. I knew there would be blessings in whatever I do moving forward, because I sacrificed one thing for Allah, and He opened more doors — He eventually did.

question: WHAT INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS ARE PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
Oh, I definitely think so. There's a lot of expectations placed on women, and I'll speak specifically about marriage. I find that a lot of Muslim women are expected — it depends on who you're marrying and who you're getting to know — but expected to leave off what they've built in order to start a family, to stay home. That can be difficult; I'm not speaking from my own case specifically, but I know some women who may have completed their PhD, and that's a lot of school, a lot of energy, a lot of work, and to be expected to, for example, be a stay-at-home wife — I think that's difficult to do. That's a huge sacrifice, and I feel like men aren't expected to sacrifice in the same way women are.

Not in all cases, but from my own experience, I feel like there's meant to be a lot of sacrifice from a woman's end.

question: INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL DIFFICULTIES WHEN ADOPTING HIJAB
answer: Actually, no, I found it was a very easy transition — I didn't really have much difficulty with that.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer:
Now, my child, definitely.

Like I mentioned, I had kind of plateaued in terms of seeking knowledge about the religion, but now that he's here — I'm someone who procrastinates a lot and lacks discipline — he's definitely helped me gain discipline. Now I definitely want to finish memorizing the Quran so I can teach him. I want to be the first person he learns from. I want to be able to grow his knowledge as well, and I would like to be the first source of that for him.

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer: I kind of think of myself as a free agent, but I'm definitely someone who's really family-oriented, and I really enjoy being there for the community. Prior to marriage and my one kid, I used to volunteer at the masjid, and I really enjoyed being there. I like baking, too, so whenever the masjid needed extra funds or there was a fundraiser, I'd bring baked goods, help sell those, and contribute — that's something I really enjoy doing. In terms of family, I take the role of mother pretty seriously, so I'm reading about parenting.

question: HOW DID YOUR FAMILY RESPOND TO YOU BECOMING MUSLIM?
answer:
I'm grateful — their response was pretty calm. It wasn't a big dramatic change; they just accepted it and we moved on, even with my transitioning from being a turban-wearing Muslim to a more modest Muslim to full niqab. Everything's been pretty seamless — the transition. I'm grateful for that.

Yes, I've stayed in contact and received family support.

I think it's cultural, because where we come from, we're not from a culture where Islam is foreign — it's pretty integrated into the culture. It wasn't something alien to them; we grew up around Muslims even before they immigrated to Canada. They were always surrounded by Muslims and knew about Islam. So I attribute it to that.

question: WHAT DOES BELONGING FEEL LIKE HERE?
answer:
Belonging — that's a good question. Honestly, I feel like as long as you're a visible minority and not of European descent, you don't really belong here. Unless you're truly assimilated and view things how they view things, you're going to be othered, if that makes sense. Especially now more than ever, I don't really feel that belonging, honestly speaking.

Or even other immigrants who assimilate well to the Canadian culture, quote unquote — maybe it's easier for them, they can easily integrate. But if you're like me, someone visibly Muslim who fully covers, I think that's kind of out the door. I may have gotten away with it in my teen years, but even then, I think it depends — they're more open to certain cultures than others.

I'll speak my mind on this — I feel like East Asian cultures are more accepted, because East Asians assimilate really well into Canadian society and culture, they can really integrate. But a lot of us who come from other Asian cultures or African cultures tend to hold on to a cultural identity a bit more without leaving it behind. If you hold on to a lot of your cultural background or identity, it might be harder to assimilate and be accepted by white Canadians.

question: HOW DO YOU UNDERSTAND ASSIMILATION?
answer: I think there's a way to be balanced, but in my opinion, the way they expect assimilation is like ignoring everything and becoming fully Canadian, if that makes sense. That's how I view assimilation here in Canada specifically. I think melting pot versus multicultural is a bit different — I think Canada is more multicultural than a melting pot, whereas in the States you can hold on to your cultural identity a bit more easily without it being such a huge problem. This is based on my own assumption and experience, but I feel like here you're kind of expected to forgo your cultural identity.

question: HOW DOES LIVING HERE SHAPE HOW YOU PRACTICE OR SHOW YOUR FAITH?
answer:
Previously it was really easy — I found it easy to be a practicing Muslim here, and I didn't find any issues. But now, especially given that I'm a lot more wary of going outside and doing my daily, mundane things, that's actually pushing me to consider moving to a more accepting environment elsewhere. I definitely feel a push to move away, for my own safety and for my children's.

Just the experiences — the hostility I'm noticing this past year only, it's becoming a bit too much to deal with. You don't want to go outside and have to deal with people staring at you and potentially harming you, and now you're seeing more instances of people being bold enough to actually harm people.

question: HAVE YOU BEEN MADE TO FEEL YOU'RE A THREAT?
answer: Not personally, I don't feel that way, but there are definitely people who could view me as a threat because of what I wear.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: I'd say I'm definitely more focused — even with the whole university thing, I always have that in the back of my head. I always want to be as conscious of sins as I can be. We're human beings, we're going to fall short, whether here or there, but always reminding myself of Allah, reminding myself that life is very, very short, and that people around us, regardless of their age, their lives can be taken — that's also a big reminder. I'm definitely not too attached to this life; we take the means, but personally I'm always remembering that this life is not everything, it is short, it's fleeting. Time is going by really, really fast lately.

question: HOW DO YOU MAKE SENSE OF WHAT IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL?
answer: If it's a difficulty, I understand it as a test, and you just have to work your way through it with patience, and eventually it'll move by. Life is definitely testing for everyone — every human being has their own tests, so you just have to accept that and move through it with grace. You continue with your life, because that doesn't stop your life; you just have to keep continuing.

question: WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR PRACTICING YOUR RELIGION IN THE LONG RUN?
answer: What matters most to me is the fact that I can still practice. I spent some time in Europe, in a certain country, and it was difficult — you could tell there was a lot of hostility towards women who wear niqab, and it was actually banned there. So I'm definitely more appreciative now of the fact that I can wear it here. I definitely do appreciate that I can still practice my religion freely.

question: HOPES FOR HER CHILDREN'S RELIGIOUS EXPERIENCE IN THE WEST
answer:
Honestly, I do plan on relocating to a predominantly Muslim nation, for the kids' sake, because I want them to have more of a conservative upbringing, if that makes sense. I'm more wary now of ever putting my child into public school, for example, just because I don't really agree with what they're teaching — it feels like it's being forced upon them. I definitely want to have control over what they're learning and their education, so I definitely want to hopefully relocate to a Muslim-majority country.

Specifically, things like the LGBTQ material — I don't think sexuality should be taught until it needs to be, and even then it should just be the biological aspects. I don't understand why kids need to be taught things of that nature; it's not their concern, and for it to be pushed on them, I think, is an agenda I don't agree with.

question: WHAT IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR HEART, INTENTION, AND OUTWARD PRACTICE?
answer:
Obviously with the hijab, because it's mundane, you do it every day and you kind of forget why you're doing it. But when I do remember, I try to remember that I'm doing this for Allah's sake — I'm not just covering my whole body and receiving hostility for no reason. I try to remember that as much as I can, just for Allah. Certain things do become mundane, because when you do things repetitively, it can become part of your routine, but I think it also depends on the state of your iman — if you're in a lower state of iman, you might not appreciate these acts of worship, but when you're in a higher state, you're more appreciative, more spiritual, more connected to Allah, closer to Him, your heart feels more full, and you feel that gratitude. It depends on the state you're in at that moment.

I'd say I try to be intentional about my acts of worship, because I want to be rewarded ultimately for what I'm doing — I don't want it to just be a wasted effort.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer: Submission to Allah means listening to His commandments and obeying. I don't think there should be arguments about what we hear from the Quran or the Sunnah — it might be difficult for some, but I feel we should try our best to obey the commandments that have been sent to us. Especially with things like the example of the student loan — it might be difficult to pay off your tuition, but I think it's better to do it slowly instead of putting yourself in debt with the sin of riba. I definitely think we should avoid major sins as much as we can.

question: HOW DO YOU UNDERSTAND LIBERATION?
answer: Liberation in terms of what? It depends on the context. As a Muslim woman, my ideas are based on my belief system, so I think the only way to truly be liberated is by obeying what Allah has commanded us to do, because He created us and knows what's best for us. If He's telling us to cover ourselves, it's for a reason, and you should be liberated that way. Personally, I don't feel objectified wearing niqab — that's how I see it as liberating. What's funny is that even when I'm fully covered I'm still approached by men, but I feel better knowing that I'm not actually seen by them, that they don't have access to me. That's definitely liberating, and I see the wisdom in why we should be covered. Men are wired a certain way, and maybe they can't always control how they think or feel — maybe they shouldn't act on certain things, but we can't control how people act, so it's better to keep ourselves safe. I definitely think hijab is a safety net for us women.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer: I would say, in the fact that I'm a niqabi, I do feel liberated. I feel free — I feel like I don't have to conform to how society wants me to be. Women get so much pressure to look a certain way, to have their bodies look a certain way, to always get manicures, pedicures, their hair done — wasting all this money. If you want to do it, go ahead, but if there's pressure to do it and you feel insecure without it, that's a huge weight that nobody should really be carrying, unless you genuinely want to do it, not because of pressure.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer:
An ordinary day in my life isn't very exciting. My life in Canada — I'm a mom of three, so it's mostly getting them ready, getting them off to school, their activities, whatever they need to do. I have multiple roles: the mother, the taxi driver, the cook, the cleaner, the event coordinator, everything. At the same time, I'm doing my PhD, so pretty much I'm home twenty-four seven — once the kids are out of the house, I'm working, either on my PhD, another research project, or teaching part-time at the university: preparing lessons, meeting with students, responding to emails, serving on committees. That's pretty much my life. I don't really have a social life right now outside of that.

Yeah, that's a good question. Faith kind of structures the day. Alhamdulillah, I pray five times a day — getting up on time for Fajr, and on the times my alarm's gone unheard, I pray when I get up a bit later. The breaks I take throughout the day, how I schedule my routine and meetings, I try to schedule those around the prayer times. Sometimes it doesn't always work — I'm stuck praying in random places if I have to leave the house for meetings. But the prayer kind of guides most of the activities happening. And obviously during Ramadan that leads to a whole new schedule — alhamdulillah, given my work at the university, my schedule switches a little so I can sleep in a bit in the morning and do more work in the evening, because I get tired during Ramadan and fasting. Other than that, in Canada I wasn't really involved in a lot of religious-based community groups, just because I was so busy with my PhD and kids. So I'd say the salah and the fasting during Ramadan are the biggest ones, and then opening up the Quran and reading here and there, or reading a religious book — but I wouldn't say that's an organized, structured part of my daily routine.

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer:
I recently met someone — this was early spring. He worked for the property management company that managed the house I was renting; they do yearly inspections to check things like smoke detectors. He'd seen the pro-Palestinian sign in my window, since I'm a pro-Palestinian supporter, and he commented on it, and that led to us discussing Islam. He was saying there's going to be a civil war in Canada because Muslims want to take over, and I was like, what? No, I don't think they do — as a very visibly Muslim woman, I'm telling you they don't want to take over Canada and impose their own culture. One of the things I said was, even within Muslims, we come from so many different cultures — which culture would you even impose? We're very diverse. I guess he's just thinking broadly of Islam and Sharia law. So that's my tangent — I feel like lately there's just a rising fear of Muslims, and it's media-led, especially social media, where they have these ideas that Muslims want to take over and impose our own ideas.

To more specifically answer the question, I'd say that we are everyday people — we believe there's just one God and that the last messenger was Muhammad, peace be upon him, and we live according to the main principles of Islam, the Sharia. But it's not this evil thing where we want to take over the world and dominate — we're everyday people, we have everyday lives, our jobs, our kids, we want good for them, we want them to be successful, to do the things that are good and lawful, and stay away from the haram. We just want to lead positive, successful lives. That's the frustrating thing — what social media and the news try to present as Islam and Muslims, and what we actually want and do.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO ISLAM?
answer: I was actually thirteen years old, in a school that was predominantly white Catholic. I'd met some friends outside of school, and it was Christmas time — I asked one of the boys what he was doing for Christmas, and he said, I'm Muslim, I don't celebrate Christmas. It was a huge shock to me — I was like, what do you mean you don't celebrate Christmas, everybody celebrates Christmas, this is normal. He explained, no, I'm Muslim, this is what we believe. I was just fascinated, and I asked my mother, who's now deceased — I asked her, okay, what's the proof that Jesus is the son of God, that Christmas is normal and everybody should celebrate it? And it's actually her response that led me to learning more about Islam and eventually becoming Muslim. She said, there's no proof, it's just something you have to believe. I was like, what do you mean there's no proof, there has to be proof. And that's when I started learning about Islam, and I actually wanted to become Muslim from that age, but when you're young and scared — I knew those guys, but they weren't close friends I'd see every day at school, just from the neighborhood — so I felt like I couldn't do it on my own, and I only actually became Muslim in my early twenties. It took me quite a while to get there. I always had the intention, but to actually do it, I think I was just scared and needed someone to hold my hand.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer:
I think I've changed a lot. When I first became Muslim, I believed the basics — the articles of faith, the pillars of Islam, all the fundamental parts of the religion. To wear hijab was a big no — I said, I'll fast, I'll pray, but I'm not going to wear hijab. But subhanAllah, I think it was within less than six months I started wearing hijab. I did focus on praying first — that was a big struggle in itself, to build that routine and discipline. Having discipline is something that has greatly improved since I became Muslim, and choosing to be a practicing Muslim, because you have to have that discipline to make sure you're praying five times a day, on time.

My sense of understanding the world, and the things happening around me — although we don't always have specific reasons and can't rationalize why things happen — it's ultimately having the understanding that everything is in the power and control of Allah. We are the creation, not the creator, whereas before I think I was more controlling. Now it's, okay, I'm not actually in control — yes, I'll put effort into what I'm doing, but ultimately, whatever happens is under the command and control of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. That gives me a lot of peace, in a way, and whatever the outcome is, I know it's for the best, even if it's something we don't always like — we accept that's what Allah decreed. I don't spend so much time mulling over it or being angry about an outcome that wasn't in my favor. I think it's just really putting that trust and faith in God that things will work out in the best way, however it's meant to happen.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, AND HOW?
answer: No. When I was younger, not married, no kids, I did — I would attend classes every week; I even managed a Quran center for a while. It was really nice to be in that environment, where women and children were coming to learn and memorize Quran. But especially since I had my youngest — even with my eldest, we used to attend a lot of halaqas and go to the mosque — my youngest was more challenging, so that made it difficult to attend anything regularly. Some of the halaqas I used to attend were online, so if I wasn't completely exhausted, I'd log in and listen to the lectures, or once in a while I'd download lectures onto a USB and play them in my car while driving. So I can't say I regularly sought knowledge, but at the same time I didn't completely abandon it.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
My hijab story — I can't even put a finger on what really led me to accept it and decide to do it. It was just a feeling, I guess — when Allah puts something in your heart, it changes the heart, and you go in that direction. I've been wearing it for almost twenty-three years now, so it's been a while. In the initial days, when you first become Muslim and you're so excited and want everyone to know — when you don't wear hijab, nobody knows, and everybody thinks you're just a regular white girl. But I was like, no, I want people to know I'm Muslim. So that could be one thing that motivated me — I wanted to be visibly Muslim. I was in college at the time; I converted at the end of January, and I think I started having that feeling toward the end of that winter semester, around April. But I was still scared, and over the summer I'd put it on here and there, and eventually I made the choice that when I went back to work, I would wear it.

I was working with immigration at the time, and I told security, on the Friday, with no hijab, listen, I'm going to be wearing hijab on Monday, so I need a new picture — it was just a weird announcement. He was just kind of looking at me, like, okay. So I showed up on Monday, and I even emailed my co-workers, telling them there was going to be a change — I think I sent it on a Wednesday, so they had a few days to get used to it before Monday. I don't always think things through very well, but anyway, it happened.

My level of modesty and conservativeness has fluctuated. At first, when I became Muslim, I'd wear jeans with a tunic, long sleeve, a regular scarf — a bit tighter. Then I became extremely modest, wearing only big abayas and big, oversized scarves. Then I calmed it down a little and went to wide-leg pants with long, three-quarter-length tunics, still quite loose. Now, honestly, it's more out of laziness — I just wear abayas, the same three abayas and one hijab, twenty-four seven. So it's definitely fluctuated. One thing I've noticed with sisters — and I'm not trying to be judgmental, because everybody's doing their best with the knowledge they have, and different personalities align with different ideologies — is that I can't say I'm the super conservative type who has to cover my face and can only wear abaya. For me, as long as you're trying to be modest, that's what matters.

Going back to what it does in my life — I still very much feel that I want to be visibly Muslim. I'm proud to wear it. It's second nature now; I just put it on, and I forget I'm even wearing a hijab among all these other people who aren't. But at the same time, I do very much want to be known as a Muslim, a proud Muslim — I have no fear in that. I've noticed that a lot of men became more respectful once I started wearing hijab — it sets a boundary for how they need to interact with me and the limits of those interactions. I used to experience a lot of sexual harassment, and that stopped once I started wearing hijab. So identifying as a Muslim woman is important, and it establishes those boundaries with the men I interact with. That comes from my appreciation and love for my faith, and wanting to visibly represent what I believe it means to be a Muslim woman. And also, it's a commandment from Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala — a commandment I'm happy to abide by, and I don't feel any negativity about it, or that it's a burden.

That understanding — that it's a commandment of Allah — came from when I started learning, at thirteen. I read a lot of books about Islam, the basics, the translation of the Quran, listened to lectures. I learned a lot in the early years, and even though I knew intellectually that I had to do it, I felt like it was something I'd never actually do. But as I progressed — after I said the shahada, started praying — I think my iman grew stronger, and then I was like, yes, I definitely want to do this.

question: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN OR HIJAB?
answer: There's definitely the misunderstanding that women are forced to wear hijab, that we have no choices and aren't able to think or make decisions for ourselves. I can say that I have many friends who wear niqab, and it was them who made the choice on their own to cover — they're the ones who told their husbands and family it's something they wanted to do, which is the complete opposite of what most people think, that it's the men who tell them they have to. From my own experience and the people I know, it's been the women who made these choices themselves and informed their male family members about it. We're not male-dominated, unable to make choices for ourselves — the women I know are pretty headstrong, and we make the choices for ourselves.

question: HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO WRONG PORTRAYALS OF MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer: Going back to that example of the man who was saying that Muslims want to take over Canada, that there's going to be a civil war — it's frustrating, because no, we're just everyday people, we're not trying to take over the world and impose Sharia law. Even though I was telling him, Muslims are everyday people, we just want a good education, good work, to raise good kids, go to nice restaurants — he was just like, no, no, no, Muslims want to take over and take control. No matter what you're saying, they're not listening — they just have this idea in their mind and don't care about anything you're saying.

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer: Alhamdulillah, Allah has tested me a lot. Going back to what I said about Allah being in control — the situations we face that we feel are negative, that we don't like, they're difficult, but there's a reason behind it, and no matter what hardship we face, we'll be rewarded for it — better days will come, whether in this life or the next. That's really what gets me through it — having that certainty that Allah is not going to abandon us, and that good will come, no matter how long it takes.

question: WHAT INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS ARE PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
That's a really hard question to answer, because the community is so diverse, and I think we have little cliques even within the community — groups that are maybe more practicing, the Salafi, the Ikhwani, this and that — we're very much divided and diverse in many ways. Within those different groups, maybe there are certain expectations. The Salafis, for example, are more conservative, and generally the women will be wearing the abaya, the niqab — though obviously it's not the same for everyone. Whereas other groups, niqab isn't even something that's discussed; some might say wide-leg pants are fine, others say you have to wear abaya. It really depends on the group and their perspective.

The weird thing is I feel like I'm just a floater — I don't fit into any one group. These are the commandments Allah put for us, but how, and whether, we implement them is really a personal relationship between the person and Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. It's not my business if somebody is wearing an abaya and black niqab, or wearing skinny jeans and no hijab. Personally, I don't even think about that — I just deal with people as they are. And, on that note, I've seen women who don't wear hijab who are more religious, more serious about praying on time, than women wearing niqab. So the dress itself doesn't always represent the level of religiosity or implementation of the essential pillars. That's something I think is important to know — I recognized years back that wearing more conservative attire doesn't necessarily mean you're a better Muslim.

Dress aside, it really depends from community to community. Some communities are more conservative, prefer women to stay home and become housewives, and education might not be so important, whereas other communities expect Muslim women to get PhDs and be successful in certain careers. And in terms of how they behave — having friends of the opposite gender, who they go out with, spend time with, smoking, those kinds of things — it really depends.

question: INTERNAL AND EXTERNAL STRUGGLES AFTER ADOPTING HIJAB
answer:
The biggest struggle from the beginning was internal. I don't know if it's just a convert thing, but it was a whole lifestyle change — not having the discipline, having to pray five times a day, and changing the way I saw the world and the things happening around me. My level of understanding all changed, so it was a huge internal struggle at the beginning. It did take some time, and I'm glad I took the time to go through it, because I think sometimes people rush through it — they're like, I'm going to be this perfect Muslim overnight, and then they can't handle it and they regress. Alhamdulillah, I took my time, focused on specific important parts and slowly implemented them before moving on to others — that helped ease the struggle, and I was able to mentally deal with everything.

The external struggle came along with the conversion too, with my non-Muslim family — they weren't very happy that I became Muslim, they were worried about what would happen to me, they thought I'd change and become this radical Muslim terrorist. Not just them — I lost friends too, especially once I wore the hijab, because then I was visibly Muslim; before that, it wasn't visible, so they could deal with it. Once I was physically wearing the hijab, the friends who weren't happy with Muslims and Islam, I lost those friendships. Externally, family members and friends really changed, even the places I went — I stopped going to places where alcohol was being served, and within my family, a lot of them aren't Muslim, so they drink alcohol, and I wasn't going to sit with them while they drank anymore. A lot of my family members didn't really know how to deal with me, weren't sure what to expect or how I'd change — it was uncomfortable at first, a lot of growing pains, but with time they saw there were some differences, I looked different, but I was still [INTERVIEWEE], and eventually they became more comfortable with that.

I'm still the only Muslim in my family, just myself and my children. Initially everybody was scared, they didn't know what to expect. I remember, maybe five years ago now, my grandmother made a comment — she said, we thought it was just a phase, that you'd go through this phase of wanting to be Muslim. They really expected that, and I think a lot of them thought I'd become this hardcore, conservative terrorist, and when they saw I was still the same person, they calmed down and became more comfortable. We settled into an understanding with each other — okay, this is how it is now: [INTERVIEWEE] doesn't come to gatherings where there's alcohol, [INTERVIEWEE] covers in front of men, [INTERVIEWEE] doesn't shake hands. It was just an understanding that [INTERVIEWEE]'s still [INTERVIEWEE] overall — she'll still sit with you, talk with you, joke with you, but there are certain limitations.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer:
Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, first and foremost — in terms of fulfilling the obligations of the salah, the praying, the fasting, all of that. After that, it might sound weird, but to myself — to be making the right choices.

A lot of my close family members are deceased. My father is still alive; we have a decent relationship in terms of communicating, but even when I was in Canada he lived in a different country, so there's always been that distance. I definitely help him when he needs it, but he's still very much independent, and it's more that personal, social communication rather than spending time together. That's why I didn't put my parents closer to the top of the list.

In terms of my relationship with Allah, it's making sure I'm fulfilling the requirements — praying, fasting. On a personal level, it's having balance between my religion and my long-term career goals and aspirations, and interpersonal relationships, with the opposite gender and with my own friends. And with my children — I guess maybe because I'm a convert and my family isn't Muslim to be there to support, I tried to raise them as best I could, when they were younger, as Muslims, especially my older son and daughter, who are eighteen and twenty now.

At the same time, I'm not the type of person to stand over them, saying you have to pray at a certain time. As they got older, I told them, you have to make your own personal choice about your relationship with Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala and your level of implementation of the religion — if you do it out of fear of me, you're not doing it for the right reasons. So although I'm not a hundred percent happy with the choices they make, I know inshallah the foundation is there, and everybody is going to stand before Allah on the Day of Judgment. I've tried my best, and the rest is for them to make their choices. My younger son, I'm spending a lot more time on now, because he didn't have those foundational classes when he was younger, so I'm trying to provide the same foundation, inshallah, that my older two had — and he'll have to make his own choice once he's older about how he practices his religion. At the same time, I'm their mother, they're my children — even if I'm not happy with the choices they make, it doesn't change our relationship.

question: DOES LACK OF FAMILY SUPPORT AFFECT HOW YOU RAISE YOUR CHILDREN?
answer: Yes and no. I don't know how it is in the United States, but in Canada these days, you see even children from Muslim families who aren't quite practicing at all, unfortunately making really bad life choices — and some of them have family members, or families, with close relationships with other community members. The Yemeni community, I'd say, and the Somali community as well, are quite tight-knit, where families spend nights and evenings together, so much time that the kids basically become like cousins. But even in situations like that, I've seen the boys or girls, as they get older, go in different directions, even though that support and foundation is there. So although I initially thought I was at a disadvantage because I didn't have Muslim family support, and my ex-in-laws weren't really involved either, when I saw other families struggling with even worse things than what I was experiencing with my kids, I changed my mind on that. And the solution for that, I don't know.

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer:
That's a good question. Within my family, especially since I'm a single mom and there are no other close Muslim family members, it's definitely my duty to keep reminding my children about Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala and their religion, and to encourage them to do good, both in terms of religion and their worldly life, and stay away from the bad.

In terms of my community, I'd say I overextended myself serving my community. I did a lot of community work, and a lot of times I really went beyond my limits, and it took away from my time with my children. Unfortunately I see this a lot with women who try to be involved in community work — just a few days ago I was talking with the woman who took over from me running the Quran center, and she's completely burned out, managing the job of two people, and nobody else seems interested in stepping up, even though it's something very much needed. There's a very small number of people who are motivated to create these community spaces and opportunities for kids and women to come learn, be with each other, support each other, have that sense of community, but unfortunately those numbers are the minority and they end up burning out from overextending themselves to keep those resources and services running.

So I'd say I'm slightly — I wouldn't say fully — recovering from overextending myself for the community. I'm trying to step back and focus on myself and my kids more, because I can't do it all, but at the same time I'm frustrated that not more people are stepping forward to work together.

I'd say it's the love of religion, and wanting that community — because life is hard, and it's easier when you have that community support, but the problem is that the people providing it are limited, and the people wanting to take advantage of it are many, so it becomes overwhelming. I know another sister who did the same thing — she'd organize weekly potluck dinners for women to gather, bring the kids, have that space to spend time and support each other, and the kids could be among other Muslim kids. But in the end she was the one doing all the cooking, so she burned out and had to stop.

question: WHAT DOES BELONGING FEEL LIKE HERE?
answer:
I think I have a different answer now, especially because of that burnout, from over-investing myself in trying to do so much for the community. When I decided to do my master's, I stepped back a lot; when I decided to do the PhD, I stepped back even more. So I don't even really feel like I fully belong to the Muslim community anymore — don't get me wrong, I definitely do, but I'm just not as involved in community events and activities as before, and I'm okay with that, because of my own confidence in myself as a Muslim woman and my own religion — I know that my religion is really between me and God, not anybody else. It's nice to be around other Muslims sometimes, but because of that burnout, I'm like, I just need to focus on myself and my kids now. At the same time, I think it would have benefited my children more if I'd stayed more involved in the community, but I wasn't comfortable continuing at that level after the burnout.

That's a tough question — because I'm feeling more and more like, wearing hijab and being Muslim, I'm labeled as not Canadian. I've had people just walking down the street tell me to go back to my country, and it's like, I'm Canadian, I'm white. Obviously, Canadians originally come from many different European backgrounds, but that's something I've struggled with, I'd say, the past couple of years — feeling not as acknowledged, wanted, and accepted as a Canadian, because I'm a Muslim, more than at any time in the past.

It's still wearing the hijab — being a visibly Muslim woman — that means you're automatically labeled as, I guess, no longer white. I'm not the type of white Caucasian that they want. It's the religion and being visibly Muslim, that's the problem.

question: HOW DOES LIVING HERE SHAPE HOW YOU PRACTICE OR SHOW YOUR FAITH?
answer: That one's also hard to answer, because we have the masajid, there are Quran classes, Islamic lectures happening — to a certain extent you're still very freely able to practice your religion however you want. If you want to go to lectures and Quran classes, wear the abaya, everything, you definitely can. The only thing is that you do somewhat feel that rising tension, that you're different, and many people no longer want you around or accept you being around. So it's this weird tightrope — you can still practice as a Muslim, but you're not quite wanted or accepted anymore.

question: HAVE YOU BEEN MADE TO FEEL YOU'RE A THREAT?
answer:
Yeah, just walking down the street and being told to go back to my country. The biggest one — like I told you, the man who said Muslims want to take over, so he's thinking we're a threat, and I'm like, no, we're not, we just want to go to good restaurants, raise kids, have a good life — but no matter what I said, he still saw us as this aggressive group of people.

Another time, there was a big storm, and a non-Muslim couple came to my house because they didn't have electricity. I had the Al Jazeera news app on my smart TV; they made themselves comfortable, had the remote, going through everything. I was in the kitchen cooking, serving them, and I heard the man comment, Al Jazeera, this is the channel of the enemy — and his wife just kind of shushed him. I didn't even know what to say or how to respond, but at the same time I was so upset — I'm a Muslim, and I'm treating you so nicely, so kindly, but you still see Islam as the enemy. By default, am I the enemy as well?

question: HOW DO WE CREATE CHANGE OR BETTER COEXISTENCE?
answer:
That's going to be very hard to do, honestly, because what's fueling that is a whole media campaign, a social media campaign — that's a hundred percent what I believe. It's not something Muslims in particular are doing, it's that social media campaign, and it's been going on for generations, from the movies to the news to everything, basically creating that fear in people. Not everybody buys into it — I know a lot of people who have Muslim neighbors, spend time with them, realize Muslims aren't like that.

Some people have open houses, potluck dinners, sharing meals, trying to show people we're happy-go-lucky Muslims — maybe some will show up and be interested to learn, but the people just sitting at home watching TV, watching the news, those are the ones who will never show up and will keep spreading the same thoughts, no matter what we do. It's hard to say. After 9/11, Muslims were totally apologetic, everybody was condemning what happened, but did that change anything for Muslims? Did things improve? We were so focused on being apologetic and trying to distance ourselves that some people even took off their hijab to fit in, to seem like, we're fine, we're regular, normal people. I don't have a good answer — on one hand I feel like no matter what we do, for the most part they're not going to listen to us, and at the same time I'm frustrated given the social media campaigns and how we're portrayed.

I think part of the best thing we can do is just keep trying to succeed in public spaces, keep showing up. I attended an awards ceremony earlier this year, for students who received scholarships at the university, and alhamdulillah, many of the top scholarships went to Muslim students, Muslim women, hijab-wearing students — I could see the non-Muslim women were so amazed and impressed at these Muslim women who, for all accounts on social media, are these oppressed people who have no rights and can't do anything, but they see us showing up in these spaces, succeeding and doing well. Even some of my undergraduate students have commented on how happy they were to see me in the classroom, as a very visibly practicing Muslim woman, being the professor, teaching them, doing research, getting a PhD — they were so happy and excited to see me there.

One time, during Ramadan, I was fasting, and the course was during the daytime, so my mouth was getting dry — it's hard to keep talking. I'm pretty easygoing, so I just said, sorry guys, I'm fasting and getting so thirsty, just give me a minute, and made a joke about leaving my kids at home sleeping while I'm here with you guys. After class, one student messaged me and said she was so happy that I was comfortable openly talking about it — it was a class of two hundred students — that it normalized it for the non-Muslims too, showing them, yes, we fast, we pray, we continue our lives and do good things, and that's it. So with all my rants and tangents, my final answer is just to keep showing up and being successful.

question: DO YOU FEEL A RESPONSIBILITY TO REPRESENT THE COMMUNITY WELL?
answer: Not necessarily — because there's still a bit of a culture where women should stay home and take care of their kids, focus on that, as opposed to being out in the community and spending all their time there. A lot of my friends would always say, you have your own problems, your own kids, just stay home and focus on yourself. So I don't think there's that pressure, necessarily, no.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: Oh, yeah, it actually plays a huge role, because I know that everything I do, I'm going to be standing before Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala on the Day of Judgment and held accountable for my actions — in terms of harming somebody, even to my own detriment, financially, physically, emotionally, I never want to be in a situation where I'm harming somebody else, where somebody can complain about me to Allah on the Day of Judgment. Honestly, in hindsight, I've even done too much, been walked over, in those scenarios, but at the same time you're trying to get the good deeds and not infringe on anybody else's rights, to make things easy for other people. Definitely knowing that I'm going to be standing before Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala and judged for my actions, and where I end up in the next life is heavily dependent on it — it plays an overwhelmingly huge role in the choices I make every day.

question: HOW DO YOU MAKE SENSE OF WHAT IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL?
answer: Beyond my control — I definitely take a step back and leave a choice for my qadar. I used to try to be very controlling, push things to go a certain way if I decided it had to be that way, but with maybe maturity and understanding in my religion, I accept that I try my best in whatever I'm trying to accomplish, but if things aren't working out, or it just seems like it's not meant to be, I'm okay stepping back and saying, it wasn't meant to be like that. That goes even with the death of non-Muslims in my family — some people dwell on it, and it's hard for them when a non-Muslim family member dies. For me, I don't know, maybe I'm just built differently, but the death itself is difficult, obviously, but in terms of their own afterlife, it's under the control of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala — I have zero control over that.

question: WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR PRACTICING YOUR RELIGION IN THE LONG RUN?
answer:
It's hard to say, because on one side I very much believe that religion is a personal choice and a personal implementation. I'm a woman, so I don't have to go to the masjid five times a day — I just pray at home, or wherever I need to pray, I find a place. I pray outside, in hallways, stairwells, changing rooms — I find a place to pray. And that's in the West — I've generally never had any issues finding a place to pray and praying. Same with fasting during Ramadan — it's a personal thing, nobody can force you or control when you can and can't fast.

Even if it came to a point where there were no Quran classes, no Islamic lectures, alhamdulillah, everything is online — the resources are always there for people to find and practice and implement.

What I really miss, and didn't like, is not hearing the Adhan, not having a wider community always remind you of Allah SWT. Now that I'm here in [CITY 1] — a few weeks ago I was in a taxi, and the driver was asking me questions because he knew I was a foreigner, and he asked, are you Muslim? He said, your answer is wrong — I said, what do you mean my answer is wrong, your question is silly — and he said, no, you should follow it with alhamdulillah. I just stopped and said, you're right, thank you for that. So sometimes it's those little interactions with fellow Muslims that remind you of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala — that's something you miss if you're living in the West and not among a lot of Muslims. Obviously you see a lot of bad behaviors too, but it's those little things, those reminders, that make a difference. So my answer is that living in the West, you're still able to practice Islam, because nobody can force it on you — you can still pray at home or other random places, learn as much as you want, it's your personal choice. At the same time, I personally felt like something was missing.

question: HAVE YOU NOTICED CHANGE IN HOW MUSLIM STUDENTS ARE TREATED ON CAMPUS?
answer: It's a hard question for me to answer. After 9/11, I was in college for most of my college years and wasn't Muslim, and didn't spend time with Muslims. When I did convert, I mostly hung out with MSA groups, the more practicing Muslims. For my bachelor's I did it online. For my master's, I did it as an adult, and I pretty much just went from class to home because I had kids. Same for my PhD now. So I can't really comment on Muslim students then and now — it's hard for me to do that, honestly.

question: WHAT IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR HEART, INTENTION, AND OUTWARD PRACTICE?
answer:
It's hard to answer, because of the layeredness — where do I even start. I've always had it at the back of my mind, the desire to be in a Muslim country — this was from years ago, but it was always delayed, because I felt I needed more education, needed to finish this or that. My intention was, I'll get a good job and come here with a job, which is basically not what I've done. But it was always delayed because of needing to accomplish something else first. At the same time, I strongly believe in what was written to happen — it was just meant that I didn't come in the past, and I'm here now. Even coming here, I had that layered intention — I was going to wait until after my PhD, but then I thought, it's taking me forever to finish, am I going to keep delaying things? So I decided to take the jump, throw myself in the deep end and just do it, whatever happens happens. I have somewhat of a plan, savings and so on — not no plan at all.

In terms of how I feel in my intentions, there's nothing better than hearing the Adhan — I love hearing the Adhan. My first apartment here was right beside the mosque; if you missed Fajr in the morning it's because you were dead asleep, it was so loud. Here you can hear the Adhan, but if you have the TV on or other things, you won't — which actually upset me, because I really wanted to be able to hear it loudly. At the same time, I can't say I'm spiritually different between Canada and here — I still feel the same. I can't say being in a Muslim country has increased my religiosity; I'd say it's still the same, whether I'm in Canada or in Egypt — praying, ibadah, everything is the same. Although, fasting the days of Ashura here, I was so thirsty — fasting in Canada is so much easier than fasting in Egypt — but that increases the reward. From a religious perspective, I don't feel different.

Fasting Ashura is something from the religion that's recommended to do, a commemoration of what Prophet Musa went through with his companions and how Allah saved them, and it's recommended to fast the day itself as well as the day before or after. As for the intention behind it, it's generally my practice, even in Canada, to try to do as many of the recommended days as possible — a regular practice, though I don't generally do the white days, I'll be honest, but the special days that come a few times a year, I make an effort to do those. That's nothing new — I'd do it whether I'm in Canada or here in Egypt. It's what I want for myself, what will remain no matter where I am.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer: Submission to Allah means that I'm trying to abide by the commandments of Allah as much as possible, and do my best to fulfill them as they've been commanded. Obviously we all have weaknesses and shortcomings, but that means praying Fajr on time, not just Fajr, all the salah, praying them on time, trying to do any additional salah, fasting during Ramadan, trying to do any additional recommended fasts, giving charity, going for Umrah, Hajj, helping the community, helping the poor — the things Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala has asked us to do, commanded us to do, and recommended for us, again with the Akhirah in mind, that you want your scale of good deeds to be heavy when you meet Allah.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer:
It's a hard question — I don't feel that I'm not liberated. When you ask that question, I go back to the whole stereotypical standard that we're oppressed, we're not free, we're forced to wear the hijab and do all these things — and I just reject that, that I'm not even liberated to begin with. I'm a free woman, and even being a woman, I don't feel like it stops me. I know sometimes people see these patriarchal societies, how women need a man to do everything, but I don't feel that way — there's no man who's ever made me feel that I can't do something on my own, that I need a man to do anything. So in terms of where and how I feel most liberated — the whole world.

As a woman, Allah created us free. I know there's that stereotype that we need a man to do everything, that we're behind the men, but I don't feel that way at all — I've never been made to feel that way, no matter where I am, in Saudi Arabia, in Canada, in Egypt, or anywhere else I've traveled. I've never felt that I'm a second-class citizen, or that I'm not free. I guess that's just how I see it — maybe I don't have the cultural baggage; people with more of the cultural norms and expectations from quote-unquote Muslim countries might feel differently. Just as a convert, I've never felt that way.

I'd say it's the same — the only thing that's changed is my mindset, my way of viewing the world and processing what's happening around me. But in terms of feeling liberated, I'd say it's the same, whether before or after I became Muslim.

question: DO YOU KNOW ANYONE ELSE WHO WOULD BE WILLING TO SPEAK WITH ME?
answer:
I have a friend — she's Nigerian, immigrated to Canada, lived in many different countries all over the world, and now she's in [CITY 2]. She's been there at least four years.

My father is French Canadian, so I could speak to it a little. [CITY 2] is very diverse. Even in [CITY 2], I've been told to eff off and go back to my country while walking down the street, but at the same time, my friend has had really good experiences — nobody's ever been rude or racist to her at all. I don't know how she gets that, being both Nigerian and Muslim, no racism, nothing. At the same time, I think other parts of Quebec would be a very different experience than living in [CITY 2] — other areas aren't quite as tolerant, partly because of a lack of diversity and education. The town my father's from is about two hours from [CITY 3], and people there aren't very educated, so their mindset is very different than people in, say, [CITY 2], where people are more educated. So it really depends. Even now, because of the newer laws, my friend is saying she doesn't know if she wants to stay in a province that's very clearly Islamophobic — not because of something that's specifically happened to her, but because Muslim women who work in schools and daycares can no longer wear hijab there.

She does consulting work for another province's government, living in [CITY 2] because she likes it there, but she's involved in a lot of activities and things socially. She's even had good luck in places where I've had bad experiences, like Italy — so I don't know what to tell you, she'll tell you a lot of great things, whereas I'm like, Quebec is horrible and nobody should go there.

You hear it's become normal now to hear that a girl has had her hijab ripped off, or been physically attacked — especially women more than men, I guess because of that visible representation. I was just thinking, while you were talking — I haven't talked to her in a long time, so I hope she'll even respond, but [NAMED PUBLIC FIGURE] — I never say her last name properly — she used to hold [A FEDERAL ANTI-ISLAMOPHOBIA ROLE]. Would you like to try to talk to her? She's no longer in that position since the new prime minister took over and relieved her from it, but I can send her a message with your information, though I haven't talked to her in so long she might just ignore me.

I'll try to think — I'll go through my contact list and see if I can think of anyone else who could speak to their lived, everyday experiences. Since I started my PhD I've really just been antisocial, so I haven't kept up those social connections — it's like I have to apologize to everybody first for ignoring them so long, and then ask them to participate in your study.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer:
Now I don't work — I'm on maternity leave, so it's a little different. When I was working, I was finishing my studies, so I worked in a public hospital where the hijab isn't authorized. I would wake up, put my hijab on over a surgical cap, and go to the hospital. Before arriving, I would take off my hijab and go into the wards wearing just the surgical cap. It's been an issue in almost every ward I've worked in, except one. I'd live my day normally, and at the end of the day I'd put my hijab back on and go home. Now that I'm on maternity leave, I don't think my hijab disturbs my daily life — sometimes I ask myself more questions about it, but now I wake up, take care of my baby, and go out and do whatever I want whenever I want. I don't have a lot of limits because of my hijab.

Faith is the center of my life. I make decisions based on my faith, I educate myself with Islamic content, and I pray wherever I am — I always find a place, especially in stores, like in the changing room of a clothing store. There are very few places to pray, even a mosque, in [CITY 1], especially for women. There are some for men, but except for the big mosque, the smaller mosques don't let women in. They say there's only one room and no one to supervise it, so they give it to the men and say it's obligatory for men (to pray there) — maybe women should pray at home instead. I don't know, but this is something that bothers me. So I pray in shopping malls, in little clothes shops. A few times I've prayed in a public park, but I was so scared that it's really only happened a few times. I think wearing the hijab is a demonstration of our faith in the street, especially in France. I'm in [CITY 1], or near [CITY 1].

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer: I would say I'm French, I feel French, and that I worship only God and pray five times a day. I think if you haven't seen a Muslim woman before, there's nothing that special about us — maybe the hijab, but that's it. I would say we are a community that always tries to do good and avoid the bad, and something I really like is that people do things for Allah's sake. That's really different from the French people I know, who are mostly atheist — they tend to only do something if there's something in it for them. You will rarely see someone do something good out of nowhere. So I'd say we try to do good actions just to please our God and to have good deeds in the balance.

question: WHAT DOES BELONGING FEEL LIKE HERE?
answer:
Of course, I was born here, and I feel a strong belonging — I don't know if that's the right way to put it, but I feel I belong to Western culture. It's a mixed feeling, unfortunately, because I also feel that my society is rejecting me, especially politically. Our politicians say so many things against us, it's crazy. Our Prime Minister recently talked about forbidding hijabi women from doing sports in high-level competition while wearing the hijab, and on TV, at the end of his remarks, he said "à bas le voile" — "down with the veil" — the way you'd say "down with the king" during a revolution. I was so shocked. Around the same time — it's quite recent that I started wearing the hijab, in 2023 — our education minister said it was forbidden to go to school wearing abayas. It was at that time that I was traveling for six months, and I felt so free. I couldn't stop thinking — the question wasn't when or why I would wear my hijab, it was why I wasn't wearing it, when I felt so free. So I decided to wear my hijab while traveling, and when I came back it was really hard, because I didn't know if I'd be able to stick with it. The abaya ban happened while I was traveling, and it made me even more attached to my hijab. I think that's one of the effects of events like that: people who are in the middle either become more attached to Islam or become more discreet about it. That's what happened for me.

It's not only about religion, because here in France we have this saying that religion isn't a hundred percent about the hijab — you can't say someone who doesn't wear the hijab isn't religious. You can have great faith, do many good deeds, and be very close to Allah, but not wear the hijab because it feels impossible. That was the case for me, because I was in medical studies, and it's forbidden in the hospital. It felt impossible. Every year it stayed on my inshallah list, and it seemed impossible until I traveled, especially to Malaysia and Indonesia, where I saw everybody wearing it and everybody was fine with it. I thought, so it is possible. It's so carefree and lightweight there — you see Muslim women in hijab everywhere, on buses, in hospitals, doing whatever they want.

It's forbidden for people who represent the state, like doctors, to wear hijab, but it's fine for patients — as someone representing a public service, it's forbidden for me. It shouldn't apply in private hospitals, but a lot of private hospitals make their own rules against it too; there, it's the head of the private institution who decides whether he wants to allow it or not.

question: HOW DOES LIVING HERE SHAPE HOW YOU PRACTICE OR SHOW YOUR FAITH?
answer:
It's really difficult — you can't talk about faith in France, that's my feeling. If you say "I believe in God," people look at you like you're dumb, like something out of the 1950s, like a hippie or someone crazy. So I only talk about my faith with Muslims; with non-Muslims, it's one word and the conversation is over. It's taboo. For example, I was recently looking for activities for my son, and near my home there was a place called [FAMILY ACTIVITY CENTRE 1] that offered psychomotor activities for kids. It was free, so I went, and everyone was very friendly — even nicer than usual. Someone asked how I'd heard about them, and I said Google Maps. The next time I went, I noticed a cross in the building — it was a Christian organization. I wasn't sure if it was okay for me to be there, but I told myself it was fine. Someone asked me what my son's name, [SON'S NAME], meant, and I said it was from the Qur'an, and after that it was like "okay," and no more conversation. I've had the same experience in other places — at a mother's coffee morning, I was speaking French to my son while my husband spoke Arabic to him, and a French woman married to an American asked why I was teaching him Arabic, as if I should just be teaching him values. I said it's so he learns about (his) religion, and she just said, "okay."

I think it's the same with all religions — people are very faith-free here, especially in [CITY 1]. There's a lot of atheism. There are some Jews who sometimes talk about their religion. There are Christians who don't go to church and don't practice — they're Christian by culture, not really by faith. I even met someone who had her child baptized, not because she believed in it, but because she wanted him to get into a good Catholic school. And yet, in that church, the people were strangely warm and friendly — I think because they were practicing Christians, welcoming and polite.
