So I think people of faith understand each other more than we understand atheists.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, AND HOW?
answer: Yes, I try to. I'm learning Tajweed at a mosque, and I try to read — I read books quite frequently, I listen to podcasts, and I watch YouTube videos, like Omar Suleiman's.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
I always knew it was something obligatory — although at one point someone told me it wasn't obligatory, it was just about control, and that suited me at the time because it was difficult. So I just lived like that. Then I traveled, and I felt so free. I went to Malaysia or Indonesia — I don't remember which — and I was in the countryside. We met some local people, and I told them I was Muslim too, and one woman said, "Muslim? Where's your hijab?" I thought, she's right — that's something you'd never hear in France. That's how I began to think about it. I was learning a lot at that time, listening to a lot of podcasts, and I was also so grateful, because traveling the whole world for six months had been my dream. Out of that gratitude, my way of saying thank you was to wear the hijab.

I felt free while traveling, so I decided to put on the hijab because I didn't feel the pressure I felt in France. Before that, I thought I felt free in France, because I didn't realize how much pressure I was under. It was only when I went to other countries that I understood what it meant to be free of that pressure. In South America, for example, we were always trying to find places to pray. Once, at a hotel where we hadn't even slept yet — we'd just left our luggage there — we asked if we could pray somewhere, and they said, "yeah, of course," like it was nothing. In France, if people say okay to that kind of thing, you feel like you have to thank them five times over. It will never feel as easy there. That's one thing that made me realize how much pressure there is in France, from society.

It's pressure to hide, of course, because here in France, on television and in political speech, they say the hijab is a tool of Islamization — that we're trying to Islamize people, that it's political, that we're trying to prove ourselves in public space. In France they say faith should be private — you can have your faith in private, that's fine — but the French idea of religion is that you're not supposed to show your faith. You're supposed to keep it private.

question: HOW AND WHERE ARE YOU ABLE TO PRAY DURING YOUR DAY?
answer: At times I've prayed in the toilet, but I asked and was told that wasn't okay, so I've prayed in the shower — in the surgical area, not the changing room, there's always a shower — or in a patient's exam room, not where the patient sleeps, just where you examine them. When there's no patient, I pray there, behind the door, and I lock it if I can. If I can't, I pray just behind the door, so if someone comes in on me I can just stop. Some hospitals even have chapels, but they forbid staff from using them — they say it's only for patients, and practicing (Muslim) staff aren't allowed in.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer: I think it protects me in a lot of ways — you become more aware of your behavior. I'm proud to be a representation of Islam in the streets; I'm trying to be a doctor while wearing my hijab. I feel like I can be an example for young girls, and even for racists — there's this big idea in France that Arabs are just here to take public money, to have children and live off the state, so I'm proud to show something different. I also think it's good protection against men's looks, even if sometimes it doesn't stop them.

question: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN OR HIJAB?
answer: I think they need someone to blame because of poor economic policy. Maybe they also want to preserve some idea of French identity. Mainly, I think it's a way to cover up political mistakes — it's easier for people to look at Islam than to look at what's really happening in politics.

question: HOW DOES YOUR EXPERIENCE DIFFER FROM A MUSLIM MAN'S?
answer: It's so different, because you often can't tell a Muslim man is Muslim just by looking at him — he could be Jewish, Portuguese, Spanish. So we, (women,) are the main target, for sure. And it's not only about the political representation of Islam — they hate the hijab because, to them, it represents submission: submission to men, submission to Islam. Their vision of freedom is that to be free you have to be free of your clothes, so to speak, and by wearing the hijab we're seen as submitting to men. That's seen as really against French feminism.

question: WHAT DOES FRENCH FEMINISM MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
I think the French woman (ideal) is someone who doesn't care about anything, who can live the life she wants — any job, any lover. Marrying, for example, is seen as really old-fashioned by my French friends and even my co-workers. I remember being at work, talking with my boss, who was just a few years older than me, and I mentioned I was married. She asked at what age. I said twenty-five, and she said that was so young — she couldn't imagine being married before thirty, that it was crazy. At the beginning, I didn't tell people I was married; I said "boyfriend" instead, because I knew it would lead to the same reaction: married, at what age, that's crazy. It's easier to just not say.

Another thing that happened: I'm a hospital specialist, and at the first meeting of my cohort, there was a buffet, and I was talking with someone a few years older than me. A waiter came around with food, and I asked if there was meat in it. When the waiter said yes, I said no thank you, and the older man I was talking to asked, "Oh, you're vegetarian?" I said yes, and then he asked why, since when. I thought, okay, I actually eat ham — I'll just stop the lie right now. It's just so much easier to say I'm vegetarian, but even that didn't work. It shows you it's easier to talk about nothing with them.

Another thing that happened — a doctor at a well-known center in [CITY 1], who's Tunisian, was talking about his upcoming marriage, which was arranged. People around him reacted like, "Oh my god, arranged marriage, that's crazy," and he ended up not getting the job because of it — they said they couldn't work with someone like that. So, the less you say, the better, I think.

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer: I think it's part of the difficulties I have to face, but I think it's okay — it makes sense because I'm representing Islam. If I left France, who would stay to represent (us)? I'll have, inshallah, the means to manage, and I feel like if I left, I'd just be leaving people who are less educated or poorer to face Islamophobia on their own, whereas I can be an example of good social integration — a hijabi who works as a doctor. I think that's a good image for people, so I see it as my contribution.

question: WHAT INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS ARE PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
Not that much, I think — I don't know, because I'm not so involved in the community; I mostly have Muslim female friends, so maybe I'm just not close enough to it to feel it. It is quite sad that there's often no space for women to pray at small mosques. I don't go to the mosque often, just for classes or for Eid — for Jumu'ah you have to check beforehand whether there's a place for women. I think there are some women who go regularly.

I see it on social media, but not so much in my daily life. If anything, I see a lot of people trying to ease into the hijab by wearing a turban first, especially in the Algerian community. In France, that community has a difficult history — we were under colonization for a long time, a hundred and forty years, and destroying our culture, especially the hijab, was part of French policy. After decolonization there was a civil war against Islamists — Islamists against the Algerian liberation movement — so there's a lot of trauma around this in Algerian families. When I wear my hijab, I see it in my parents' generation — not my own parents, but for example my friend's father looked at me like, "whoa, that's so radical, that's too much." They're frightened, I think, because of the civil war — they saw so much, and in the 1980s a lot of girls in Algeria were forced to wear it just for their own safety, and that's stayed in the minds of that generation. I'm also thinking of a friend's mother who is starting to wear the hijab, but very slowly — just covering the neck at first — because she has a whole social circle to navigate, and when you wear the hijab you're always worried people will say you're becoming radicalized.

Muslims and non-Muslims (both say this). Personally, I was afraid of being seen as radicalizing — we hear so much about "radicalization" on TV, like it's the worst thing on earth. They don't say it outright, but what's implied is that when you radicalize, you're against people, against the state, a danger to others, closing yourself off, not wanting to be seen. I saw a clip from a French TV show where a man said, "Do you realize how violent it is for me to see a woman in hijab? She's telling me I'll never be with her" — as if she's telling the whole world it's impossible to have her. It's crazy. I've also seen, on social media, people say that hijab isn't part of Amazigh culture, as if Amazigh women don't wear it — I can't imagine it's even harder for them.

I think the real issue isn't either of those things — it's that I felt like I had to say goodbye to a part of my identity before the hijab. When you put it on, you know a lot will change. When I came back to France wearing my hijab, I went to ask for information at a desk in the métro, and I was spoken to so rudely — before, I had a kind of "beauty privilege," where everyone was nice and easy with me, and with the hijab I never felt that again. But on the other hand, I felt like Muslims would come up to me, like they recognized a sister. Another time, cycling, I didn't stop at a red light — which is really common here, cyclists never stop — and a man got angry and called me "sale hijabi," dirty hijabi, meaning it as an insult. Another time, passing a café, a man who was drinking alcohol said, "Hey you, why do you cover your hair?" and I told him, "Isn't it your dream to see my hair? It's your dream." Then I just walked away. But there are things like that. On the other hand, when I'm cycling in [CITY 1], sometimes Muslim men will see me and say it's good to see a hijabi cycling.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer: Of course, because in Malaysia I'm a nobody — I don't have social connections there the way I do here. At work, for example, I was talking about the hijab, and a young woman I thought was fairly educated asked me, "Oh, so did you start wearing the hijab when you got married?" I said no, and you have to explain, again and again. I just finished my studies this year — six years as a student, then six years as a resident, so you're a full-time specialist, but still a resident. I need one more year in the public hospital, inshallah.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer:
First, Allah. In the work environment, of course, I'm always afraid of my superiors, of people reporting to the administration that I wear a hijab, so I modify my behavior. In the last ward I was in, I never ate with my co-workers at the hospital, because you might run into someone from the administration, and if they see you in the surgical cap, they'll keep track of you until you can't wear even that anymore — because even the surgical cap is forbidden.

I hide when I can and try to be as discreet as possible. For example, when you start in a new ward, they take a photo of you for the hospital website — I let them take it, but then I asked the photographer not to post it anywhere, because I knew it could lead to me having to take off the surgical cap. I also don't let myself speak at conferences, because I don't want the extra attention — I don't want extra work for myself, I just want to finish my studies. I'd wear the hijab, but I don't want to speak publicly, because there's this idea in the public sector that the hijab is political — I don't want them saying, "you see, she's showing off her religion." I don't want the extra problems. It's worth it (to stay quiet).

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer: In my family, I try to be as good as I can — I try to educate my son, who's still very young, but I take it seriously, trying to give him love for Allah and for practicing the religion. In my community, I try to act mainly in an educational way. I've participated in meetings where I talk about my job and help medical students study, and I take part in mock exams — I sit on the jury and see the students. I think that's my way of helping the community.

question: DO YOU FEEL YOU BELONG HERE — ARE YOU SEEN AS FRENCH/QUEBECOIS?
answer: I'm not sure at all. One of the men in my family married a French woman, and when she met me she asked if I was born here. So I'm not sure — I don't think they see me as French. When they see the hijab, I don't think they do. Just recently I took my son to the doctor, and it was an Arab woman like me, but I felt like she looked down on me, like I was stupid. Since I'm also a doctor, I felt I shouldn't have to ask questions, but she was like, "no questions, just listen." It was for a BCG vaccination, and I hadn't had it done yet because we'd traveled to Algeria — it's actually best to get that vaccination before traveling there — and she said, "oh, you took him to Algeria, that's not good, not good to go without the vaccination." I wasn't even surprised. I don't know if she's Muslim, but probably. I've also had French people talk to me really slowly so I can understand, when maybe I speak (French) better than they do.

question: WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR PRACTICING YOUR RELIGION IN THE LONG RUN?
answer:
Honestly, I have very little hope that things will change for the better. I'll teach my son as much as I can, especially prayer — I want that to be the most important thing, praying on time, even if that's not the easiest thing here. I don't think it can get better, honestly; I'd be happy if it just stayed like this.

What I fear is — there were social reasons why my generation didn't learn Arabic; it was treated as shameful to speak Arabic, and our parents wanted so much to protect us from being mocked, so a lot of people in my generation never learned the language. I'm glad my husband can teach our son. I fear him learning to hate himself — in French, détestation de soi, self-hatred, I hope that's a good translation — because we see so much negative talk about Muslims on television, and I don't want him to feel that. For example, I know of a boy at school who didn't want to wear nail polish, and the school called his mother in to explain why she was "forbidding" it, as if the boy should be free to wear it. Another story: a boy saw someone fall at school and said, "Allahu Akbar," and his parents were called in — "you said Allahu Akbar, that's crazy, radicalization," and so on. I also know a ten- or twelve-year-old girl, Arab but from a non-practicing family, who heard "Allahu Akbar" during prayer and asked why (Muslims) say it "like terrorists." I think it's not as intense now as it was after Bataclan and the big terrorist attacks in France, when "Allahu Akbar" really did mean "terrorist" to people. I feel that's slowly changing — maybe people are starting to understand that we say it in prayer.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: I wish it shaped it even more, but it makes me try to learn Qur'an, try to do good deeds, and make a lot of du'a. I don't know that it shapes it beyond that.

question: HOW DO YOU MAKE SENSE OF WHAT IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL?
answer: For the moment, it's still okay to wear the hijab in public space, so I can still do the things that are obligatory in our religion. As for the other difficulties, I think they're meant for us, and that they become good deeds for us — when you have difficulties, it's only so you have fewer bad things weighing on your balance. So I try to take it in a good way, to tell myself it will benefit me in the end, inshallah.

question: HOW DO YOU UNDERSTAND LAÏCITÉ, AND HOW DOES IT AFFECT YOU?
answer:
It's a big word here. It's everywhere in the hospital — every time you start in a new ward, you get a PowerPoint about laïcité. It's crazy, really — laïcité, laïcité, you can't wear a surgical cap, it's forbidden, laïcité. But you'll see people wearing a cross necklace, and that's not a problem. Legally, laïcité just means a public agent has the obligation to be neutral — to show no sign of belonging, of religious affiliation. But in French politics they want to expand it to any individual in public space, and even ordinary French people who aren't politicians tend to think that's what laïcité means.

I know laïcité is really just a pretext for Islamophobia — it's very clear. Co-workers will report you to the administration if they see a surgical cap, but if they see a cross, they won't call anyone. Now hospitals even have people whose job is to be the "laïcité police" — they're literally called the chief of laïcité, and they go looking for surgical caps on our heads.

There's a story from my hospital. For a while it was okay for me to wear the surgical cap, but they always made it clear they were doing me a favor. Then one day, someone wrote a letter saying an employee wasn't respecting laïcité — it wasn't even about me, it was about someone at the front desk who wore her hijab visibly, while I just wore the surgical cap in the back. But because of that letter, it became a huge issue. They called me into the office and told me, in no uncertain terms, that I couldn't wear it anymore. I was so desperate. I went to another office, to the ward administrator, and she said she was sorry, and suggested I go to occupational health to see if a doctor could give me a note saying I had a medical need for the surgical cap. I didn't want to lie, but I went anyway, crying, and the doctor asked me what my husband thought about it. I thought, why does it matter what he thinks?

I went back to the administration, still crying — crying with rage — and she asked the same thing, what does your husband think? I said, it's not possible, leave me alone, I'm thirty years old, I'm a doctor, what does my husband have to do with this? I had even more rage after that. I called in sick for a week because I was so desperate.

Then I came back and took it off. It felt like taking off my dignity. It was terrible, I hated it. The administrator told me I was so brave, but it wasn't bravery — it was humiliation, an obligation, there was no bravery in it at all. I thought about it for weeks, and I couldn't accept it, so I put it back on. The head of the ward called me again, surprised, and I told him I'd gotten legal advice, so I was putting it back on — even though the legal advice I'd actually gotten was that there was nothing I could do, that I should just take it off. But I tried anyway, and they let me keep it for the rest of my internship, because it was only one more year, and I'm a surgeon (so they needed me). They wouldn't give me a research contract though — I think because they knew I'd be leaving anyway. I emailed to ask about a position for this year and never got an answer. During that search, I had an appointment with another ward chief where I wore just a turban, styled to look neat, but that felt undignifying too, I hated it. He seemed to like me — he'd already written to HR saying they had a doctor — but at the end of the appointment he told me there was no way I could keep anything on my head, because he was the chief of laïcité at his hospital too. So I didn't get that job either. I did find something else, but I don't know yet how they'll respond to the turban or the surgical cap — I had one appointment with the chief there and he didn't say anything, so it will be a surprise once I actually start.

It's okay for a hijabi woman to be a cleaner, but not to be a doctor — cleaning staff can wear a cap, even if it's not technically legal, because no one minds. I'm sure that's also post-colonial — it feels comfortable to people to see someone in a hijab in a position "lower" than them. That's just how it is.

question: DO YOU FEEL OPPRESSED BY THE STATE?
answer: Yes, of course. Especially around political symbols — it's crazy what they say.

question: WHAT IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR HEART, INTENTION, AND OUTWARD PRACTICE?
answer: I'm always worried someone will find out — that's for sure — but I do it because I have to, and in a sense I can be proud that I'm doing it. Even if I have to pray in the changing room, I'm doing what I need to do, so I feel happy about that.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer: I think it's believing in what He gave us. I think it's trying to be near Him, trying to have tawakkul, (trust in Allah). That's mostly how I'd put it.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer: In my case, I felt liberated by wearing the hijab, I think. When I go to the hospital I feel oppressed, because I have to take it off, but when I don't have to take it off, I feel liberated, because I'm doing what I want in order to please Allah — I think that's what makes me happy.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer:
I wake up in the morning, I do my worship, say my prayers, and go about my daily business — making breakfast and so on. I do a lot of volunteer work, I help people, and I do all the other things a regular person does, except I just dress differently.

I live my faith. I say my regular prayers, I follow the guidance in the Qur'an, and I feel that my religion doesn't interfere with my daily life — it is my daily life. I had a successful business running with my husband, and I was out meeting people and so on, and I always had a very good reception.

question: HOW AND WHERE ARE YOU ABLE TO PRAY DURING YOUR DAY?
answer: Yes, I am. I just excuse myself for five minutes — it doesn't take more than that. I go to the washroom, wash up, go to a corner, take my five minutes, and that's about it, then come back to my meetings and my work.

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer:
I would tell them we're no different from you — we just believe differently, but we worship the same God.

You'll be surprised: I think the people around me are my community. It doesn't matter if they're French Canadian, Christian, Jewish, Bengali, Pakistani, or Indian — it doesn't matter to me. My community is the people around me. I don't associate only with a certain community, because I believe everybody is a human being and everybody's creator is one creator. For me it's been very good — up until now I've had a very good experience here, except for a couple of times in the fifty years I've been here.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer:
I've lived here almost fifty years — this September it will be fifty years. I came here in September 1976. I've had good experiences, except when I've heard horror stories about the government making laws to discriminate against Muslim women. On a personal note, I have French Canadian friends and English-speaking friends, and I don't see a difference. I'm perfectly comfortable, except with people dealing in areas where the education level is a little lower than where I move around, because the government creates an atmosphere of fear against "the other," and then the other looks at me as the other and is scared. For instance, after 9/11, I was wearing the scarf and working in an office building on the seventh floor, and I noticed that as soon as I got into the elevator there was this barrier of cold air around me, like people were scared of me. So what I used to do was start talking to them with a big smile — "oh, that's a nice bag, where did you buy it," "those shoes look nice on you, are they comfortable" — and once you start a conversation, I could literally feel the ice melt away. They'd have a smile on their face and chit-chat with me until I got to my floor.

I think everybody should do that — I don't think it's only because I wear this scarf and I'm visibly Muslim that I do it, but I make a point of it because I know the other person is scared of me, because fear-mongering has taken its toll. I want to break down their fears, show them I'm just another human being like them — I go about my business, I eat my food, I do my exercise, I go for walks, just like them. I only believe differently, I only dress differently. It's part of my wardrobe, part of my practice — it's not something to be scared of.

I didn't wear the hijab until 1997, after I did my Hajj. As I understand my Islam, I have to dress modestly — I don't have to cover my head, I don't have to flaunt my hairstyle, but if I'm modestly dressed and covered, I don't have to wear this. But since I went for my Hajj, I understood it differently: when I stand in prayer I cover my head, so I understood that maybe I should always cover my head. I also found it easier for me, because whenever I'm out somewhere and it's prayer time, I don't have to look for something to cover my head — I'm always ready for prayer. There were many reasons. One was that I wanted people to know it's not your dress that matters, it's what's inside you, what's inside your brain, that matters. When I communicate with others, I want them to feel I'm no different from them.

question: HOW DOES LIVING HERE SHAPE HOW YOU PRACTICE OR SHOW YOUR FAITH?
answer: I have to share with you that I haven't had that experience. There have been many occasions where I was the only hijabi woman among thousands of non-hijabi women, Muslim and non-Muslim, and I haven't felt uncomfortable at all. Sometimes I even forget I have it on my head — I'm driving, somebody cuts in front of me, I scream at them, and then think, "oh my god, they're going to think this is what a Muslim woman is like." For me this is just part of my dress now — I've been wearing it almost twenty years. My math isn't all that good, but I don't feel different.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, AND HOW?
answer: Absolutely. I read a lot of books, and I've read ten to fifteen different interpretations of the Qur'an. For the last thirty years, maybe more, I've made it my mission to read a different translation every Ramadan, just for my own knowledge, because you really can't translate the Qur'an, you can only interpret it. An elderly person once told me that if you want to understand the Qur'an, you have to read different interpretations, because no two are quite the same — each gives a different perspective, because it's the translator's perspective, and the Qur'an is written in metaphors. So I've made it my mission to read as many translations as I can, though there are a few I keep going back to. I've also read good authors like Karen Armstrong and others. I want to build my own knowledge — I don't want to just listen to somebody else. I do listen to religious podcasts, but I form my own impressions and my own understanding. I don't like anyone telling me what's right or wrong. In fact, I encourage everyone to seek their own knowledge and understanding, because the Qur'an tells us that each soul is responsible for its own actions — we don't have the right to tell anyone they're practicing wrong, whether they wear a hijab or a niqab or neither. It's about how each of us understands our faith and practices it.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
I started wearing the hijab when I went for Hajj — you have to cover your head there, and of course, when you pray, you cover your head. I understood it as a mark of respect to my creator, and that's why I kept it on: I said, I'm going to leave it on, it's a mark of respect to my creator. Since I have to cover my head whenever I stand in prayer, I thought, why not cover it all the time? I haven't faced any aggression, except two or three times in fifty years, as I told you, so I'm pretty comfortable with my scarf.

It gives me peace, because I know I'm respecting my creator. When we stand in prayer we're standing in front of our creator, in communication with Him. So if I'm already covering my head when I come before my creator, then by leaving it on, I feel I'm always in His presence. That's why I left it on, and it hasn't had a negative impact on me.

You could call it subconscious — that's my personal understanding, and someone else might understand it differently. For me, when I have my head covered, I feel I'm in the presence of my creator all the time, because I used to cover my head only when standing in prayer.

question: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN OR HIJAB?
answer:
All the time — I'm giving interviews all the time, to the media, to PhD students like you, so many interviews in my life.

I blame my own community for a lot of this misunderstanding — we should have been more open, more willing to reach out and show people we're just the same. When I moved into this neighborhood in 1977 — I'd lived in an apartment building for a year before that, but nobody wanted to rent to us after that because we had four young children; they thought the children would destroy their apartment. So we bought a townhouse instead. When I moved in, I made a point of going out and mixing with the neighbors. My next-door neighbor, a Catholic woman, used to fast with me — when Ramadan came and she saw me fasting, she asked about it, and said she wanted to fast with me too. I asked her, don't you feel hungry, don't you feel thirsty? Because I knew that during Ramadan God gives us the strength to fast. She said no, whenever she felt hungry or thirsty she just offered it up to God, and then she was okay. On the twelfth of Rabi' al-Awwal, she baked a cake and brought it to my door — "this is for your Prophet's birthday." I've had very good experiences. She was French Canadian, and she used to come to my house for dinner, and we'd have coffee together.

There was another neighbor, a young English-speaking woman, who told me that when I first moved into the neighborhood, people were scared — "oh, Muslims are moving in, they're taught to keep their houses dirty, they don't live well." Then she said, "I come to your house and it's just the same as mine." I said, of course it is — people have these misconceptions about us, and it's up to us to remove them.

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer:
By the grace of God, I've never really had difficulty other than financial difficulty — when we moved here with young children and my husband didn't have a job, we had a difficult time financially, but I've never had any other kind of difficulty in life. I've always had very positive responses and feedback from people. We got through it by budgeting.

I said a lot of prayers and asked for God's help, and I got it. I went back to the Qur'an, to the verses in Surat At-Talaq — I think chapter 65, from the second verse to the end of the third. That's a very good ayah for getting over financial difficulty, because God says in the Qur'an, "I will give you from whence you know not" — if you have faith in Him, if you ask Him, He will give you from whence you know not. So I prayed a lot, and I was okay — my husband found a job, we budgeted, our children went to school, and we were good, masha'Allah. Sometimes now I just think, my God, where did all that come from? I don't know, but it's exactly as Surat At-Talaq says: He will give it to you from whence you know not.

question: WHAT INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS ARE PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
I don't go to the mosque — I'm sorry to say that, but I feel very insulted that women are pushed into a corner, behind curtains. I've been a secretary at my mosque, and I was on the board of a masjid — the only Muslim woman on the board here in [CITY 1], actually the first Muslim woman on that board — and I saw how our Muslim men operate: my ideas were totally discounted. It's the Muslim men who need to evolve. Muslim women have evolved, but the men need to.

Yes, and it's up to us Muslim women to rise up against those biases, against those expectations. It's turning — it will take time, but it will turn, it will be okay. Women are standing up because they're getting more knowledgeable, learning their rights, saying, "no, this isn't in the Qur'an, you can't ask me to do this because it's not in the Qur'an." It's knowledge that we need more of. Things are changing because women are getting educated and learning their Islamic rights, because Islam gave women their rights more than fourteen hundred years ago, but the colonizers came and changed all that, and Muslim men took advantage of it and changed the religious knowledge, kept women uneducated — they said women don't need to go to school, just learn to read and write a little, do the household accounting, and that was it. Men needed the higher education, they said, and the women were left financially suppressed, without the means to stand on their own two feet. But now it's changing — now women are understanding that they have Islamic rights.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer: My family — I'm responsible for bringing up my children. I taught them how to read the Qur'an, and I used to stand in prayer with them, because my husband traveled a lot for work, so I was alone with the children most of the time. I gave them whatever Islamic education I had, and I prayed with them. Now they're all grown and gone. My son lives in the States — he calls me every day, because I've told him not a day should pass without my hearing from him, since I worry. Every day I ask him if he's applied for anything over here. I don't like that he's there, honestly, to tell you the truth.

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer:
An educator, in every aspect of my life. I try to make life easy for others — God told us that, and that's what my father told us too, to help others. To tell you the truth, I don't make a difference between friends, family, outsiders, Muslims, non-Muslims — whoever needs my help, I'll help in whichever way I can.

Yes, absolutely — I was on the board of [COMMUNITY ADVOCACY ORGANIZATION 1], and on the round table of senior citizens of [SUBURBAN REGION 1]. I'm very involved in the community, and I feel everyone has to be, whether it's a Muslim community or not — a community is a community, and how will non-Muslims know who Muslims are if we don't get involved? In my family, I'm a leader — I lead my family toward goodness. I try my best.

question: WHAT DOES BELONGING FEEL LIKE HERE?
answer: I belong to Quebec, but the government keeps telling me, over and over, that I don't belong. It's a huge — I can't find the word — the government tries its best to make me not feel I belong, although I do feel I belong. Because I've lived here — I've never lived anywhere else for this long. It's been fifty years. I was only twenty-eight when I came here.

question: DO YOU FEEL YOU BELONG HERE — ARE YOU SEEN AS FRENCH/QUEBECOIS?
answer:
I have to share this with you. The government can keep on talking, but the people around me, they make me feel good. They don't discriminate against me, and life goes on as we want it to go on. The government can keep making rule after rule — who's following that rule? You will have one or two here and there, hijab-wearing women who have been discriminated against, and again I'll take you back to the reason I didn't feel discriminated against: first, I was raising my family and didn't go out to work, and then I had my own business, so I wasn't exposed to that part of society where I've heard horror stories of women being pushed down escalators because they were wearing a hijab. I have a friend who is a PhD, and when she'd just finished her PhD, she applied for a job at a university and got it, over the phone and by email — she was a hijab-wearing woman — and when she went in for her final interview and the man across the table saw her in the hijab, he completely did not hire her. All her credentials worked, her timing worked, her salary was fixed, everything was done — but when he saw her in a hijab in person, he didn't hire her. I haven't faced those situations, because I didn't go out into the world to work. I was home raising my children, because my husband and I had decided he would go out and earn the money, and I would concentrate on our family here. If I'd gone out to work, all my salary would have gone toward babysitting for four children — it wouldn't have worked out, budget-wise. So I said I'd rather give my children security and bring them up properly, and we'd make do with less.

My faith is my own faith. The province doesn't have any business in my home, and it cannot control my faith. I know Quebec has a history with religion — the Catholic Church used to be very imposing on people, and they resent religion because of that — but I don't resent my religion. My faith is my faith, and I'm a very good citizen: I've paid my taxes, I've done a lot of volunteer work, I've done a lot to help others, and they can't interfere in my faith. So I have no problem with it, although many times we've asked for a face-to-face meeting with government officials and they haven't responded.

question: DO OTHER FAITH COMMUNITIES FACE THE SAME RESTRICTIONS?
answer: The Jewish community here is a very old, well-established community — Jewish people are involved in politics and everywhere, so they're very well established, very powerful. We can't compare ourselves to them; we're not that powerful yet. The Muslim community is very new, and it will take time to establish itself. We have to be more involved in the community, more involved in politics, more involved in education — a lot more involvement. That's how you control many aspects — you control the narrative.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer:
I live toward the Akhirah — when I follow my faith, I'm taking care of my Akhirah. I live according to how the Qur'an guides me, and that's supposed to be my Akhirah. If I'm not doing anything wrong, if I'm not cheating, if I'm following the commandments God set out in the Qur'an — I counted twelve, I don't know why — I should be fine, inshallah.

I'll share a story with you. There was a Christian woman I knew who was diagnosed with a terminal illness, and she explained everything to her pastor about her funeral arrangements — what dress to bury her in, to put her Bible in her right hand. Then she said, "oh, I forgot one thing," and asked him to also put a fork in her left hand. He asked why, and she said: at church suppers, they used to call out from the kitchen window, "hold on to your forks, there's dessert coming." So she wanted to be holding her fork, because she was expecting something good to come — that's her Akhirah, holding the fork, expecting dessert from God. I thought that was such a good idea. When she passes on, she's going to get dessert. That's what shaped my thinking — that I should do everything good, and have my fork in my hand, ready.

question: HOW DO YOU MAKE SENSE OF WHAT IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL?
answer: It's very easy, if you're a person of faith — my life is very God-centered, Alhamdulillah. If something goes wrong, I believe there must be some wisdom in it, and I ask God to show me that wisdom — that something went wrong in my life for a reason, because there must be something good in it. The Qur'an tells us not a leaf falls but that it is in His knowledge.

question: WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR PRACTICING YOUR RELIGION IN THE LONG RUN?
answer:
No, my children don't have children yet. One of my daughters is a professional athlete. My daughters don't wear the hijab, and I've never asked them to, because hijab is something you have to be comfortable in — if you're not comfortable in it, it doesn't serve its purpose. As long as you're modestly dressed, that's between you and your Lord, your creator.

I'm holding the fork in my hand — I hope the future is good. I'm expecting God Almighty to have mercy on us and show us the way, although we're going through very dark times. I would like us — and when I say us, I mean the whole of Quebec — to understand each other: you're Christian, you're Jewish, I'm Muslim, you're Hindu, you're Buddhist, you don't believe in anything — but we are all human beings, and we should learn to respect each other's beliefs and move on as human beings doing good things for each other, who don't have to be enemies. We are all God's children.

question: HOW DO YOU UNDERSTAND LAÏCITÉ, AND HOW DOES IT AFFECT YOU?
answer: I don't get their version of laïcité. For me, laïcité means I'm allowed to do and believe and wear whatever I want — if I want to walk around in shorts, that's none of their business; if I want to wear a bikini, none of their business; if I want to cover and wear a niqab, that's also not their business. Laïcité means freedom of thought, to me. How is it laïcité if they're imposing something on me? That's not laïcité, to me.

question: HAVE SPECIFIC LAWS (BILL 21, BILL 94, BILL 9, ETC.) PERSONALLY AFFECTED YOU?
answer: I have speeches on that — if you want, I can share them with you and you can take excerpts. But I'm not really the right person to ask, because, as I told you, I've never personally had problems because of these laws.

question: WHAT IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR HEART, INTENTION, AND OUTWARD PRACTICE?
answer: I'm a very peaceful person — nothing really bothers me, honestly. If I have good health, food on my plate three times a day, I don't need much. Of course, three cups of coffee during the day is good too — one in the morning, one mid-morning, one at three p.m. — and I'm happy. I'm the kind of person who feels everything can be solved with dialogue: if you have a problem with me, sit down across the table, ask me questions, and I'll answer honestly. That's all.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer: Everything. Submission is everything — if I'm not submitting to the will of Allah, then I'm not a Muslim.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer: Liberation, to me, means doing things that make me happy, that make me comfortable. I don't really know where — I'm always liberated. I speak my mind; what I have inside comes out of my mouth. I speak my mind. I'm liberated.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer:
Oh my goodness — an ordinary day in my life? There are several, I would say. I've had several stages in my life, because now I'm a very senior person, and what I've done as a routine has of course varied depending on my age. So where do you want me to start? Because if you say today, my routine today is very different from my routine fifty years ago.

Let me start from the beginning, and the beginning would be my beginning in Canada, since you're interested in the history of women who have lived in Canada. I'll start there — not that I think my life is interesting, but since you asked, I'm going to respond to the best of my knowledge. I came to Canada as what at the time was called a landed immigrant, so I came as an immigrant knowing that I would become Canadian, quote-unquote, after three years. I was here as a student. This is how I started. I had hopes of getting a PhD degree, and I came against my parents' wishes — they thought I'd be here just for a couple of months, and that it was lunacy to be alone in Canada. I wasn't married at the time, so they just let me go. I had saved enough money to pay for my ticket, and I had five hundred dollars in my pocket. That's how I started here. I worked at [UNIVERSITY 1] as a teaching assistant, and I also enrolled in courses for my degree, what I hoped would be a PhD degree — and this ensured that I was more or less financially independent.

I was twenty-eight years old at the time. I came to [CITY 1] because I knew I spoke French — I was educated in a French lycée — and I liked the fact that it was a bilingual city at the time; this was very attractive to me. I was kind of disappointed, because I thought [CITY 1] was a small city compared to where I came from. I came from Egypt, and [CITY 2] was celebrating two thousand years of history at that time, so [CITY 1] seemed quite provincial to me. But very soon I discovered how convenient it was to live in this city — the water pressure was excellent, the phone lines worked without any hindrance, and this is how I started.

Now, if you want to know about my faith: I grew up in a conservative Muslim family, and I had contacts here with the Muslim community. At that time it was basically more Asian, so Pakistani, and maybe not as many Arabs — sixty-forty percent. I can't give you exact numbers, but there was just one mosque in [CITY 1]. I used to go to the mosque, I enjoyed it, and this was my first contact with the Muslim environment here. It was a Muslim non-Arab environment, but nonetheless there was a Saturday school for kids that I participated in, and I really enjoyed it. I liked my life in [CITY 1] — I used to spend an inordinate amount of time going to the stores and seeing what there was available at the beauty counters. And politically, I thought there was more freedom, although I came here with the idea that I was fed up with politics, that I didn't want to know anything about the Arab-Israeli conflict, that I just wanted to be free and live my life. But in fact politics here took hold of me — I was interested in politics, and I did appreciate that you could be involved, that you could go out in demonstrations. Although in the first few years I wasn't politically active, I was more religiously active, because this was my main attachment to the community, to the Muslim community, through the mosque.

At that time, I must say, there was no marked Islamophobia as there is today — so we're talking about the mid-70s. People would see my brown skin and they would think, "oh, so you're Pakistani." That was the first reaction. I'd say, no, I'm not Pakistani, I come from the Middle East — but usually it was the same place for people, you know, there was no difference, and nobody would address me as Muslim or would be aware that we were so different. That was [CITY 1] in the mid-70s.

Now, things began to change after the Islamic Revolution in Iran. I can place it very distinctly, when Khomeini — the late Ayatollah Khomeini — came into power, the Islamic Revolution in '79. People now would start using the word "Ayatollah," for instance, and "Muslim revolution," and "Islam." And there was a very popular book called Not Without My Daughter, by Betty Mahmoody. That was the story of a mother who was married to an Iranian; she thought it was a repressive marriage, an unhappy marriage, and she wanted to leave Iran, but she had a daughter and her husband wouldn't allow her to leave. Betty Mahmoody wrote about her experience, which was an allegory for all the fantasies that Western women have of the Muslim world — that the husband is oppressive, and so on. Anyway, this was the novel, and it had great popularity. It was translated into French, and you would hear about it everywhere. There was also the fact of the American hostages who were taken in Tehran. So this played very vividly here in the media and in the subconscious of Quebecers, of the Canadians here. That was the first exposure, I would say, to the Muslim world, and to the beginning of Islamophobia.

Then in the 80s there were the Lebanese immigrants who came from Lebanon, from the civil war in Lebanon, so we had more Arabs here, we had more religious Islamic centers in Quebec — this was the second wave. In the 90s we had the immigrants coming from North Africa, in particular from Algeria. As the number of immigrants from Muslim countries increased, our problems also increased, because immigrants come and they settle here — they don't settle in faraway places, in the farms, where no one hears about them or sees them. They come here to [CITY 1]. This made a difference. We were seeing more halal restaurants, more young men coming either to study and then to stay. I mean, it was a good thing to see the community grow — we would hear more Arabic on the streets, more specialized grocery stores, restaurants. But at the same time, the international context was, how would you say, coloring the way local people here, local Québécois and local Canadians, were looking at us.

All this was before 9/11 — so the 90s and the turn of the century. Then, of course, there was 9/11, the war in Afghanistan, and everybody wanted to go and fight in Afghanistan to free the women, right? So the woman was a very central part of the Islamophobic context, because of the way they were depicted: they're submissive, they have no agency, they're repressed — in other words, they're covered, you don't see them, they're silent, so they have no role in life except to reproduce. That was the image that was circulated. And of course the Western world was going there to liberate them — this is a very good cause, you know, you can't argue with that.

Now, what was special about Quebec is that there's the French influence. There's influence from France, and the secularism law, what we call laïcité, has also been imported from France, and here it was taken up. With the number of Muslim immigrants doubling every decade — coming whether from North Africa or from the Middle East, and I include here Afghanistan, and Iraq, Turkey — this coincided with the rise of a nationalist view of what people should be, look like, dress, eat, think, speak. That was all taken up by the nationalist Parti Québécois as a banner, as what they thought would be defending the Quebec national values, what they call Québécois values. All this put together gives you an idea about the build-up of Islamophobic trends in Quebec, and especially — I'm speaking for [CITY 1], but this is true throughout Quebec — most of the immigrants, about eighty-nine percent of Muslim immigrants, are based in [CITY 1].

question: WHAT DOES BELONGING FEEL LIKE HERE?
answer:
Absolutely, I feel I belong. What helped me to integrate was that I married a man — my late husband was from Quebec, but he was from the English-speaking minority in Quebec. He was not French-speaking, he was English-speaking. But I felt integrated because I had in-laws who lived here, who lived in Quebec. I also worked in the English colleges, what they call CEGEPs here. I never felt like an outsider, because I was a hundred percent engaged in the community, and I never wanted to isolate myself. As I said, maybe being married to a Québécois did help me, but also I think of myself as an active member of society — when I was working, I was earning money, I was paying taxes, and I thought that politically I was very engaged as well, not only on the international level, more on the international level, but also on the Quebec provincial level, a little bit less on the municipal level, I do regret to say. I'm only becoming more involved now on the municipal level, with the problems that we have with the unhoused people, and garbage collection, and so on. I'm not happy with the services that the city is offering, but this came at a later stage.

You can't do everything — I mean, you can't be at the international level and the Quebec level and the municipal level. But maybe the municipal level is something that we as immigrants should get more interested in, because this is more immediate. From my experience as an immigrant, I'm always attached to my home country, so I follow what's happening over there. And although when I came I said, okay, I'm not going to live my life worrying about Israel and Egypt and Palestine and so on, I became increasingly involved in politics, and in Islamophobia. At the beginning, when you live normally, when nobody points at you and says that you're a Muslim, you don't pay as much attention to it — you don't have to defend it, you don't have to explain, you don't have to prove yourself, not as much, at least. But with increasing Islamophobia, yes, I think this is an added challenge. This is more of a challenge also for younger women who are in the workplace — we're very aware of that, especially now that we have laws that curtail what professions they can do, how they should be dressed, what conduct they should adopt in the public place. I'm very much aware of that. Now that I'm retired, I'm not employed, but I do have a business, I do have a rental business, so I'm still active, and I'm very much involved in the community, and I hope I'm doing something that would be of benefit to other Muslim women.

I don't think I deserve all this. I just have to be honest and say I lived my life. I was mentioning to my nephew that I haven't accomplished the things that I thought I would accomplish in Canada, and he said, do you live the life you wanted to live? So that is true, but there's nothing to gloat about.

question: HOW DID FAITH SHOW UP IN A GIVEN DAY?
answer:
What I found — and this was maybe in the 80s and in the 90s — was the difficulty, for instance, of praying. That is a big hurdle for Muslims, because you can't just say, well, I want to find a space, a private space, for praying. And then you have to justify it. People would say it's very well accepted to have breaks — a coffee break — but when you talk about a break for prayers, that is not so well accepted. And now there are laws that prevent schools from having a space for prayers for the young people.

Whereas when I first came to Canada, at the [UNIVERSITY 3] there was a chapel. There is still a chapel at [UNIVERSITY 2]. [UNIVERSITY 1], for instance — they refuse to apply this new law that says you cannot pray in a public space, because they have so many international students, and they are selling this as an advantage, that students have a place to pray, a musalla. So it's a room, and it's divided — the place for men, and next to it for women. That is [UNIVERSITY 1]. At [UNIVERSITY 1], at [UNIVERSITY 2], it was a yearly fight, from day one, from forever — I remember it was always difficult to have a space for prayers. There was a space given, allowed for Friday prayers, but not a permanent place. It was always a fight to get a place to pray. And now, with the new law, I'm not sure — I'm not sure if there is going to be a musalla, or even Friday prayers.

question: HOW DID THE NEW LAW COME ABOUT?
answer:
I can tell you how the new law came about. This is part of the CAQ, the Coalition Avenir Québec, and that is invoking not neutrality but secularism, laïcité — that you cannot have prayers in public space. What triggered it was that during the demonstrations for Palestine, sometimes they coincided with the afternoon, because here in [CITY 1] in the winter it's almost Asr prayers — you pray noon at twelve, and then ten minutes after two p.m. it is Asr. So in some instances we had to pray standing in the street, just to have a space to pray. And there were also some instances where, at Eid for instance, families came into the park and prayed in the park.

This didn't go well with the members of the CAQ. So they introduced this new law that you cannot pray in a public place — but then they didn't want to put it so bluntly, so they nuanced it. They said, unless you obtain permission from the municipality and you don't hinder traffic. Which was already the case, because whenever we had demonstrations for Palestine, we did have to take permission from the police, and it was well announced, and the area was cordoned off, so there was no hindrance of traffic or any other activity. It was just that we were praying, and this was part of marking our presence, let's say, or our protest.

And so after that they did elaborate on it, and said, okay, a public place — well, what is a public place? A school. Of course schools are a public place, so you can't pray in a college, what they call here a CEGEP, and so on. There are a lot of ramifications to this law, which is Law 94, and this was an extension of another law. So they're just building it up, and going the way France is going, because in France those laws are en vigueur — in other words, they're circulated. So here we're copying France. This is the model for Quebec.

question: DO THE OTHER UNIVERSITIES HAVE A CHAPEL OR A MUSALLA?
answer:
I would say musalla here, because there are four universities in [CITY 1] that I could talk about. So there is [UNIVERSITY 2] — and I think I did mention [UNIVERSITY 2]. [UNIVERSITY 1] has a specific place for prayers for Muslims, so a musalla. There is the [UNIVERSITY 4] — I don't know what the situation is there. Same thing for the [UNIVERSITY 3], I don't know. What I can tell you is that the students — and this I heard from somebody who is doing some research, a French intern, actually, who is doing research there — he told me that he and the other young men have to bring their prayer carpets with them, and they pray in a hidden place, but there is no central place for prayers.

No, no, they don't have a chapel. In fact, [UNIVERSITY 2] has a chapel, and they have a department of religious studies, so it's integrated there. And I can tell you that at the [UNIVERSITY 3] there was a chapel in the 80s — so a church, a chapel — and then they turned it into a morgue. They thought the space would be better used that way. Yes — for a morgue. That's what happened to it. Now, at [UNIVERSITY 4], I don't know what the situation is there, but for sure now they cannot have a musalla.

question: IS THE LAW TARGETED AT MUSLIMS, OR APPLIED TO OTHER RELIGIONS TOO?
answer:
Absolutely. Well, the law doesn't say we are against Muslims. Muslims are the most affected by it. When we think of the increment in the Asian immigrant community, there is no debate about being a Buddhist, or about synagogues, for instance. It says "religious symbol," but it's not only the law, [INTERVIEWER], it's how the law is applied. And maybe we are more visible.

Although — the second group that is more impacted are the Sikhs. There was a big controversy about the kirpan, the small dagger, the ceremonial, symbolic dagger that Sikh men were wearing, and this was a big issue here at one point, in the schools, for instance. And lately, I just read recently, there was a Sikh man — and it's Sikh in English; I don't want to say a sick man, like someone who's ill. He's also an influencer, so he takes photos of himself and so on. He was working out at the gym, and he was wearing a long dagger — because the daggers that are allowed only have to be seven inches long, and his dagger was obviously longer than that; I've seen him in the photo — and he also had a turban. Apparently one of the employees came and told him, you have to leave. Why can't I stay in the gym? Because you have a weapon on you. And there was a big controversy — should he leave the gym, yes, no, why, and so on.

But these are still affecting a minority. What makes us more of a target is the numbers. Not that this should matter — I mean, one person is one person too much, that's discriminated against. But over and above the law, it's how people even would discriminate against Muslim women who are wearing the hijab, even if the law doesn't say you have to discriminate against them.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer:
I see that there are more challenges, and this has actually encouraged me to learn more about Islam — when you're going to debate, when you're going to talk about your religion, you have to be informed. So I try to have solid arguments. I read, and I don't know whether the articles I've written are still on the website of [MUSLIM WOMEN'S ORGANIZATION 1].

What I write about now is very different from what my sister, who lives in Egypt, is interested in, in the kind of religious knowledge (she seeks). Here you have to convey more basic knowledge, and also to address the attacks and the concerns, so we would look at a different kind of source, a different kind of knowledge, if I may say. I'll give you an example. My sister is very much interested in how you read the Qur'an and the rules — what we call tajweed. I wouldn't have the luxury to just sit down and study those rules, but I would write about the history of Islam, misconceptions of Islam, because this is what I'm confronted with. Nobody will ask me how you read the Qur'an, or whether you read it correctly or not correctly. So there is a certain balance here. Although I know it's very important to read correctly, I would rely on listening to the Qur'an and reading it in the same way, rather than being knowledgeable about how to read the Qur'anic text — because you can't do everything. You have to specialize, specialize in the areas where you would be useful, useful in the sense of being accessible, acceptable, of explaining, in the sense of facilitating integration. That is the objective now, let's say, my primary interest, my contribution or participation. This is what is needed, or what I feel is needed, or what I feel I can do or contribute.

question: HOW DO YOU SEEK THAT KNOWLEDGE, AND HAS THAT CHANGED WITH THE POLITICAL ENVIRONMENT?
answer: Books. And yes, it has changed, because at the beginning there wasn't so much Islamophobia, not so many attacks directed so directly at the religion. I was also more on the political side rather than the religious side, because in the Middle East — I come from Egypt — during those fifty years it was always a kind of turmoil, whether it was repression, or seeking to support those who were repressed, political prisoners, whatever. It has been an ongoing upheaval, and that took precedence over Islamophobia. But since 9/11, I would say Islamophobia has become so marked. And we are in Quebec, where we receive blows from both sides, from south of the border and from France — so it's like somebody slapping you on both cheeks, one from the States and one from Europe. Not me particularly, but it's like we are in a sandwich.

question: IS ANY OF IT DIRECTED AT MUSLIMS HERE, OR AT MUSLIMS IN GENERAL?
answer:
In general, what's happening in the States is not kind to Muslims either. I get the emails of CAIR, C-A-I-R, and it's not — how do you say? I don't want to use the word pleasant. It's not reassuring, let's say. It's not reassuring.

However, the difference between Muslims in the States and Muslims here is that in the States fifty percent of them are natives. So the African American Muslims are aware, politically, socially, whether that comes with advantages or disadvantages. But here, most of the Muslim population is either first-generation immigrants — now we have a second generation — but we are not considered natives in the same sense as African Americans.

question: WHAT DOES INTEGRATION MEAN TO YOU, AND WHAT DOES IT LOOK LIKE?
answer:
One word: integration means that you have access to the job market. This is the best way to get integrated. The immigrants who come here from Muslim countries are, of course, not seniors — they are at a stage of their lives where they are active members of society. And how do you become active, how do you become integrated? By having a place in the workforce. There is no other way, no better way to be integrated.

Well, it starts with economic integration. You can't just be — how are you going to be living? This is all you have. You have to have an income, you're not going to live on thin air, you have to have a means of living, and the economic side here is very important. I would say we are living in a society where your value is based on how much money you make. It's as simple as that.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DID IT DO FOR YOU?
answer:
I don't wear a traditional hijab like the hijab you are wearing. My story is very different, because when I grew up — the 60s, the 70s, in Egypt — the women didn't wear it. It wasn't known as such. There was a national attire, but the word "hijab" didn't even exist in our vocabulary. It was more those who went out with a black wrap around their head — not a chador, we didn't have this.

There was also a divide in the society, where the upper class was imitating the Western world — very much influenced by colonialism. I myself went to a French school, so it was also about looking at France as the model: whether I wanted to dress like the French girls, act like them, speak like them. My whole environment was very much influenced by this colonial mentality.

That was one side of the family. What made a balance is that my father was very religious, and that he had studied in England, so he could see the colonialism, he could see the imperialism — he was more aware of it. He was in England for his studies and then came back — this was in the 40s. But Egypt had both English and French colonial influences. My mother sent me to a French school because this was thought to be an advantage — a young woman of my society should speak French, and it looked good when you sat among people in society to be able to speak French. It was a kind of refinement, if you want. Whereas boys would go more to an English school. My father, being an Arab nationalist, wanted his son to go to a national Arab school, so my older brother went to a national Arabic public school, and I and my sisters went to the lycée.

Going back to the question of hijab: the question of identity, of Islamic identity, came into play after Egypt was defeated by Israel in the 1967 war. That was the beginning of the call for more Arab Islamic values. And this is how it started — a prominent family from high society started wearing the hijab, and then it filtered down to the society, even up to the 80s. Since I was here, the hijab was not so dominant. I started wearing a kind of hijab, covering my head, after 9/11.

I did it for two reasons. For me, there were always norms of decency that were enforced. For instance, my sisters and I would never wear miniskirts, although in the 60s that was the fashion, the rage — the miniskirts. So we wouldn't wear miniskirts, we wouldn't wear sleeveless blouses. There were terms of decency that were, let's say, unwritten — we would know what would be considered osé, or not acceptable — but the hijab was not part of it. So this was introduced gradually in Egypt and became the norm, and it spread because it became — how do you say — fashionable; it became not acceptable but high class to wear the hijab, you see. So it's a religious component doubled with a societal component — it was a kind of distinction to wear the hijab.

The hijab, what we call the Egyptian hijab, which is basically what you are wearing — there is some historical precedence, in that at the time when Egypt was under the Turkish influence, and was actually a Turkish wilayat, part of the Turkish empire, then men and women used to wear the niqab, cover their face. But this again was a kind of distinction. This was the upper society: you wouldn't reveal yourself, or show your face, to somebody who's not from the immediate family. It was something for the upper class. It was not for, let's say, the farmers, the Egyptians who were working the fields, or in some other menial jobs — it was for the very upper crust. So that has a certain resonance. And so now the niqab is quite different, but it is not popular; the niqab comes from a Saudi influence. In Egypt at the time, for instance, my great-grandmother used to wear what would be called a niqab today, but she only wore it when she would meet men from outside the family, or go outside the house — for instance, her driver or her cook would never see her face. She always had this kind of makeup (underneath). So that idea of supremacy, or upper class, I would say, played a role in the adoption of the hijab in Egypt. For myself, it was more in solidarity with those who wear the hijab, after 9/11. I think it's quite complicated.

question: WAS THERE MORE ISLAMOPHOBIA AFTER 9/11, AND DID PEOPLE TREAT YOU DIFFERENTLY?
answer:
Absolutely. Nobody attacks me. I rightly think that it's out of modesty, perhaps, that I'm covering my head. I don't look typical — I dress modestly, but I dress off the rack here. I buy my clothes mostly here from Winners; I don't know if you have Winners and others. And so I'm a Muslim, but perhaps they don't think that I'm a very conservative Muslim — or I'm a Muslim that passes. And when I walk in the street, I pass. Now, in the job market, it's a different story. But there isn't as much animosity (toward me) as toward somebody who is wearing a full hijab, whom they perceive as wanting to impose themselves as Muslim. You see the difference?

It's not that I'm not at ease — no, I'm totally at ease about being identified as a Muslim. I even had some cases where a woman would come and ask me, "so are you a Muslim, or a Jew?" And I would say, no, I am a Muslim, that's quite clear. But people here think, or have an idea, that Muslims who wear the hijab do it because they want to impose (their faith), or they want others to convert. They think it's more aggressive, rather than out of faith or out of conviction. So that is the perception. And so I kind of pass — especially because I speak French, and I speak good French. And I'm old also, because older women in France, at a certain time — I'm not saying now — would be more or less dressed like me.

No, I didn't notice a change — not with the way I dress. And also because I was not on the job market at the time — I was self-employed, I had my own business. So it was not like somebody who is entering the job market, or even studying to become a teacher, wearing the hijab.

question: WHAT DOES THE LARGER PUBLIC IN QUEBEC GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
Absolutely, (there is something they get wrong). There is a fear. Quebec has not had a good experience with the (Catholic) church, and that gets projected onto Muslims. They wanted to liberate themselves from the grasp of the church, and that is what they perceive as real liberation. So when they see Muslim women so attached to their religion, they say, you are bringing us back to the dark times, when the church had all the power over women — they were against the pill, for instance, they wanted women to have as many children as possible, and they also had a monopoly on the economy, on society, and on the education system. Once Quebecers got out of the shackles of the church, they don't want to see any going back, any being respectful or mindful of religion. It brings back bad memories, and they say, well, we don't want any religion in our life, and we don't want to be with people who seem backward, in a sense, or not liberated. So this is the problem here.

I should get statistics on that before I speak, but originally, yes, they are Catholics — mainly Catholics, the French Québécois majority. Now, with the statistics — and we can look the statistics up — you can also identify as a non-believer, as an atheist, so I don't know what the proportion is. There's also the question of being baptized: traditionally, officially, you're Catholic, but then you don't believe and you don't practice, so you're a non-Catholic (Catholic). The relationship with Catholicism here is rather, you know, not a complex one.

Yes, but even during the time of what they call the Révolution tranquille — which would translate, I would think, as not soft transition; I don't have the exact translation, but a revolution that isn't a fiery revolution — the nuns opted to wear secular clothes, not to be dressed as nuns, and to wear a small cross instead of a big cross. So that was part of the evolution, if we don't want to use the term revolution.

question: HAVE YOU PERSONALLY ENCOUNTERED DISCRIMINATION, BEFORE OR AFTER YOU STARTED WEARING HIJAB?
answer: Yes — there was discrimination when I was applying for a job, for sure. I did feel that there was discrimination. But you know, Madame, I think at that time I brushed it off. I didn't want to dwell on it. Whereas now I see it more clearly when it happens to others.

question: FEEDBACK ON THE STUDY'S QUESTIONS
answer:
We should identify the sample. So, for instance, we should say this is geared to Muslim women, Muslims who identify themselves as Muslim, and also to women who wear the hijab — that's another aspect. Then the age group. I'm very sensitive to age now, with a mirror, since I'm a senior, so I can see that in the different phases of my life I had a different outlook on things, and the way you ask some of the questions, I think, is time related. So it's good to have age groups — not giving your exact age, but where you think you fit. I'm not going to say I'm thirty, but if we shifted to the senior category, that's where I would be. The usual age groups, I think. And if you want to add whether you're a student, or a housewife, or a mother — how you identify yourself socially — because some of the questions are very socially oriented, I would say. It's also good to have a sense of who is being interviewed: social and marital status, whether you're working or at home and so on. This is what I was thinking of.

Then there was a question about what kind of difficulty you encountered. It comes somewhere here, I have it, but I thought it would be good to break it down — what kind of difficulty, whether it's in the workplace, or in the family, or other, because we face different kinds of difficulties. That would be a distinction: if I talk about a difficulty at work, it's very different from when I talk about a difficulty socially, when I had to bury my husband, for instance. Those are the ones that come to my mind, what I jotted down.

We touched on some of the first questions, so if you don't mind, I'll just read the question and tell you where I thought I was irrelevant, in a sense — because I was talking too much, and I don't think that would help. We're not going to mention everything that happened in Quebec and the waves of Islamophobia. All of that is documented historically; it's not only my interpretation or my point of view, and you have better sources for that. So it doesn't make sense to me to include it in the interview, or to give it any weight, let's say. For me it's a background, to explain my — how do you say — in French you say parcours, which doesn't mean my evolution but what I went through. But that's general; I wouldn't say it's specific to me.

question: WHERE, IF ANYWHERE, DOES FAITH SHOW UP IN A GIVEN DAY?
answer:
Let me see. Tell me about an ordinary day in your life — I think that one is an icebreaker, more or less, unless there was something specific behind it, because the second question is related to it: where, if anywhere, does faith show up in a given day. This is crucial, I think. If we identify ourselves as Muslims, the first thing is that I pray — we have five prayers per day, and the day follows the schedule of those prayers. If you ask me about Ramadan, for instance, that's another feature of my days during Ramadan. So that is where my faith shows up, in the sense that as Muslims our faith guides us; it's in everyday life. In other aspects too, I do reflect — we face so many situations where we have to decide, how is this consonant with your religion, how would you deal with this given that you want to practice, to live as a Muslim. So that is a constant. If you say that you're a Muslim, it's a way of life. So how are we living in the West as Muslims? That would be the question. I'm not going to say it bothers me, but I do reflect on it, and sometimes I can come up with an answer — it's not always easy.

Let's take a very simple question, a very simple situation. When you go to meet politicians, they want to shake your hand — so do you shake hands or don't you shake hands? Sometimes they know that you may not be comfortable shaking hands, so they refrain from giving you their hand, whereas you would have liked to show that you're friendly. So there's that kind of situation. Or at work, when they have a gathering, a cinq à sept after work, and they meet in a bar or some other place where they're going to drink, even if it's beer or something like that — do you go, or don't you go? That's the kind of thing, at a very practical level.

There are also other questions where you would reflect as a Muslim, as a general policy. For instance, at school, if you have kids and they have classes where they talk about transgender and so on, and that you don't have to be a girl or a boy, you can be something in between — I don't have to tell you, you know better, but this is the kind of situation that comes to your mind. Or when you get a grant from the government: [MUSLIM WOMEN'S ORGANIZATION 1] is getting a grant, and they have to talk about diversity, they have to have a session about gender and so on. I may not feel comfortable with that, you see, because here there is a clear conflict between what we know from the guidelines of Islam and the society where we are living.

So when you say, how does faith show up in a given day, I can tell you it should. It really should, as Muslims. We should be reflecting on how we, as Muslims, are living in the West. It doesn't imply that in our home countries we're not going to face those problems, but there the burden, the responsibility, is usually taken by the society, and you just follow. Here in the West you have more individuality and much less, I would say, leadership, or light to guide you, so you have to adjust your own compass. It's your responsibility in front of Allah, which is a part of Islam. We don't have a Pope. We don't have somebody to dictate to you what you should be doing — you do to the best of your knowledge, you could be right, you could be wrong, and Allah is going to judge us. So this, I thought, is a very deep question, if you ask me.

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY TO SOMEONE WHO HAS NEVER MET A MUSLIM WOMAN?
answer:
This is where we talked a lot last time. Just one notice here: I think that there are now a lot of visible Muslim women, because of the immigration in the city — many, many visibly Muslim women wearing hijab and so on. It's outside [CITY 1] that Muslim women have no presence, and there they are represented by the media negatively, unfortunately. So this question — how would you describe yourself? I don't know; maybe you should ask somebody who has never met a Muslim woman. How would you view a Muslim woman? Where do you get your views of Muslim women from? Have you ever met a Muslim woman?

Maybe — I recall that we talked a lot about this, so at this point I wouldn't want to elaborate, because it also depends on who is asking. And in fact, when I first came there were a lot of — I was invited, as I think I mentioned, by a lot of Catholic nuns who wanted to know about Muslim women, and this is one setting where I remember clearly that I had to say what I think I myself represent, or what I am doing, or what I am thinking.

As for how long I have lived here, and how my sense of myself as a Muslim has changed over that time — I think we did broach on this.

question: ARE THERE PLACES WHERE YOU FEEL YOU CAN OR CAN'T BE VISIBLY MUSLIM?
