answer: This is regulated by law now in Quebec. There are places where you can't pray, whether it's at school, at work, or in the park. No, you can't be visibly Muslim, in the sense that you can't practice your religion. It's okay if you wear a hijab, but if you are going to pray for Eid, let's say collectively, then this new law bans such a manifestation. So in a sense they don't want to see Muslim women — they don't want to see anybody identified as Muslim.

question: HOW DO YOU MANAGE THE EID SALAH IN [CITY 1]?
answer:
This was a new phenomenon — as I mentioned, this came about after the protests that we had for Palestine. Usually we didn't have Eid Salat in the park. One reason is the weather, and another reason is that we all restrict ourselves to mosques. But then it became popular after the demonstrations, that people want to pray outside.

So the new law says you can't pray in a public place, but it puts the responsibility of denying it on the municipality — it says unless the municipality allows it. So it's a bit complicated, in a sense, because usually when you have a congregation, whether it's for a protest or anything else, you have to have a permit from the police. Now the new law says, no, you get the permit from the police because the police assures that you're not going to impact the traffic or the parking — just some logistical matter. But now, in addition to this, the municipality has to decide if it is desirable or not desirable, and how it will fit with the laïcité. Is this a religious sign or not?

Because the Catholics also have processions in the street at Easter. This is why there was a controversy about it. It's a procession, and they go with the big cross, so it's obviously religious, and they were walking in a public place, it's in the streets. So we're not going to prohibit this, of course. So who takes the responsibility here? They found that it's a little bit more difficult to navigate than they originally thought. So there is the law, and there is the interpretation of the law.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE?
answer: Yes, actively. Yes, I would say only in times of crisis. On a daily basis I don't read much about religion, except for the Qur'an and the prayers. When do I seek knowledge? When I want to write an article, let's say for the Islamic New Year, or for the birth of the Prophet, peace be upon him, this kind of thing. That's where I try to get more educated about religion, and there are tons of books coming out. In other words, I seek knowledge when I want to say something, when I am in a situation — but not routinely, not routine-like. I don't say, okay, I'm devoting half an hour to bettering my knowledge about religion. No, it doesn't work that way, to be honest with you.

question: HAVE YOU ENCOUNTERED REPRESENTATIONS OF MUSLIM WOMEN THAT WERE INACCURATE, AND WHAT DID YOU DO?
answer: I would write — whether it's to the editors, whether they publish it or not, but I do react.

question: A DIFFICULTY YOU FACED, AND HOW YOU MADE SENSE OF IT
answer:
No — when we face difficulties, we don't make sense of them, otherwise we would accept them. But in general, there are different types of difficulties, right, whether it was at work or whether it was socially and so on. So I don't know where you would want the focus to be.

Well, as a Muslim in general, we have the coping mechanism of sabr, patience. This is something that's very much praised in Islam — that there are difficulties in life and you go through them, that you have to be resilient, you have to be strong.

One of the difficulties I can tell you about is that I wanted to get married to a man who was not Muslim, and he was not really very keen on converting, so it took me a long time to convince him. He finally converted, but it was not easy sailing. So this is one kind of difficulty, but I stuck to my guns. He knew that if he wouldn't convert, I wouldn't marry him — although he was very open to being married civilly, in a civil court, like we have here. We didn't have to be married religiously, and the marriage would have been accepted socially; here in Quebec people can just register as married, they don't have to go through the church or the mosque to have a religious marriage. So that was one difficulty. How did it make sense to me? No, at that time I really found that it was very difficult to be a Muslim and to abide by this rule that you can't marry a non-Muslim. That, there's no denying.

My first thought was that I didn't want to go against my religion, so that was a very strong argument, and then I also didn't want to — how to say — to pain my family, because my family was conservative, and although they were delighted to see me married, it wouldn't have been acceptable. But basically, I knew that I couldn't accept being married to a non-Muslim. So this is a kind of my faith that sustained me. Although I wasn't that young — I was in my 30s, and I was alone. And frankly, I didn't have many suitors at any time of my life, so that was a good opportunity, that at least this man loved me and he wanted to marry me. But it was also a big sacrifice on his side, because he had to leave his religion.

question: DID THEY IDENTIFY WHAT THEY WERE DISMISSING YOU FOR?
answer:
Other difficulties that we can mention are at work, for instance. I felt that at one time I was dismissed just out of discrimination. So this is the kind of difficulty perhaps that you want to ask your interviewees about — just to put more emphasis on the workforce and the conditions here in Quebec especially.

This is quite painful to recall, but I do remember clearly that I was a teacher, and at the end of the year they had to make a review of whether I would become permanent or not. So they did this review, and they decided that no, they wouldn't let me become a permanent teacher, but that they would kind of let me teach the way you fall back on the ladder — you don't go further, you fall back. Okay, so you can say it's quite justified: I didn't meet their expectations or the standards, so I didn't deserve to be a teacher, a permanent teacher. That's acceptable. However, I had a colleague, a white man, and he was in the same situation. So he was automatically promoted and became permanent without any review, and the reason at that time was, oh, we forgot that we had to review him. So they remembered very well that they had to have a review for me, but for him it just slipped their mind — they didn't know that he was coming up for tenure. And so that's it. It just passed like that.

question: HOW DID YOU RATIONALIZE THAT SADNESS?
answer:
Absolutely, absolutely, yes, that was — I didn't rationalize it. I refused, really, to go back down and start from the beginning. Essentially what they were saying was, okay, you can teach, but you wouldn't be permanent, you would be just teaching certain courses — so it's like you're starting over. I said no, I'm not staying, and I'm going to have my own business and start something new and so on, and my husband did encourage me. Which I think was not — it would have been better for my career if I had relented and started over, because eventually I would have been on a tenure track after two years. But I was so hurt, and I thought I didn't get a fair shake, so I said, okay, no, I am going to do something else.

So that is it. Now it's debatable whether this was the best reaction or not. This is now water over the dam, as they say. But this is me, and this is what I did at the time. I don't know if I'm answering your question, if I'm giving you the right answers.

question: ARE THERE INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer: The external, this is easy to answer. I mean, there are so many stereotypes about Muslim women, so I don't have to elaborate on what they are, because you know them, and you know how Muslim women are viewed outside, or how they are represented in the media. Let's say that that would be a good representation, or a good image, of what they see Muslim women as being like.

question: IS THERE A TIME YOU FELT THAT EXPECTATION WAS PLACED ON YOU AS A MUSLIM?
answer:
Yes — all the laws that come from the government of Quebec. This is what they think Muslim women are: submissive, with no agency, you name it. It's as if we had no personality, as if I'm not like other women in general. So yes, not only by the government, but by the media, which is essentially what people are reading and seeing. I don't think people think much; they just take what they get, in terms of what they see on TV, or the narrative, or what they see abroad. That's an important point — when they talk about Muslim women, it's always Muslim women in Afghanistan, in Saudi Arabia, in such places, not women who live in the West, not me, not our reality or our life. It's always an image, generally negative, projected on us.

The internal expectations — this is a minefield, I have to tell you. Whether it is in the family — now, my husband was not an Arab Muslim, so I can't speak from my own experience, but I can speak from what I've seen, women coming and talking about what they have lived through, or what expectations men put on them. So we have this at the internal level, the family, the domestic experience. And I can mention it because I was with [MUSLIM WOMEN'S ORGANIZATION 1]. Now, this happens in all communities, it's not only for Muslims, and I wouldn't say it's more prevalent in our community than in others, but certainly in general women are expected to do more than men, let's say, in a marriage. I'm not going to dwell on that, because it's not first-hand experience — it is something that has been reported to us.

However, when it comes to the people who want to represent themselves as spokespersons for the community — whether they're imams in mosques, or whether they call themselves quote-unquote leaders of the community — how the Muslim community views us women, that's another story. That's really another story.

I want to share with you an experience that I am still unhappy about. Myself and another lady — we had knowledge of someone, a man in our community, very politically active, very astute, very vocal, very connected, I would say. We had complaints from women that he had, let's call it, inappropriate behaviour towards women. So we wrote a letter — he was of course at the head of an organization — asking questions, and he sued us for defamation.

Oh, I could say that he got more sympathy from the establishment than anyone else; we were viewed as troublemakers. The case was a little more complicated than that, because there was one woman who complained bitterly about him and then changed sides at one point, and she accused us of trying to build a case against this man, (said) that this is not what she meant, and that she didn't want to have anything to do with this court case. So we were stuck. And it did eventually — we won the case. The judge was very good, because he saw through what was going on. We were awarded a sum of money, a respectable sum of money, as compensation. But in my view, that didn't change the dynamic, the situation — I still find that men would side with men, and that this questioning was not welcome in the community, which is unfortunate.

I must say that the responsibility falls also on these women who complained, and who, when it went to court, didn't want to testify. This, I think, was not in our favour. Somebody comes and says, oh, this man did this and that, and then finally you ask, okay, are you ready to come and say your name and say this publicly? No, no, no, I wouldn't say it, because I'm married, and what would my husband say? That kind of thing.

There were also some financial irregularities. But basically our questioning, our letter was about — we heard, it was brought to our attention, that some women complained, and we wanted some explanation. And it seemed that this is not the kind of thing that we Muslims should be raising. Quite to the contrary: women would have rights in Islam, and certainly a case of sexual abuse or sexual exploitation would be something un-Islamic. It happens in other religious communities, I believe, but you asked about internal and external difficulties.

And of course this man went around saying that he was so generous, so flexible, that he let us off the hook, and everything was settled. Yes, after we won the case. But we don't have access to the establishment, to the men. You don't go around saying, no, that's not true, we won the case. And of course he never said that he paid compensation.

I think I'm going off track here. I'm bringing it up because I think it's an important aspect of our community. We have to look inwards. We always look at the threat from outside, but we also have to have the courage to look inside our community and try to be righteous — not only to cater to the reputation of such and such, but to ask what is right, what is morally right, what is acceptable, what should be upheld, rather than what would tarnish the reputation of such a person because he's good, because he talks to politicians. Anyway, this is my view on the situation. So this is just for you, [INTERVIEWER] — I don't know if it's going to be relevant, but we have problems. We have internal problems.

question: WHO ARE THE PEOPLE YOU FEEL MOST RESPONSIBLE TO?
answer: Responsible to, or responsible for. I understand, but I don't feel responsible to anyone. That's the case now, for sure. I felt responsible towards my parents and my family in the sense that I didn't want to hurt their feelings, although when it came to my life versus their feelings, I chose my life. That is a very simple situation: I wanted to immigrate to Canada and they were against it, and this caused them a lot of pain, but I did finally immigrate, because I wanted to live in a free country where I could be politically active.

question: LOOKING BACK, DID YOU GET WHAT YOU SET OUT ON?
answer: Yes, I think. I lived my life — I'm not going to say I lived the life I wanted to live. It doesn't mean that it was successful, it doesn't mean I have much to talk about, to brag about. I thought I'd make a lot of money, I thought I would be in a career, I thought this and that, which didn't happen. But on another level, I lived the way I wanted to live.

question: AND WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE FOR?
answer:
So this is responsible to. Now, responsible for — not a hundred percent, not directly, but I still feel I have a responsibility towards my sisters, towards nephews, nieces, the extended family. I feel that I'm still very much attached to them. I feel responsible in a broader sense for Muslims — and this is political, of course, because they're Muslims. Talking about Egypt, I mean, there is an organization that is very active, was very active, not as much now, but I'm very active, for instance, for Palestine, for Egypt and so on, without knowing that there are Christians and Muslims in Egypt. So I would say it's more political than strictly Islamic.

Although — for instance, I would feel that I have a responsibility towards the Uyghurs in China. I don't come from that geographic place on the earth, but because they are Muslims. And I follow Justice For All; I don't know if you're acquainted with this organization. They deal with news coming from Muslim minorities, whether it's in China, the Rohingya in India, Kashmir — a lot of places where there are Muslim communities and minorities.

question: HOW DO THOSE VALUES SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer: Choices as an activist — let's say that I make time for my activism. First of all, to get informed: this takes a lot of time, I do read a lot politically. And also acting, whether you're writing, meeting politicians, taking positions, signing petitions. Believe it or not, this takes a lot of time. So those are the ones that shape my choices.

question: HOW DO YOU UNDERSTAND YOUR ROLE WITHIN YOUR FAMILY AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer: Those are two distinct things, although related. One hadith that comes to my mind, [INTERVIEWER] — I'm paraphrasing here — is that the best Muslim among you is the one most useful to the community. This has been really a leading principle for me: that your religion is not only about dogma, it's not only about praying. I'm not saying it is not, but it's not only about the practice — it is also about your feeling, your connection to the ummah in general, and that you have to be actively an asset to your community. You feel that you are not an individual, you are part of the community. This is very important for me.

question: WHAT DOES BELONGING FEEL LIKE FOR YOU HERE IN QUEBEC?
answer: I think we have covered this. Am I seen as a Québécoise — not Québécois, you have to put the feminine of the word? Yes and no. I am definitely a Québécoise — I mean, I love Quebec, I love my life here, so yes, I feel like a Québécoise. No, because people make you feel different. It's not that I feel different; it's how people look at you and how they treat you differently. This is why they would tell you, you are not a Québécoise.

question: IS THAT THROUGH THEIR WORDS, OR THROUGH THEIR ATTITUDES?
answer: Through their words, for sure. There is a distinction between a native Québécoise and an immigrant — and it's not only terminology, it's also laws, it's a lot of things.

question: WHO IS A NATIVE QUÉBÉCOIS?
answer: They would define native Québécois as white Catholic — that's it, white Catholic. Born in Quebec — okay, not even. (An Egyptian Muslim born in Quebec,) no. It certainly has a racial connotation, yes. And also, now they are excluding the English minority, although there is a sizable English-speaking minority in Quebec. It's difficult for me to be very precise here, because it's more a perception, what they would call native — and as you would ask, okay, what about Aboriginal people? No, they wouldn't be Québécois. I mean, there is the legal term, and there is what is understood in the parlance of every day, like whether you would say, oh, she's a Québécoise, or she's not a Québécoise. So there are many nuances, and I don't think I am ready to delve into this, because it's very nuanced, and it has so many legal — there is a legal connotation.

question: ARE YOU SEEN AS A QUÉBÉCOISE?
answer:
That's in response to the question — let me see here — are you seen as a Québécoise? That's the actual question, and the short answer is no, except of course that since I live here, I'm a resident in [CITY 1], and I do pay taxes. For that purpose I'm certainly a Québécois. Otherwise, no — no one would qualify me as a Québécois, because as we said, Québécois is more white, French-speaking. Even those Québécois who are of English descent, they would say Québécois anglophone. They would always qualify it. For the rest, no.

People tend more to say — all right, there is the term néo-Québécois, but it's not used, I mean, I don't hear it often. And I also refer to the term native, which is born in Quebec; I'm not too sure whether that one is also widely used. Usually, for immigrants, we are referred to by our ethnic background or our origin, or even being a Muslim is a strong marker, so they would say she's a Muslim. Period.

Those are all the nuances, I would say, the identity markers — and if you read my last email, these identity questions are very important here in Quebec. I have a book in front of me about it. It says, Who Belongs in Quebec, and the subtitle is Identity Politics in a Changing Society.

question: WHAT HAPPENS WITH THE SECOND AND THIRD GENERATIONS, BORN HERE?
answer:
That's a good question. I don't have much experience with the kids, so I'd rather not answer this question, but I would refer to a journalist, actually, at [PROVINCIAL NEWSPAPER 2], which is a very big newspaper — her name is [NAMED COLUMNIST], and she's not Muslim, she's Christian of Lebanese extraction. She mentions comments like, "go back to where you came from," and she says, I came from [CITY 1] — and she even mentions a district in [CITY 1]. So she's born here. And yet people are judged — it's a racial distinction, I think. It's by the color of your skin.

So how would the kids refer to themselves? I prefer not to answer. I prefer not to answer, because I don't have enough knowledge. I know of some kids who would say that they belong to the country of their parents, but I don't want to generalize. So let's just leave it. As far as I'm concerned — no, I'm not concerned, except for the taxes.

question: HOW DO YOU EXPERIENCE THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR FAITH AND QUEBEC?
answer: I think it's a strange relationship, and I think it's not understood. I don't think we're given credit for loving Quebec, or for wanting to contribute to the welfare of Quebec. This is the general political speech — that immigrants are seen as a problem, and that our contributions are not valued as they should be. After all, if we came to Quebec, it's because we were accepted by Quebec; it's not that we imposed ourselves. It was a mutually beneficial agreement — you come to the country because the country needs you, and you need to be in this country, you chose to be in this country. But lately, and this is a later development than when I first came fifty years ago, it's more, oh well, we have a housing crisis because of the immigration, and so on. That's the short answer.

question: HAVE YOU BEEN MADE TO FEEL OR SEEN AS A THREAT?
answer:
Afraid? No, no, I wouldn't go as far as that. Perhaps not welcome, because of my ideas — especially because I'm such a strong advocate for Palestine. So when I was in a working environment, I was seen as hostile to Jews, as anti-Semitic. That would be more the attitude.

Since you mentioned the word threat — yes, there is this theory. The CAQ says that Muslims in general, not me personally, but Muslims who are visibly Muslim, are a threat to Quebec values. You hear that phrase a lot, valeurs québécoises. So what are those values? We don't know, except that they want to convey that they are not following the church, not dominated by the church, and that Muslims want to take them back to that time when religion was omnipresent in their lives, controlling their lives and so on. So in that sense, a threat — taking away their culture, in the same way that they would say immigrants are more anglophone, or want to be anglophone, that they don't want to speak French, and that this is a threat, quote-unquote, to the French language. As a woman, I'm not a security threat — let's put it that way. If we talk about threats here in Quebec, I would qualify a security threat as something going towards men; as a woman, no. As a Muslim, though, I'm a threat to Quebec values. Although again, personally, I'm not perceived as a militant for imposing a Sharia doctrine in Quebec.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: If you want to say that you're a believing Muslim, you have to factor in the Day of Judgment. Everything is projected with the idea that one day we're going to have to answer for our thoughts, for our acts, for how we're spending our money, how we're disposing of our knowledge. I think that's basic and central to the faith. So depending on how much faith you have, you would fear, or you would think of, the other (world). I think this is a religious question more than a question about our situation here as Muslims in Quebec.

question: WHEN SOMETHING IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL, HOW DO YOU UNDERSTAND IT?
answer:
This again is a philosophical question, [INTERVIEWER] — what do you want me to say? We Muslims believe that our life is predetermined; I don't want to say only a certain part of our life. That this was our nasib — is this a word familiar to you? Very much so in our Arab Muslim culture: if things happen to you, then inshallah, mā shā'a qadara, which means whatever God has decided for you. In a sense that helps you to accept what is beyond you, knowing that you're not going to be able to change it, but that you have to live with it, that this was what was prescribed — your destiny.

I even think that in Egypt especially — I'm talking about Egypt because this is what I know — people tend to be resigned to their fate, to what happens to them. So I wish we were more militant, I wish we would be more questioning of what's happening. That is my take on the question. Take patience, for instance: there's a fine line between being submissive and reacting, being active. So I don't think that as Muslims we have to bend at every turn, but there's certainly a part of it where we have to accept that you can't change everything — not everything is within our control.

question: WHAT MATTERS MOST OVER THE LONG RUN FOR MUSLIMS BEING ABLE TO PRACTICE THEIR RELIGION?
answer: I think, again, that we have to be flexible, in the sense that religion is not only — frankly, is not — outside manifestations. It's also how you behave, how you live, how you treat others. Maybe this relates a little to a previous question, where I mentioned the hadith that the best Muslim is the one who is the most useful, the most helpful, to the community. So preserving my religion is to a great deal about me, rather than about taking an antagonistic approach, which I don't think would help. There is a balance again here. Those are the things that come to my mind.

question: WHAT DO YOU THINK ABOUT THE NEW LAW ABOUT PRAYING OUTSIDE?
answer: I think it's a discriminatory law, and I think it's politically motivated. We're heading into elections, and it gives the politicians an opportunity to elaborate on a familiar theme — that we Muslims are strange, that we have strange habits, that we practice the religion only in order to impose it. That's what has good currency here: that we want to convert the West, that we want to make it an Islamic state, that we want to impose the Sharia. They don't understand what those words mean, but those are words that have special connotations here, and the nationalist party is building its popularity on them. So that's what I have to say.

question: HOW DO YOU UNDERSTAND LAÏCITÉ, AND HOW DOES IT SIT WITH YOUR OWN LIFE?
answer: Laïcité, in the strict sense of the word, is that the state, l'état, has to be neutral in terms of religion — not favoring one religion over the other. For instance, in the so-called Muslim countries, because they're not Muslim any more — again, I'm referring to Egypt — on the Islamic occasions the head of state would be filmed going to a mosque and praying with the others. That here wouldn't be acceptable, because there the government is not secular, whereas in a secular government, the government should not have a religion that the people in the government are following. We agree with that entirely. But it doesn't mean that it should strip citizens of their identity, which is what is aimed at here by those secularism laws — they don't want to see that you are a Muslim in a special place, in what they call places of authority, and they keep on expanding what those positions are.

question: WHEN YOU SAY PLACES OF AUTHORITY, DO YOU MEAN TEACHERS IN PUBLIC SCHOOLS?
answer:
Yes, yes. First, with Bill 21, they had designated specific people — teachers, judges, prison guards, and what else? There was a fourth category also, where they would say those are women. They didn't say women, so it would be women and men in places of authority — in effect, where you would have influence over others. But with the new law, which is Law 94, they expanded this. So now it's not only teachers who are wearing a visible religious symbol — they wouldn't say hijab, they would say religious symbol, as if it were not aimed at Muslims. Then they said anyone: a cook, for instance, in a cafeteria, wearing a hijab, would not be acceptable; a cleaning lady in a school. So essentially anybody working in the school, not only teachers, and whether they have direct contact with the kids or not. In a public school, you cannot have this.

It also included the garderies, the daycare centers, where in [CITY 1] a majority of the caretakers are Muslim women. At first they were not covered by Bill 21, but now they are covered — although I think there's a clause that says if you're already in the position, you wouldn't be banned from the position, but you cannot as a new entry be qualified to be in a garderie. So this is actually an extension of the law.

question: HAS THE LAW PERSONALLY TOUCHED YOU?
answer: No, no, because I go back to the fact that I'm not in the work market, I'm retired, so it is not affecting me directly. But it's affecting me in the sense that all our efforts at [MUSLIM WOMEN'S ORGANIZATION 1], when I was part of it, were directed towards defending those women, writing about how unfair this law is going to be, how it's affecting the women — and not only the women, because women are not isolated, women are part of the community. I see kids who suffer anxiety because of those laws. I don't know if their mother will be working, if they're going to be able to have the toys they want. This becomes a family discussion, and the most vulnerable segment in our society, which is the young people, they are also impacted. So it's a whole community. And moreover, it's not only the law: it also gives bigots the freedom, how to say, to be more nasty.

question: DO YOU FEEL THE STATE OPPRESSES YOU?
answer:
Yes, definitely. I think this is a kind of oppression. It goes to your pocket, and that's very important — especially in a materialistic society like the North American context, where money is so important. People see you here, and the first question that comes to their mind is, how much money do you make?

In many instances, you're judged by how rich you are — what assets do you have? It's talked about all the time, and it's given value, I would say, beyond anything else. Before, you would say, she's a kind woman, or she's devoted to her family; now people say, oh, where does she work, how much money does she make? That kind of thing — it seems to me, anyway.

question: WHEN YOU WEAR HIJAB OR PERFORM AN ACT OF WORSHIP, IS THERE SOMETHING GOING ON INWARDLY?
answer: Yes, it was a pleasure, but this is a personal question. Awareness, yes — certainly when I cover, before going out, I am aware that I am covering because I'm a Muslim, and that this is the way I want to be dressed and to be seen.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer: Again, I think you're getting into questioning to what extent we are practising our religion, or bringing forth things that are more intimate. I wonder — let's skip that one.

question: HOW DO YOU UNDERSTAND LIBERATION?
answer: How God has sent liberation — this is quite clear to me. It's to act according to what I want for my life — very much so — within the limits of my religion, rather than being limited by conventions, traditions, society, that kind of thing. I want to live my life the way I want to live it. This being said, I wouldn't say that it was a successful life, but for me, I can say I lived my life, and this is sufficient reward for me personally.

question: IS THERE SOMETHING I SHOULD HAVE ASKED THAT I DIDN'T ASK?
answer:
Yes, I think perhaps we should talk about the contribution to the community. Most of your questions were personal. I feel that perhaps you should add: how far have you been engaged with the community, what have you done for the community — that kind of question.

Absolutely, you're right. I'm sorry — I even have a notice here, this is question sixteen, how do you understand your role within your family and your community. I would have liked anyway, for my case, to separate them. Family is one thing for me and community is another thing, maybe — it's like private and public spaces.

What I would like to add is that being part of the community is very important in the West, because our families here are nuclear families, not the extended families that we had in our home countries. So as a compensation, it is very important to be aware, with others, of our role within the larger Muslim community.

question: WHAT HAVE WE GAINED FROM THE WEST?
answer:
I wonder if you would be interested also in knowing what we have gained from the West. We talked at length about our concerns, but what makes us stay in the West, if it is a choice? We're not compelled to stay here, by and large — we're not refugees. Speaking about myself, I came here willingly, knowing to a certain extent what my life would be.

What have we gained here from the West? First of all, physical fitness. For women especially, there are more venues, opportunities and encouragement to be physically active here and to look after my health than I had back home — whether in terms of physical installations, or in how society looks at someone who wants to be physically active. Even beauty standards: in some poor countries, or even not so poor countries, a woman who is well, who is round — who has round forms, let's say — is deemed more attractive than somebody who is athletic and wiry. And this, of course, stems from the fact that somebody who is well-nourished is a sign of wealth — you're not skinny.

So that is one thing I gained from the West. Another thing is that I have the opportunity to voice my political opinions, which was very vital for me, very important. Back home, no, you can't do that — not fifty years ago, and unfortunately not up till today. So I feel that people are living in a cage; even if it's a golden cage, they can't go outside certain limits. And here in the West there is a price to it — let's not gloss over it and say it's something that you can do every day in every situation. No, there is a price to it, but still you have choices.

I also find that in the West there is more awareness about gender equality, which did not necessarily prevail where I came from. I find there is more awareness of the rights of women in the family, whereas in Egypt it was more — it depends. Men perhaps want to be seen as the deciders, although it may not be the case, but they wanted to be seen as such. So there are nuances, of course. Let's say that my place as a woman in a Western society pleases me, or is more in agreement with what I want to be.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer: An ordinary day in my life: I wake up early, before dawn, to do my prayer, then go back to sleep. I wake up again when my alarm goes off at seven, have some breakfast, and sit on my balcony to look at my little flower garden, which is beautiful, and get some sunlight. Then, depending on what the plan for the day is, I usually do some writing or some kind of creative project, because that's what I enjoy doing with my time. I'm in my mid-sixties now and I live alone, so I have more free time than I've ever had, and that's wonderful. I make my midday prayer. Sometimes I go into my part-time job at [NATIONAL POSTAL SERVICE], three days a week. Other times I may go visit family members or other members of the community, or I might go shopping — I don't do that very much because I'm opposed to consumer culture. Cooking, chatting, following politics, watching streaming shows on my computer, reading books — I regularly download books. At the moment I'm doing some research on Fatimah al-Zahra, and that is fascinating, absolutely fascinating. I'm not quite sure what I'm going to do with it yet, but maybe I can work it into some kind of piece.

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer:
Myself and my community — okay, I am a Western-educated Muslim convert. I came in through Islamic Sufism. I've written about my experience. I met a Sufi sheikh in Switzerland many years ago, and I converted to Islam a year later — actually in Turkish Cyprus, which wasn't part of Europe at that point — and then I married and came to Canada from Europe.

Somebody who's never met a Muslim: well, the converts from the West who went into Islam are a pretty unique demographic. I don't know if you've ever met any of them. It sort of started before then, but it became more significant in the 1960s and 70s. I converted in the mid-80s, by which point there were — I wouldn't say quite a few of them, but a significant number. Interestingly enough, many of them were from secular North American Jewish backgrounds. The man I married had converted ten years previously in [CITY 5] — it was the hand of Allah, the will of Allah. So I'm part of that community, and I do have friends who are raised Muslim — you found me through [MUSLIM WOMEN'S ORGANIZATION 1], the majority of whom are born Muslim and immigrants. So my background is a little bit different, and one of the reasons I wear hijab — I don't wear it all the time — is as a cultural signifier, because nobody, including the Muslims, believes that I'm actually a Muslim, because of my unusual cultural background. So I wear it to kind of prove that I am a Muslim. Well, because I'm white, because of the way I speak, because I was raised in England, and people don't realize that now the only people with faith in England are the Muslims. They're becoming a bit more aware of it, but the stereotype of British people is different to what I am.

I see that as a very positive thing. When I lived in England, in the mid-80s, the first wave of large-scale Muslim immigration was establishing itself, and there were the beginnings of communities in parts of the north of England where the industrial base had collapsed. I thought it was wonderful. I wasn't Muslim at that point, but I lived on a street in [CITY 3] that was full of Muslims, and the culture for women there was that they didn't really communicate with people outside their community, but we had some very pleasant interactions over the years — some lovely acts of kindness shown to me by Muslims. But I never thought that Islam was something that was viable for me, partly because of the hijab, also because of the cultural closeness at that point. I think in that first wave, Muslims coming over deliberately chose not to integrate with mainstream society because they were fearful or they didn't like it, so there wasn't much cultural exchange or dialogue, as they call it now. But that's changed radically.

Interestingly enough, I had an uncle — well, first of all, my father, before he was married, lived in [CITY 4], Iraq. He worked as a doctor there and was very fond of the people he met and his time there, and he talked about it in a very positive way — that was when I was a child growing up in England. My uncle, because they were part of the British colonialist thing (I have to deal with that too), came over from Malaysia, where he was working, and brought someone who worked for him to get treatment because this person had tuberculosis. He stayed with us, and that was the first Muslim I ever met, and the first person of color I ever interacted with. I was seven years old and had never interacted with somebody who had such a different life experience. That was wonderful, because I thought this person was absolutely amazing — stunningly good-looking, extremely kind, and with such wonderful manners. There was always this emphasis put on us growing up that we should have good manners, but this person's manners were next level, they were really good. So that was very positive and inspiring, and I never really bought into the anti-immigrant rhetoric that was around, because it was clear to me that the people coming to my country were better raised and educated.

In [CITY 1]? Well, I've grown up with the community, I raised my children with them, I'm very aware of what's going on with them. My most positive link with a community at this point is with the Turkish mosque. There is a very old friend who's Turkish, she's in her 90s now, and (her husband has) always maintained [MASJID 1] as a very safe space. He's linked with the Unitarian Church now, and it's become a kind of repository for immigrants — he's got all this stuff stored all over the place, and most of the born Muslims really don't like it, because it's a bit like going into a recycling store — in the masjid, well, the basement of the masjid, but also in the masjid itself. At one point he had all these kids' toys, and then the people praying there objected. Anyway, that is a place where I enjoy my interactions. That's where I go for Eid prayers and things.

Well, it's very varied. Now it's majority Francophone, because those are the people who are coming in. The group running that particular mosque at the moment is a little bit marginal in the Muslim community because they differ about the direction of the Qibla — they're called the Habashis, because they're related to a certain shaykh, and it's to do with the way they calculate it. It's towards the Kaaba, it's not towards Jerusalem or anything, but they calculate the direction of the Kaaba in [CITY 1] differently than everybody else does. Allahu a'lam. Yes, they are Sunni. Honestly, there's just all kinds of variety, it's incredible — practically every cultural community now has its own mosque. I've been in Canada since the mid-80s, so I've seen a lot of changes, and over the years I've negotiated and adapted to nearly all the communities — there are some exceptions. So I've become agile at what they call — I don't know, they have words for it now, like switching — anyway, I've gotten used to that, and I go into these contexts and just do my best to make alliances based on my understanding of deen. I was lucky enough to go on hajj, and one of the things I marveled at was the cross-section of humanity that you would not find anywhere else. It was wonderful, wonderful.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer: Oh, yeah, that's interesting. When I first became Muslim, I was sort of trying to be Turkish, because my shaykh was Turkish, and his wife and his daughters introduced me and taught me about Islam — that's Hanafi Sunni. So when I came in and was newly married, I was forced to internalize that when I was confronted with the Muslims at that time, because their interpretation of Islam was very influenced by the Salafi mindset, and it was very rigid, I would say. Within Sufism we're more flexible, let's put it like that — we try not to judge, we try to see everybody as a person of God. So I had this sort of Turkish persona almost. I would say over the years I've internalized my faith more and more and linked it with the person I was born and raised to be — there was this discrepancy between the child who grew up in [CITY DISTRICT 1] and was raised in a certain cultural background, and the person who converted to Islam, got married, and became a sort of trad wife before that term existed, then later got divorced and had to start her own business and survive. So yes, it's definitely evolved, and it's become internalized, and it's actually become stronger. Several years ago, I met my sister-in-law on a visit to the UK, and she said, "Oh, so you've stopped the Muslim thing," and I said, "No, the Muslim thing has become even stronger." Because it's coming from in here — it's coming from my reading of the Quran, my prayers, my interaction with teaching and podcasts and all the wonderful resources that are out there now for us.

question: HOW DOES LIVING HERE SHAPE HOW YOU PRACTICE OR SHOW YOUR FAITH?
answer:
Well, I'm a hidden Muslim. Publicly, I do not wear hijab. I do not want to go around with a target on my back. That started around 2010, when I had to go out and get a job. I had to interview for a job, because I knew perfectly well that nobody was going to hire me as a converted Muslim. The Muslim businesses themselves were not going to hire me because I wasn't part of their cultural community, and it was problematic — plus they had their wives already working there for free, so why would they? And, well, we're under national socialism now — the situation for Muslims in Quebec is the worst it's ever been. It's always been bad, but now there's so much prejudice, a lot of open, active hostility towards Muslims. The incidents of racism — Muslim women being attacked on the metro, having horrible things said to them, treated with prejudice and disrespect constantly. When I was married and wore hijab, I did experience some of that, but to a certain extent I was protected from it, because I was married and in a secure economic position. It would happen when I was driving — there would be these big black trucks behind me, kind of menacing me. That doesn't happen to me now that I'm not wearing it. It's bad, and people are not embarrassed or inhibited about doing it. In [CITY 2] it's way better — not so much [PROVINCE 3], there are far fewer visible Muslims, but in [PROVINCE 2], in [CITY 2], it's fine to wear hijab and be Muslim. Not in Quebec.

I didn't have to remove it, I chose to remove it, and now I use it as a cultural identifier — so when I go into what I'd describe as a Muslim context, I wear hijab, but when I'm in a secular context, I don't. Now I work at [NATIONAL POSTAL SERVICE], which is an interesting example, because it's one of the very few organizations that will not discriminate against women wearing hijab — there are hijabi women working at the federal government and at [NATIONAL POSTAL SERVICE]. However, I've noticed that many of them have swapped the hijab for a beanie or a hoodie. In the winter I do that too, because it's cold in the warehouse — I cover my head in various ways. A traditional hijab and an abaya, I'd wear to Eid prayer, but I certainly wouldn't wear it to the grocery store.

Prejudice and hostility — that's what was in my environment, and it's everywhere. You can have this thing about educating people about Islam, but honestly, look at Muslim men — most of the time, apart from their skin color, you can't tell that they're Muslim men. So why should I go around with a target on my back or on my head? I read a fatwa that said originally hijab was to protect women, and I agree with it — it's become the other way around, especially in Quebec. Wearing hijab is not protecting you, it's opening you up to hostility and Islamophobia and anti-immigrant, racist rhetoric.

It's gotten way worse, the situation has really deteriorated, and unfortunately the CAQ government, which is in power at the moment, has perpetuated and encouraged this. It started with 9/11. Shortly after, my husband, who is very intentional about appearing as a Muslim male — he always wears a hat and these kinds of outfits from his Turkish tailor, he looks outrageous — people used to call him Osama. We were traveling to Jordan and we were at Schiphol Airport, and a woman got on the lift and said, "Are you crazy? Are you out of your mind? What are you doing going around dressed like this? Do you realize how much they hate us?" I've never forgotten that. That was at Schiphol, in Europe, shortly after 9/11. But then it started in Canada too — everyone was like, "Who are these people? What's going on, they're terrorists, they're trying to take over, they're trying to blow us up." And unfortunately this kind of garbage has continued.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, AND HOW?
answer: I consider it one of my pillars of faith to listen to and watch and read Quran, listen to tafsir, learn — anything I can. I see my faith like a part of my body, if you like. I have to nourish it with good food, I have to make sure it gets exercise and water, that it flourishes and grows, because honestly, if you don't feed it, it will wither. I think it's true — I think we all have to do that.

question: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN OR HIJAB?
answer: Honestly, at this stage in my life, I don't expect people to understand. I don't place the burden on them of understanding who I am and my journey — that's one of the reasons I wrote this book, just to document it. My daughters read it and they were like, "Oh wow, we never realized," and I'm like, well, why would you? It's been a very long journey, and I'm old now — like I said, I'm in my sixties, so a lot has happened, a lot has gone on, and it continues.

question: HOW DO WE CREATE CHANGE OR BETTER COEXISTENCE?
answer: Well, I think the secret lies in our humanity, in our hearts and our intentions. If our intention in our interactions with others is to nurture the faith of that person and meet their heart to the best extent that we can, then I think we're going to be fine. But if our intention is to try to force some kind of ideology on them, or to force a language or a way of life on other people, which is the direction of the CAQ, then there's going to be trouble — Islamophobia, racism, and so on. When people have positive interactions with Muslims, they think of Muslims in a positive way. You've got your typical Canadian who lives in [PROVINCE 2] in a suburban house — he has a Muslim neighbor, the kids play together, the wife brings over sweets, they talk over the fence, their reactions are very positive, people are living peacefully. When that person hears "they're trying to take over society," he's going to think, well, Zaid's okay, I know Zaid, he's fine — or the guy who works in the office, Abdulrahman, he's a good guy, he stayed late and helped me with a project, he always says hi to me in the lift and asks about my family. They've been inoculated against this. The problem is with people who have no experience of Muslims, so they can buy into the idea that "they're a threat, they're here to steal jobs" — as if they're here to speak English. Most of the Muslims are from North Africa, that's why they're here — if they came here speaking English, they'd be out of here as quickly as they could. What else is the sentiment? Well, "they're foreign, they have different values, they're not like us, they're primitive" — it's coming directly from France, what you hear in France is what you hear here — "they have to integrate, they have to be part of our society, our culture" — which leads me to ask, well, what is your culture? I could get nasty, but I'll try not to. What is this so-called culture that the Muslims are supposedly trying to take away from you? Think about it.

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer:
As a revert — as a convert, I prefer to call myself a convert rather than a revert, because a revert sounds to me like a diagnosis — a big problem for me is the way I get treated by the mainstream community when I go to a mosque or a community gathering. There is often prejudice, condescension. I'm an old woman, but many Muslim males will not interact with me at all, out of what they think is politeness. They seriously believe that pretending I don't exist is a polite way of dealing with the problem of someone like me in their prayer space, in their club. So yeah, that's a difficulty.

A typical example: I go to a mosque, I'm told I can't go in — I'm shooed out of the main entrance, "get out of here, go around the back." So I go around to the women's space, which is filled with sad women in difficult situations, many children crying and upset because there's nothing to entertain them and their needs aren't being met, and then there's a giant TV screen on the wall broadcasting the imam talking non-stop, usually in another language — sometimes the language of the cultural community of that mosque, frequently not even that language. I don't know quite what that's serving, but it has happened. I wouldn't say frequently, but when it does, I find it disturbing, disruptive to my faith — it hurts my heart. Sometimes I just leave, it's my choice to be there. Sometimes I make a complaint, sometimes accommodations are made because I'm making a fuss, but just the fact that I have to do that — I make alliances with other women in the same situation, and we push and petition together.

question: WHAT INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS ARE PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer: I think there's both. Generally, Muslim women put far too much pressure on themselves — I'm not surprised there's this rate of depression, mental illness, and anxiety among Muslim women, I've witnessed that many times, and it's systemic, tied to the isolation and the kind of family structures they're expected to maintain. For some convert women, there are pockets of communities where women who were raised in the West, in [PROVINCE 2] for instance, are expected — and put it upon themselves — to wear niqab and homeschool their children, meaning they're responsible for the education of five or six children all day, every day, in addition to living life in the West and supporting their husbands. I don't think it's surprising that a lot of them struggle. Anyone would. They put far too much pressure on themselves. That's also true of working Western women generally — the plight of working women with children is far too much pressure whether you're Muslim or not, because you don't have your mother and your aunts or your sisters there to help you the way you would in a traditional context. If you're leaving the house every day, in a traditional context there's somebody there for when the school calls because your kid has thrown up in the classroom — for these women there isn't anyone, so it's on them. I think they could really lighten up, because Islam is in your heart, Islam is in your journey, Islam is in your salah and your relationship with Allah. This is your Islam. Your Islam is not in what you're wearing, how you're living, or where you're living — you should be able to practice it anywhere.

question: HOW AND WHERE ARE YOU ABLE TO PRAY DURING YOUR DAY?
answer: Well, now there is a law that we're not allowed to pray in parks — it's kind of treated like taking drugs, not allowed in public places. At [NATIONAL POSTAL SERVICE], when I first started working there, there used to be a prayer room, but because it's Quebec, they closed it and used the pandemic as the excuse. So they just locked it. Now when Asr comes in while I'm at [NATIONAL POSTAL SERVICE], I go into the lunchroom, and there's a group of Maghrebi brothers who sort of acknowledge that I'm Muslim and sort of don't — and I definitely don't (make a point of it either). It is what it is, it's fine, they don't have to understand me, that's okay — Allah understands me, I understand me, it doesn't matter. There's a chair in the back corner of the room that's facing the Qibla — that's the prayer chair. I sit in it, wrap something around my head, and do my prayers. If someone else comes in while I'm sitting there doing my salat, the Western people just kind of stare at me, but the Muslim brothers politely ignore me, and that's that.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer: I do (need to prove it) — that's kind of all I can say. Members of the Muslim community recognize other Muslims, especially within the cultural communities, by their affinity with other members of their group — it's kind of an anthropological thing. This is less the case with younger Muslims who've been through the Western education system, but with the men, most men, and with some women — I used to go quite regularly, and they would make me recite the Shahada or say some surahs, like a kind of parrot performing to entertain them, to prove that I was a Muslim.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer: Well, obviously my family — not so much my ex-husband, although we're friends and remain in contact, like he tells me when Ramadan's beginning (though I can tell anyway because I get the alerts on my phone), but that sort of thing is helpful. My daughters — I have three daughters, they're absolutely wonderful, I feel most responsible to them, to be there for them and my grandchildren. I do feel responsible to help my Muslim friends too — these are friendships that go back thirty or forty years, we've always been there for each other, so when they have hospital visits and things, I try. And who else do I feel responsible to? I feel responsible to Allah — that's who I feel responsible to. How do they shape my choices? Well, they're shaped through my heart — what my conscience is telling me is the right thing to do is what I try to do.

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer: My role within my community, at this point, I've decided is through my writing — as a writer and a Sufi, someone who's promoting spirituality. That's what I see my responsibility and my role as. Within my family, my responsibility is as a mother, a coach, a support.

question: LEARNING TO SPEAK FRENCH IN QUEBEC
answer: In England we all learned French at school, and it was always my worst subject — possibly I was even worse at Latin, but that's a close call, since they let me stop doing Latin within a year. I had to take what we call the O-level three times; I think in the end they gave it to me because they felt sorry for me and I kept trying. So I'm not good at languages. But since I've been in Quebec, especially at [NATIONAL POSTAL SERVICE], I have a lot of fun with the Quebec people who work there — not so much the women, who usually hate me, but the men, and we have this banter. I've learned to speak what they call joual — there's this whole prejudice against Quebec French, but what they speak is a dialect that's actually much closer to medieval French than the French spoken today. I've learned to speak that particular dialect, and I have that accent, and I'm very proud of it, because when I speak to them, they look at me, they know I'm an English immigrant, and then I speak with this joual accent and deliberately use these little aphorisms and phrases — they think it's hilarious, they love it, and I love it too, because it's such fun.

question: DO YOU FEEL YOU BELONG HERE — ARE YOU SEEN AS FRENCH/QUEBECOIS?
answer: No. When I first came here, my husband — third generation Quebecer — and I were talking to a very nice, very respectful Quebec man, and I said, well, my husband's a Quebecer, [HUSBAND'S NAME]'s a Quebecer, because he was born here and his mother was born here, and he said, "mais il n'est pas Québécois de souche" — which means, essentially, that he's not "pure wool." There was this phrase, which they seem to have dropped now, fortunately, that if you're not one of the people who came over back in the 18th century, then you're not really a Quebecer. No — I joke with other immigrants, I say, well, we're Quebecers, and we both laugh. I've been here since 1986. I think of myself as Canadian too — I have a Canadian passport, and I say I'm more Canadian than I am British because I've been here longer. It's true, I am much more Canadian, but the British thing still comes through when people hear me talk. And no, the accent doesn't show up in my French, because I've got this joual thing going.

question: HOW DO YOU UNDERSTAND LAÏCITÉ, AND HOW DOES IT AFFECT YOU?
answer:
I really like the traditional Catholic identity of Quebec, because it promoted belief in God in the daily life of people, so I appreciate that. I live just outside [CITY 1], in a place named after the Virgin Mary — that's Hazrat Maryam. I like that. Although the Muslim community has this thing where they say, oh, Christians believe in the Trinity, so they're wrong — I've made alliances with Christians as people of faith, very positive alliances, and we build each other up, because the darkness of secularism in Quebec is affecting everyone who believes, not just the Muslims. The Muslims are a visible target, but it's affecting the Sikhs, some of the Jews, the Christians too. Now their churches have to pay taxes, so they have to fundraise to support their buildings, and their buildings are all going to be demolished — I recently read an editorial in [PROVINCIAL NEWSPAPER 1] saying, well, wouldn't it be so much better if we could just use it all as public housing?

We have to support each other, because Christians are people of the book, despite what you might think about the way the Catholic Church has behaved over the years — they're people of the book, and the people of the book are the believers, and we treat them differently. To me, the problem isn't so-called polytheists or shirk, it's not the Hindus — the problem is consumer mentality, secularism, and liberalism, especially when it's aligned with communism or socialism. This government describes itself as national socialist, and that is the problem.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: Okay, well, I'm answerable. I have this understanding I received many years ago from a wonderful sheikh — not Sheikh Nazim, but another sheikh I studied with — who said you really don't have to worry about judging the actions of others. It's good to say something is wrong, it's good to speak truth to power, but you don't have to get into a terrible state about things that are happening, because everyone is going to be judged and Allah will deal with them. So one of the things I say to myself is: it's okay, Allah will fix them. I find that thought comforting, and I also believe it's true — nobody gets away with anything. People can make billions on cryptocurrency, oppressing others, supplying them with arms, this and that — but they're not going to get away with it. So you better be responsible about the way you behave, responsible for every interaction and every intention you have, because your intention shapes your actions and your actions shape who you are. If you wish to be a Muslim, you have to align your intentions and your actions to aspire to the character the teachings of Islam would want you to be.

question: HOW DO YOU MAKE SENSE OF WHAT IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL?
answer: Again, it's in the will of Allah, and it's not something that as an individual I can control, not something I have a voice in — my saying "this is terrible" isn't going to be acknowledged by governments in power. I don't believe in activism, honestly. When I was a teenager, I used to go to protests about things I didn't really know that much about, and I was just being manipulated. I actually see quite a bit of manipulation going on in the Muslim community too, by various political forces, and that concerns me. Allah is in control — it's the will of Allah, and I have a responsibility, as a servant of Allah, to bring about the best outcome I can within my limited capacity.

question: WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR PRACTICING YOUR RELIGION IN THE LONG RUN?
answer: What matters to me most is that they have a vital and living relationship with Allah. Because I believe if they have that, then Allah will be in their hearts, and if Allah is in their hearts, their deen will follow. When I was raising my daughters, I was perhaps too liberal, and they had friends whose parents were extremely strict about how they were raised — today those girls have basically abandoned eighty percent of their parents' belief. Allah alim, I don't know about their prayer life, but they're one- or two-pillar Muslims — if you ask them, they'll say, yeah, I believe in Allah and the oneness of Allah, and I don't eat ham, but that's about it. I would aspire to something more than that — an interior experience of connection with the Creator of everything.

question: HAVE SPECIFIC LAWS (BILL 21, BILL 94, BILL 9, ETC.) PERSONALLY AFFECTED YOU?
answer: They've affected my community. Honestly, I think people are afraid. Many years ago, when we had Jumu'ah, we'd meet for picnics in the park, and we'd all be sitting there, and then the men would get up to pray, we'd put out a blanket, and the sisters would pray behind them — we prayed publicly, that was part of our association as people of faith. None of that is allowed now. If we were all hiding, nobody wearing hijab, nobody praying, presumably there wouldn't be a problem — but nobody's doing that.

question: DO YOU FEEL OPPRESSED BY THE STATE?
answer: Absolutely, yeah, absolutely. It's like — it's like in communist countries. Yes, the experience here is different than the rest of Canada.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer: Aligning my intention with the will of Allah.

question: WHAT IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR HEART, INTENTION, AND OUTWARD PRACTICE?
answer: It was my path. Initially, again, it's the way I came into Islam — I came in through Sufism, so I'd say that's informed by Sufi spirituality, and it's nurtured and encouraged by my interactions with other people aligned with these values — for instance, Abdul Hakim Murad, who teaches out of Cambridge Mosque, and to a certain extent Hamza Yusuf. He's also part of the Haqqani (order), which I had experience with — that's the sheikh who told me about the judging thing, he was one of the Haqqani, and that stuck with me. So yes, those people.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer: Liberation — well, I guess when you die, inshallah, your spirit will be liberated from your existence in dunya, with all the struggles of dunya and all the suffering and pain and tribulation you undergo, so you'll be liberated then, inshallah. I just think you have to keep struggling — you get up every day, you do your salat, you do your best, you show up, that's what you're required to do. You're not going to find some kind of spiritual state where you're floating like the Buddhist thing, whatever — don't get me started on that. You're not going to find some special spiritual state where nothing bothers you, and if you did find that, it would be very problematic, because you'd be completely oblivious to all the suffering going on around you.

question: WHO GETS TO REPRESENT MUSLIM WOMEN IN RESEARCH, MEDIA, OR AI?
answer: As for the impact of AI — if AI can help us be more human and more accepting of our limitations and difficulties, then I think it can be a very positive thing, so I don't mind AI learning from me. AI is much better at quite a lot of things, but AI has nothing to do with faith — AI, unlike a human, does not have a heart. As for "Sheikh AI" and all that business — I think humans will transform AI, they're already doing it. It's kind of like the pet rock phenomenon: people would have a pet rock and attribute all this consciousness and all these qualities to it. People do it with their pets, and I think they're going to start doing that with AI. Well, they already are. Not a Muslim marriage, though.

question: HAS WEARING HIJAB CREATED BARRIERS IN EDUCATION OR EMPLOYMENT?
answer:
Oh god, no — never, never, I don't think you're allowed to attend [UNIVERSITY 1] as a hijabi, I don't think you would be. When I was there, they were openly racist, openly — I didn't survive, I left after two terms. I think there's probably a law about it — there was a whole thing about not being allowed to wear hijab in high school, not allowed to wear it in educational institutions at all, not allowed to access government services wearing niqab. At one point they wouldn't let people on buses wearing niqab, and then the pandemic came — masks, that was great, to me that was one of the last little jokes. But anyway, I think about screening people so they can't get into buildings.

Many years ago, I did another interview about hijab, and when I told the interviewer that I didn't wear hijab all the time, he was a Black Muslim from somewhere in the States, and he just gave me this whole lecture — his wife lives in [STATE 1] and always wears hijab, wouldn't go out of the house without it, okay, fine. But I was divorced at that time, and I had made the choice, in order to survive economically, that I would not wear hijab. And there we go.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer:
I wake up — it depends if I have school or work or not — but I wake up, get ready for the day, and then if I have work, I go to work, if I have school, I go to school. If I have plans with my friends, I go to that. I can't really remember, because it's summer, so all my days look different, I don't really have much of a routine, but yeah, I go out, come back home.

It shows up in everything I do. Depending on your intention, anything can be an act of worship, so I think faith is everywhere in my day, but tangibly, I wear hijab. So when I get ready, I have this in mind, this act of worship — when I go out, it's part of me and my identity and how I show up in the world. I make sure to do my five prayers during the day, whether I'm inside or outside, so when I go out I'll find a place to pray, look for a mosque, or make sure that wherever I go there is a place to pray nearby. I'm studying Islamophobia mainly, I have a Muslim lens on my research. I'm also very involved in my community, so it does come out. I also have primarily Muslim friends, or even the friends I have who aren't Muslim — we have some talks about faith. So I think it shows up a lot.

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer:
I think if I were to describe myself, I wouldn't necessarily start with my faith, although it is something people would see first because I wear hijab — I would start with the basics: we believe there's only one God, and the last messenger is Muhammad, peace be upon him. That actually came up a lot — I went on vacation in Costa Rica, and I was a lot of people's first Muslim woman, so I've done this quite a bit over the summer. They would ask me a lot of questions about hijab and why I wear it, and I'd tell them it's because I'm a Muslim woman, and they'd ask the basic questions — can you take it off, when can you take it off, who can see your hair, why do you dress like this? I answer these because I think if people encounter a woman in hijab and don't know a lot about Islam, they start asking questions, because there are a lot of misconceptions, and it's nice when they ask respectfully — every single one of my interactions has been respectful, alhamdulillah. They usually ask why I wear the hijab, and I tell them I believe in one God and the last prophet. I also make sure people can make links, so I talk about the differences between Christianity and Islam, because a lot of people already know a lot about Christianity, and making those links makes Islam seem less like the "crazy religion" it's made out to be in the media. I make those links to help humanize us, because we're really dehumanized in the media.

The community I'm involved in, alhamdulillah, is very good-willed. I admit I've also been a little bit swayed by media representations of Muslims — not by the West, but by Muslims themselves, the way they represent themselves on social media, a lot of the extreme viewpoints that appear there. So when I got involved in the community I came in with some doubt, but it's honestly been such a good community. I'm especially involved with women, because that's what my research is about, and I've always been a feminist — even before, I involved myself with non-Muslim feminist groups, and now I involve myself with groups that help women's rights. It's very respectful, we try to build a community, really rely on one another. Fun-loving at times, especially the younger part of the community — the older people too, but because I'm younger I can enjoy the more fun parts of it. Very educational. I had this image that there would be a lot of misogyny, and that has not appeared — in fact, people have advocated for women in many ways within the community, which is really different from the way we are perceived in the media, whether it's how we're portrayed or how we portray ourselves.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer: I was born and raised where I live — always in [CITY 1]. Alhamdulillah, I don't think I've had some sort of identity crisis, I think I've had a very easy life when it comes to my faith. When I was very young, the political climate made people very Islamophobic, and I watched my mother struggle with that. That's kind of shaped who I am as a person — not necessarily my faith, but my sense of justice, and a lot of what I do now in my master's has been shaped by these early experiences. Other than that, until I got involved in the Muslim community, we weren't really involved apart from Quran school and things like that, so I don't think I really had an identity crisis when it came to my faith, because when I was young I didn't really think about it — I just knew I was Muslim, I knew what I was taught in Quran classes, I believed in one God, and I didn't bother with much more than that. In high school, I went to a school with a lot of my community, so I never really had any struggle with Islam, because a large majority of the students were Muslim — I didn't feel any of the Islamophobia. I started to really look into Islam when I was a little older, around eighteen, nineteen, and that's where I started my journey with Islam — learning about it through social media discourse at first, which was really detrimental to my faith, so I stopped, because I thought, if God is the most merciful, why are these people saying things about God that aren't merciful, that aren't just? So I started to look into Islam by myself, with the Quran — I started to really focus on my prayers, started wearing hijab, and that also came at a time when I was doing research about Islamophobia.

question: HOW DOES LIVING HERE SHAPE HOW YOU PRACTICE OR SHOW YOUR FAITH?
answer:
I don't have anything to compare it to, because I've never lived anywhere other than Quebec. I never thought it was much of a struggle until these laws — personally, I'm not affected by the laws about secularism, so it hasn't changed a lot about how I practice, but when it comes to prayer, the laws are starting to affect everyone, because one of them closes down prayer rooms in universities and CEGEPs. Alhamdulillah, this law came in right when I started at a university that doesn't have a prayer room — my first year there, so this past year has been kind of hard on my faith when it comes to prayer. I was looking for a place to pray, afraid, trying to find places to sneak into, because I'd been spoiled by the prayer room back at my old university. Alhamdulillah I have an office now, because I'm a graduate student, so I just pray in there and I'm no longer on campus that much. In my adulthood I've held on to my community, and I think that's what truly helps and makes being Muslim anywhere very easy. Muslims who live in Muslim-majority countries have community, they're the majority, so holding on to your community, your friends, your family really helps — and it doesn't even have to be in a setting where you talk about or practice Islam, just being with people who think like you and accept you truly helps. My non-Muslim friends are also very open-minded and encouraging — because they know my faith means a lot to me, whenever we go out they make sure it's not at a bar, or if they're going to a bar they won't invite me, they make sure there's a place for me to pray, they worry about my prayers, if my hijab is slipping or my hair is showing they'll fix it for me. Being with people who truly understand and accept you, whether they're Muslim or not, really helps in being Muslim, not just in the West but anywhere.

I think a lot of women have had really bad experiences. Alhamdulillah, I haven't had many. I think the worst that's happened to me is crazy people talking to me on the metro, saying Islamophobic things or sexualizing me because I wear hijab. I'm not going to pretend my experience is the only experience, but alhamdulillah I've had a good one — I'm not very affected by the laws, though I still think they're very discriminatory, they shouldn't stay, they don't have legitimacy. I've been Muslim in Quebec, my sister has grown up Muslim in Quebec, and we've had good experiences, so I don't think it should discourage Muslim women from living in Quebec or from starting to wear hijab if that's where their journey takes them. But I do know some women — I don't know if it's a lot — have very bad experiences being visibly Muslim in Quebec, and some women don't at all.

question: HAVE SPECIFIC LAWS (BILL 21, BILL 94, BILL 9, ETC.) PERSONALLY AFFECTED YOU?
answer:
There are three laws. The first was Bill 21, which basically does not allow anyone who wears religious signs to work in a government job in a position of power — this affects lawyers who represent the court in Quebec, judges, police officers, and, really importantly, school teachers, because it's a female-dominated field with a lot of Muslim women teachers, in high school and elementary school — it's a very big community, and the educational system is already underfunded and understaffed. The law came into effect in May, and from that point no one could be hired into one of these positions of power representing the government of Quebec. People who already had a job could stay, protected by a grandfather clause, but they couldn't be promoted or change positions — if you're a woman teaching third grade, you'll teach third grade for the rest of your life; if you're a sergeant in the police force, you'll be a sergeant for the rest of your life. You can't switch schools even if you move far away. There's a real focus on education because that's where Muslim women are concentrated, but it's affected a lot of other fields too — anyone studying education who was a Muslim woman wearing hijab, that dream was dead to them unless they worked at a private school.

Then Bill 94 came into effect, after they found that one or two cases in the entirety of Quebec didn't follow the rules, and made this big law focused on the educational system: no one who works or volunteers in a public school in Quebec can wear a religious sign — teachers, psychotherapists, speech therapists, parent volunteers (and the Quebec educational system relies heavily on parent volunteers because it's understaffed), library volunteers, volunteers who take kids to field days, janitors, school lunch staff. It's truly erased religious signs from the view of children — supposedly to protect them, because Quebec has a long history with the Catholic Church being restrictive and oppressive, and when Quebec liberated itself from the Church it made everything secular. Quebec is secular, Canada is secular, but we had an open secularism that allowed people to be who they are and live, without laws dictated by any church. Now it's honed in specifically on Muslims, I think, because of our portrayal in the media — Quebec is openly trying to be like France, to remove religion from everything, and this shows up specifically targeting Islam because the media only ever talks about Muslim women when discussing religious signs and secularism, saying very dehumanizing things, and they have since 2012–13, when they were trying to establish the first law, the failed Charter of Values.

Bill 94 also prevents students from wearing niqab at school. And Bill 9, the newest one, prevents every student in CEGEP and university from wearing niqab, and extends the restrictions to any school that receives government funding, even religious schools, and to daycares — Muslim women who wear hijab can't wear religious signs in subsidized daycares. It closed down prayer rooms in CEGEPs and universities, and limited the halal menu at cafeterias — some schools have halal, kosher, vegetarian menus, and now you can't fully ask for one, I can't remember the exact rules on that. It made public group prayer illegal, so you can't pray in public in a group. The thing with these laws is that legislators didn't really think through how they'd be implemented, so they're still trying to figure it out — but yes, that's how they appear.

They're relying on school boards to enforce these laws — yes.
