There hasn't been a case where a board refused, but [ENGLISH-LANGUAGE SCHOOL BOARD 1] sued the government over Bill 21 — they still comply, but they've taken part in a lawsuit now in the Supreme Court, already debated, and we're just waiting for the verdict, it's been months. No school board has failed to comply. In cases where people haven't respected the laws, those specific professors or teachers are just fired.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer: I've worn hijab for almost four years now. My story was very spontaneous. I was sitting down — I was not a religious person, I was not practicing, unfortunately, almost at all. I did not dress modestly, I did not pray, though I did fast. I had a lot of struggle with religion and didn't care that much — I had some feeling of guilt, but not enough to change it. It was a Tuesday, I was writing a paper — I do my research on Islamophobia, so I was writing about Bill 21 when it was fairly new — and I couldn't pray because I was on my period. I felt this feeling that I really wanted to do an act of worship, and I was like, oh, I can't pray, I really wanted to go back to prayer in that moment. There was a Quran in front of me, and I wasn't informed enough to know you can touch the Quran on your period — I'd been told the main opinion is that you can't. So I couldn't read it, and I just thought, what if I start wearing the hijab? And that's what I did, alone in my house, and I started wearing it the next day, but the decision was made that same day. As for what it's done for me — truly, everything, because the moment I started wearing hijab is the moment I really started my religious journey of knowledge. I started to learn more about Islam because I told myself that the way wearing hijab in the West works out, it's really only materially negative — everyone assumes I'm subject to Islamophobia, dehumanization, and also assumes I'm a religious woman — so I told myself, since I'm putting myself in that position anyway, I might as well be ten toes down and start learning and practicing my religion properly. Since then, alhamdulillah, it's been going so well.

question: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN OR HIJAB?
answer: Yes, a lot. I think people have a lot of misconceptions about hijab and Muslim women — people think we are oppressed, brainwashed, that we don't have agency, that we're submissive, that all women who wear hijab are one type of woman — quiet, submissive, kind of childlike, reduced to a childlike state because we wear it. That's part Islamophobia, part misogyny, and it's not true. We're all very different people, with different opinions — even though what we share is belief in Allah and Rasulullah and wearing hijab because of it, the reasons why we wear it are different, our religious opinions are different, our personalities are different — we can be strong, loud, bubbly, we can also be quiet, creative, alternative, anything. At the end of the day, the way I see it, hijab is just an adornment you wear because you believe in it enough to wear it, but it doesn't change anything about who you are on the inside. And while it's true some women are oppressed, that's true of every woman, Muslim or not — we're all oppressed by the patriarchy. We're old enough to make our own choices and think for ourselves, and it doesn't necessarily have anything to do with men or anyone outside of God. One of the biggest misconceptions is that we wear hijab just for modesty, just to be protected from the male gaze — that's a really dangerous misconception, because it takes away from our agency and makes it sound like we can't think for ourselves. It really diminishes what hijab truly is, which is an act of worship to God — it's about you and God, about being recognized as Muslim, about altering the beauty standards. The way I see it, Islam is not just haram and halal, it's a lifestyle that gets you to detach from material things and focus on the immaterial, on the afterlife to come — kind of how Buddhist monks shave their heads and live in a monastery with very little clothing. We wear the hijab to divert away from material things, from beauty standards, to focus on what's truly important — our relationship with God, helping people, the community.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, AND HOW?
answer:
I already had the basics — my mom put me in Quranic school, and my parents taught me religion — but I wanted to rework the basics, and I'm still on this journey. I started to wear hijab at a time when I saw a lot of people converting to Islam online, and I decided to pretend I was a revert and start truly from the basics — the five pillars, understanding the importance of the Shahada, prayer, fasting for Ramadan, and having a relationship with the Quran, because the Quran is the word of God, the one thing we know for sure is His word, so we should have a relationship with it. I had never fully read the Quran, even though I'd been Muslim my whole life — I didn't even know what religion I was truly participating in. So I started with the basic knowledge anyone curious about Islam would want — why people pray five times a day, what the Shahada means. I'm still working through it, it's a big text to digest, but it's made my first connection to God the Quran itself, and not other people's interpretations of Islam, which has really weeded out a lot of the bad things that come out within our community.

I have a Quran class, so I memorize with a class and have a teacher, but I also do a big part myself. I read from a Quran that has the Arabic, transliteration, and a lot of context — pages and pages of historical context. I started reading the Clear Quran, which is a very good resource, but I found it lacking in places — when you don't know the context, some of what you read seems a little unfair, especially since I started from the beginning, from Al-Baqarah and the surahs that came later, which are more about rules, wars, and history. As you know, Islam introduced the Meccan surahs first, to get to know God, and the rules came later, but I started the other way around, with the rules coming first. My Quran offers a lot of social and historical context — it makes links to the Bible, to Greek philosophers, to Shakespeare, so it really connects to a more contemporary reality.

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer: Right now I'm struggling with finding a job. I have little jobs, so I have a steady stream of income, alhamdulillah, but it's still very small. I'm used to having multiple jobs at the same time for a bigger income, and being busier — right now the job that's usually my main job, I don't have, so I'm underemployed, still struggling to find one. The way I make sense of it: alhamdulillah, I live with my parents, I still have some income, I'm never truly in a place where I'm really struggling, I feel very blessed, and I remember that whatever is meant for me will come for me — God has a way of always providing some stable income even when I don't have a stable job. It is a struggle at times, because I'd love to have some routine, something steady, some security, but I make a lot of du'as and remember that at the end of the day, I am safe in the hands of God.

question: WHAT INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS ARE PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
Yes, a lot — internal and external. We have expectations from our community and from outside it, and it's truly a lot of pressure, because we have everything coming at us — Islamophobia, patriarchy, and the two coming together, an intersectional experience. Within our community, depending on where you are and who you turn to, we're not fully supported when we talk about the misogyny within it, and we don't really have a space to do that — if we want to talk about Islamophobia, Islamophobes say "but you're oppressed within your own community too." So we're oppressed within our community and also oppressed outside of it as Muslims — it's a struggle to balance everything. I think the best way to fight it is by doing it ourselves, fighting both the misogyny in and out of our community and the Islamophobia that affects us, our men, and our children.

There's a lot of pressure surrounding the hijab, because it's the factor that shows you're Muslim — you get a lot of looks, and because people know you're Muslim, people feel comfortable coming to tell you what you're doing wrong, whether outside the community or within it. If someone feels you're doing something haram, whether you are or not, they feel comfortable giving you "advice" — and I put that in quotes, because it's not necessarily well-meaning or useful. We get policed on our bodies, in the community and outside it, because we're visibly Muslim, and outside the community people feel free to victimize us because we're women and obviously Muslim, and say whatever comes to mind. There are good experiences, where people ask about Islam in a nice way and you have interesting conversations. But there are also experiences where you get hate-crimed, dehumanized in a conversation you never asked for, when you're just trying to get home. The eyes on us, and people thinking they can police our bodies because we wear hijab, is very difficult, especially because it comes from inside our community and outside it both.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer: It depends what my role is in that case, but generally I feel responsible towards my family. I feel like we owe something to everyone — I don't have a very individualistic mindset, I love community, I love helping out and being there for people, so I do feel a sense of responsibility for a lot of people around me. I guess that informs what I do now in my career and education, but when it comes to my own personal actions, I only feel responsible towards God. If I wanted to take off the hijab today or tomorrow, I wouldn't care as much about what people think or say, or my responsibility towards them — when it comes to my personal actions, I only feel responsible to God. But I do think we owe each other something — community, respect.

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer: There's not a specific one, I just use my skills to help in any way I can. With my family, I'm very present, emotionally and physically as much as I can be — they're people I care about, so I want to be there for them and help them as much as they need. It comes from a place of care rather than obligation. I know I'm a very vocal, opinionated person, so my role comes out a lot in advocacy — I'm involved in a lot of it, because it really takes nothing from me except time to be vocal about the things I care about and for my community.

question: WHAT DOES BELONGING FEEL LIKE HERE?
answer:
I wouldn't say I feel like I belong in the Quebec community as a Quebecer — I would say I am a Quebecer, but it depends who's asking. Seeing as we're very obviously not accepted by a lot of Quebecers, when people ask where I'm from, I give them my parents' nationality, even though I was born here. But if someone told me I'm not a Quebecer, I'd say I am, I was born here, you can't tell me what I am. I don't have much attachment to the land itself, or the culture — I just don't really care that much.

Very difficultly, in a very difficult way. I'm blessed to have had few bad experiences, but seeing people be so Islamophobic has brought me closer to my faith — that's something that happens when you feel you're not accepted, you hold on to your community. It's brought me there, but what's kept me there is Islam itself — I don't feel like I have trouble reconciling the two, because I am who I am, and you can take me or leave me. There are a lot of Muslims in Quebec, I live in a big city, so it's not like I'm the only Muslim in a small village where everyone else is Quebecois — I don't feel too much trouble reconciling them.

I don't know if they accept me as Quebecoise, and I don't care if they do. I know the Quebecois I surround myself with do. I don't even know if I come off as Québécoise — even my accent isn't very Québécois, so maybe they don't accept me because of how I talk, and maybe they do — but their acceptance doesn't change the fact that I am Québécoise.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: It shapes fully what I think. Whenever I'm going through something hard, I remind myself that this life is temporary and very short compared to the Akhirah — whatever trouble I'm going through, I'm going to die in a few years, inshallah, maybe ten, twenty, thirty, it doesn't matter, even if I live to be a hundred it's not a long time on this earth. That helps me get through the bad things, and it also helps me truly enjoy the good moments, because I'm not going to be here long, and life can be so beautiful and so painful. Because we have an afterlife, I can enjoy the time I have and also get over whatever bad thing I'm going through. The fact that there's a hell and a heaven really helps me navigate things — for example, the genocide in Gaza. One of the things that's helped me navigate it is knowing there is a hell for people committing this genocide, and the victims will have their justice, in this life and the next. The concept of martyrdom helps reconcile the feeling of helplessness we have, being so far away, unable to do much — I'm involved in advocacy for Palestine, but you can make all the effort in the world, and if the people in power don't listen or care, it won't happen in the time you want. It helps me to think that the moment their blood touches the ground, they're transported into the feeling of heaven, they see what heaven is like, they have their justice in the grave and will have it in the afterlife, and the people committing this will be punished for it. It really helps with the whole justice of it.

question: HOW DO YOU MAKE SENSE OF WHAT IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL?
answer: I have a lot of trouble with that, because I do love control, but I try to tell myself that everything is beyond my control, in a good way — that I just have to learn to let go, that the only thing I can control is myself, and I will do my best, and what happens, happens. You just have to believe that God truly loves you and will take care of you — you have to hold that belief and try to let go, and that's a lot easier said than done. I still struggle to implement it in my life.

question: WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR PRACTICING YOUR RELIGION IN THE LONG RUN?
answer: I really hope the laws are reversed, and that we can openly (practice) — because where it's going in Quebec, they're trying to erase Muslim women, to erase religion from the public eye. I feel nervous, and I really hope it doesn't get as far as it has in France, because I know that's their goal, as they say very openly.

question: HOW DO YOU UNDERSTAND LAÏCITÉ, AND HOW DOES IT AFFECT YOU?
answer: I do believe in laïcité, just not the way it's done in Quebec — the way it's done in the rest of Canada. I think it's good to separate religion from the state, but the laïcité present in Quebec is what we call, in the rest of Canada, "une laïcité ouverte," an open secularism, where the state and the church are separated but people are free to practice however they want, or not practice at all. The closed secularism, "laïcité fermée," seen in Quebec, is based on discrimination and Islamophobia, because the entire media discourse around why we should adopt secularism only ever talks about Muslims and Muslim women — it's discriminatory, it's really bad for society, because outside of discriminating against Muslim women, it also removes religion from education. There's a curriculum reform too — we used to have a program called Éthique et culture religieuse, ethics and religious cultures, which taught us about different religions, gave us the basics, let us know other religions and other people aren't evil. That's been changed to Culture et citoyenneté québécoise. Taking that away really takes away the knowledge part, because now, especially in regions without many Muslims, all people know about Islam is what they see on TV — that we're oppressive, terrorists, basically Orientalist views. I see this type of secularism as really bad, but otherwise I love the concept of open secularism we have in the rest of the provinces in Canada.

question: WHAT IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR HEART, INTENTION, AND OUTWARD PRACTICE?
answer: I try to connect with God while I do these practices. Sometimes it's not very easy or obvious, but when it does work, when I do feel a connection with God as I'm doing an act of worship, I feel very good inside, like my soul is elevating. (My intention is) to worship God, so it helps inwardly — when you change your intention towards anything, even something worldly like work, if you do it with the intention to worship Allah, worldly things won't affect you as much, because your intention has changed, and barakah comes out of it.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer: Submitting to His will, to whatever happens — that is what happened, it's out of my control. This is primarily what I struggle with, accepting the lack of control, so submitting to Allah, to me, means releasing control, letting go, learning to let go a little. It's kind of like the secular idea of manifestation, leaving it to the universe, except I'm leaving it to God.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer: I think none of us will be liberated until all of us are liberated — from all the systems of domination, imperialism, patriarchy, capitalism, white supremacy. Until we're collectively liberated, we won't be liberated individually. In the meantime, until that happens, inshallah, detaching from the world helps you feel liberated. It's a mix of the two — individually trying to detach from worldly possessions and material things, while at the same time seeking a collective liberation from the systems of social domination.

question: DO YOU FEEL OPPRESSED BY THE STATE?
answer: Yes, they are (oppressive). The laws take away from Muslims, not just from people who wear religious signs — they take away choices in life, the ability to participate in society, to have a job. They take our rights away, so by definition it's oppressive. And paired with the media discourse, it leads to a dehumanization that's also oppressive — it's not just the government or the laws, but the discourse around them that allows these laws to be adopted, and that's dehumanizing and oppressive too.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer:
I'll do during the school year. Usually I get up, get ready, and I have a work shift — I usually work at a Muslim summer camp, and right now it's a summer camp, but during the year it's a school, so I usually have a two- or three-hour shift there, and then I go to my university classes at [UNIVERSITY 1]. I come home, do homework, chores, things like that, and go to sleep.

During my prayer — my five daily prayers, that's how I start my day, that's how I end it, and it comes up throughout the day too. At work, of course, I teach Quran, so that's religious as well. Conversations with friends — I'd say in every aspect of my life, what I'm eating, what I'm doing, it shows up everywhere. It influences my career decisions too, what I want to study.

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer:
I think for someone who has never met a Muslim, I would say everything we do revolves around intent. Being Muslim first and foremost means someone who has submitted their will to God, so whatever we're trying to do, it's for the will of God. If I were to go more into our religious beliefs, I'd say it revolves around being conscious of the fact that there is one Creator watching what we're doing.

I would say we're a very closely-knit community — family matters a lot, the community matters a lot, making sure we're helping each other out. Charity projects are very common, and looking out for the vulnerable — we volunteer at women's shelters a lot, homeless shelters a lot. It's something that's definitely very important, looking out for one another and making sure no one's in need. One other thing that's quite important to us is that our morals are reflected within our communities — if we think an action isn't aligned with our morals, correcting it is also important.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer: I was born and raised in [CITY 1], I've lived here my whole life. How has it changed over time — I would say more or less it has stayed the same. I went to a hyper-Christian school ([PROTESTANT DENOMINATION]), and that made me very vigilant of my identity, so it's something I had to decide and settle early on in life. I don't think it changed much from there. Trying to think of anything that could have evolved — I'd say one thing is that I became a bit more shy over the years, I think I was more outspoken when I was younger.

question: HOW DOES LIVING HERE SHAPE HOW YOU PRACTICE OR SHOW YOUR FAITH?
answer:
I think it made me practice more vigilantly, because especially at the Christian school I felt like I was the only one — the only Muslim, the only hijabi — so I felt the need to show a good example. If I was about to do something disrespectful, or that didn't align with my values — say I'm at the metro and my classmates are there and I forget my [TRANSIT CARD], even though it's relatively common for someone to jump over the bars, I wouldn't do that, with the only fear being that people are watching and might blame all Muslims for what I'm doing. That was constantly in my head, because I was always afraid that if I did something, they'd equate it to all Muslims, which I've seen happen. So I was super vigilant of the fact that I was the only one, that I needed to showcase my religion properly — I always felt that pressure.

I became hijabi when I was eleven years old, and I was at that school until I was fifteen — my elementary and high school were the same school, so around grade six. In school, yes — I never had any particularly disrespectful incidents. Maybe later on, in the last years of high school, we had a few teachers change, so it got a bit more difficult, but in the first year I was wearing it I was very comfortable. I remember my teachers complimented me a lot, because it's also part of their faith, and even though they don't always follow it, they recognized that, and praised me for it. My first years, when I was eleven, twelve, thirteen, it was okay, I didn't face any discrimination — that came later, but by then I was very proud of my identity, so it didn't affect me mentally, I'd say — emotionally, maybe.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, AND HOW?
answer: Yes, I do a lot of self-study — whatever I learn at the mosque, if there are any halaqas or religious gatherings. I think the biggest source these days is YouTube, any courses you can find online — I can name some scholars if that would be helpful, some of the most famous ones, almost like influencers, they have long series on YouTube on specific surahs, for example. I think that would be my main source — reading Quran and listening to prominent scholars online.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
So this is kind of unconventional, but I'm from Pakistan, and in Pakistan it's common to wear — not on your head, but a shawl on your shoulders. I remember in elementary school, before I started wearing hijab, I went to Pakistan and saw everyone wearing it, so I started wearing a shawl around my neck or shoulders. But at school we had a strict uniform and weren't allowed to wear shawls, and I did not feel comfortable at all without it, because I was so used to having something on my chest. I didn't cover my hair at the time, but I did not feel comfortable without my shawl, and they told me to take it off because it wasn't part of the uniform. However, I remember on the agenda — they'd give us a lot of pamphlets on rules — there was a line that said you cannot add anything to the uniform unless it's for religious obligations. So I actually took my shawl and put it around my head, because then I'd be able to cover my chest.

It was something different to them, and I had no familial influence either — no one at school, no family influence — I just didn't want to be without my shawl, so I decided to do it. That's how I started wearing it — at first only at school, because I wasn't allowed to wear my shawl otherwise, so I'd drape it over my head and cover my shoulders that way. Then slowly, as I started researching more about Islam, I became more and more attached to it, so within two years I started wearing it full-time.

I think the most important part is that it sets certain boundaries for whoever meets me. I'm happy that without even meeting who I am, someone can tell I'm Muslim, and there are boundaries they'll keep. For example, if I'm about to buy something that has gelatin in it, I've had experiences where the cashier will stop me and say, hey, just so you know, this has gelatin, are you comfortable with it? There are so many examples where someone identifying you as Muslim really helps. Another example I really appreciate is that if I see another hijabi woman on the street, she'll always smile and say salaam, and that can really make your day — you could be feeling really down, but if someone smiles and says salaam, it lifts your mood. That's how I feel, personally.

Definitely being recognized as such. I also think sometimes someone will come up to you for help just seeing that you're wearing hijab, so there's some sort of bond. At university, at college especially, that's the first way I'll make friends, or people will be friends with me — they see my hijab and they see what values I have, and in friendships it's very important to know where your values align. Maybe the most important point is also that it's a constant reminder to me of who I am, what my values are. I remember in middle school, grade seven, grade eight, we'd have picture day, and I'd see everyone with their hair out, someone would dye their hair or make new braids for it, and I'd think, oh, I wish I could do that too — but then I'd remember, hey, I don't come to school for this reason, I'm not here to show off, and I'm also not in this dunya to show off. I come to school to study, and I'm in this dunya to pass a specific test. So it was a constant reminder of why I'm here, and that's the most important part — it's a reminder of who I am, and a reminder to others of who I am too, and I think that's what it says in the Quran.

question: HAS WEARING HIJAB CREATED BARRIERS IN EDUCATION OR EMPLOYMENT?
answer:
Well, this story is from about ten years ago, when I was in high school, so I don't know if they've had to change it now — it was also a private school, so I don't think the same legislation applies, so of course it's very different. I do worry, though, that if they continue making these regulations stricter and stricter, about my younger sister, for example — she's in elementary right now, in public school, so I do worry about what changes might come. But I'm happy in the sense that that one line made the whole difference for me — the fact that I could wear a certain symbol if it was religious, giving that permission really changed my life, a very important aspect of it. I'd say it was such an important part of my journey, and the fact that others might not have it — my sister might not have that same encouragement, that you're allowed to wear what you want for religious reasons — it's concerning.

Well, they don't apply in public schools, not that I'm aware of — they don't apply to students, they apply to teachers. But the way it's been going, it's getting stricter, so it is concerning that something like that could happen to my sister, for the teachers, the workers. Yes, to school, yes, but not as an employee. The rule is that if you got a job in the last two years, you're not allowed to wear your hijab in public institutions — court, the police force, schools, government positions — but if you've been working for more than two years, they're not forcing you to take it off. I have heard of stories where both happen — employees who've been wearing hijab for more than two years, working at a specific institution for more than two years, and still had to take it off because of pressure. But I've also heard stories where they let it go — my mother, for example, works in a school, she's been working for less than two years, and even though she was initially given an email saying no religious symbols would be allowed after a certain date in March, no one forced her to take it off, she was just sent an email. So I've heard both sides of the story. But one thing I'd say for sure, it's definitely becoming harder for Muslim women to get jobs. I got a teaching job at a Muslim school, so of course they weren't going to tell me to take it off, but I've had friends who've applied for jobs and found it harder to get hired — not necessarily because the employer or HR is racist, but because they're concerned, they see these laws being passed, don't know what's going to happen, so they don't hire you.

Yes, (my mother is) working in a public school. It shouldn't be (up to the school) — the government wouldn't want that, the government would want its rules followed, but I feel like they haven't come up with anything to enforce it yet. Personally, my mother has a good relationship with the school, she's done a lot for it, she's close with the administration, and she knows they would never ask her to take it off.

question: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN OR HIJAB?
answer:
Oh yeah, for sure — I've had a lot of instances where people assume certain things, like that I'm oppressed in some way, or being forced to wear it. I've had this conversation with many people — my family never influenced me in any shape or form to wear it. My mother wears it now, but when I started wearing it, she wasn't. That's one thing people assume, that I was forced. Another thing people assume is that we wear it to not attract attention from the opposite gender, that they think that's the sole reason we put it on — so I've explained the misunderstanding around that, what I believe are the nuances behind wearing hijab, my own perspective.

Yes, I can give examples. One other thing I'd say is that people assume I'm Arab — I'm from South Asia, from Pakistan, but it's very common for all hijabis to be considered Arab. Perhaps another misconception.

A specific example, yes, definitely, about the part where they assume you're forced to wear it. I remember I was in a friend group and I showed them a picture of my parents — we were somewhere, I was wearing hijab, my mother wasn't, and someone said, oh, she tells you to wear it but she doesn't wear it herself, and I said, no, no one told me to wear it. They were very shocked. I think that's really changing now — a lot more people, I feel, because of all the emerging hijabi influencers online, are starting to realize not everyone is forced to wear it. Social media is really helping with that — it wasn't the same five years ago.

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer: It was an interview for a specific program — you have to pass several stages, examinations, grades, and so on, so getting to the interview level was very difficult, with CV checks and all that, and then I did not clear the interview. That was very difficult for me, because I really felt like I had spent the last four years of my life just preparing for this moment. I think in general I'm just not very adept at interviews. How did I come out of it? Well, religion plays a role in all my decisions, so I held on to the fact that things in life might not always go as you plan, but Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala always has a better plan — if He closes one door, He'll open another. One thing I really believe is that sometimes you want something really badly, but it's just not good for you, and you might not see why. Holding on to that belief, and reciting Quran — that's such an important part of my life, reciting it again and again really calms me down — those two things really helped. And alhamdulillah, two years later, I did realize that program just wasn't right for me, and I'm happy now, alhamdulillah.

question: WHAT INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS ARE PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
Internal expectations, yeah, definitely — expectations revolving around family, family values, are placed on us in the Muslim community. Having children, having a family, I think that's an expectation placed on women. Other expectations — especially regarding hijab, maybe it's more of an issue with the younger community, but you're expected not to mess up, not to make the mistakes everyone makes, lying for example. But again, with knowledge, with social media, it's changing.

I do think so, yes — they expect us to be a certain way too. I had a conversation once where someone said, oh, you have a very bubbly personality, you're very loud, and I said, oh, okay, and she said, because I always expect a woman to be quieter and things like that. I don't know where she got that from. So there are stereotypes about Muslim women, both within the community and from outside it — people expect us to be a certain way, but it hasn't impacted me in any significant way, I'd say.

Have I resolved internal expectations? I don't know if I'd say I've resolved any. External expectations, it's kind of easier, because you can explain to them what's halal and haram, what we have to do and what we don't, so if they think you're supposed to be a certain way, you can say, no, this is what I believe. But you can't always say that to another Muslim, because they're part of your religion too, so you'd think they'd already know.

Like I said, I don't think they've impacted me, so I wouldn't say it's something I have to resolve — any expectation someone has on me, I have my own expectations for myself, and the expectations my family has, that's what matters to me. I have to follow the Quran and Sunnah to the best of my ability — after my religion, my family comes first, so it's about pleasing them, I wouldn't care much what the wider community has to say.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer: My parents, definitely, my mom and dad. Before taking any decision, I would ask them for permission — if it's a job offer, for example, I would consult them before taking academic decisions too, so just consulting them before any major decision, that's the main way it impacts things. And of course, if they encourage me to try something, they've never been forbidding or forcing about anything, but I would still ask them for permission and consult them first.

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer: My role in my family — well, I'm the eldest child, so I do take it upon myself to set the example. In my community, as an Islamic school teacher, there are certain responsibilities I have, setting a good example, following the rules within the religion, setting the right values for the children I teach. It varies — I've been a tutor for a long time, but at the specific school I'm teaching at, I taught math and science to the higher grades and Quran to the lower grades.

question: WHAT DOES BELONGING FEEL LIKE HERE?
answer: What does it mean to belong to Quebec — I guess it would raise the question, do I feel like I belong to Quebec? No. I think my values are different from Quebec's, even though I grew up here. Given all the rules and regulations, and now they're even banning halal food in schools, it's clear that they don't want someone like me here, but I don't have a choice — I grew up here, so it's my home, they're going to have to put up with me. But I would not say I belong in Quebec.

question: DO YOU FEEL YOU BELONG HERE — ARE YOU SEEN AS FRENCH/QUEBECOIS?
answer:
At (university), I was just walking around campus one day and someone visiting said, oh, I moved recently into this neighborhood, and I was just seeing the place as a university campus. I said, yes, it's a university campus, here's the main building, here's this — it was near the biology center building, and they were asking me what the buildings were. Then we crossed [ISLAMIC STUDIES LIBRARY], and I said, oh, this is [ISLAMIC STUDIES LIBRARY], there's a really cool quiet study room here if you ever need a quiet place to read. My focus was on the buildings themselves, but then they started asking me questions like, how is this allowed, how is an Islamic studies library allowed? I started explaining a bit of the history behind having one, that there was nothing like it before.

The person was Quebecois, not Muslim. I was wearing hijab. We were just talking about the buildings and directions until I mentioned [ISLAMIC STUDIES LIBRARY], and then he became visibly upset about why there's an Islamic studies library, and it led to, oh, I don't even know how you're allowed to wear hijab on campus, it's not allowed in France. And I said, but we're not in France, we're in Quebec. I could tell he wasn't happy about me wearing it — he said, you can do it at home. And I said, I should have the choice of what I want to wear outside and inside my home. Incidents like these — they're not numerous, maybe around five or seven in my life — but they make me realize that Quebecers don't want me here, personally, they don't want me to wear the hijab, they don't want me to be me.

question: IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR FAITH AND QUEBEC STRAINED?
answer: The relationship is strained. It's not that they don't give us religious freedom — there is religious freedom, they just want us to keep it indoors, and to a certain degree I'd say they have the right to say that. For example, I think it would be wrong of us to say, we want to give the adhan loudly in the neighborhoods — that might disturb them, so that's understandable. But then there are things that to me aren't understandable, like why that man had a problem with me covering my hair on a university campus — it's not hurting him, it shouldn't be disturbing him in any way. So yes, the relationship is strained, but I wouldn't say the relationship between my faith and the province is strained — it's more the relationship of me showing my faith and the province that's strained, or tense.

question: HOW AND WHERE ARE YOU ABLE TO PRAY DURING YOUR DAY?
answer:
Yes. However, before, they've always let us pray — we have a prayer room, it was amazing, and they let us rent out a bigger room for Jumu'ah on Fridays. However, recently the government has tried to close down our prayer room, I think twice during the semester, and more times at other universities I've heard of. At our prayer room specifically, news reporters tried to come in and ask us questions about whether it was closing or not, and there was talk of it happening, to which the MSA, the Muslim Student Association at my university, said they'd hire lawyers if need be. There's been talk of it closing, but I haven't had any experience where I wasn't allowed to pray in the prayer room.

Not the university — the Muslim Student Association, we have our own student groups within the university. I don't think [UNIVERSITY 1] itself would hire lawyers to fight our case, it would be the MSA or [STUDENT SOCIETY 1], the student society, the group that represents students, not the university itself. There have been discussions, but I'm not part of the administration segment of the MSA — there's a hierarchy within it, and I'm not part of those who communicate with the university, but I know they've had talks, I don't know what came of it. I think [UNIVERSITY 1], universities in general, the Muslim population is so large that they won't be successful in shutting it down — people would really pull together resources and get lawyers. But the case for smaller colleges and CEGEPs, which in Quebec are the two years after high school before university, is harder.

In CEGEP it's harder, especially for smaller CEGEPs. The CEGEP I went to, [CEGEP 1], there were very few Muslim students, and we had a very small room to begin with — maximum six people could fit, for a student population of maybe fifty to seventy Muslim students. It wasn't called the Muslim prayer room, it was just called the prayer room, and we had Bibles, Torahs, all religious texts, prayer mats, Catholic rosary beads, and the misbaha that Muslims have too — we had everything, though people from other religions rarely came, I saw Christians there maybe twice in the two years I spent there. What happened was that it was called the multi-faith room, but then they changed the name to the meditation room, because there could no longer be symbols of any religion — that's the law from Quebec, you cannot show religion openly. It wasn't successful at [UNIVERSITY 1], I think because of the huge population there, but at [CEGEP 1] they tried to get it shut down and weren't successful, so instead you can pray in it, but you have to keep all the symbols away — you use the mat, but have to put it away in boxes on shelves. The religious books also have to be kept covered, they can't be on display, and the same goes for the rosary and the tasbih.

Yeah, actually, before I came to the college we had a larger room, and then they shifted us a few years later. The MSA tried to contest it, but we were unsuccessful. You could see there was a need, because we would line up outside before prayer time — in the winter especially there were long lines, so you can't say there wasn't a need. But we were still very thankful for the small space we had, because we knew that in French colleges and universities — the ones I've attended were English — there is no prayer room at all, and you're not allowed to have a Muslim Student Association.

[UNIVERSITY 3], [UNIVERSITY 4] — they don't have an MSA either. But [UNIVERSITY 2], [UNIVERSITY 1], [CEGEP 1], [CEGEP 2], [CEGEP 3] all have prayer rooms. I don't know exactly why, but I can tell you for certain it's not because Muslims aren't trying — I have friends at [UNIVERSITY 3] who tried to get a prayer room and were unsuccessful. I don't know if it's because they're more Quebecois than the English colleges — I can't give you a certain reason. The student life animators had the keys to the prayer room, and they were enforcing the fact that everything was hidden.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: Kind of tying back to what I said before, I live with intent. So if I have free time, I will try to do something productive, something that will help with my akhirah. If I feel like anything I do might negatively impact my akhirah, I think about that. It influences what I do, what I say, what I watch, what kind of friendships I make.

question: HOW DO YOU MAKE SENSE OF WHAT IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL?
answer: Just like what I said about the interview — to me, it's always beyond my control, Allah is in control, He's the one who plans everything, so it'll work out for me in the end. If I can't change it, I'm not going to stress about it.

question: WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR PRACTICING YOUR RELIGION IN THE LONG RUN?
answer: Well, of course, for me it's being able to show my identity. I know I might be very comfortable with mine, but it's not the same for the younger generation growing up in public schools, hearing things like, oh, yesterday government officials couldn't wear hijab, today it's educators who can't wear it anymore. I'm definitely worried about my own career too — I don't envision myself working as a teacher my whole life, I'm working part-time as a student teacher, but I wanted to go into healthcare, and slowly they're enforcing the same rule there, that you can't wear hijab anywhere in the public sector, so I'd be confined to the private sector, which is concerning. But the biggest thing is not being able to show it — for prayer, for example, I think I'd find a way to do it. That's one of the arguments that came up when there was talk of closing our prayer room — people said, we'll just pray under stairwells like we did before there was a prayer room, it's not going to stop us. But wearing hijab, that's going to directly stop me from a career in the public sector. Even then, I have a choice, I can work in the private sector, private clinics for example. But I worry about future generations, because they might not have the same confidence I did, they might not be able to make that decision for themselves.

question: HOW DO YOU UNDERSTAND LAÏCITÉ, AND HOW DOES IT AFFECT YOU?
answer: It's definitely a barrier, I would say, because of this value — I don't know if I'd call it a value exactly, but this idea that's very prominent in Quebec culture, it's a word we hear all the time. It means keeping your beliefs private, not showing them in any shape, way, or form.

question: HAVE SPECIFIC LAWS (BILL 21, BILL 94, BILL 9, ETC.) PERSONALLY AFFECTED YOU?
answer: Just one incident, where a woman said, oh, soon, in the metro, soon you won't be allowed to wear it. Other than that, it hasn't impacted my career or education or anything. It was very random — I submitted this as a report to [MUSLIM ADVOCACY ORGANIZATION 1] as well. She was preaching, had a Bible in her hand — sometimes there are preachers in the metro. I was trying to ignore her as best I could, but then she started yelling "Allah, Allah" at the top of her lungs, and the metro was packed, so everyone was looking at us, and then she said things like, pretty soon you won't be allowed to wear it, and, are you jealous of me because I don't have to wear it, and, if you want to wear it, go back to where you came from — things like that.

question: DO YOU FEEL OPPRESSED BY THE STATE?
answer: Oppression is taking away someone's power, and I don't think they're able to do that — I think oppressed is a strong word, I wouldn't say oppressed, but it does affect our quality of living, definitely, taking away some of our freedoms. But not oppression, I wouldn't say it oppresses us.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer: Submission to Allah means accepting whatever comes your way, not questioning it, not saying why, why me, why did this happen to me — accepting His rules and His commands.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer: It kind of depends what sense you mean, but in general — being free to practice your beliefs, not being constrained by other people's values or beliefs. Yes, I do feel liberated.

question: CAN SOMEONE REPORT YOU FOR WEARING HIJAB IN QUEBEC?
answer: Workplaces can — public schools, but I'm not working in a public school. Universities, as a student, no — we have full liberty to wear it as students, it's just as workers in the public sector. Someone could report it to HR, but I don't think there's anything they could do to report you to the government, for example, to get a government fine — I think that's the case in France, but not here.

question: ORDINARY DAY AND WHERE FAITH SHOWS UP
answer: At the moment I am in summer school and I'm also working, and I have a roommate who's also a hijabi Muslim woman like myself. Usually I'll wake up around 5:30 — sometimes I'll miss Fajr, but I do my best to pray on time most days. I take Arabic classes with a teacher in Egypt, so I have my classes usually at six for an hour, and then either I'll go to work or have class. Depending on where I'm going, I dress a little differently — I've been trying to wear abayas every day when I can, but sometimes I'm not so confident, so I sort of base what I'm wearing on where I'm working that day. Right now I just finished a contract job as an educator, in a reading intervention program for children with autism and ADHD. On days I have class, I'll go to class and then study afterwards, come home, make dinner, pray, call my parents, and then I'll usually scroll or text my friends until it's time to go to bed.

question: HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOURSELF AND YOUR COMMUNITY?
answer:
I feel like a lot of existing as a Muslim woman is really hard to put into words, because I find myself trying to prove myself to my own Muslim community and also to non-Muslims a lot of the time. I would describe myself as a student before anything, and I find that to be a very important part of my faith too — my studies, and trying to establish myself academically so I can build a career for myself that is halal and represents my values. I'm a very ambitious person, and my friends would say I'm someone who wants to change the world — I don't think that's necessarily how I see my day-to-day character, but I find that as I've gotten older, I've become a lot more insecure and struggled a lot more with my long-term goals because of the hijab and because of living in Quebec. In recent years I've also been really involved in activism around the various wars and genocides that have been taking place against Muslims globally, and that's really shaped my identity — it's the first thing I want to talk about if I get to decide where a conversation goes, and I think a lot of people associate me with that. When they get to know me, they usually get to know me based on what I'm studying and my work, which I always politicize very heavily. I think it's hard to balance being feminine and soft, the way I feel my culture often expects me to be, and also being a powerful, ambitious woman, the way I feel is often expected in the West. I don't even know where I fall on that spectrum, because it changes so much based on who I'm around and what I'm doing. But when it comes down to it, I'd say I'm just a student.

Well, I'm Arab, and I'm not necessarily speaking to the Muslim community as a whole, but within Arab culture there's a very strong expectation for women to be soft-spoken, patient, nurturing — expectations of a certain way of carrying myself that are a lot more passive, I guess, whereas in the West there isn't necessarily that same framing of how women should be, there aren't the same social scripts for women. But I'll give so much credit to my culture for the weight it gives to education, to educating yourself and equipping yourself to be productive in society and give back to your community — I don't see that as much here, and that's something I value so much as a person. I see that as the most central thing to myself, wanting to give back to my community and wanting to be educated in order to do that.

I think that we're very collectivist, which people here aren't super familiar with — we care a lot about appearance and how we treat and appear to others, more than we necessarily care about personal successes in career, etc., and we're the most generous and hospitable people ever. I think if more people got to know my community — I'm Palestinian, and I just think there's so much hate going around, assumptions about what a Palestinian is. Of course there are so many different people in every society and culture, but across the board I haven't met a Palestinian who isn't so excited to share their food and share what they have with others. So I would say we're generous.

question: HOW HAS YOUR SENSE OF YOURSELF AS A MUSLIM WOMAN CHANGED OVER TIME?
answer: I've lived here my whole life. My family is in Palestine, but I've grown up here — I used to visit them regularly, up until the war started; in 2023 I'd visited maybe five or six times before then. I'd say the hijab definitely changed me a lot, because it changed how other people treated me, which in turn changed the way I behaved. When I was younger, I used to do a lot of sports, I wanted to go to the Olympics, and then I wanted to be an actor — my family never pressured religion onto me at all, although there are people in my family who are very, very practicing, much more strict in their religion than I am, but it was never forced on me in any way. My brother is very different from me, we went in kind of opposite directions. But as I got older and became more religious on my own, I became a lot more intentional in what I do, more selective about who I spend time with and the hobbies and things I invest myself in, so my goals became a lot more focused. I went from wanting to change the world on a really big scale to wanting to help individual people a lot more, and I went into education and working with children because I see that as a really practical way of helping people. I think also naturally, for any woman, once we hit our teenage years we get really insecure, and that shaped me a lot too. Also, just living in Quebec in the past couple of years, I've had a lot of Islamophobic encounters that have really changed the way I behave and see others — now my assumption when I'm meeting people, when I'm out in public, is that people are hostile towards me before they do anything, and that will only change if I have a positive encounter with them, whereas when I was younger I'd always assume the best in others. But I think I've also just become a lot smarter.

question: HOW DOES LIVING HERE SHAPE HOW YOU PRACTICE OR SHOW YOUR FAITH?
answer:
It's really blatant in some ways — there are laws that prevent me from practicing my faith to a degree. I'm a student, and this coming fall, Bill 9 is about to shut down all the prayer rooms on university campuses, so that's going to be really major in terms of how I structure my days at school as a practicing Muslim who needs somewhere to pray on campus. But I think it's also really inhibited me in other ways — I wanted to wear hijab long before I actually did, because I was really nervous about how people would treat me. And even now, I feel like I could easily wear abayas every day, but depending on where I'm going I might not be totally safe like that, and I've had interactions that have proven it to me, so I definitely don't feel great. Even though living downtown, in [CITY 1], is pretty manageable because there's a lot of diversity, there are still a lot of hateful people, and I don't think there's much accountability when they act on that hate. It leaves a lot of us feeling very scared.

I don't know specifically about francophone universities, because I don't go to them, but I do know that, for example, [UNIVERSITY 2] does not have a prayer room. [UNIVERSITY 1], which is where I go, we have one of the oldest Muslim student associations. We have a massive prayer room on both of our campuses, and they also organize Jumu'ah prayers every Friday, and all of these things are being shut down. Bill 9 is basically calling for no more religious spaces on campuses, but there are exceptions for heritage sites — there's a chapel on one of our campuses that's still allowed to operate as a chapel, and the irony of that is not lost on a lot of us. These spaces are very used, people love them and rely on them, and I think it's pretty clear to see, even if it's not written directly, that these laws are intending to target Muslims disproportionately. There's also new legislation now around street prayers and prayers in public, which also has a lot to do with the protests that were happening against the genocide in Palestine, and the fact that there were prayers taking place at those protests, which pissed a lot of people off.

question: HAS WEARING HIJAB CREATED BARRIERS IN EDUCATION OR EMPLOYMENT?
answer:
Muslim women, I feel like we gravitate towards careers in education — I'm not a sociologist, but I see a trend, there are a lot of Muslim women in my program and in this field generally. I feel really disappointed, because the laws here now are saying that no one can wear religious symbols even into schools — even if they're a parent volunteering on a field trip, even a janitor, even a tutor representing the school from their own home, they cannot wear religious symbols. You cannot work in a public school or a subsidized private school with a hijab. And you need certain experience — childcare is one of those careers where you can have a great CV, but if you don't have substantial experience with children, you're not going to get very far, and a lot of the time that means doing a practicum during your university studies, but it also means students who've been working with kids throughout their university career are at a huge advantage once they graduate, compared to those who haven't. I think it's really disadvantaging many students. I was really lucky to get an internship at a private daycare, but it's been really complicated, and I've been speaking with and advocating for other students at my university who need to do their internships and weren't sure where to go. It ended up falling on our department chairs to coordinate exceptions, getting them into private daycares or schools, rather than the university itself. I think that's really disappointing, and it really shows that even if our university claims not to support these bills, we're not really welcome in these programs anymore, which is super sad.

From my understanding, complaints can be made to the government by basically anyone, and that could result in a fine on the institution and likely the termination of that teacher. Other times the institution just won't be comfortable taking that risk, so they'll fire the teacher outright, or won't hire them, or they'll share the government's politics in believing it's a detriment to students' education. We've been in conversations with our university administration since December of last year, asking for details on how they're going to enforce this, and they haven't given us any meaningful response, despite meeting with them almost five times, repeatedly asking, repeatedly going into meetings — we've just been told, oh, we don't know yet. And now these bills are allegedly going to be enforced next month, and there's still no details, so I'm feeling worried and disappointed about that. I don't think our university is planning to sanction students for praying, but if a complaint is made, they're not going to want to pay a fine, so they might have to take action. Nine and 94 are the ones I'm familiar with.

question: HAVE YOU EXPERIENCED HOSTILITY FOR BEING VISIBLY MUSLIM?
answer:
I've had people spit at me, I've had people call me a pedophile-worshipper randomly — at one point I was just walking down the street near my house and a man passed me and spat at my feet and said something under his breath. I've had people come at me on the metro, always a man — I had a man corner me and swear at me for three stops straight, getting really close to me, and it was a full metro and nobody did anything, and that reinforced my fear of going out, because I felt like no one was going to protect me if something violent happened. I've also had kids I've worked with say things that have been really disappointing, because I know they're hearing it from somewhere — I had an eleven-year-old with autism last week look at me and say, "I hate Muslims, especially Pakis," and I asked him, do you know that's a slur, do you know what it means, do you know that I'm Muslim? This kid had no idea, it's just something they heard someone say and are repeating, and if they're not given the opportunity to have Muslim educators or interact with Muslims, that's just going to be what they carry with them until they're adults, and that's how they'll treat people. It's beyond disappointing.

In other circumstances I've gone into a daycare for the first time and a toddler will run up to me for a hug, and the manager says, oh, her mom wears the hijab, or another kid will come up and say, I like your hijab, my mommy wears it too — that gives me so much joy, knowing there's that representation, but it's also heartbreaking that it's about to be taken away from so many of these kids, and they're undoubtedly going to have classmates whose parents have told them things. It's not just affecting educators and their careers, it's also affecting Muslim kids. A lot of times it's just a look someone gives you — I think we're all aware enough to know when a look is a look of disgust, just based on what you're wearing.

question: DO YOU SEEK RELIGIOUS KNOWLEDGE, AND HOW?
answer: Yeah, I try to. I don't feel super proud of myself recently, I've kind of let that go, but I used to do halaqas at the masjid I go to, and I have some apps I follow for sort of Duolingo-style Islamic lessons. Also, in my Arabic classes, I see that as a big part of improving my ability to read Quran, because I grew up here, my Arabic isn't as strong as some of the rest of my family. And I just love talking about my deen with my friends and people I come across.

question: HOW DID YOU COME TO WEAR HIJAB, AND WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO YOU?
answer:
I never had any pressure from my family. I wanted to for a long time, but I ended up putting it on only a couple of years ago — I was in university when I did. Funny enough, it was quite spontaneous — I was having a bad hair day, feeling really overstimulated by my hair kept getting in my face, and I was complaining about it to my friend, and she said, well, we're going to have to go pray anyway, let's go to the mosque at school, and why don't you just keep your hijab on afterwards — no one's going to see us, it's a Saturday on campus, I know you've been wanting to, so it's a good opportunity. So I put it on, and as we were leaving the musalla I ran into about twenty of my friends, and everyone was so excited and happy for me that I felt like, okay, I can't bail now, I've locked in — everyone was giving me hugs, being so excited and proud of me. That was the part I was most scared about, people's initial reactions, and I think that's what held me back for years, fear that people I was friends with might not see me the same way — so when I had that major reassurance, it helped me a lot. I just kept wearing it after that. My same friend, bless her, she's been an amazing support to me — she texted me that night and said, okay, I'm going to pick you up at your house for school tomorrow, you better be wearing the hijab when I get there. She helped a lot, because my parents live in a different city.

It makes me a lot more intentional about what I choose to do and how I choose to speak to people. I think it really encourages me to be a smarter person. I feel like there are bigger consequences to my actions and my words. It's weird, I feel this balance — I've said I feel unsafe in many ways here, but I also feel safe in the sense that I notice how it changes the way negative people avoid me, and also the increase in respect I've gotten from certain people within my community.

And my ability to enter certain spaces, to move more freely in certain political spaces because of my hijab, especially as a Palestinian — I think there's a certain ability to move and speak and do things when you're representing yourself as a Muslim woman that you lose without it, especially because I'm quite white-passing. I also just feel really proud of it. There are some days, even two years later — almost three, actually three years in a month — where I'm just sitting minding my business and I remember, oh my god, I can't believe I did that, that's awesome, because I struggled with it for years. When I remember that I'm just wearing it and not thinking about it anymore, I get so happy. It brings me a lot of pride, and I think it's unparalleled how good it feels when someone says salam to you on the street — that feels so good. I like that other Muslims recognize me as a safe space, someone who is understanding and there for them even if we don't know each other. I've never seen a Muslim sister and had a bad vibe since wearing the hijab, because I feel like we're immediately on the same team, so that's nice.

The best people in the world — if I could live anywhere, I would want to be in Gaza. My friends from Gaza, the people I know there, there's just a way they see the world, a way they measure their actions, that gives me chills. And I put the hijab partly because of the war as well — I felt like nobody knew I was Palestinian until I told them, which is ridiculous. People should look at me and see a Muslim, they should look at me and think, that person has a side in this — I couldn't just be wearing my keffiyeh every day, it needed to be more.

question: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG ABOUT MUSLIM WOMEN OR HIJAB?
answer:
I think a lot of people assume that I had this big family pressure and grew into it, or got over it, but my family is so relaxed about religion, very open to different faiths and lifestyles, and I think that played a big part in how resolute I am now, because I was able to really consider every possibility growing up around the religion. I think also, as a Palestinian, there's a lot of belief about "violent Islam" and a lot of propaganda around that, and people are really surprised to know that my culture values education to such a high degree — we have one of the highest literacy rates in the world, and women are very involved in politics, education, social and community building. That's something that really shocks people. When they find out I'm so deeply connected as an adult with my culture and religion, they don't see it as congruent that I'm also very outspoken politically. I think people sometimes assume I'm hateful in ways I'm really not, based on stereotypes they might have come across. To me, Islam is such a respectful, kind religion, and sometimes people assume the hijab means I dislike certain people — and they're often surprised to know that I'm just Canadian too, living here, part of this community and culture, not carrying around every day being like, I hate this person, I hate that person — no, I'm just minding my business, wearing my hijab.

Yeah, especially working with kids, I see this so much — so many kids say, "but you're forced to wear it, right?" That's the main one I get all the time, people assuming I've been forced into the hijab and resent it deeply, and I often have to say, oh no, I'm so proud of myself, I did this, this is my biggest accomplishment. I think another thing is that a lot of people find it hard to believe a woman would want to dress this way. Our culture is also very different in that people have a hard time understanding family dynamics in Muslim culture — the idea of, well, I wouldn't put up with that from my family, I'd set this boundary or that boundary — that's just not really a concept that exists for me. Family is family, we're not setting boundaries and ultimatums, we're supporting each other, helping each other grow, and accepting each other's differences. But the biggest thing usually comes down to how we dress, because people can tolerate and understand a pretty diverse range of beliefs, but once it becomes visible, they start to feel some type of way about it.

question: HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO WRONG PORTRAYALS OF MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer: A little bit disappointed, depending on how old the person is — if it's a kid, I usually think, oh, this is a great learning opportunity, but when it's coming from someone my age, I think, come on, you've been here long enough, you should have encountered enough Muslim women to know what's actually motivating our decisions. I don't get hurt by it, but I feel tired — genuinely, sometimes I'm just so tired of people being stupid. It doesn't make sense to me how a lot of people don't see the contradiction in claiming to advocate for women's rights, for women's ability to decide things for themselves, while contradicting our ability to decide to wear the hijab or believe certain things. I think that's really embarrassing for those people, and our governments view so much of it the same way — I don't necessarily blame them, but I think people need a little more critical thinking.

question: TELL ME ABOUT A DIFFICULTY AND HOW FAITH HELPED YOU MEET IT
answer:
I really struggled to secure an internship so I could set up my last year of studies. I had to do a lot of networking, speaking to people, sending emails to my department and different daycares, just to set up something I think a lot of other girls in my class get on the first try, just to be able to graduate. That was really hard, because I felt so unwanted the whole time, and I feel like our education system is already not doing great, and it's disappointing that we're pushing away so many educators — the same way we're doing with healthcare workers here. I also think I took a really big risk putting on the hijab, because now, the next time I want to go back to Palestine inshallah, I'm much more endangered by the Israeli military — it's a well-known fact that Muslim women are often targeted with sexual violence and general violence at Israeli checkpoints and when traveling across Palestine.

My parents definitely felt some type of way about my choice to do that, and the risk it was going to put on me. I've done research projects on the hijab in occupied Palestine, why it's worn in some places and not others, and I think it really is a big sacrifice in terms of mobility and rights there. But I haven't had to encounter that directly yet, because I haven't been back since I put it on.

I keep just feeling so shocked, because when you really simplify it, at the end of the day it's just blatant discrimination, blocking certain religious minorities from certain careers — that's really what it is. They can frame it as protecting children from radical religious fanatics, but at the end of the day, I live in a place where, because of my religion, I don't have the right to a certain harmless, in fact very beneficial, job for the community and society as a whole. It just shocks me sometimes — I can't make sense of it, because so much of Canadian culture is based on this idea that we're so free and fair and kind and inclusive, and then I can't get a job because I wear the hijab, and so many people just don't talk about it. I'm talking to my non-Muslim friends, saying, well, I can't work in a school anymore, and their immediate assumption is that I was convicted of some crime — I have to explain, no, the government decided I'm a threat to children, and so many of them have no idea, they say, that can't be right, not in Quebec. Really, yes, that's where we live. I really want to leave, but I also don't want to give them that, because I do feel like that's exactly what this is intended to do. Since my family doesn't live in Quebec, I've heavily considered just moving to another province where I'd have fair opportunities, because this is the career I want, this is what I studied for, and I'm not just going to throw it away because in a certain part of Canada it's not permitted.

I'm proud, because I think it's a good test, a test of my faith, and I certainly would not take off the hijab over something like this. I put it on before this law was even announced — Bill 9, Bill 94, I didn't know they were in the works or going to be enforced. So when I put it on, I still had every reason to believe I was going to graduate and get a job in a school, and when it became clear that wasn't a possibility anymore, I just thought, okay, their loss — it's really frustrating and a lot of extra work, but alhamdulillah for my hijab, because I wouldn't necessarily want to work in a province where I don't have the ability to dress how I want. Maybe I would change my mind later down the road and want to put the hijab on, and I couldn't without losing my job — better to know now than to find out or have it progress later. At least I'm at a stage where I can still plan my career and future. There are many women who've had the rug swept out from under them after twenty years of teaching, and I think that's much more vile than what I'm experiencing. But the hijab is one of the proudest things I've done, and I have no intention, I've never even once considered taking it off because of this — not for a second has that occurred to me, because it's just a ridiculous concept, to take off my hijab because of an Islamophobe. It doesn't do anything for me in that sense. It does make me want to leave, but that's about it.

question: WHAT INTERNAL OR EXTERNAL EXPECTATIONS ARE PLACED ON MUSLIM WOMEN?
answer:
We all have to assess Islamic teachings on our own — there's no forcing a woman to behave a certain way, and I think a lot of that comes from experiencing things and understanding them, whether through speaking to other Muslim women or not. I felt like when I put the hijab on — I used to do a lot of sports, and suddenly that was this amazing outlet, but suddenly there was so much shame, I was so ashamed to be seen playing soccer with my friends, I could not go to the gym.

Within the Muslim community. That said, many Muslim friends of mine are athletes, go to the gym, do these things, but they've also spoken about experiencing this idea that a woman should not be doing that in public, that it's not modest, and I think modesty is such a broad term, really hard to understand — there's not a specific line, it depends so much on the context of where you're doing something, what you're doing it with, who you're doing it with, what your intentions are, and that's so hard to understand as a young person, especially living around one culture where your friends here say this is normal and cool, and the other culture at home says a woman should not do this. I think many of our parents, if they're immigrants, don't necessarily understand the nuance that it's actually not as objectively bad to do something here, because the cultural context is different — for sure it'd be bad if I did it in a city in the West Bank, but here it's really different. I find myself hiding things from different people in my life depending on how I think they'll respond — with some Muslim friends I'll talk about the soccer game I played last week, or the event I went to, and with other friends or family I'll say I was at home studying, or I don't do these things. That takes a really big toll on someone. It causes so much anxiety — especially when you're growing up here and want to fit in, want to have the same experiences as your friends. I don't think it's that effective, what our community tells us, which is often just a flat no or a flat yes. There needs to be more conversation about that gray area, especially being second generation — it's so confusing. I think we assume young girls know what's modest and what's immodest, and I still don't really know.

I think we're expected within the Muslim community to be better representatives of the religion than non-hijabis, so when we do make mistakes, the social consequences are usually bigger. In terms of Canadian culture and the expectations on us, I think it's a lot more just assumptions that we're powerless, not in control of our lives, and I feel a lot of pressure to prove that wrong. I don't think that's necessarily bad, but I think it causes a lot of people to underestimate us and not give us opportunities we deserve.

question: WHO DO YOU FEEL RESPONSIBLE TO, AND HOW DO THOSE BONDS SHAPE YOUR CHOICES?
answer:
My parents. I feel very responsible to not disappoint them, to make sure I set myself up well so they can have a good rest of their lives, especially coming from what they've come from. It's so important to me that what they've gone through has led to an overall good in my life, and alhamdulillah, I really think it has. They've given so much for me, and I hope inshallah I can compensate for that to some degree.

It's hard, because I haven't lived with them for some time while I've been studying, but I call them many times every day, and I run everything by them — decisions about what job I'll take, where I'll live, if I'll sign a lease, if I'll buy a dress, what I'll cook for dinner — I really call them for everything, we're very, very close as a family. My parents really consult with me, they don't make me feel like they're telling me what to do, they guide me through conversations in a way that I feel like I understand the decisions I'm making, and I'm very grateful for that. Long-term, when I think about getting married, I don't want to move far from them, and I don't want to do anything that would disappoint them in a big way — that's always at the back of my mind.

question: WHAT IS YOUR ROLE IN YOUR FAMILY AND COMMUNITY?
answer: I see my role as having to transfer a lot of generational information — I try to speak to my grandmother a lot, she's still in Palestine — and I put a lot of pressure on myself to help my community, sometimes to my own detriment. I sacrifice a lot of myself to protect people, a lot of labor to give them opportunities, and especially since the war, that's been such a huge part of how I live with myself here. Within my family, I see myself as a conflict solver — that's kind of the role I've always had, very much a mediator, the person always talking things out, reconciling situations, trying to make sure everyone's on good terms.

question: WHAT DOES BELONGING FEEL LIKE HERE?
answer: In Quebec, I think it just means not feeling scared — really trusting that there's equal accountability for people who might do something hateful towards me, as if they'd done it to any other person. I don't want to feel like an exception, I don't want to feel like there's added legislation specifically for me, whether to protect me or to inhibit me from accessing certain things. I don't think Islam or hijab should be an issue in Canadian politics the way it has been, especially in Quebec. I also think sometimes people don't factor in what makes something inaccessible to a Muslim — if I'm at a job and everyone wants to go out to a bar as a social, I don't think it's talked about, like, oh, you're going to order something that's not halal for the team and not run it by anyone — I think it would be nice if that was considered more. But really, at the end of the day, it's less about stopping all hate crimes against Muslims and more about just actually treating them the way you'd treat any other act of violence. Stop it. Sometimes it really feels like there's this huge exception made for Muslims, and I've always felt there's an exception for Palestinians too, that for some reason violence against us, or laws against us, are seen as justifiable. That's really disappointing.

question: DO YOU FEEL YOU BELONG HERE — ARE YOU SEEN AS FRENCH/QUEBECOIS?
answer: Some people do, and then other people say, go back to your country. I think a lot of people presume, when they see someone wearing hijab or a Muslim, that we've come here from somewhere else, and they might not necessarily mean anything hateful by it, but I think even the most well-meaning person doesn't necessarily see us as part of the real Quebecois culture. We just don't really mesh.

question: WHAT DO YOU MISS ABOUT PRACTICING YOUR FAITH OPENLY?
answer:
I wish I lived somewhere where I could hear the Adhan, where people were praying on the streets, where during Ramadan shops don't close at night — sometimes it's really lonely here, especially during religious holidays, and sometimes just on regular days, I wish my religion was more visible. I get really homesick when I see videos where a masjid is playing the Adhan out loud, and I feel like everything is so closed off here — our masajid are old buildings designed to not look like mosques, because they'll get hate-crimed if they visibly look like mosques on the outside. I think that's just so sad.
