I don't know the history of it, but to be fair, it would never end well if a mosque were playing the call to prayer out loud here. In terms of the architecture, the official reason I've heard is that it's in part to protect against attacks, that many mosques are openly community centers, outwardly, I should say — but I haven't done proper research on that. I feel like there's a little bit of a feeling that I'm sort of secretly a Muslim sometimes, because it's complicated to ask for accommodations to go pray or to have a meal I can eat. So sometimes it's lonely.

question: HOW AND WHERE ARE YOU ABLE TO PRAY DURING YOUR DAY?
answer: Always in the musalla at school — we have a prayer room in one of the buildings on our downtown campus, and also at our other campus. The university hasn't told us yet how they're going to enforce it, but it's not going to be allowed to be used for prayer, that's what they've told us. The rooms will stay, but they won't be allowed to be used for prayer.

question: HOW DOES YOUR AWARENESS OF THE AKHIRAH SHAPE THE WAY YOU LIVE?
answer: Sometimes it snaps me back into focus — I spend a lot of time scrolling, and I definitely shouldn't. I get these bursts of motivation sometimes, always at the most random time, and I feel like I need to get my life together, that I'm so far behind, doing so many things wrong, and I wish I could leave this place and live in a Muslim country. It also pushes the way I am with my family, how I want to treat them, be there for my parents — I think that's so huge. That's also, I think, the main reason I've persisted so much with my hijab, through a lot of discrimination, when people are really hateful and I've had bad experiences — I feel very confident that there is ajr in everything, that there is for sure a reward in all of the bad we encounter here as Muslims, and undoubtedly it's khair for us, that we were chosen to be here and not somewhere else. I wish I was more consistent in the emotional relationship I have with these concepts.

question: HOW DO YOU MAKE SENSE OF WHAT IS BEYOND YOUR CONTROL?
answer: That Allah is there — I actually feel really calm when things are not in my control, it's when I feel like I could have done something differently that I find it really, really difficult. But that was something my parents really hammered into me from when I was young, that you do what you can and then you leave the rest to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, that's it, you've done your part. A lot of that, when you're helping others too, is about your intention — I find that very reassuring. I don't think I've really struggled with it as a concept in Islam, but sometimes I wonder if the reason things are happening a certain way is because I haven't been as good as I could have been — I'm working on that, because I don't think that's the greatest outlook.

question: WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR PRACTICING YOUR RELIGION IN THE LONG RUN?
answer: I think just maintaining as much of it as I can, not losing or sacrificing anything that Allah has commanded from us for comfort in dunya here. I really don't want to find myself in a position where I look back and realize I've compromised aspects of my faith and how I practice, just to fit in better. So for me it's less about being a representative, and not really so much about establishing myself either — it's really about maintaining. I don't see this as my long-term place, to be honest.

question: HOW DO YOU UNDERSTAND LAÏCITÉ, AND HOW DOES IT AFFECT YOU?
answer: I think it's just the fake way of — I mean, Quebec is founded on the Catholic Church, we have a [PROMINENT CHRISTIAN LANDMARK] at the center of [CITY 1], and our holidays at school are based around Christmas and Easter. And somehow they think it's convincing to tell us that these laws banning Muslim women from places are about keeping religion out of society, about secularism. I just think it's funny — it cannot be real, the fact that they find it convincing. But I don't want to negate the religious trauma people have had in Quebec and say religion should be everywhere — true secularism and laïcité is about removing religion from the government and allowing people freedom of religion outside of the government, and that's the complete opposite of what they're doing. They're making laws around how people should dress and behave religiously — that's the polar opposite of what that entire concept is meant to mean. True laïcité and true secularism is something I'm not at all opposed to — absolutely, the government should have no religious affiliations, I completely agree with that and would encourage it. But what they're doing is saying nobody should be allowed to be religious unless it's a religion they're comfortable enough to have absorbed into the fabric of their community. And because Muslims are seen as outsiders, that's the issue.

question: HOW ARE MUSLIM WOMEN ADAPTING THEIR CAREER PLANS?
answer: Most of us are just changing our career goals. A lot of girls are saying, oh, I'm not going to be a teacher then, I'll do that instead, or, I'm going to do grad school in [PROVINCE 2] because I can't stay here and be a teacher — that's the running theme, not so much people saying, how are we going to combat this, although I do know many people who are — I know some really, really smart, mashallah, girls who are lawyers working in activism against this. But for the most part, the ones I've spoken to in my field have just been saying, okay, I'm going to leave, or I'm going to switch to a slightly different sector.

question: WHICH PROFESSIONS ARE AFFECTED BY THESE LAWS?
answer: Not at all — it's specific targeting of teachers working in public schools. I can't remember specifically where the line is drawn, but my understanding is it has to do with a balance of power — if you're in a position where you're an educator or holding authority over someone, you're not able to wear it. I don't think healthcare workers are affected. Professors — so far it's okay, I haven't had any — oh, no, I've had one, I had an Arabic professor at university — universities are fine. It was such a shock when Bill 9 came out, because that was the first time they came for public universities and our prayer rooms, but nothing so far on who's allowed to teach. I think that would be extreme for them, and I don't know how they'd garner enough public support, because universities tend to publicly oppose their stance on "secularism," which isn't secularism, and to be honest, their base of support for these bills comes from non-city centers, the less metropolitan areas of Quebec, where there are fewer large universities and student populations. Student cities are not for this.

question: DO YOU FEEL OPPRESSED BY THE STATE?
answer: In Quebec? Yeah, one hundred percent.

question: WHAT IS THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOUR HEART, INTENTION, AND OUTWARD PRACTICE?
answer: I have some goals — I want to memorize Quran inshallah, and I want to have kids, and I really want to feel confident that when I get married, inshallah, I can be a good teacher of the religion to them. Sometimes the way I think of it is that I'm gathering knowledge that I can pass on, and obviously so I can implement it in my own life, because I've yet to learn something about my religion that hasn't benefited me. My goals really have to do with my family, being a better daughter, and inshallah someday being a better mom. It's also about understanding, because I think even within our own community women are taken advantage of for their lack of understanding of their rights, and outside our community women are taken advantage of for their lack of ability to advocate for their rights as Muslims too. So that's always beneficial. I think it's to better myself for others.

question: WHAT DOES SUBMISSION TO ALLAH MEAN TO YOU?
answer: It means not always needing to know the answer. That's deep — yeah, I don't know if I can really go much more into that.

question: WHERE IN YOUR LIFE DO YOU FEEL MOST LIBERATED?
answer: I understand it as the freedom to have all your needs met enough to discover yourself on your own terms — literally, to rid yourself of external influence on your own agency. When I am back home, or with my family, when I'm closest to my Palestinian culture and that way of living, I feel the most comfortable, the most at peace to be myself. I mean Palestine when I say back home — I grew up here, but it's always been home for me, I've gone back for summers and months at a time since I was a very young kid, and it's always felt more like home than anywhere in Canada.
